artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich- At the 17th International Conference on Advanced Automotive Lithium Batteries (ABAA-17), Gotion High-Tech laid out its latest advances in all-solid-state batteries, lithium manganese iron phosphate (LMFP), and global manufacturing capacity. Yet it was Chairman Li Zhen who, in his opening remarks, pulled the conversation back to the industry's broader cycle. During the keynote, three of the company's technical experts walked through a systematic showcase of collaborative innovation spanning the entire value chain — from base materials to finished cells. With market demand barreling toward 5 TWh by 2030, the company has already built eight global R&D hubs and 20 production bases, said Zhou Fu, president of the General Research Institute. Gotion continues to deepen its work on key materials like high-compaction LFP and high-voltage single-crystal NCM, while building a flagship product matrix — spanning G-Cycle ultra-fast charging batteries, G-Edge smart batteries, and all-solid-state cells — to underpin electrification across every usage scenario. Image source: Gotion High-Tech Zeroing in on the frontier of all-solid-state tech, Dr. Pan Ruijun, who heads the solid-state project, said Gotion has cracked the full-chain process and equipment system — from materials to electrodes to cells — along the sulfide route. A semi-dry mixing method and a novel solvent system have sharply improved slurry stability. Warm isostatic pressing (WIP) trims electrolyte membrane thickness to 35 microns, boosts cell densification by more than 20%, slashes interfacial impedance by over 99%, and pushes cell yields past 90%. At the pack level, the system is racing toward lower stacking pressure and lighter weight. Cells from Gotion’s all-solid-state pilot line are now rolling off in batches, giving the company a firm foundation for mass production. On the LMFP front, Dr. Fang Yaoguo, vice president of the International Engineering Research Institute, detailed how Gotion conquered the chemistry’s inherent flaws — low conductivity, lattice instability, and manganese dissolution — along with the engineering hurdles. The fixes rely on proprietary techniques: particle nanocrystallization, dual-ion doping, particle-size gradation, and surface structuring. The third-generation Qichen LMFP cell now hits an energy density above 205 Wh/kg and can recharge to 70% in just 10 minutes, while delivering strong cold-weather performance and lower costs. In passenger vehicles, it delivers superior power; in commercial trucks, it shines as a weight-saver. By precisely bridging the performance gaps between LFP and NCM, the cell is rapidly expanding into a wider range of applications. Li Zhen, Image source: Gotion High-Tech Li Zhen didn’t dwell on technology alone. He laid out four guiding paradoxes: the fiercer the upheaval, the greater the need to revere science and seek truth; the faster the innovation, the tighter the loop between production and research must become; the more tangled the competition, the more vital openness and symbiosis grow; and the quicker the iteration, the higher we must climb to scout the next frontier. Innovation, he stressed, must bridge the “0-to-1” breakthrough with the “1-to-100” grind of real-world refinement — turning lab advances into safe, reliable products. Gotion, he added, will stay true to its mission of making green energy serve humanity, working alongside global peers toward the shared promise of the energy transition.

artigo.texto: The Fiddler’s Ferry battery energy storage system (BESS) is redeveloping part of the former coal-fired power station site in Warrington, Cheshire. The project is being developed by SSE Renewables. With a capacity of 150MW/300MWh, it will store electricity and supply it to the UK National Grid during periods of high demand. Construction began in January 2024, following a final investment decision in December 2023. SSE Renewables appointed OCU Energy as the principal contractor and Fluence as the battery storage technology supplier. The project is listed as under construction on the developer’s official project page, with completion previously scheduled for 2026. Project Scope and Technical Specifications The Fiddler’s Ferry BESS will have a power output capacity of 150 megawatts (MW) and an energy storage capacity of 300 megawatt-hours (MWh). Therefore, the installation is designed to discharge electricity at full rated output for up to two hours, subject to operating conditions. The Fiddler’s Ferry Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project will use Fluence’s Gridstack battery energy storage platform, while OCU Energy is responsible for principal construction works. The development will occupy approximately 3.5 hectares of the former power station site and reuse the existing grid connection, reducing the need to establish an entirely new connection to the electricity transmission network. Once operational, the system is expected to provide the UK’s transmission system operator with access to stored electricity equivalent to the demand of up to 250,000 homes for as long as two hours. However, this is an illustrative equivalent rather than a guarantee that the facility will continuously supply that number of households. Construction Progress and Project Timeline SSE Renewables reached its final investment decision in December 2023 and confirmed OCU Energy and Fluence as its delivery partners in March 2024. Construction began in January 2024, with SSE announcing in March 2025 that the project was progressing and remained scheduled for completion in 2026. As of November 2026, SSE Renewables lists the facility as under construction. However, no revised commissioning date has been confirmed. The battery system has also not been confirmed as commercially operational. Reuse of the Former Fiddler’s Ferry Power Station The Fiddler’s Ferry BESS project forms part of the wider redevelopment of the former power station site. Previously, the facility ceased coal-fired generation in March 2020. Since then, Peel NRE has been redeveloping the site. Its plans include employment space, housing, infrastructure and other uses. Meanwhile, the battery installation provides a new energy infrastructure use for part of the former industrial site. By storing electricity when it is available and releasing it when demand rises, the BESS can help balance fluctuations in electricity supply and demand. It can also support the integration of variable renewable generation, including wind and solar power, into the electricity network. This is a function that is being emulated by other projects across the region, including the 442MWh Smareg 13 BESS project in Bavaria aimed at stabilizing Germany’s grid. The project’s reuse of an existing grid connection is particularly relevant because connecting new energy assets to the transmission network can be a significant development constraint. However, the facility is a storage asset rather than a power generator: it shifts electricity across time and does not independently produce renewable electricity. Fiddler’s Ferry Battery Energy Storage System (BESS): Project Factsheet Location: Former Fiddler’s Ferry coal-fired power station, Warrington, Cheshire, England, UK Developer: SSE Renewables Power capacity: 150MW Storage capacity: 300MWh Maximum rated discharge duration: Approximately two hours Technology supplier: Fluence Battery platform: Gridstack Principal contractor: OCU Energy Construction start: January 2024 Final investment decision: December 2023 Original target completion: 2026 Latest publicly stated status: Under construction Grid connection: Existing connection at the former power station site Primary purpose: Grid flexibility, electricity storage and support for renewable energy integration Fiddler’s Ferry BESS Project Team SSE Renewables : Project developer and investor. OCU Energy : Principal contractor responsible for construction and project delivery. Fluence Energy : Battery energy storage technology supplier, providing the Gridstack battery storage platform. Peel NRE : Owner and redevelopment partner for the wider former Fiddler’s Ferry power station site.

artigo.texto: Appear Inc. Begins Pre-Production of Solid-State Battery, Targets Mid-2027 Launch Field trials complete across motorcycles, e-bikes and scooters. Pre-production underway. Limited production on track for mid-2027, with full-scale production in 2028. SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Appear Inc., a San Francisco-based developer of next-generation solid-state battery technology, today announced that it has moved from proving its technology to producing it. The company has completed field trials on three types of electric vehicle: motorcycles, e-bikes and scooters. It has also completed advanced manufacturing trials and started pre-production manufacturing with a manufacturing partner. Alongside this technical progress, Appear has added new distributors and strategic partners in selective established and emerging markets. The company remains on track to begin limited commercial production in mid-2027, followed by full-scale production in 2028. The technology Most electric vehicles today run on lithium-ion batteries, which use a liquid electrolyte to move charge between the electrodes. Solid-state batteries replace that liquid with a solid material. This is widely seen as a path to safer batteries, with no flammable liquid to leak or ignite, and to more energy in a smaller, lighter cell. Watch the video: https://youtu.be/W2H44vFPjXY Appear's solid-state technology is built around three priorities: safety, performance and manufacturability. For motorcycles, e-bikes and scooters, where weight, range and safety matter on every ride, that combination is especially valuable. From the lab to the production line Following its advanced manufacturing trials, Appear has moved into pre-production with its manufacturing partner and is refining its processes for volume manufacturing. Building a route to market New distributors and strategic partners in selective established and emerging markets are expected to give Appear regional market access and distribution channels at launch. Partner details remain confidential. "We are moving beyond development and validation and into commercialization," said Prashant Rurs, Founder & CEO of Appear Inc. "We remain on track to begin limited production in mid-2027 and to scale up to full production in 2028." About Appear Inc. Appear Inc. is a San Francisco-based company developing next-generation solid-state battery technology for electric mobility and other energy storage applications. artigo.texto: CATL's Deal Spree Meets a Blunt Test: Can It Hold Price Per Unit? Published on 11/09/2026 at 16:41 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL shares slipped 2.2% on the day as investors weighed a fresh wave of partnership announcements against a tougher earnings backdrop, with the central question being whether new business actually translates into profit. The stock's decline came amid reports of automakers broadening their supplier base and unconfirmed local accounts of a possible construction pause at a Beijing battery project. Those concerns sit alongside a more concrete pressure point: JPMorgan cut its earnings forecasts for Chinese battery makers, CATL included, on Friday, citing lower assumed profit per unit and growing difficulty in passing battery-tax costs through to customers. JPMorgan Trims Its Targets The US bank lowered its price target on CATL's H-shares to HKD420 from HKD440, keeping a Neutral rating. Its A-shares, by contrast, retained an Overweight stance — a split verdict that underscores how the house sees value in the mainland listing even as it tempers expectations for the Hong Kong line. That combination frames the debate. Automakers and energy-storage integrators have been pushing back against absorbing the battery-tax costs, making cost reduction more important than ever. Technical collaboration therefore carries extra weight for investors — but only if it protects earning power. A Flurry of Agreements CATL has spent the past several days stitching together alliances across materials, recycling and energy supply. On Thursday it sealed a strategic cooperation with China Aluminum Group (Chinalco) covering new non-ferrous metal materials, metal recycling, and the linking of green power with storage. The pact also takes in grid and storage projects at high altitudes plus support for global supply chains. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? A day earlier, on 1 November, came a collaboration with Shanghai Electric spanning carbon-neutral industrial parks, energy storage, green transport and international business. And on 2 November CATL closed a deal with Blue Vector to develop an aviation battery specifically for its SKYLA V30 aircraft, named as exclusive battery partner — a customer-specific assignment that could strengthen its hand with a single buyer, provided the economics hold up. The most concrete volume commitment comes from INTILION: 3 GWh of CATL energy-storage systems are planned over five years across Germany, Switzerland, Austria and further markets. That project is grounded in a letter of intent rather than a binding contract, so its eventual contribution hinges on execution. Breadth Is Not the Same as Depth The strategic thread running through these deals is clear — CATL is reaching beyond the battery cell itself, tying materials research, recycling and power supply into its industrial chain. For shareholders, the measure of that breadth is whether it delivers resilient returns. A partnership can impress on strategy while adding little at the earnings line if it lowers costs, improves market access or binds customers more tightly. Rising activity on weaker per-unit returns would be a far less convincing signal. The bull case needs several pieces to fall into place at once: storage projects that actually get deployed, credible progress on the materials side, and steady profit per unit. Where the Risk Bites The flip side is additional opportunity colliding with softer margins. If CATL can only partially pass on higher tax costs, those expenses could erode the benefit of new projects — larger volumes would then only make sense if their terms adequately compensate for the extra burden. The agreements also differ in how binding they are. Chinalco is a multi-theme strategic cooperation; INTILION rests on a letter of intent. Their future earnings contribution depends on how each is implemented. CATL at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. For cautious investors, the analyst action carries more weight as long as the expected hit to per-unit profit is confirmed. The bearish scenario is a combination of more projects and falling unit returns — broader collaboration that opens operational doors while doing little for the earnings outlook. What to Watch Next Execution of the INTILION storage rollout stands out as the nearest concrete checkpoint. Progress on actual projects, and firm word on their terms, could make the earnings picture more tangible. From Thursday's Chinalco agreement, what matters is which material, recycling or storage projects emerge. The weighting for any investment case is therefore straightforward: the partnerships argue for additional upside if their execution supports profitability, while Friday's lowered earnings expectations argue for caution while pressure on unit returns persists. Operational progress will be judged against exactly that threshold. Ad CATL Stock: New Analysis - 9 November Fresh CATL information released. What's the impact for investors? artigo.texto: Política Acre avança em negociações na Turquia para certificação internacional de créditos de carbono O Acre deu mais um passo nas articulações para obter a certificação internacional de seus créditos de carbono. Durante agenda na Turquia, representantes do governo estadual se reuniram com a diretora associada da Art Trees, Lucia Madrid, para discutir o avanço do processo de certificação. O encontro contou ainda com a participação da presidente do IMC, Neidinha Lima, e do consultor internacional de mercados de carbono, Victor Hugo Rondon. A iniciativa busca ampliar as oportunidades de investimentos para o estado, fortalecendo a política de preservação ambiental e criando possibilidades de geração de renda e desenvolvimento econômico. A expectativa é que a certificação internacional valorize os resultados das ações de conservação da floresta amazônica e garanta benefícios às comunidades que contribuem diretamente para a proteção do meio ambiente. A proposta é transformar a preservação da Amazônia em oportunidades concretas, promovendo mais qualidade de vida para a população acreana.

artigo.texto: 9 de novembro de 2026, às 14:00 Por João Caires Brasília, 9/11/2026 – O Ministério das Comunicações informou nesta segunda-feira, 9, que o governo federal planeja investir R$ 46,3 milhões no desenvolvimento de uma plataforma de gerenciamento e distribuição de dados entre mini data centers no Brasil. Batizado de Prisma, o projeto utilizará inteligência artificial para identificar onde e como os dados devem ser processados, distribuindo automaticamente os recursos computacionais entre diferentes infraestruturas. Na prática, o Executivo espera que a tecnologia reduza gastos com energia e custos operacionais, acelere o acesso às informações e aumente a proteção de dados estratégicos. Os recursos serão administrados pela Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep), e o projeto será executado pelo Centro Brasileiro de Inovação em Tecnologias da Informação e da Comunicação (CPQD). O prazo de execução é de 36 meses, a partir da celebração do convênio de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação entre a Finep e o CPQD. O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico Filho, afirmou que o projeto possibilitará maior autonomia e soberania no tratamento de dados no País. “Investir em tecnologia nacional é garantir que o Brasil tenha mais autonomia para proteger suas informações e desenvolver soluções para os desafios do futuro. Estamos fortalecendo a inovação brasileira e criando condições para uma infraestrutura digital mais moderna, segura e sustentável, reduzindo nossa dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior”, afirmou em nota. artigo.texto: O governador Otaviano Pivetta (Republicanos) participa, hoje, na Turquia, do primeiro dia da conferência mundial do clima com presidentes de diversos países e delegações, cientistas, pesquisadores que encaminham decisões sobre proteção ambiental e reduções dos impactos no meio ambiente. A cúpula dos líderes políticos é hoje e amanhã, com temas centrais no financiamento climático para países em desenvolvimento e planos de adaptação climática, transição energética e redução de combustíveis fósseis e eletrificação. “Estamos na COP 31 com uma missão importante: apresentar o trabalho de Mato Grosso na redução do desmatamento e buscar reconhecimento internacional para nossos créditos de carbono. Também vamos conversar com investidores e mostrar que é possível unir conservação ambiental, desenvolvimento e novas oportunidades para o nosso Estado”, disse Pivetta, há pouco. “Uma agenda de muito trabalho e diálogo”, acrescentou. O tema de mercados de carbono: do potencial brasileiro aos investimentos em escala será debatido amanhã. Dia 13, será a implementação do mercado de carbono no Brasil: avanços e próximos passos’ A delegação de Mato Grosso tem a secretária de Meio Ambiente, Mauren Lazaretti e o deputado estadual Beto Dois a Um. O presidente Lula e ministros também estão na conferência. O governo instalou o Pavilhão Brasil que tem debatido inúmeros temas ambientais desde o último dia 9. Na programação de hoje também estarão sendo debatidas ‘energias da floresta: inovação aberta para transformar o acesso à energia’. artigo.texto: Masdar, a global leader in clean energy, and Endesa today commemorated the start of construction on three battery energy storage projects in Spain. These projects will add 60.16 megawatts (MW) of battery storage capacity and 120.34 megawatt-hours (MWh) of storage capacity to solar plants in Extremadura and Andalusia, representing a joint investment of €25.2 million. The projects are Ardila, at the 44 MWp solar plants in Fregenal de la Sierra (Badajoz), and La Vega I and La Vega II, at two solar plants in Teba (Málaga). By storing some of the electricity they generate, they will contribute to integrating more renewable energy into the grid and making the electrical system more flexible. These projects are the first energy storage developments under the Masdar-Endesa alliance, established in 2014 when Masdar acquired a stake in a portfolio of Endesa photovoltaic assets in Spain. Dr. Ibraheem Almansouri, Masdar's interim chief operating officer, said: "Spain is one of the fastest-growing economies in Europe, and this growth requires a secure and resilient electricity supply. These projects will help integrate more clean energy into the grid and strengthen the stability of the electricity system. They demonstrate how strategic partnerships can accelerate the deployment of advanced energy technologies, reinforce grid resilience, and support sustainable economic growth, and they consolidate the strength of our alliance with Endesa while expanding our portfolio in the Iberian Peninsula. We look forward to continuing to invest in Spain and support the country's economic ambitions." Continue reading All three systems will use lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries with grid-forming inverters. This technology provides synthetic inertia, mimicking the behavior of a conventional thermal or hydroelectric generating unit, and responds almost instantaneously to sudden changes in grid conditions, thus contributing to the stability of the electrical system. Ardila will provide 36.10 MW (72.20 MWh) of storage in 12 battery containers, enough to store the equivalent of the daily electricity consumption of approximately 8,100 Spanish households. La Vega I and La Vega II will each provide 12.03 MW (24.07 MWh) in four battery containers per site, which together is equivalent to the daily consumption of approximately 5,400 households. All three projects are expected to be operational by the end of 2027. In total, 50 jobs will be created during the construction of three projects, with a commitment to using European-sourced components and services, including inverters, auxiliary systems, communications, and integration, thereby boosting the regional energy storage value chain. In Ardila, the partners will also collaborate with the Fregenal de la Sierra Town Council to identify local improvement projects, allocating part of the budget to training. The research and technical validation will be carried out with CIRCE and the Institute of Research in Technology (IIT) of the Pontifical University Comillas, including on-site tests and studies of the operation of the electrical network. Masdar currently has 4.1 GW of operational capacity in the Iberian Peninsula, with approximately 1 GW under development. These projects further Masdar's strategy of collaborating with industry leaders to drive the deployment of renewable energy globally, with the goal of reaching 100 GW of global capacity by 2030.

artigo.texto: Struggling marijuana farmers pivot to becoming AI data center sites to escape falling weed revenue — existing water and power infrastructure makes cultivation sites ideal for decentralized ‘mini data center nodes’ Let's get high... on AI. The AI data center boom is bringing hope to struggling cannabis farmers as they face increased competition, costs, and taxes amid reduced demand for marijuana. According to Arizona Public Media, the cannabis industry is in decline, with sales peaking in 2024 and oversupply driving prices down. And now, several growers are considering selling their cultivation facilities or converting them into “mini data center nodes.” These facilities already have many of the ingredients needed for AI data centers, such as the increasingly hard-to-get supply of electricity and water infrastructure. "For some reason, there's a lot more cannabis grown in Arizona than Arizonans use. And so, a lot of folks are getting out of that business, like myself, at least on the cultivation side. But these facilities can potentially be repurposed to be mini data center nodes," Moe Asnani, the former owner of two Tucson D2 Dispensaries, told the public broadcaster. He also added, "The whole idea is if you create these smaller nodes where people control their own data, where they're not at the mercy of other people's updates and things like that — that's kind of where the idea came in, because I believe in decentralization." Cannabis farming is both power- and water-intensive. Forbes looked at a 32,850-square-foot cannabis facility in Kalamazoo, Michigan, which is currently wired for 1.5 megawatts, which can be expanded to 2.5 megawatts in under a year and 15 megawatts in the long term. It's also provisioned for fiber internet and equipped with a state-of-the-art HVAC system for climate control, which should make it a tempting property for anyone wanting to put up a small data center — something that even OpenAI and Anthropic are interested in as massive hyperscale sites face opposition from the community. This concept is dubbed "adaptive reuse," with Tucson City Council member Paul Cunningham saying that it’s a more palatable alternative to massive, purpose-built sites sitting on the outskirts of town. "Data centers are dirty words, and everybody knows that. And no one wants to build a brand-new data center anywhere," the politician said. "But if we have buildings that were using that amount of water and that amount of energy already in their previous function and [it] can be done without being invasive, I'm OK with exploring that option." There is massive demand for data centers, but it’s not a guaranteed payoff for struggling cash-strapped growers looking to unload their unprofitable properties. Niki Krear, vice president of acquisitions of real estate investment trust New Lake Capital Partners, said that there’s a sweet spot between connectivity, costs, and regulation that data center operators look for in a site. "It’s a combination of finding affordable power, dense fiber networks, and favorable tax policies," Krear told MJBizDaily. Even though many cultivation facilities already boast higher-than-average power capacity for lighting and climate control, data centers often demand twice to thrice more, with upgrades possibly taking up to five years. Data center operators looking for smaller sites may also have to contend with NIMBY — not in my backyard — fights from neighbors. Additionally, there may be zoning restrictions, moratoriums, and regulatory hurdles, and the lack of economies of scale could end up costing operators more. As these new AI GPUs become available, data centers will need to sell their existing equipment and buy new hardware to remain competitive. Because suppliers usually offer favorable pricing for larger orders, upgrading these smaller sites will likely end up being more expensive on a per-unit basis. That said, growing opposition toward large new projects could make these former cannabis farms suitable alternatives for operators desperate to get more compute online quickly, provided they check all (or most of) the boxes they need. artigo.texto: 10 de novembro de 2026, às 07:34 O SoftBank Group registrou prejuízo líquido trimestral, pressionado por perdas em investimentos e por perdas extraordinárias ligadas a mudanças no plano de compras de equipamentos para geração de energia em projetos de data centers nos EUA. A holding japonesa de investimentos em tecnologia divulgou nesta terça-feira (10) prejuízo líquido de 1,115 trilhão de ienes (US$ 7,06 bilhões) no trimestre encerrado em setembro. O resultado contrariou a estimativa de lucro de 53,5 bilhões de ienes em pesquisa com analistas do Visible Alpha. No mesmo período do ano passado, o SoftBank havia registrado lucro líquido de 2,502 trilhões de ienes, impulsionado por ganhos de bilhões de dólares com o investimento na OpenAI. A empresa informou uma perda de 597,2 bilhões de ienes relacionada a alterações no plano de aquisição de equipamentos vinculados à geração de energia para data centers de inteligência artificial nos EUA. Segundo o SoftBank, uma de suas unidades revisou a estratégia de compras diante da evolução das exigências dos projetos em andamento e planejados. O resultado fraco se soma a contratempos recentes. A China bloqueou a aquisição de US$ 5,4 bilhões do negócio de robótica da ABB, anunciada em outubro de 2025, que buscava combinar IA e robótica. O SoftBank pretendia usar a unidade – fabricante de braços robóticos e outros dispositivos empregados em manufatura e logística – como vitrine de uma ofensiva mais ampla em aplicações físicas de IA. Nos EUA, a SB Energy, empresa de data centers apoiada pelo SoftBank, adiou o IPO após enfrentar resistência do mercado em relação à avaliação. A rival da OpenAI, Anthropic, pretende manter o plano de abrir capital ainda neste mês, apesar da volatilidade recente ligada a investimentos em IA, segundo o The Wall Street Journal. A OpenAI, por sua vez, levantou menos da metade do valor inicialmente pretendido em sua rodada mais recente, e a avaliação ficou abaixo do alvo, em US$ 1,25 trilhão. O SoftBank tem ampliado suas apostas em IA nos últimos anos, deixando para trás a estratégia anterior de investir em um portfólio diversificado de startups. Em outubro, a holding informou que aportou mais US$ 10 bilhões na OpenAI, elevando o total investido na dona do ChatGPT para US$ 64,6 bilhões e a participação para cerca de 13%. Na semana passada, a Arm Holdings, empresa britânica de design de chips controlada pelo SoftBank, informou lucro trimestral acima do esperado, com a demanda por IA sustentando o crescimento. artigo.texto: The city of Fort Worth held the first of two public hearings Nov. 10 in regards to a possible moratorium on accepting, processing and approving data center applications. Council voted to initiate a moratorium process at the Aug. 11 meeting, but the earliest it could be approved is Feb. 23, 2027, according to the presentation. What they’re saying The public hearing lasted more than one hour with each speaker in favor of implementing a moratorium on data centers. Before the public hearing, city council received a 156-page report from the Fort Worth Data Center & Infrastructure Commission. Resident Letitia Wilburn questioned holding the public hearing just an hour after the report from the commission. “The public hasn’t really had enough time to go through it,” she said. Other speakers voiced concerns about approving local rules that do not meet state regulations that could be passed or crafted by a new state legislature in 2027. “I think it’s really incumbent upon us academics to work with our elected officials, not to lecture at them, but to sit down together and say what do we know and what do we need to find out before we make real long-term decisions [about data centers],” said Michael Slattery during the presentation on the findings of the commission. Zooming out Of the four existing data centers in Fort Worth, three are in council District 10, according to previous reporting. Another is under construction in council District 7, and there are four proposed data centers in Districts 3, 6, 7 and 8. The Fort Worth Zoning Commission voted July 8 to deny a proposed ordinance that would restrict where data centers could be located in Fort Worth, according to previous reporting. On Sept. 21, Gov. Greg Abbott said Texas environmental regulators must stop issuing new permits for data centers, according to previous reporting. His order expands an existing pause on data center development in the state and stops new data center permits while the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, which operates the state power grid, conducts an audit of proposed data center projects. Despite the existing pause, a permit for a $430 million data center in the Alliance area of Fort Worth was filed Sept. 22 with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, according to previous reporting. Looking ahead The second public hearing is slated for Jan. 12, a week later than planned earlier this summer. The moratorium on development and permitting could start if passed following a second reading Feb. 23. If approved in February, a 90-day moratorium would run through May 24, 2027. The city could approve a second 90-day window, but 180 days is the most allowed under state law, Assistant City Manager Jessica McEachern said. She added the moratorium does not apply to planned or approved projects or projects with zoning applications already submitted. McEachern said that under state law, data centers already in the works can choose to develop under the current standards or they could voluntarily develop to meet the higher standards. Hannah Norton contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: The University of Michigan-Dearborn has been named to a new national consortium to accelerate the transition of battery energy storage solutions from discovery to domestic manufacturing. The effort, led by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, is known as the Battery Manufacturing (BattMan) Accelerator. Jie Xiao, the Boeing Martin Professor of Mechanical Engineering at the University of Washington and a Battelle Fellow at the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, will serve as the accelerator director. “Breakthroughs in battery science must be matched by our ability to manufacture them at scale,” says Xiao. BattMan will bring together national laboratories, universities, and industry partners to address critical barriers in scaling next-generation battery technologies. The accelerator will focus on lowering manufacturing costs, speeding up development from the lab to commercial scale, and boosting U.S. leadership in energy storage manufacturing. Associate Professor of Mechanical Engineering Lei Chen will serve as the co-principal investigator from UM-Dearborn. Chen also is affiliated with the electric vehicle center (EVC) at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. He notes the accelerator’s goals align closely with EVC’s efforts to advance battery safety, sustainability, and manufacturing efficiency, and to train the next generation of EV engineers. “As we become increasingly reliant on stationary energy systems, continued advancements in battery manufacturing will be integral to keeping the U.S. at the forefront of innovation and competitiveness,” Chen says. “This consortium brings together the technologies, data, and partnerships needed to accelerate market-ready solutions and quickly scale them for Michigan’s auto industry and many other sectors.” Chen’s research contributions will focus on super intelligence-driven modeling and computational simulations for battery manufacturing. In addition, he will be developing and teaching a course on super intelligence for battery manufacturing to help train the future workforce in this critical area. UM-Dearborn is one of five university partners in the consortium. The others are Arizona State University, Binghamton University, University of Alabama, and University of Washington. Argonne and Oak Ridge National Laboratories also are partners. DOE announced the consortium earlier today. The accelerator is actively establishing collaborations with companies within the battery and materials manufacturing sector.

artigo.texto: The growing adoption of renewable energy changes the energy infrastructure in many ways. In particular, solar photovoltaic (PV) systems become one of the main elements of such infrastructure providing a flexible source of clean energy at utility, commercial, industrial scales and even at remote infrastructures. Nevertheless, solar energy alone does not guarantee continuous power supply because of its generation dependency on weather conditions, daylight and seasonality. With the rising share of renewables, the ability to store the energy becomes crucial. One of the technologies designed to address this issue is battery energy storage systems (BESS). Meanwhile, the industries requiring a continuous power supply, including telecom facilities, consider solar and storage systems as a promising way to increase the reliability and decrease dependency on conventional energy sources. Thus, a combination of solar PV, battery storage and energy management turns out to be a promising solution to improve the resilience of energy infrastructure. Why Solar PV Requires Energy Storage As was mentioned, energy production using solar energy is highly variable. During daytime hours PV systems are able to produce more electricity than necessary. During nighttime or periods of insufficient solar irradiance, the production falls sharply or even stops. Thus, without efficient means to store electricity, a company is forced either to export surplus generation or even to curtail the generation depending on electricity market conditions and system design. Battery storage becomes a solution helping to store extra solar generation and consume it later. A typical hybrid solar-plus-storage system is composed of PV modules, battery modules, power conversion system (PCS), battery management system (BMS) and energy management system (EMS). These elements allow coordinating the generation, charging, discharging and consumption processes. For commercial and industrial applications, such system allows achieving the following objectives: - Energy shifting - Peak shaving - Provision of backup power - Integration of renewable energy - Implementation of microgrid operation The required storage capacity will depend on the specific load profile, generation of solar energy, backup time and operating strategy. Particularly, modular and containerized solutions turn out to be very helpful for flexible scaling of projects' capacity. The Growing Role of Containerized Battery Energy Storage Systems As energy storage projects grow larger and become more complex, integrated solutions for battery storage become of increasing interest. Containerized BESS combines battery modules, power conversion equipment, thermal management, fire protection and monitoring into a compact solution. Such system architecture can facilitate transportation, installation and system commissioning process. Compared to assembly of separate equipment at construction site, pre-assembled solutions can reduce on-site integration efforts and provide unified equipment configuration. Another advantage of this solution is scalability: depending on the specific of the project, multiple storage modules can be combined to achieve required power and energy capacities. It makes the technology applicable for renewables power plants, industrial applications, microgrids and grid services. However, there are many parameters to be considered when choosing a solution including: - Battery chemistry and cycle life - Rated power and usable energy capacity - Round trip efficiency - Cooling and temperature management - Fire detection and suppression - Battery management and energy management functionalities - Ability to work in grid-connected and off-grid mode Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries are extensively used in stationary energy storage applications owing to high level of thermal stability and positive cycle-life characteristics. Thus, for the project developers and system integrators, containerized battery energy storage systems can be viewed as a practical reference allowing to evaluate BESS architecture, capacity options and renewable energy applications. Solar and Battery Storage for Telecommunication Facilities Telecommunication facilities represent another type of application where power supply becomes very important. Cellular base stations, microwave transmission towers, wireless repeaters and remote communication facilities operate 24/7 and any interruption in power supply will have negative consequences for the network availability and quality of service. In urban environments, the telecom sites usually have access to power grid although some issues such as blackouts and voltage variations can become a problem. However, remote facilities face additional challenges in terms of limited access to power grid, difficulties with transportations and high expenses for diesel generator operations. Solar energy generation combined with battery storage turns out to be a good solution in this case. A typical hybrid telecom power system may include: - Solar photovoltaic modules; - Lithium battery storage; - Hybrid power controllers; - AC/DC power conversion equipment; - Backup from grid or diesel generator; - Remote monitoring and energy management. This system can use solar generation first of all to power the equipment and charge batteries from surplus energy. In case of shortage of solar energy, the stored energy can be used to power the equipment. Backup power from the grid or diesel generator can be used to supplement the lack of renewable energy and stored energy. Such approach allows reducing operating time of generator, expenses for fuel and maintenance costs as well as maintaining continuous power supply. However, the design of telecom power system requires thorough analysis of specific conditions. artigo.texto: Corrida por energia para IA leva data centers a buscar turbinas e motores de avião usados Boom da tecnologia está aumentando a demanda por turbinas, elevando os preços e afetando diversos setores Internacional|Da Reuters LEIA AQUI O RESUMO DA NOTÍCIA Produzido pela Ri7a - a Inteligência Artificial do R7 Concessionárias de energia, desenvolvedoras e companhias que correm para garantir o fornecimento de energia para data centers de inteligência artificial estão vasculhando o mundo em busca de turbinas a gás usadas, reativando máquinas desativadas e convertendo motores de avião aposentados, já que os prazos de entrega de novos equipamentos, cada vez mais caros, se estendem até a próxima década. Apesar do crescente ceticismo em relação aos riscos da tecnologia de inteligência artificial e de uma recente onda de venda de ações do setor, a demanda por data centers que consomem muita energia está disparando, criando um gargalo crítico para a infraestrutura e os equipamentos essenciais de energia, como as turbinas. “As negociações para entregas estão firmemente focadas no período de 2030 a 2031”, afirmou Aurora Tenorio, analista sênior da consultoria de energia Wood Mackenzie, sobre o mercado de turbinas dos EUA. Veja Também - Portal EdiCase Treinamento corporativo com IA caminha para se adaptar ao perfil de cada funcionário - Inovação & Negócios ‘O diferencial é ser humano’, diz executivo sobre o avanço da IA nas empresas - Portal EdiCase Posso perguntar à IA se estou doente? Especialista explica o que vale pesquisar e o que exige cuidado Isso está levando algumas empresas a buscar equipamentos usados e recondicionados, bem como turbinas baseadas em motores de aviões, em vez de esperar que a carteira de pedidos seja atendida, de acordo com mais de uma dúzia de corretoras, empresas de serviços e fornecedores. “Esse mercado secundário está muito, muito aquecido no momento”, disse Ana Amicarella, presidente-executiva da EthosEnergy, uma prestadora de serviços de equipamentos. “Também temos observado um aumento nos preços dos produtos que as pessoas estão procurando.” Será que esse mercado pode ser a resposta para a escassez no fornecimento de energia? Provavelmente apenas em parte, disse Noor Qureshi, da Enverus Intelligence Research. “O mercado já está apertado, com excesso de oferta limitado, então é improvável que ele compense uma parcela significativa dos atrasos”, disse ela. As turbinas são apenas um dos obstáculos, já que licenças ambientais, acesso à rede elétrica e outros fatores também causam atrasos. Não há estimativas confiáveis de quanto o mercado secundário está contribuindo para o fornecimento global de turbinas, avaliado em cerca de US$ 25 bilhões (cerca de R$ 137 bilhões) por ano. Seu próprio surgimento, porém, atesta o profundo impacto que o boom dos data centers teve em todos os setores. A empresa de infraestrutura de IA Crusoe, por exemplo, encomendou em abril 13 das chamadas turbinas a gás aeroderivadas da ProEnergy, sediada nos EUA — que se baseiam em motores a jato fabricados pela GE Aerospace —, descrevendo a ação como uma medida estratégica para crescer rapidamente. As turbinas, com capacidade conjunta de 650 MW, serão implantadas nos projetos de data centers de IA da Crusoe nos EUA. A ProEnergy e a Crusoe não responderam aos pedidos da Reuters por informações adicionais. Os data centers e suas operadoras surgiram como grandes clientes de turbinas a gás, um mercado que, até alguns anos atrás, atendia quase exclusivamente às companhias de energia tradicionais. Hoje, os pedidos mundiais ultrapassam 100 GW, de acordo com a Wood Mackenzie, bem acima da capacidade de produção global estimada, que varia entre 60 GW e 70 GW. Analistas do banco de investimentos Jefferies estimam que somente os data centers dos EUA representam quase 17 GW da demanda neste ano e que esse número pode mais que triplicar até 2028. Embora a capacidade global de fabricação de turbinas a gás esteja crescendo e deva atingir cerca de 87 GW em 2028, ela ainda ficará bem aquém dos 129 GW previstos para a demanda por energia das turbinas, afirmaram eles. A Siemens Energy, a GE Vernova e a Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, que dominam o mercado, afirmam que o boom da IA levou os pedidos a ultrapassar sua capacidade de produção. Nos Estados Unidos, a entrega de uma turbina a gás leva agora, em média, seis anos, disse Tenorio. Equipamentos usados, recondicionados ou reaproveitados trazem seus próprios desafios. Turbinas recondicionadas podem ter históricos de manutenção pouco claros, vida útil residual limitada e assistência técnica de longo prazo precária, disse Tenorio. Motores a jato convertidos levantam dúvidas sobre sua adequação para o trabalho contínuo como geradores de energia. Ainda assim, os tempos de espera que se estendem por anos garantem o apelo do mercado. “De poucas em poucas semanas recebemos uma solicitação do tipo: ‘Vocês conseguem encontrar uma turbina a gás usada para instalar em um data center?’”, disse Darayus Pardivala, que lidera os negócios de pós-venda da Sulzer nos EUA. Pardivala não revelou detalhes sobre os clientes nem sobre a localização dos data centers. Os custos também são importantes. Unidades usadas em bom estado de conservação podem ser vendidas por cerca de US$1,5 milhão a US$1,7 milhão por MW, e unidades recondicionadas por cerca de US$1,3 milhão, de acordo com Zach Machuca, sócio-gerente da Origin Partners, empresa que adquire equipamentos de energia para desenvolvedores de centros de dados. Esse valor é significativamente menor do que o de turbinas novas, que custam cerca de US$ 2 milhões a US$ 2,5 milhões por MW, segundo a Aurora Energy Research. artigo.texto: Moura investe R$ 200 milhões para ampliar fábrica de armazenamento de energia em Pernambuco Com a chinesa CATL na comercialização, empresa mira o primeiro leilão de baterias do País, em dezembro, e projeta capacidade acima de 8 GWh por ano Clique aqui e escute a matéria O Grupo Moura vai investir R$ 200 milhões na expansão da fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia (Bess, na sigla em inglês) instalada em Belo Jardim, no Agreste pernambucano. O aporte busca colocar a empresa entre os principais fornecedores nacionais do segmento no primeiro leilão de baterias do País, marcado para dezembro. Com a expansão, a companhia projeta produzir mais de 8 GWh por ano. A iniciativa conta com a chinesa CATL, parceira da Moura. A informação é da Broadcast e foi publicada pelo jornal Estadão. A aliança com a CATL não começa agora e se estende a outras áreas, como a eletrificação de veículos, contou à Broadcast o diretor de operações de lítio do grupo, Spartacus Pedrosa. No caso das baterias, a Moura banca sozinha a fábrica e a CATL assume a venda dos sistemas, já que tem mais bagagem em disputas de leilões em diversos países, incluindo a América Latina. Cabem à brasileira a fabricação, a industrialização e o controle local. Novo mercado O leilão pode dar fôlego ao armazenamento no portfólio do grupo, hoje centrado em baterias para veículos. Perguntado se o Bess poderia virar um dos maiores negócios da empresa no País, Pedrosa afirma que o potencial existe. O executivo vê no certame um ponto de inflexão para a indústria nacional e para a segurança energética, num cenário de avanço da geração eólica e solar e de mais episódios de cortes na geração, conhecidos como curtailment. Há cerca de 10 anos no armazenamento, a Moura trabalhou até agora com projetos menores para comércio e indústria. O leilão abre a porta para o chamado utility scale, de grandes empreendimentos, com sistemas maiores e requisitos mais rígidos. A empresa já tem produtos de 30 MWh e agora mira projetos a partir de 120 MWh. Valor flexível Os R$ 200 milhões anunciados podem crescer, avisa Pedrosa. O número final depende das regras do edital, de quantos projetos forem contratados e de novas etapas de nacionalização e ampliação da produção. Em alguns cenários analisados pela empresa, o aporte total para atingir 8 GWh ultrapassa essa cifra. Em Belo Jardim, a Moura vai receber os módulos e montar o equipamento final, um contêiner de 20 pés equipado com refrigeração e sistema contra incêndio. A empresa trabalha com parceiros nacionais nessa etapa, o que também ajuda a reduzir a dependência de fornecedores chineses. Conteúdo local A exigência de conteúdo local ligada ao financiamento do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) é central na estratégia. Montar as baterias no País é o caminho escolhido para cumprir os índices do banco, com nacionalização entre 50% e 60%. Pedrosa explica que essa rota faz a bateria, item de maior peso no investimento, contar como conteúdo local. Por isso, a empresa diz ultrapassar sem dificuldade o patamar de 50% a 60%. A ampliação inclui ainda a compra de equipamentos adicionais encomendados na China, com chegada prevista para 2027. A produção da fábrica deve começar a partir do fim do primeiro semestre, para atender os projetos do leilão em que a Moura espera fornecer os sistemas.

artigo.texto: A Engie Brasil Energia está avaliando oportunidades de aquisição de ativos renováveis em operação e vê no armazenamento de energia por baterias uma alternativa para o desenvolvimento de novos projetos. A companhia considera difícil ampliar sua atuação em geração renovável por meio de novos empreendimentos, mas mantém interesse na compra de ativos existentes. “A gente acha que renováveis está muito difícil de crescer em greenfield, exceto em baterias”, afirmou o gerente de Relações com Investidores da Engie, Leonardo Depiné, durante teleconferência de resultados realizada nesta quarta-feira, 11 de novembro. Segundo o executivo, a empresa tem analisado oportunidades de aquisição de ativos brownfield, mas ainda não há nenhuma operação concreta. No desenvolvimento de novos projetos, classificados como greenfield, a companhia considera os sistemas de armazenamento por baterias entre as possibilidades de expansão. A Engie também pretende participar do leilão de baterias previsto para dezembro, caso o certame seja realizado, levando em consideração as condições macroeconômicas e a rentabilidade dos investimentos. A companhia seguirá avaliando oportunidades nos próximos leilões de transmissão. No certame realizado em outubro, disputou lotes, mas não apresentou propostas vencedoras. Segundo Depiné, a empresa chegou perto de conquistar dois lotes, mas manteve os limites de retorno estabelecidos para seus investimentos. Curtailment e ressarcimento Na mesma apresentação, a Engie informou que ainda não reconheceu contabilmente os valores que poderá receber pela compensação dos cortes de geração de energia eólica e solar ocorridos entre setembro de 2023 e novembro de 2025. Segundo Depiné, a companhia ainda não tomou uma decisão definitiva sobre a adesão ao mecanismo de compensação. A expectativa é de que o eventual ressarcimento ocorra em 2027, quando os valores também poderão ser reconhecidos no balanço, caso a empresa decida aderir. A compensação foi estabelecida pela Lei 15.269/2025 e regulamentada pela Portaria Normativa 140/2026 do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME). O mecanismo contempla cortes provocados por restrições de confiabilidade elétrica e indisponibilidade de instalações externas às usinas, mas não inclui aqueles decorrentes de excesso de oferta de energia no sistema. O procedimento prevê uma manifestação prévia de interesse das geradoras, cujo prazo foi encerrado em agosto, com participação da Engie. Para que a adesão seja vinculante, será necessário assinar um termo de compromisso que prevê a renúncia a determinadas reivindicações relacionadas aos cortes, como ações judiciais. A Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE) será responsável por operacionalizar os cálculos e os pagamentos, após a apuração dos dados pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS). Depois disso é que as empresas vão decidir se assinam ou não o acordo vinculante. No terceiro trimestre de 2026, o curtailment atingiu 26% do potencial de geração eólica e solar das usinas operadas pela Engie, ante 23% no mesmo período de 2025. O percentual foi igual ao registrado no Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Entre as eólicas da companhia, os cortes passaram de 19% para 22%, enquanto nas solares recuaram de 37% para 36%. No conjunto eólico Santo Agostinho, no Rio Grande do Norte, o curtailment alcançou 59%, ante 35% um ano antes. Revisão tarifária da TAG A Engie também comentou os efeitos da revisão tarifária do transporte de gás natural sobre os resultados da Transportadora Associada de Gás (TAG), da qual detém participação direta de 17,5%. A contribuição da TAG ao resultado da Engie Brasil Energia caiu de R$ 166 milhões para R$ 144 milhões no terceiro trimestre, redução de 13,3%, ou R$ 22 milhões. Segundo o balanço, a diminuição decorreu principalmente da menor receita da Malha Nordeste, que ainda depende da conclusão da revisão tarifária para o ciclo de 2026 a 2030. Durante a teleconferência, Depiné explicou que a TAG vem contabilizando provisoriamente uma redução de aproximadamente 50% na receita da malha sujeita à revisão, que representa cerca de 23% da receita da transportadora. Os valores serão ajustados após a conclusão do processo regulatório. A discussão envolve a metodologia utilizada pela Agência Nacional do Petróleo, Gás Natural e Biocombustíveis (ANP) para calcular a Base Regulatória de Ativos (BRA), considerada na definição da remuneração dos investimentos por meio das tarifas de transporte. Em outubro, a diretoria da ANP adotou o Método do Capital Recuperado e estabeleceu uma base regulatória de abertura de R$ 0 para a Malha Nordeste da TAG, por considerar que não há capital prudente ainda não recuperado nesses ativos. A decisão diverge da metodologia defendida pelas transportadoras. A TAG ainda acompanha o processo e avalia as medidas cabíveis para buscar o reconhecimento da metodologia que considera mais adequada à remuneração de seus ativos. Na segunda-feira, 9 de novembro, a ANP decidiu suspender por 15 dias a terceira etapa da revisão tarifária, após receber informações do MME sobre possíveis negociações entre a Petrobras e a Nova Transportadora do Sudeste (NTS) para reduzir os custos de transporte. A agência também determinou a avaliação da possibilidade de soluções negociadas com outras transportadoras e seus contratantes. Depiné afirmou que a Engie aguardará a conclusão do processo para avaliar seus desdobramentos, ressaltando que eventuais medidas relacionadas à revisão cabem à TAG. O executivo também disse não esperar que a metodologia adotada neste ciclo seja necessariamente aplicada às próximas revisões, uma vez que, segundo ele, a ANP indicou que cada processo poderá ter sua própria metodologia. Questionado sobre uma eventual indenização relacionada à TAG, o executivo afirmou que o contrato de compra da transportadora prevê mecanismos de proteção contratual, mas disse não ter detalhes sobre como eles poderiam ser aplicados em relação à Petrobras. artigo.texto: A Microsoft vem pressionando o governo do presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, a suspender os planos de proibir as importações chinesas de um componente essencial utilizado em data centers de inteligência artificial, segundo três pessoas a par da situação. A Reuters noticiou em agosto que o governo Trump pretende proibir a importação para os EUA de novos modelos de transceptores ópticos chineses, que permitem que os dados trafeguem por cabos de fibra óptica à velocidade da luz dentro dos data centers. A preocupação é que eles possam ser usados por Pequim para roubar dados, instalar malware ou interromper o serviço nos data centers dos Estados Unidos. A Microsoft tem 35 data centers em construção nos Estados Unidos e outros 134 planejados, de acordo com a Cleanview, uma empresa de inteligência de mercado que acompanha o desenvolvimento de data centers. A startup faz parte de um grupo de empresas e associações setoriais que argumentam junto ao governo Trump que tal proibição poderia prejudicar irreparavelmente a vantagem dos EUA sobre a China na corrida pela IA, ao retardar ainda mais a implantação dos data centers, disseram as fontes. A empresa de nuvem e software foi uma das poucas que se reuniu com autoridades do Escritório de Política Científica e Tecnológica da Casa Branca e do Conselho de Segurança Nacional em setembro para alertar sobre os desafios na cadeia de suprimentos que tal proibição representaria, disseram duas das fontes. “Isso realmente ameaça, sem dúvida, paralisar (a implantação dos data centers)”, disse John Miller, consultor jurídico geral do Conselho da Indústria de Tecnologia da Informação (ITI), um grupo de lobby do setor de tecnologia, que instou publicamente o governo a não seguir adiante com a proibição. Ele disse que muitas empresas de nuvem já adquiriram os chips de IA necessários para a implantação. “Esses chips, sem transceptores ópticos, poderiam literalmente ficar parados lá, sem uso, até que você realmente tenha os transceptores para conectá-los”, acrescentou. Alguns data centers precisam de milhões de transceptores ópticos para conectar servidores, roteadores e switches. A Comissão Federal de Comunicações dos EUA (FCC), que supervisiona o setor de telecomunicações do país, está trabalhando na proibição. Os esforços da Microsoft e de outras empresas, que não haviam sido divulgados anteriormente, mostram como as deliberações da agência despertaram preocupações em um setor que se esforça para atender à crescente demanda por serviços de nuvem e IA, apesar da crescente reação negativa dos consumidores em relação ao aumento dos custos de energia e do consumo de água. A Microsoft se recusou a comentar. A Casa Branca, a FCC e a embaixada da China em Washington não responderam imediatamente aos pedidos de comentário. artigo.texto: Alberta's Gigawatt Play: Why Building Data Centers Means Building an Industry Key Highlights - Alberta's transition from data center planning to execution is testing whether its workforce, infrastructure and supply chains can scale alongside gigawatt-class projects. - Industry self-awareness and voluntary commitments on water, emissions and community benefits are becoming more prominent, even as public opposition intensifies. - Unrealistic development proposals can undermine legitimate projects, making credible power, appropriate siting and early-stage development discipline increasingly important. - Alberta's experience raises broader questions about regulatory fairness, community trust and the growing association between AI and the physical infrastructure supporting it. For Alberta's emerging data center industry, the difference between a roadmap and an excavator has become increasingly consequential. A few years ago, Western Canada's data center conversation revolved around the possibilities: abundant energy resources, available land, a favorable climate and the prospect of attracting hyperscale investment to a region better known for oil, gas and other industrial development. Today, earthmoving equipment is preparing the ground for what is expected to become Canada's largest data center, and the questions facing the province have changed accordingly. The shift was on display at Data Centre West 2026, held in Calgary in September, where some 500 industry and government leaders gathered to examine the infrastructure and policy requirements of Alberta's rapidly expanding digital economy. But for conference founder Vlad Oujegov, the most revealing development wasn't simply the appearance of projects measured in gigawatts. It was the growing recognition that building those projects will require Alberta to develop an entire supporting industry, while confronting the environmental, political and community questions that increasingly accompany large-scale AI infrastructure. "The theme last year was the data center roadmap," Oujegov told Data Center Frontier Editor in Chief Matt Vincent during a new episode of the Data Center Frontier Show podcast. "This year's theme really to me was about execution and actually getting things done, actually seeing projects materialize and construction beginning." Oujegov is president and founder of the Western Canada Data Centre Alliance, which organizes Data Centre West, and serves as National Data Center Power Systems Lead at Schneider Electric. His perspective draws on both Alberta's emerging development pipeline and the wider industrial ecosystem now being assembled around it. In DCF's earlier reporting from Data Centre West 2026, the central question was how quickly Alberta could convert growing hyperscale demand into deliverable capacity. The latest podcast conversation takes that question further, examining what happens when a relatively small digital infrastructure market begins preparing for growth on a scale that can transform its regional economy. The resulting challenges extend beyond power availability and construction schedules. They encompass skilled labor, service networks, development credibility, public accountability and the increasingly complicated relationship between the data center industry and the communities being asked to accommodate it. From Roadmap to Earthworks The clearest example of Alberta's transition is Meta's newly announced data center campus in Sturgeon County, northeast of Edmonton. Announced in July 2026, the planned 1-gigawatt, AI-optimized campus represents an investment of more than CAD $13 billion and will become Meta's first data center in Canada. The company anticipates approximately 3,000 construction workers at peak activity and more than 300 permanent operational jobs, along with approximately CAD $60 million in local road and water infrastructure improvements. The campus is located in Alberta's Industrial Heartland, an established industrial region supporting energy production, petrochemicals and related infrastructure. The provincial government's major projects registry identifies the development as under construction, with site grading having begun under a permit issued earlier in 2026. Its supporting energy infrastructure represents another substantial undertaking. The development is paired with the planned 932-MW Greenlight Electricity Centre, a dedicated natural gas generation project intended to help supply the campus. While construction activity has begun at the data center site, full delivery of its associated power infrastructure remains a longer-term proposition. That distinction matters. Breaking ground is an important step toward execution, but it is not the same as delivering a fully commissioned gigawatt of computing capacity. Nevertheless, the physical progress is striking for a market that Oujegov estimates had less than 100 MW of total data center load only a few years ago. A single development now under construction is larger than the province's earlier installed base by an order of magnitude, illustrating both the scale of the opportunity and the challenge of accommodating it. For Oujegov, satellite images showing the site's developing earthworks provide a tangible illustration of how far Alberta has moved from theoretical discussions. "It's really cool for me to see," he said, pointing to visible construction activity following years of preparation. The project also illustrates a broader change in the province's industrial positioning. Alberta is no longer simply attempting to persuade global operators that it belongs on the data center map. It must now demonstrate that its utilities, suppliers, construction industry and local institutions can support developments of a size and complexity previously uncommon in the region. artigo.texto: By Shereen Siewert | Wausau Pilot & Review Weston residents can weigh in Thursday on draft goals for the village’s next comprehensive plan, including a proposal to restrict hyperscale data centers. The “Shaping Weston’s Tomorrow” workshop runs from 5 to 7 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 12, in the board room of the Weston Municipal Center, 4747 Camp Phillips Road. The session is open to the public. “It’ll only be as good as the people that are here,” a village staff member told the Plan Commission on Monday. The draft economic development initiatives propose supporting industrial growth while restricting hyperscale data center projects, according to a Nov. 4 report from Planning and Development Director Jennifer Higgins. Staff has begun researching zoning rules for large data centers, and the topic came up at a meeting of the steering committee guiding the plan update. Marathon County is weighing a countywide data center ordinance, and Weston staff completed a county survey on data center planning last week, the report says. Staff also flagged the need to coordinate with the Town of Weston in the shared extraterritorial zoning area. No formal policy recommendation has been made, and any future ordinance would go through the Plan Commission and Village Board. At a state planning conference in October, Higgins attended a session recommending that communities define data centers as a land use and regulate their effects through measurable standards, including noise, lighting, heat, stormwater, landscaping and demand on utilities. Those lessons will inform the village’s ongoing rewrite of the zoning code, her report says. Thursday’s workshop will open with a short presentation from consultant MDRoffers Consulting, similar to one the steering committee heard earlier. Residents will then split into small groups by topic, such as transportation and land use, to discuss draft goals and objectives and report back to the full room. Staff hopes to record the session and is considering an online option for people who cannot attend. The draft goals draw on community surveys and steering committee work. An initial 2026 community survey drew 681 responses, and a separate questionnaire for young adults closed Sept. 18. Steering committee members showed strong support for an alternative draft vision statement, according to the report. Plan commissioners are not required to attend. Staff said they want the room filled with residents, since commissioners have already had their say through the steering committee. Input from Thursday will be compiled, and a joint committee will review a draft of the plan’s Vision and Directions volume this winter.

artigo.texto: The Dade County Board of Commissioners has unanimously approved a 90-day moratorium on new data center development, following news that an Atlanta-based company is exploring building a large facility in the county. At 300 megawatts, the potential data center would consume enough energy to power 250,000 homes for an entire year, according to estimates from the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Dade County has approximately 7,500 homes, according to 2025 numbers from the U.S. Census Bureau. That means the power draw of the prospective facility could power every home in the county for the next 33 years. The moratorium adopted Nov. 5 would prevent any new data center from being developed in the county for three months, time that would allow officials to draft regulations governing new data centers and residents to voice questions or concerns, said Commissioner Melissa Christiansen Bradford, who placed the proposed moratorium on the board’s monthly agenda. Evan Stone, executive director of the Dade County Industrial Development Authority, told commissioners that Atlanta-based Masterworks previously contacted the board about exploring a data center location in its development park.

artigo.texto: FAIRFIELD — The City Council on Tuesday night unanimously placed a 45-day moratorium on a type of project that does not yet exist in the city. And by the tone of the council members' comments, and that of the majority of speakers at the special meeting – time to study the issues surrounding data centers is exactly what is needed for Fairfield. There was even a hint that an extension is a foregone conclusion. "We need a moratorium, there is no debate about that," Councilman Manveer Sandhu said, though not specifically about an extension. City Attorney David Lim cautioned the council about getting too far ahead of itself, and clarified that the moratorium applies to the entire city and not just the possibility that a data center could be built within the 300-acre Planning Area 6 of the Fairfield Train Station Specific Plan. That site had most of the focus because the city went to NorthPoint Development to test its interest in developing a data center. The initial answer, City Manager David Gassaway said, was NorthPoint was not interested. However, that position has changed. Gassaway made the presentation to the council, seeking direction on the kind of information it would want to see if such a project did go out to Area 6. He asked about location, buffers from urban development, water use, noise, environmental impacts, density – perhaps using just 100 of the 300 acres – the type of buildings, community benefits and utility taxes. But that brought at least one public comment that the staff should not be asking the council about helping to develop regulations for a project that the speaker – and many others – do not want near the One Lake community, and more than a handful do not want in Fairfield at all. The primary issues raised by the public were about water use, power use, noise, fire risk and response, pollution and to no small degree, the proximity to the One Lake community. A buffer of 3,000 feet that Gassaway suggested was viewed by many as not nearly enough. Ed Fischer said the city Fire Department is not equipped to deal with the kind of fires that data centers can generate, and Alicia Minyen added that substations with lithium battery technology would only heighten that risk. There were voices against the moratorium, primarily from representatives of the trade unions that believe the data center would create jobs – maybe not the center itself, but the other businesses that would be attracted to having a data center nearby and the energy infrastructure that would come with it. "The idea of opposing data centers (completely) is like walking around with blinders," said Dave Harrison, with Operating Engineers Local Union No. 3. He said the U.S. is already trailing China in the development of data centers, and that by simply wishing them away will not stop them from coming. Planning was needed, but through the land use standards not a moratorium. The economic promise is a big reason city staff approached NorthPoint in the first place, that and what Gassaway suggested would be a benefit to Travis Air Force Base. However, Councilman Doug Carr said he would want to hear from Travis AFB officials directly about whether they support a data center in the area. Clearly, more power capacity is a big issue for the base. Gassaway said the city has already lost a $400 million project because the energy infrastructure needed to support the company could not be developed in time to meet the deadline. Mayor-elect Pam Bertani said in a recent interview that economic development is at the top of the city's agenda. "We have been talking about economic development for years ... and this is what economic development looks like," Councilman Scott Tonnesen said. But he too had a laundry list of concerns he said would have to be addressed in the staff report on potential impacts. "It's not saying no to economic development," George Kennedy, chairman of the Planning Commission, said about the moratorium. He was speaking as a citizen. "It's talking about planning for it." At the end of the 45 days, which would be Dec. 25, the council could extend the moratorium another 22 months and 15 days. That decision would likely be made on Dec. 15, the last scheduled meeting of the council this year.

artigo.texto: The Cromwell Board of Education was asked for its stance on a proposed data center that would be situated near a middle school. A formal application for the data center developed by Global Common has not been submitted yet, according to the town. Still, concerned residents and parents sent inquiries to the board for their input. Stream Connecticut News for free, 24/7, wherever you are. The board agreed to issue a public statement in the near future laying out its priorities, which are the safety, education, and health of students. “I think we can continue to say that and continue to hold to those values and participate in the dialog representing what is so important to our students, to our families, and to our public schools," Alyssa Goduti, the Cromwell Board of Education Chair, said during Tuesday's board meeting. Cromwell Middle School is about half a mile away from the proposed site on Geer Street. Julie Burland, a parent, brought up her concerns about data centers at the meeting. “They operate 24/7, generating continuous equipment noise, including low-frequency humming that can travel beyond property lines and potentially affect nearby homes, schools and outdoor spaces," she said. Local The developer, Global Common CEO Bob Foxen, has said the data center would use little water and be powered by fuel cells, which he said are quiet. The town’s planning and zoning commission is considering a six- month moratorium on data centers. They’re holding a public hearing on Dec. 3. The board did not say whether it's in support, or against, the data center, but all at the meeting tonight agreed students are the priority. "We don't know what the health effects would be on our children," Susan Vanveldhuisen, a resident, said. "And they should come first."
