artigo.texto: DECATUR, Ga. — DeKalb County commissioners delayed action on two major data-center proposals Tuesday, Nov. 10, deferring one measure and withdrawing another after extended debate over what the county needs to know before deciding how to regulate the facilities. The DeKalb County Board of Commissioners deferred Commissioner LaDena Bolton’s proposal to broaden how DeKalb defines and classifies data centers until Dec. 15. Commissioners took definitive action on Commissioner Ted Terry’s separate proposal for an independent health and environmental study, voting 5-2 to withdraw it. The votes come as DeKalb remains under a moratorium on accepting applications for new or expanded data centers while county officials consider how to regulate the industry. Bolton’s proposal would ask the administration to classify data centers based on factors beyond a facility's physical size. “Define, study and protect has always been the mission,” Bolton said. She said the county should first establish what kinds of data centers it is dealing with before deciding what regulations may be appropriate. The classifications could consider factors such as a facility’s type of operation, tier classification, energy and water consumption, backup power and noise. Terry said he had sent Bolton proposed amendments and wanted the committee to consider those changes. “That’s how the democratic process works,” Terry said during a back-and-forth over how commissioners should handle changes to the measure. Bolton responded that some of Terry’s proposed amendments, including setback requirements, went beyond the purpose of her resolution. “This is not regulating,” Bolton said. “This is defining.” Shadowbox pushes for study before limits The debate followed public comments from both residents concerned about data centers and executives from Shadowbox Studios, whose south DeKalb property has become a focal point in the county’s discussion. Shadowbox CEO Peter Rumbold told commissioners the company supports an independent study of data-center impacts but said the county should focus on measurable standards rather than begin with conclusions about what size developments should be allowed. “The question should not be whether a data center development has impacts,” Rumbold said, “but rather what those impacts are, how they can be measured, how they can be mitigated.” He said a study could establish thresholds for issues such as water consumption, noise, emissions, light and stormwater and examine ways impacts could be reduced through buffers, infrastructure improvements or other requirements. Jeff Weber, Shadowbox’s chief development officer, also challenged discussion of a 1-million-square-foot limit on data-center development. “What scientific or empirical evidence supports that particular number?” Weber said. “Define the uses now, study the impacts next and then establish appropriate development standards once you have the facts,” Weber said. Residents speaking Tuesday urged commissioners to take a more cautious approach. Jackie Malcolm, who said she lives about a mile and a half from Shadowbox, raised concerns about potential health effects and property values near large data centers. “Your job as commissioners is to protect our health, our property,” Malcolm said. She called for an independent health and environmental analysis examining areas within five miles of proposed data centers. Resident Rosalind McIntyre questioned what would happen to economic incentives tied to Blackhall Studios, and later Shadowbox, if the property were used for data centers. McIntyre cited a $68 million incentive package and a commitment to create 2,400 jobs. She asked whether the incentives would carry over to data-center development or be rescinded, and what would happen to the promised jobs. Independent study withdrawn The board later returned to Terry’s proposal, which would have required an independent third-party health and environmental study before DeKalb could lift its data-center moratorium. Terry questioned county administrators about what research had already been completed as part of the administration’s work. An administration representative said staff had begun evaluating needs and discussing water and sewer impacts, but did not yet have findings ready to present. Terry then asked whether that work specifically included health and environmental impacts. The representative initially expressed uncertainty about whether those issues had been part of the water and sewer discussions and later said the administration would return with a timeline for its broader work. “A moratorium in and of itself is not enough if we don’t have the evidence to back it up,” Terry said. Commissioner Nicole Massiah said she still had questions about how the proposed study would work. “What is the testing technique?” Massiah asked during the discussion, also raising questions about peer review, potential error rates and how commissioners would ultimately use the findings. She said answering those questions could help the board reach agreement on what kind of study would be useful. Terry said the resolution had already changed in response to earlier concerns about who might conduct the study. “We took the organization out,” he said, noting that the proposal would instead direct the county’s procurement process to identify an independent firm. Commissioner Mereda Davis Johnson then made a substitute motion to withdraw the proposal. She argued that the county’s existing moratorium gives officials time to gather more information from residents and from state and federal discussions before deciding what questions an independent study should answer. Commissioner Michelle Long Spears said she did not support withdrawing the measure, noting that it had been moving through the county process since January. artigo.texto: Quincy, Wash. — Quincy's long-running push for data centers has brought jobs, tax revenue, a new hospital and a new high school, while also fueling concerns about water, farmland and a planned high-voltage transmission line. NonStop Local spoke with residents and officials in Quincy to get a closer look at what operating data centers mean for that community. At L and R Cafe II, owner Ibis Ortiz says main street businesses, like hers, are doing well in Quincy. "Probably our biggest in the morning is our breakfast burritos," said Ibis Ortiz. Quincy once leaned on food manufacturing and field work, but city leaders said that was not enough to keep people from leaving. "We survived on a food manufacturing plant and field work. That's what drove the city of Quincy. And we were seeing lots of people leaving," said Quincy City Administrator Joe Harris. The city then worked to recruit fiber companies and build around key amenities the area offers. "... low-cost power, from the hydropower, easy planning and permitting nothing to it, and the land," said Port of Quincy Commissioner for Dist. 1, Curt Morris. That effort helped bring eight data center campuses now operating in Quincy, each with multiple buildings. Expansions are expected. Various officials say those centers store online information tied to banking, medical records, insurance, airline ticketing, entertainment and other services people use every day. Morris said Quincy's facilities were not built as superscale artificial intelligence, generative AI or bitcoin mining sites. "This Microsoft plant isn't considered a mega, super-scale data center. I don't think that'll necessarily fit here because infrastructure will dictate how big you can make it. No, but having another one the size of 80-acres, 100 acres, Yeah, we take all those all day, There's just too much confusion between AI and data centers," said Morris. Water use is one concern. Quincy told NonStop Local the city's data centers use 8% of the city's water, but more water sources are needed for expected residential and industrial growth. "...either more re-use water, or water out of the Columbia Basin Irrigation District, or the Columbia River itself," said Quincy Q-1 Water Program Manager, Bob Davis. Officials said Microsoft already has a re-use water system that it funded, and the city runs for Microsoft. Quincy aims to have another re-use plant operating in 2029. "Most of the cooling water will come from re-use water," said Morris. The port explained that reuse water is treated and sent to data center campuses and to other non-potable uses such as park irrigation. Companies started building these data centers 20 years ago. Now, older facilities are being replaced with more efficient ones. "They will be replacing them with higher efficiency and lower energy use and water use. They will be much more efficient," said Quincy Municipal Services Director, Carl Worley. Davis said newer data centers are also using less water to cool their systems. "Data centers today are installing non-evaporative cooling systems. They're using mechanical chilled systems," said Davis. "So, is the turnaround that they use more electricity?" asked Meili. "Yes, mechanical-chilled uses more electricity," answered Davis. The Port of Quincy said nearby farmland that might sell for $15,000 an acre for agriculture could bring about eight times that amount, if it's within the technology growth management map. "As industrial property, with the services we're working on, it'll be $125,000 an acre," said Morris. City officials said the much higher valuation of the city, and tax revenue from the data centers have drastically cut what citizens pay for many levies and bonds. "When we go out to the community and we say, hey, we need to build a new hospital, a new high school, a new police department, a new city hall, whatever that whatever that build, that ask is we're asking the citizens to fund that using $0.88 per $1,000 of their assessed value instead of $3.12 per thousand," said Harris. The city administrator adds that revenue linked to data centers helped Quincy more than double its police force. "A lot of cities in Washington don't even have one officer per thousand residents. Quincy has got 2.3 officers per thousand," said Harris. That same tax base also helped build new city, police and fire facilities, an aquatics center and a new high school. Quincy Recreation Director Russ Harrington pointed to the aquatics center's family features. "Youve got your lazy river, the slides and the kids' area that goes to the box pool," said Harrington. Quincy Public School Superintendent, Dr. Nik Bergman toured us around the new high school and said the bond support reshaped local campuses. "The voters passed a $108 million bond that would support the brand-new high school that we're being interviewed in today. It also built brand new elementary gyms. Every single one of our elementary schools has a new gym. It also helped us renovate the existing high school to make it into a middle school," said Dr. Bergman. Quincy Public Schools also partnered with Microsoft on a Data Center Technician Program. "A kiddo can leave Quincy High School and go right to work the data centers and earn a family sustaining income." said Dr. Bergman. "It starts over $60,000 plus. We have students who have come out from a year ago with the Data Center Technician Program and are going into jobs with that," said Lisa Karstetter with Microsoft Community Outreach. Quincy estimates data centers employ about 1,000 full-time workers, with more than half at Microsoft. This does not include contractors. Quincy estimates that each data center job creates four more good paying jobs. Back at the historic L and R Cafe II, one farmer told NonStop Local he sees the data center industry as a stronger job option for his son. artigo.texto: Sediar data centers pode ser caminho positivo para o Brasil na corrida da IA, diz especialista Superávit da China ultrapassa US$ 1 trilhão impulsionado pelo boom da inteligência artificial, mas incertezas podem deixar economia vulnerável Tecnologia e Ciência|Do R7, com RECORD NEWS LEIA AQUI O RESUMO DA NOTÍCIA Produzido pela Ri7a - a Inteligência Artificial do R7 Carros autônomos, androides lutadores e atletas robôs são comuns na China, um dos principais polos globais de desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial. O superávit comercial do país ultrapassou a marca de 1 trilhão de dólares, mas a economia enfrenta o risco de desacelerar no cenário de uma eventual baixa na demanda por IA. “Muito se fala do boom das IAs, que alguma hora ou outra isso vai demonstrar que era uma aposta do mercado que não necessariamente resultará em benefícios ou em resultados econômicos. Mas, sem dúvida nenhuma, hoje é a grande corrida mundial”, analisa o advogado especialista em Direito Digital, Luiz Augusto D’Urso. No programa Conexão Record News desta terça (10), o especialista usou a crise de espionagem interna da Nvidia — empresa produtora de chips utilizados na montagem de computadores — como exemplo da instabilidade do setor, mas não descarta as oportunidades que a tecnologia traz, especialmente para o Brasil. “O boom da IA que está exportando não só a tecnologia, mas essas situações para sediar data centers. [...] Pode ser um caminho interessante para o Brasil se aproximar, do ponto de vista econômico, desses países e trocar não só questões econômicas, mas tecnológicas”. D’Urso, porém, aponta cuidados que o país deveria ter nesse eventual cenário: “Sediar os data centers é uma coisa. Ter certeza de que a informação não sai para esses países é outra. Então, também nós, sediando esse debate, podemos de alguma forma brigar por ter confiança nas informações, e o Brasil está nesse momento no meio de toda essa negociação, mas para a gente é positivo.” Análises, entrevistas e as notícias do Brasil e do mundo estão na RECORD NEWS. artigo.texto: Com venda de elétricos em alta, BYD antecipa terceiro turno na fábrica de Camaçari, na Bahia Novo horário de produção, que estava marcado para começar no final deste ano, iniciou nesta segunda Atualizado Com vendas de carros elétricos em alta e demanda pelo seu novo modelo Atto 2, a chinesa BYD antecipou do final do ano para esta segunda-feira, dia 9, o início do terceiro turno de produção na unidade de Camaçari, na Bahia, que passa a operar 24 horas. Com a contratação de mais dois mil trabalhadores para este turno, o complexo industrial baiano alcança mais de dez mil funcionários desde o início da produção, no ano passado. As vendas de carros eletrificados têm crescido a um ritmo de dois dígitos no Brasil. Em outubro passado, foram emplacados 54.486 veículos eletrificados, um crescimento de 154,9% em relação ao mesmo mês de 2025, quando foram comercializados 21.369 exemplares, segundo a Associação Brasileira do Veículo Elétrico (ABVE). Entre janeiro e outubro, foram vendidos 436.809 veículos elétricos e híbridos no Brasil, uma alta de 158,8% em relação ao mesmo período de 2025. O Dolphin Mini e o Dolphin, ambos da BYD, lideram o ranking dos carros elétricos puros mais vendidos no varejo, e a marca chinesa já é a quarta que mais vende carros no país, atrás de Fiat, Volkswagen e General Motors, segundo ranking elaborado pela Bright Consulting, consultoria especialista no setor automotivo. O recém-lançado híbrido plug-in flex Atto 2 registrou 10.329 pedidos e 5.012 unidades emplacadas em pouco mais de 40 dias úteis, segundo a BYD. Além do terceiro turno, a BYD está concluindo os testes finais das áreas de soldagem e pintura — etapas decisivas para a produção 100% nacional. Na Bahia, são produzidos o elétrico Dolphin Mini, o sedã BYD King (híbrido plug-in) e o SUV BYD Song Pro (híbrido plug-in), e agora com a expansão, o Atto 2. — Estamos acelerando a produção porque o consumidor brasileiro está respondendo, e os números do Atto 2 deixam isso muito claro. Temos uma demanda expressiva para atender e uma fábrica preparada para acompanhar esse crescimento — afirmou Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente sênior da BYD do Brasil e head comercial e de marketing da BYD Auto do Brasil, que lembra que os novos turnos já foram estruturados com jornada semanal de 40 horas. Um estudo do Observatório da Indústria (Sistema FIEB) em parceria com a BYD mostrou que o impacto da retomada das operações na unidade de Camaçari, depois que a Ford saiu do país e deixou a unidade, retomou cerca de 22 mil empregos (diretos, indiretos e induzidos) e a operação vai movimentar cerca de R$ 1,03 bilhão por ano em salários. O investimento total anunciado pela BYD para o complexo industrial de Camaçari é de R$ 11,3 bilhões, nos próximos anos, com capacidade inicial de produção de 150 mil veículos por ano. Já foram investidos R$ 5,5 bilhões. A BYD está anunciando ainda uma parceria com a TIM para fornecer soluções de conectividade embarcada para toda a frota de veículos leves da marca em circulação no Brasil. A parceria terá a implantação também de infraestrutura de redes 5G e 4G na fábrica de Camaçari, com sete pontos de cobertura externa e 63 equipamentos distribuídos entre os galpões e as áreas operacionais, permitindo conectar colaboradores, visitantes, sistemas operacionais e os próprios veículos ainda durante a fabricação, facilitando a comunicação entre diferentes etapas da produção.

artigo.texto: PowerX, a Japan-based grid-scale BESS manufacturer, has signed a non-binding partnership agreement with Energy Vault Japan, a subsidiary of Energy Vault Holdings. The two companies will explore the supply of up to 1.5 GWh of the Mega Power series of PowerX, which is to be deployed in the US in 2027. That series includes a containerized BESS, a grid connection package and a modular data center with a built-in BESS. The products would be made at the factory of PowerX in Japan and designed to meet the Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements of US federal law. Those requirements apply to storage projects that seek federal clean energy tax credits. The two companies also intend to work together on BESS and data center projects in Japan, Australia and the US, with the scope to be decided project by project. artigo.texto: Brussels, 9 November 2026 The European Commission has today published the 2026 EU Climate Action Progress Report and Carbon Market Report, showing that EU greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions continue to fall, clean technologies are expanding, and an increasing amount of ETS revenues are available to EU Member States for investments in decarbonisation. These developments show how the clean transition continues to support the EU’s wider objectives of strengthening competitiveness, enhancing energy security, reducing dependencies and becoming climate resilient. The Climate Action Progress Report confirms that EU net GHG emissions fell by 1.6% in 2025 compared to 2024, according to provisional data. Emissions covered by the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) decreased by around 2% in 2025, while emissions in sectors covered by the Effort Sharing Regulation (ESR) remained broadly stable, and provisional data show an improvement in the EU land carbon sink. Emissions are now 39% below 1990 levels, while the EU economy has grown by 74% over the same period, decoupling one more year the growth of our economy from its decarbonisation, further reducing emissions. This year’s Carbon Market Report also finds that EU ETS revenues grew to €43.2 billion in 2025, an 11% increase compared to 2024. The EU also strengthened its longer-term climate framework this year by establishing a legally binding target to reduce net GHG emissions by 90% by 2040 compared to 1990 levels, with the entry into force of the amended European Climate Law in April 2026. Stepping up 2030 implementation across the EU While the EU remains fully committed to reducing net GHG emissions by at least 55% by 2030, the slower pace of emission reductions in 2025 means that efforts will need to accelerate across the economy in the second half of the decade. The report indicates that emissions covered by the Effort Sharing Regulation (including domestic transport, buildings, agriculture and waste) are currently expected to fall by around 38.5% by 2030 compared with 2005, slightly below the EU-wide target of 40%. The assessment shows that nine EU Member States are not making sufficient progress towards meeting their 2030 ESR targets. The Commission will request that Austria, Croatia, Cyprus, Germany, Italy, Ireland, Lithuania, Malta and Sweden each submit a corrective action plan to accelerate the implementation and development of emission reduction measures and investments. Provisional data show that net carbon removals from the land sector increased by around 11% in 2025 compared to 2024. Despite this improvement, current projections for the land sector also indicate a gap of 40–55 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent towards the EU’s 2030 land-use target. Clean transition strengthens energy security and competitiveness The accelerated deployment of clean technologies in 2025 continues to help reduce Europe’s dependence on imported fossil fuels and limit the impacts of volatile fuel prices on citizens and businesses. While EU cleantech manufacturing has expanded significantly, the report highlights that further economic opportunities for European industry can still be captured, which will as a result mobilise investment. Registrations of battery-electric cars increased to 1.9 million in 2025, the equivalent of roughly one in six new car registrations. EU wind and solar capacity increased to 611 GW, or around 49% of total electricity generation capacity. The installation of heat pumps also accelerated, with estimated 41 GW of additional capacity installed in 2025, up from 26 GW in 2024. Climate resilience increasingly urgent Climate-related extreme events have caused an estimated €822 billion in economic losses in the EU since 1980. Around €70 billion per year will need to be invested in adaptation up to 2050. The reports emphasise the rapidly growing impacts of climate change, with severe impacts in 2026. The new EU Climate Resilience Framework, presented in October 2026, will strengthen Europe’s ability to anticipate, prepare for, and manage climate risks with a proposed Climate Resilience Law underpinned by a common reference trajectory for global warming. EU ETS continues to be a well-functioning carbon market The 2026 Carbon Market Report shows that EU ETS revenues amount to €43.2 billion in 2025. More than half this amount (€23.9 billion) went directly to EU Member States to finance decarbonisation measures for households and industry. Increasing the share of ETS revenues invested in decarbonisation, and maintaining the system’s integrity, will ensure that the EU ETS meets its 2030 target of a 62% emissions cut below 2005 levels. Emissions from industrial installations decreased by 3.3% from 2024, mostly driven by the iron and steel, cement, and chemical sectors. Maritime transport emissions decreased by 4% while aviation emissions grew by 0.2%, confirming the pressing need to decarbonise this sector. While overall ETS emissions remain below the cap, emission reductions have slowed compared to previous years. In July 2026, the Commission proposed a reform of the EU ETS for the decade 2030-2040. Background The Climate Action Progress Report shows annual progress towards the EU’s emission reduction targets and includes information on different climate policy areas, legislative progress, climate finance and adaptation. artigo.texto: Strengthening the Luzon grid: BESS at Magat supports flexible renewable integration Customer Story | 4 min read SN Aboitiz Power (SNAP) operates several of the Philippines' most important hydropower assets, including the Magat Hydroelectric Power Plant in Ramon, Isabela. The plant delivers up to 388 MW of dependable hydropower capacity to the Luzon grid. It is also a strong contributor to the Philippines’ Energy Plan 2023–2050, where the government aims to raise the country’s total share of renewable energy to 50 percent by 2050. To strengthen operational flexibility and support the country's clean energy ambitions, SNAP implemented a battery energy storage system (BESS) with grid-forming capability at the Magat site in two phases. The first 24-MW system entered commercial operation in January 2024 and demonstrated ancillary services performance under real operating conditions. Building on this result, SNAP launched a 16 MW expansion in 2025, which entered commercial operation in June 2026. The two battery energy storage systems operate independently, each with its own control architecture and operational boundaries. When dispatched together, they can inject up to 40 MW of fast-response power at the site’s common point of coupling, strengthening grid support for the Luzon system. As the share of Variable Renewable Energy (VRE) on the Luzon grid continues to increase, system operators require faster and more reliable resources to maintain frequency stability and ensure secure operation. For SNAP, this challenge was particularly acute at the Magat site, where hydropower plays a dual role in supporting both electricity supply and critical irrigation needs. Any additional grid support capability would need to perform reliably under real operating conditions and respond predictably during system events. At the same time, it had to integrate with existing plant infrastructure without introducing operational complexity or disrupting established processes at the site. SNAP required a solution that could deliver dependable contingency reserves, maintain stable behavior during grid disturbances, and provide clear visibility for operators. Just as importantly, the approach needed to be scalable and proven in a way that would allow future capacity decisions to be taken with confidence, based on performance rather than assumptions. To meet these challenges, SNAP adopted a phased deployment approach to strengthen grid support at Magat while managing risk and ensuring continuity of operations. The first phase, a 24 MW BESS commissioned in January 2024, demonstrated dependable ancillary services performance in day-to-day conditions, providing the firm operational basis for SNAP's 16 MW expansion, which entered commercial operation in June 2026. With two independently controlled BESS units operating at a shared single point of interconnection, Hitachi Energy supplied the power conversion solutions, plant-level controls, SCADA integration, and engineering support across both phases, establishing consistent response characteristics and sitewide visibility through cloud-based remote monitoring while preserving independent operation. Using a consistent system architecture across both phases reduced integration risk, supported lender confidence, a key consideration for project bankability, and established a repeatable approach for scaling storage within the existing site framework. Each unit maintains its own plant controller and operating parameters, and when dispatched together the two systems can inject up to 40 MW at Magat's common point of coupling, meeting the grid's requirement for fast response while keeping the assets logically separate for operations and maintenance. The phased deployment at Magat has strengthened SNAP's ability to provide fast, dependable grid support on the Luzon system, improving frequency response capability and enhancing stability during system events. Operationally, each system maintains independent control and clearly defined operational boundaries, preserving the ability to dispatch, maintain, or modify one unit without affecting the other. Both installations feed into SNAP's Integrated Remote Operations Center (iROC), providing centralized visibility that supports timely and informed operator decision-making without adding complexity to site operations. By building on the proven performance of the initial installation and maintaining continuity in system execution, SNAP has established a repeatable pathway for scaling energy storage at Magat. SNAP's decision to award both phases to Hitachi Energy reflects a partnership built on demonstrated performance, a practical indicator of confidence as the site scales its storage capacity. In doing so, SNAP has demonstrated that storage and hydropower can be scaled together in a way that is technically sound, commercially repeatable, and directly aligned with the Philippines' ambition to make renewables the backbone of its energy future.

artigo.texto: NEGÓCIOS NA COP31 JBNews Por José Teixeira O governador Otaviano Pivetta participa, a partir desta segunda-feira (9), da 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP31), em Antália, na Turquia, com uma agenda voltada à abertura de oportunidades econômicas para Mato Grosso por meio da comercialização internacional de créditos de carbono e outros ativos ambientais. A missão ocorre em um momento em que o Governo do Estado busca estruturar instrumentos jurídicos e financeiros para transformar resultados de redução do desmatamento em receitas destinadas à conservação ambiental e à implementação de políticas de desenvolvimento sustentável. A COP31 será realizada de 9 a 20 de novembro, reunindo representantes governamentais, instituições financeiras, empresas e organizações internacionais para discutir medidas relacionadas às mudanças climáticas, ao mercado de carbono e ao financiamento da preservação ambiental. Pivetta integra a delegação mato-grossense acompanhado da secretária de Estado de Meio Ambiente, Mauren Lazzaretti, responsável pela condução das políticas ambientais estaduais. Entre os compromissos previstos estão reuniões com representantes de investidores internacionais ligados à Coalizão LEAF, iniciativa que mobiliza recursos públicos e privados para apoiar a proteção de florestas tropicais e a redução de emissões provocadas pelo desmatamento. A participação de países como Reino Unido e Noruega nesses mecanismos de financiamento representa uma oportunidade de aproximação de Mato Grosso com compradores internacionais de resultados ambientais certificados. A intenção do governo é ampliar a confiança dos investidores em créditos de carbono gerados a partir de reduções de emissões registradas no território estadual. Para que esses resultados sejam comercializados, entretanto, é necessário atender a exigências técnicas de certificação, monitoramento e verificação, além de demonstrar que as reduções de emissões são reais, mensuráveis e adequadamente contabilizadas. O trabalho está associado ao mecanismo conhecido como REDD+ Jurisdicional, que permite desenvolver programas de redução de emissões por desmatamento e degradação florestal em escala estadual. Durante a conferência, integrantes do Consórcio da Amazônia Legal também deverão apresentar ações realizadas pelos estados brasileiros para estruturar esse modelo de financiamento ambiental. Em Mato Grosso, uma das principais medidas relacionadas ao projeto é a proposta de criação da Companhia Mato-grossense de Ativos Ambientais S.A. (CMAA). O projeto de lei foi encaminhado pelo governador à Assembleia Legislativa e prevê a constituição de uma sociedade de economia mista destinada à estruturação, gestão e comercialização de créditos de carbono, créditos de biodiversidade e outros ativos ambientais gerados no território estadual. A nova companhia deverá funcionar como instrumento empresarial para organizar operações ligadas à economia ambiental, respeitados os limites estabelecidos pela legislação e pelas regras de certificação dos ativos negociados. A proposta também está associada ao compromisso anunciado pelo Governo de Mato Grosso de alcançar a neutralidade líquida de emissões de carbono até 2035. A criação da empresa, porém, ainda depende de autorização legislativa e dos procedimentos necessários à sua constituição. O encaminhamento do projeto não significa que a companhia esteja em funcionamento ou que já existam contratos internacionais firmados. A importância econômica desse modelo decorre da possibilidade de Mato Grosso obter receitas a partir de resultados ambientais, sem depender exclusivamente das atividades tradicionais de produção agropecuária e exploração de recursos naturais. O Estado possui áreas dos biomas Amazônia, Cerrado e Pantanal, que apresentam características ambientais diferentes e exigem estratégias específicas de conservação. Ao mesmo tempo, Mato Grosso ocupa posição de destaque na produção brasileira de soja, milho, algodão e proteína animal, tornando relevante a relação entre expansão econômica, preservação ambiental e exigências dos mercados consumidores internacionais. A criação de instrumentos de comercialização de carbono poderá ampliar as fontes de financiamento para projetos de prevenção ao desmatamento, recuperação ambiental, proteção da biodiversidade e valorização de comunidades que participam da conservação dos recursos naturais. No entanto, a dimensão financeira dessas oportunidades dependerá do volume de reduções de emissões que receber certificação, dos preços negociados, das condições contratuais e dos compromissos assumidos pelos compradores. Até a abertura da conferência, os comunicados oficiais consultados não apresentavam novos contratos assinados durante a COP31 nem confirmavam receitas efetivamente ingressadas nos cofres de Mato Grosso em razão da missão internacional. A programação da delegação também contempla discussões sobre riscos climáticos, prevenção e combate a incêndios florestais, economia florestal e estratégias para enfrentar crimes ambientais. Outro aspecto importante da conferência será a discussão sobre mecanismos capazes de ampliar o financiamento climático destinado a regiões que concentram grandes áreas de vegetação nativa. Essas negociações podem influenciar diretamente os interesses de Mato Grosso, especialmente em relação às condições de certificação, pagamento e reconhecimento internacional de resultados de conservação florestal. A cúpula de chefes de Estado e de governo está programada para os dias 11 e 12 de novembro, quando deverão ocorrer reuniões e pronunciamentos de alto nível sobre os compromissos internacionais de enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas. Pivetta permanecerá fora de Mato Grosso até 18 de novembro, conforme a programação divulgada pelo Governo do Estado. artigo.texto: Com 3125 MW de baterias em operação, outros 3017 MW em fase de testes e 5130 MW em construção , o Chile enfrenta novos desafios para manter a rentabilidade do armazenamento de energia, em um mercado marcado pela rápida incorporação de projetos de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) e pelo crescimento limitado da demanda por eletricidade. “Há tantas baterias que a arbitragem está sendo diluída e cada unidade de armazenamento adicional dilui essa receita”, alertou Alfredo Solar , Gerente Regional do Chile e Cone Sul da Atlas Renewable Energy, durante a Future Energy Summit (FES) Chile 2026 . O executivo explicou que os sistemas visam armazenar eletricidade durante os horários de pico de geração solar, quando os preços se aproximam de zero, para posteriormente vendê-la a preços superiores a US$ 100/MWh. No entanto, ele observou que as descargas já estão ocorrendo a preços praticamente nulos. Mario Acevedo Bilbao , Gerente de País e Mercado da DNV , destacou: "Se você observar o modelo financeiro de dois anos atrás, verá que ele é muito diferente agora." O especialista observou que os bancos já estão solicitando cenários de sensibilidade que consideram uma maior incorporação da capacidade de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), inclusive acima das projeções inicialmente utilizadas. Mais baterias e novas opções de financiamento. Segundo as estatísticas de setembro da Associação Chilena de Energias Renováveis e Armazenamento (ACERA) , os projetos em operação, teste e construção totalizam 11.272 MW e 49.413 MWh , embora nem toda essa capacidade esteja disponível comercialmente. A capacidade operacional praticamente dobrou em comparação com os 1575 MW registrados no final de 2025. Além disso, o portfólio inclui iniciativas ambientalmente aprovadas e outras em avaliação, que poderão expandir consideravelmente a oferta nos próximos anos. Solar comparou essa evolução com a expansão experimentada anteriormente pela geração fotovoltaica no Chile, quando o aumento da capacidade resultou em desperdícios, menores rendimentos e dificuldades econômicas para alguns desenvolvedores. “É preocupante que o armazenamento no Chile continue a crescer ou a ficar sobrecarregado, para além do que é razoável”, disse ele. Além da arbitragem, foram identificadas pressões sobre os pagamentos de capacidade, outra fonte de remuneração que faz parte dos modelos de negócio. Ao mesmo tempo, Acevedo alertou que a rapidez com que as obras estão sendo executadas dificulta prever como o sistema elétrico evoluirá em períodos relativamente curtos. Ele explicou que algumas instalações podem ser concluídas em aproximadamente seis meses, enquanto certos ajustes regulatórios e operacionais exigem prazos consideravelmente maiores. “Os bancos também estão pedindo coisas como: vamos adicionar mais 2 GW, vamos reduzir outro em tanto, o que acontece se essas condições mudarem?”, exemplificou ele. O representante da DNV comentou que essas simulações fazem parte das avaliações de risco exigidas para novos investimentos e operações de refinanciamento, considerando as possíveis variações nos custos marginais e nas receitas esperadas. O cargo e a remuneração, sob escrutínio. Em setembro, os sistemas de armazenamento de energia injetaram 584 GWh no Sistema Elétrico Nacional , o equivalente a 7,9% do total de injeções por tecnologia, segundo a ACERA. Esse volume representou um aumento de 216,3% em relação ao ano anterior. Em paralelo, a Solar defendeu a aceleração da implementação de mecanismos que incorporem o custo de oportunidade no planejamento do uso de baterias , conforme previsto na regulamentação do setor elétrico chileno. O executivo explicou que as decisões de descarregamento devem levar em consideração o valor da conservação de energia para uso futuro, em vez de concentrar as operações em determinados momentos e causar novas quedas de preço. “Dois anos é muito tempo”, questionou ele, referindo-se ao prazo de implementação das ferramentas operacionais mencionadas durante a reunião. Ele também alertou que esses recursos estão sendo usados para atender às necessidades do sistema, como variações repentinas na geração de energia solar, sem necessariamente receber uma compensação equivalente ao serviço prestado. “Se eles estão usando isso como um serviço complementar, sejamos claros e digamos: este é um serviço complementar”, argumentou ele. Seguir leyendo A proposta surge num momento em que o Chile continua a enfrentar dificuldades na utilização de toda a sua capacidade de geração de energia renovável. Entre janeiro e agosto de 2026 , registaram-se cortes de energia de 3.014 GWh , em comparação com 3.125 GWh no mesmo período do ano anterior, segundo a ACERA. Acevedo concordou com a necessidade de melhorar os sistemas de remuneração e mencionou alternativas utilizadas em outros mercados, incluindo mecanismos baseados em ofertas. “O importante é, além de falar, executar”, enfatizou ele. O especialista lembrou que o Chile já enfrentou diferenças entre os tempos de expansão da geração fotovoltaica e o desenvolvimento da infraestrutura de transmissão, por isso considerou necessário evitar novas discrepâncias com o crescimento das baterias. Contratos, cibersegurança e garantias para sustentar investimentos A Solar identificou os contratos de compra de energia (PPAs) de longo prazo como uma ferramenta fundamental para apoiar novos empreendimentos. A Atlas possui aproximadamente 1000 MW de capacidade de armazenamento de energia com duração de quatro horas no Chile e uma capacidade solar equivalente, associada a acordos com grandes consumidores dos setores de mineração e indústria, incluindo a Antofagasta Minerals, a Codelco e a CAP. artigo.texto: Astella, do Grupo ABL, inaugura data center em Curitiba com investimento R$ 60 milhões Entre 2027 e 2028, grupo brasileiro de tecnologia prevê investir mais R$ 300 milhões em centros de dados com recursos próprios e expandindo a operação a outros estados A empresa Astella, do Grupo ABL, estreia no mercado de centros de dados para serviços de nuvem e inteligência artificial com a inauguração de um data center em Curitiba (PR). O grupo investiu R$ 60 milhões na operação entre 2025 e 2026, em energia, refrigeração e cibersegurança do data center. Até 2028, a meta é injetar mais R$ 300 milhões no negócio, com recursos próprios, expandindo a operação para outros estados. O data center inicia um projeto de rede nacional e descentralizada de computação em nuvem, inteligência artificial e soberania de dados, diz o presidente do Grupo ABL, Agnaldo Lopes, ao Valor. “Em 2025, decidimos retomar a operação de data center na esteira desse movimento do mercado para atender à demanda da IA. Vimos uma oportunidade de retomada”, afirma. O centro de dados com capacidade inicial de 3,5 megawatts e está instalado em um edifício de 16 andares e 8.800 metros quadrados de área útil, no centro de Curitiba. O prédio foi vendido pela Vivo, do Grupo Telefônica, ao grupo ABL em 2018. O imóvel era o principal data center da Vivo no Paraná desde a aquisição da GVT pela operadora. O primeiro projeto da Astella prevê uma rede em forma de estrela que leve o tráfego de dados do data center de Curitiba a outros pontos de conexão de rede (nós) localizados em regiões que não possuem grande concentração de centros de dados. A ideia também é conectar essa rede aos pontos estratégicos de troca de dados como São Paulo e alguns estados da região Nordeste até o final de 2028, acrescenta o executivo. O Paraná possui cinco data centers em operação, enquanto São Paulo reúne 133, segundo os dados atualizados no fim de agosto pelo Mapa de Datacenters do Brasil, criado pelo centro de inovação do Rio de Janeiro em parceria com o site Startups. Fundado em 2000, o grupo ABL atuou no setor de data center no passado. "Em 2015, nós inauguramos um dos primeiros data centers de nuvem privada no Paraná", recorda Lopes, sócio fundador e majoritário da companhia. A empresa também foi provedora de acesso à internet em banda larga, entre 2014 e 2021. A operação foi adquirida pela Copel, que criou o provedor Ligga Telecom, vendido em fevereiro à Brasil Tecpar. A soberania dos dados é um dos pilares da atuação da Astella. "Quando olhamos para o mercado vimos que 80% das estruturas atuais pertencem a grandes empresas internacionais", afirma Lopes. "Entendemos que precisamos criar um modelo que atenda estrategicamente também a soberania nacional", ele acrescenta. As operações de data centers são financiadas com capital próprio, informa Lopes. O executivo controla o Grupo ABL, com 90% do capital, e detém 100% da Astella. O grupo de capital fechado projeta fechar o ano de 2026 com um faturamento de R$ 100 milhões, o que pode representar um crescimento de 28,2% ante o resultado de R$ 78 milhões em 2025. A margem de lucro antes de juros, impostos, depreciação e amortização (Ebitda na sigla em inglês) estimada para 2026 é de 58%, ante margem, Ebitda de 57% no ano passado. A companhia não informou o valor do lucro líquido.

artigo.texto: Calibrant Energy, a leading provider of on-site energy solutions, on November 10 announced the close of a $145-million debt facility led by Investec for solar and battery storage projects across multiple U.S. power markets. The portfolio includes a 120-MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) serving a hyperscale data center customer in the PJM territory. Citi, Liberty Bank, and Siemens Financial Services also participated in the facility. Data center operators are looking for ways to get online faster as PJM and federal regulators work through how large power users connect to the grid. Calibrant’s engineered BESS solutions give energy-intensive facilities greater control over how and when they draw power. This flexibility supports faster interconnection timelines and reduces the need for costly grid infrastructure upgrades that would otherwise be passed on to other ratepayers. “Data center operators are choosing on-site energy storage because it is a fast, reliable, and effective way to get online and operate as responsible grid citizens,” said Phil Martin, CEO of Calibrant Energy. “With this financial close and site mobilization for a hyperscale data center, Calibrant continues to demonstrate that large-load flexibility is not just possible but a commercial reality today.” Calibrant’s turnkey, zero-capex solutions unlock the path to reliable power that the world’s largest power users need to grow their businesses. “Investec is proud to support Calibrant and Macquarie on this transaction,” said Fred Petit, co-head of Energy & Infrastructure North America at Investec. “We value the opportunity to partner with experienced investors and operators, and to provide financing that advances the energy transition and the critical infrastructure needed to meet growing power demand across the U.S.” Calibrant Energy now has more than 5.9 GWh of battery storage capacity in operation, in construction, or under exclusive development agreements, including additional sites with the same hyperscale customer. This growth reflects rising demand from large power users for on-site energy solutions that accelerate speed to power while easing strain on the grid. It also reflects customers’ preference for a trusted, experienced partner that can develop, own, and operate these solutions and deliver the power outcomes their business plans depend on. —This content was contributed by the communications team for Calibrant Energy.

artigo.texto: Viridi and Good Carbon Deploy One of the Largest Indoor Battery Energy Storage Systems in an Occupied US Residential Building BUFFALO, N.Y., Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Viridi, the industry leader in fail-safe distributed energy storage systems, and Good Carbon Co., today announced the deployment of a 3.75MWh lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) at Peace Bridge Place, a 105-unit affordable housing apartment building in Buffalo, New York. The project is one of the largest indoor lithium-ion battery systems in an occupied residential building in the United States. At Peace Bridge Place, Viridi’s RPSLinkIN indoor BESS is part of a broader clean energy strategy that includes geothermal heating & cooling, domestic hot water, and high efficient building envelope upgrades. The 3.75 MWh system is designed to provide extended backup power for the fully electrified building during outages, while also helping reduce demand on the local grid during peak periods. Good Carbon Co., which focuses on revitalizing multifamily properties in communities throughout Western New York, selected the system to strengthen energy resilience for residents and enable the property to enable flexible, grid-responsive energy management. Adam Serbert, CEO of Good Carbon Co, said: Energy is one of the biggest operating costs in multifamily housing, and how you manage it directly affects the long-term performance of a property “At Peace Bridge Place, Viridi’s battery and energy management technology will help us reduce peak demand, avoid higher-cost periods and participate in demand response programs. That means lower operating costs, new revenue opportunities and a stronger economic foundation for keeping the property affordable and well maintained. For us, this is not just about one building — it is about creating a model we can apply across future multifamily projects.” Viridi’s intelligent Energy Management System automatically stores and discharges electricity based on the needs of the fully electrified property and the local grid. It allows Peace Bridge Place to reduce electricity demand during peak periods and respond to utility signals when additional grid flexibility is needed, while providing greater energy resilience for residents. By reducing peak demand and participating in demand response programs, the system can help lower the property’s energy costs while creating new revenue opportunities. The New York State Energy Research and Development Agency (NYSERDA) is providing support to Good Carbon Co. for the Peace Bridge Place project through its Future Grid Challenge. The Peace Bridge Place project is a National Grid pilot focused on integrating flexible, grid-responsive technologies into its distribution network. Viridi’s energy storage and energy management technology will work in coordination with EnergyHub’s Edge Distributed Energy Resource Management System (DERMS), enabling the property to respond to National Grid signals during periods of peak electricity demand. Doreen M. Harris, President and CEO, NYSERDA, said: Peace Bridge Place demonstrates how forward-thinking energy storage solutions can ensure New York’s multifamily buildings are meeting the energy needs of its residents while creating a more reliable and resilient electric grid, “Projects like this embody NYSERDA’s mission to spur innovation that drives New York toward a clean energy future.” Distributed across seven battery rooms, the 3.75MWh system is integrated with Viridi’s proprietary Energy Management System (EMS), which optimizes the property’s electricity use while enabling it to respond to changing conditions on the local grid in two key ways: - Peak Shaving: As the building’s grid energy draw approaches a monthly peak, the battery automatically discharges to keep demand below a target threshold, reducing peak demand and associated $/kW demand charges. - Seasonal Demand Response: During peak events, National Grid dispatch signals are delivered through EnergyHub’s platform to Viridi’s energy management system, which then coordinates the response across the building’s battery and other energy systems. For participating residents, smart thermostat setpoints can be adjusted to “pre-cool” or “pre-heat” apartments before the event, enabling reduced HVAC consumption during the event while the battery discharges. Residents can opt out of individual events at any time. Together, these actions allow the property to reduce its net electricity demand while the local grid is under the greatest strain. Deploying lithium-ion battery storage indoors at this scale requires rigorous safety standards. The risk of thermal runaway — and its potential to propagate from cell to cell — has historically constrained where lithium-ion systems can be installed. The RPSLinkIN system is designed to address that challenge through Viridi’s proprietary Fail-Safe Anti-Propagation architecture, a passive safety layer designed to prevent thermal runaway from spreading between cells. That safety architecture has undergone industry-standard testing designed to evaluate how battery systems behave during a thermal runaway event. During UL 9540A testing, a cell was intentionally driven into thermal failure to determine whether the event would spread to surrounding cells. Viridi’s technology prevented cell-to-cell propagation, with no detectable release of heat, sparks, smoke, gas or flames. RPSLinkIN has also earned UL 9540 Listing from TÜV Rheinland, providing third-party certification of the complete energy storage system. Jon M. Williams, CEO of Viridi, said: This project demonstrates what becomes possible when energy storage is designed to serve the building and the grid at the same time, “Peace Bridge Place will now be able to reduce peak demand, respond when the grid needs support and strengthen resilience for the people who live there. https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBM.resumo: O Governo do Brasil irá investir R$ 46,3 milhões no desenvolvimento de uma tecnologia nacional que visa tornar os data centers mais eficientes, seguros e sustentáveis. A iniciativa, aprovada pelo Conselho Gestor do Fundo para o Desenvolvimento Tecnológico das Telecomunicações (Funttel), prevê a criação de uma plataforma inteligente para gerenciar e distribuir dados entre diferentes estruturas de processamento, o que inclui mini data centers instalados em diversas regiões do país. Batizado de Prisma, o projeto utilizará IA para identificar onde e como os dados devem ser processados, distribuindo automaticamente os recursos computacionais entre diferentes infraestruturas. Na prática, a tecnologia poderá reduzir gastos com energia, diminuir custos operacionais, acelerar o acesso às informações e aumentar a proteção de dados estratégicos. “Investir em tecnologia nacional é garantir que o Brasil tenha mais autonomia para proteger suas informações e desenvolver soluções para os desafios do futuro. Com o apoio do Funttel, estamos fortalecendo a inovação brasileira e criando condições para uma infraestrutura digital mais moderna, segura e sustentável, reduzindo nossa dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior”, afirma o ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho. Os recursos serão administrados pela Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep) e o projeto será executado pelo Centro Brasileiro de Inovação em Tecnologias da Informação e da Comunicação (CPQD), em Campinas (SP). Uma das frentes do projeto é estimular a expansão de mini data centers em diferentes regiões do Brasil. “O objetivo é desenvolver e disponibilizar uma plataforma nacional segura e sustentável para setores como saúde, defesa, segurança pública, educação e telecomunicações, apoiando, assim, a transformação digital de setores estratégicos”, explica a superintendente da Área de Saúde e Transformação Digital da Finep, Joana Meirelles. Para o diretor de Tecnologia e Inovação do CPQD, Gustavo Correa Lima, a distribuição de mini data centers pelo país também representa um avanço na aproximação da infraestrutura digital dos usuários. “Além de tornar mais rápidos o processamento e o acesso às informações, essa arquitetura permite maior controle sobre o dado que está na borda”, destaca. Além de ampliar a capacidade de processamento de dados, o Prisma busca reduzir o impacto ambiental dos data centers, estruturas que demandam grandes quantidades de energia elétrica para funcionar e manter seus sistemas de refrigeração. Entre os resultados esperados estão a redução do consumo energético e da pegada de carbono, o aumento da resiliência contra falhas no fornecimento de energia e a proteção contra ataques cibernéticos.  A plataforma também contemplará soluções de armazenamento de energia elétrica para garantir maior autonomia e continuidade dos serviços em situações de instabilidade no abastecimento. A proposta prevê, ainda, o fortalecimento da governança nacional de informações críticas, seguindo padrões internacionais de segurança e as diretrizes da LGPD. O prazo de execução é de 36 meses, a partir da celebração do convênio de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação entre a Finep e o CPQD.

Hyderabad-based energy storage company TREX Energy has begun lithium battery manufacturing at E-City in Maheshwaram, using an automatic module assembly line that produces 12 parts per minute. The plant will make 52S battery packs for 261 kWh and 5 MWh storage systems, supporting a product range that runs from 5 kWh home units to 5 MWh utility-scale BESS. The company has also received four acres of land from the Madhya Pradesh Government for a Phase 2 unit, though the plant’s capacity and timeline are yet to be confirmed. TREX Energy, an Indian energy storage company, has opened its lithium battery manufacturing facility at E-City, Raviryal, in Maheshwaram, Hyderabad. The plant was commissioned in late September, and the company formally announced its opening this week. It has a 12 PPM automatic module assembly line built to produce 52S battery packs, which are used in 261 kWh and 5 MWh energy storage systems. The plant comes at a time when India is adding renewable energy capacity quickly, and industries, utilities and households need more storage as a result. Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and other energy storage system (ESS) products help manage swings in power supply, handle peak loads and provide backup power. According to the India Energy Storage Alliance (IESA), India added 7.9 GWh of BESS capacity in the first half of 2026, taking its operational capacity to 8.5 GWh. TREX Energy said the Hyderabad unit will serve this demand through local manufacturing. It plans to build products suited to Indian operating conditions, reduce dependence on imports and shorten delivery times. Bharat S. Chhittarka, Director, TREX Energy, said the company was focused on lowering financing costs so that BESS becomes more affordable and reliable for the Indian market. He added that energy must be available when it is needed, and BESS was a key solution for this. The assembly line makes battery modules at a rate of 12 parts per minute. The company said automation will help keep production consistent, improve efficiency and maintain quality control as demand grows. Roshan Shaik, Technical Director, TREX Energy, said the line was a significant step forward for the company’s manufacturing capabilities. He said it allows the company to produce battery modules efficiently and consistently for BESS solutions ranging from 5 kWh to 5 MWh, and strengthens its ability to meet India’s rising storage demand with scalable and reliable products. The portfolio includes C&I BESS for factories, offices and commercial facilities looking to manage energy use, ensure backup power and improve operational resilience. It also covers utility-scale BESS for grid applications and large renewable energy projects, residential energy storage systems, home inverter batteries, and battery packs and ESS configurations, including the 52S packs for 261 kWh and 5 MWh systems. Earlier this year, the company launched its REX BESS, a liquid-cooled 125 kW/261 kWh cabinet system for commercial and industrial users. A few months later, IESA named it the C&I Company of the Year. For its next phase, TREX Energy has been allotted four acres of land by the Madhya Pradesh Government for a proposed Phase 2 facility. The expansion is expected to enlarge its manufacturing footprint and help it serve customers in more markets across India. Details of the facility’s capacity, development timeline and commissioning are yet to be confirmed. The company said it will continue to invest in manufacturing, technology and local talent as it expands. TREX Energy, which carries the tagline “We Store Electrons”, has registered offices in Hyderabad, Telangana, and Pune, Maharashtra. The new plant adds to a growing cluster of battery units around Maheshwaram, where Cygni Energy opened a 4.8 GWh BESS facility last year. India’s cell manufacturing is still at an early stage, so most local assembly units continue to depend on imported cells. Demand, however, is expected to keep climbing, with the Central Electricity Authority estimating a need for 236 GWh of BESS capacity by 2031-32. How quickly TREX firms up the capacity and timeline for its Madhya Pradesh unit will show how seriously it plans to compete for that demand. Source PTI 9th Nov, 2026 8th Nov, 2026 7th Nov, 2026

artigo.texto: QUINCY, Wash. — In the national debate over the rapid expansion of data centers, Microsoft has pointed to Quincy, Washington, as an example of how the industry can benefit a community. However, the utility serving the city has restricted more development until more electricity can be brought to the community. Twenty years after Microsoft opened its first data center in the small Grant County city, seven other companies have followed. The growth has brought significant investment and tax revenue to a community of roughly 8,200 people. Locals point to new schools, a fire station, a hospital and other improvements as evidence of the transformation. “Anybody who comes to town who hasn’t been here in years, I’m like, ‘Oh, you need to take a drive because things are different,’” said Tina Stetner, owner of Quincy Hardware & Lumber. Stentner has watched farmland give way to data centers and housing, but she says it’s giving the next generation opportunities she did not have growing up. “I think it’s fun and exciting,” she said. “A lot more opportunities for our kids as they grow up.” The Quincy School District has also benefited from the enormous property values associated with the data centers. District officials say that tax base helped pay for 54% of its school construction projects while reducing the property tax rate associated with those projects from $1.94 to 84 cents per $1,000 of assessed value. “Without the data centers, it would be really difficult for this community to carry that tax burden,” Dr. Nik Bergman said, the district’s superintendent. Microsoft says 700 people will work at its local data centers by the end of this year, along with another 200 security employees. Microsoft also points to one electrical contractor it works with that has grown from about 50 employees to 550. “There’s been a lot of good financially for the city of Quincy,” said homeowner Jaque Rasmussen, who previously taught in the local school district and taught in the high school paid for by the increase in property taxes. Lately though, Stetner has noticed a slowdown. “The construction has kind of settled a little bit, or quite a bit,” Stentner said. The industry’s continued expansion is creating new challenges. The large amount of electricity required by data centers is putting pressure on the system that delivers power to Quincy. Grant County PUD has placed limits on additional data-center load growth because of concerns about outages and grid instability. “Load-growth limits are not unique to Grant County. Utilities across the United States are grappling with the same concerns as power-intensive artificial intelligence services housed in data centers are placing increased pressure on power systems that are close to capacity,” the utility said on its website. The restrictions can be eased as additional electrical infrastructure comes online. Grant PUD has a series of capacity expansions planned to meet growing demand. The first would bring power from the Wanapum Damn to Quincy through a 32-mile transmission line. The planned line would cross nearly 40 private properties, requiring easements along portions of farms and homes. Some of the transmission structures would stand roughly 135 feet tall, triple the heigh of the distribution poles currently in front of homes. Grant PUD is using eminent domain proceedings to acquire property rights needed to construct the transmission line. Alan Rasmussen said some of the tallest structures would sit along the edge of his property. Some of the affected families have owned their land for decades. “It’s kind of sacred ground to us because our parents sacrificed, worked so hard, almost lost it back to the bank a few times,” property owner Lisa Marcussen said. Marcussen says the line will reduce her farming income. She uses circular irrigation and the placement of the pole will cut the usable acreage of her property. “The burden of growth should not be on the back of the private property owner when we are not paid fair, equitable, and annual income from these lines that these data centers and some of these companies are going to be making millions of dollars a day,” Marcussen said. Ten property owners have fought the condemnation proceedings, though Marcusen says there is a petition with 145 signatures opposed to the plan. Their dispute goes beyond losing the use of portions of their property. The landowners question why Grant PUD selected this particular route when multiple alternatives were considered. Plans from the PUD showed four other routes, all of them cheaper and crossing fewer private properties. The selected project’s estimated cost has climbed to roughly $86 million, more than double its original estimate. “We’ve made payments on our place for 35 years, and then for somebody just to take that land and say, ‘We want it now,’” Rasmussen said. Rasmussen says the valuation the PUD used was significantly lower than what realtors and licensed appraisers put on the property. She ran, unsuccessfully, as a write-in candidate for Grant PUD to change an internal policy that the PUD will pay 25% of market value for residential property and 40% for farm property. Alan and Jaque Rasmussen said they were offered slightly more than $7,000. “It was insulting,” Jaque Rasmussen said. Grant PUD says it considered public feedback when selecting the route, including 10 comments supporting the chosen route. “Despite the higher initial estimated capital construction costs of 4B relative to alternative Routes 1, 2 and 3, the expectation was that those higher costs would be more than offset by the benefits of reduced regulatory and permitting complexity, and the shorter timeline required to complete the line, which accelerates the flow of revenue from customers served by the line,” the PUD said on a page about the route. artigo.texto: MEMPHIS, Tenn. - A clerical error on Tuesday's Memphis City Council agenda briefly created confusion over the future of several major data center ordinances, making it appear the proposals were headed for a vote when they were not. The mistake caught even some council members off guard and raised questions about measures that would help shape where future data centers can be built in Memphis and what requirements those developments would face. According to Councilman J.B. Smiley, those ordinances were not up for action Tuesday because the council previously combined two third-reading measures into a single ordinance that passed two weeks ago. The focus now shifts to developing the zoning guidelines that will govern future data center projects. “I think what's of particular interest to the community is whether or not there will be a moratorium,” Smiley told FOX13. “There will be a 135-day pause or moratorium. That gives the administration time to put forth zoning rules that the council can then adopt or amend.” The proposed pause would give city leaders time to craft zoning regulations before additional data center development moves forward. For some residents, the ongoing debate is less about timing and more about ensuring Memphis establishes the right guardrails before approving additional projects. “I am for delaying data centers' foothold in Memphis for as long as possible,” said Midtown resident Lucy Chambliss. “It's a little tricky with these ordinances because we don't actually have anything in place stopping them right now.” While broader questions about data center development remain unresolved, council members did take action on one related measure Tuesday. The council approved Ordinance 5989 on second reading. The proposal would create a nonprofit community benefit agency responsible for receiving, managing, and distributing funding tied to community benefit agreements associated with data center projects. Supporters said the agency would provide transparency and accountability by ensuring those dollars are properly tracked and directed to community needs. That issue is particularly important for residents who live near existing or proposed data center sites. “I know some friends personally that are affected by the data center and that live nearby it, and I just want to see that their lives improved,” Memphis resident Rigo Able said. The ordinance must still clear additional readings before becoming law. Meanwhile, debate over data center development in Memphis is far from over. City leaders continue working on potential zoning changes and development standards that could determine how, and where, future data center projects are built across the city. artigo.texto: Política Governo de MT vai a COP 31 com missão de ampliar credibilidade da comercialização de créditos de carbono Liderada pelo governador Otaviano Pivetta, a comitiva de Mato Grosso deve cumprir agenda de reuniões com investidores da Coalizão Life O Governo de Mato Grosso participa da 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas, a COP 31, que acontece de 9 a 20 de novembro, na Turquia, com a missão de ampliar, junto a investidores internacionais, a confiança dos créditos de carbono provenientes da redução de desmatamento no estado. Liderada pelo governador Otaviano Pivetta, a comitiva de Mato Grosso deve cumprir agenda de reuniões com investidores da Coalizão Life, que reúne países do Reino Unido e Noruega, que detém hoje o maior volume de recursos para aquisição de redução de carbono. Segundo a secretária de Estado de Meio Ambiente, Mauren Lazzaretti, o governo do estado busca a certificação internacional de créditos de carbono gerados nos últimos anos. A intenção é demonstrar aos investidores a credibilidade desses créditos, transformando a comercialização em mais conservação ambiental e inclusão social. Durante o evento, a força-tarefa dos governadores do Consórcio da Amazônia legal deve apresentar as medidas adotadas pelos estados para construção do modelo de Redução de Emissões por Desmatamento e Degradação Florestal (REDD+Jurisdicional). Em Mato Grosso, esse processo está na reta final. O governador Otaviano Pivetta enviou à Assembleia Legislativa projeto de lei que autoriza a criação da Companhia Mato-grossense de Ativos Ambientais S.A. (CMAA), uma sociedade de economia mista destinada a estruturar, gerir e comercializar créditos de carbono, créditos de biodiversidade e outros ativos ambientais gerados no território do Estado. A nova empresa busca dar suporte institucional ao compromisso assumido por Mato Grosso de zerar as emissões líquidas de carbono até 2035, além de ampliar a capacidade do Estado de captar investimentos nacionais e internacionais ligados à economia de baixo carbono. Durante a COP 31, a comitiva de Mato Grosso participa ainda de debates sobre riscos climáticos , combate a incêndios florestais, economia florestal, estratégias de enfrentamento aos crimes ambientais, entre outros assuntos. O grupo permanecerá na Turquia até o dia 18.

artigo.texto: California Tribal Fire Station Adds Vanadium Flow Battery to Solar Microgrid A solar-powered microgrid at the Soboba Fire Station near San Jacinto, California, now includes a vanadium flow battery system designed to provide at least 10 hours of backup power during grid outages and Public Safety Power Shutoff events. The system serves the Soboba Band of Luiseño Indians' fire station and emergency response facilities, helping maintain operations when utility power is unavailable. The installation also is expected to help reduce the facility's energy costs. Representatives of the Soboba Band, GRID Alternatives and battery manufacturer Invinity marked the project's completion with a ceremonial handover last week. The microgrid is particularly important for the Soboba reservation, which is located in a Tier 3 Extreme High Fire Threat Zone. The area has experienced repeated grid outages, some lasting more than 24 hours. During major incidents, the fire station serves as an emergency response facility, incident command center and community resource. The battery uses vanadium flow technology, which stores energy in liquid electrolyte tanks. Unlike lithium-ion batteries, vanadium flow batteries use a non-flammable electrolyte and do not have the same potential for thermal runaway, according to Invinity. The project was developed by GRID Alternatives with funding support from the California Energy Commission as part of the state's efforts to demonstrate long-duration energy storage technologies that do not rely on lithium-ion chemistry. The installation provides the Tribe with an additional source of backup power for critical emergency services while demonstrating how solar generation and long-duration storage can support energy resilience at community facilities.

artigo.texto: PRESCOTT, AZ – Watters Garden Center, Prescott's premier destination for horticulture and mountain gardening expertise, proudly announces a major leap forward in sustainable business practices: the installation of a comprehensive solar energy system complete with Tesla battery backup. This state-of-the-art infrastructure upgrade strengthens the family-owned garden center's commitment to environmental stewardship, builds vital power independence, and gives back to the local APS power grid. Since Harold Watters opened the doors in 1962, the garden center has pioneered solutions for Northern Arizona's unique needs. As detailed in the "Watters Garden Center Culture," the company is built on four core cultures: Honesty, Fun, Success, and Beauty, alongside a deeply rooted philosophy of treating the community like family. Adding renewable energy aligns perfectly with these values, pushing their legacy of Eco-friendly solutions into the next generation. "My father taught the importance of our environment, shopping small and keeping it local,” says Lisa Watters-Lain, owner of Watters Garden Center. "The garden center has always been green, but we look for ways to be even better stewards of what we've been given. This is yet one more step in the right direction." Power Independence and Grid Support Integrating Tesla battery technology gives Watters Garden Center crucial power independence. In extreme mountain weather or unexpected grid outages, the batteries ensure the center's climate-controlled greenhouses, sophisticated digital point-of-sale systems, and vital irrigation lines remain fully operational. This resilience allows Watters to continue serving the Prescott community without interruption, protecting its living inventory and ensuring customers always have access to the plants and expertise they rely on. This expansive solar array is designed to generate more power than the garden center consumes during peak daylight hours. This excess clean energy is fed directly back into the APS power grid. By reducing strain on local utility infrastructure, Watters Garden Center helps stabilize the grid and provide clean, renewable energy to neighbors throughout Yavapai County. A Legacy of Community & Environmental Care This solar initiative is the latest in Watters' long history of sustainable practices. In 2015, the center became the first retailer in Prescott to transition to 100% post-consumer recycled color-packs for their plants. They have consistently championed organic, locally formulated soil products, drought-resistant native plants, and biodegradable options that thrive in the local microclimate. As a third-generation business currently guided by Ken, McKenzie and Lisa Watters-Lain, Watters views this investment not just as an operational upgrade, but as a community service. The center is renowned for giving back, donating significantly to local non-profits like Rotary International and Big Brothers Big Sisters. As founder Harold Watters famously stated, "We are not in business for profit alone, but to share God's love and beauty with the community." By embracing solar energy and Tesla battery storage, Watters Garden Center ensures this legacy of beauty, sustainability, and community support will continue to thrive for decades. About Watters Garden Center: Founded in 1962, Watters Garden Center is a multigenerational family business dedicated to providing the Prescott area with the highest-quality garden advice and expert plants that inspire being outdoors.

artigo.texto: What to know: - Moratorium on new data centers: Michigan governor-elect Jocelyn Benson is proposing a pause on new data center construction until the state establishes regulations to protect communities and natural resources. - Community input required: Developers would have to hold public hearings before projects move forward, giving residents an opportunity to ask questions and voice concerns. - More transparency: Companies would be required to disclose information about proposed projects to prevent behind-the-scenes agreements that exclude residents. - Protecting water and land: Developers would have to demonstrate before construction that their projects would not harm Michigan’s natural resources. Recommended Videos Michigan governor-elect Jocelyn Benson is proposing a moratorium on new data center construction in the state until regulations require developers to meet specific standards for community transparency, environmental protections, and energy costs. Under the proposal, Michigan would not allow new data centers until rules require companies to negotiate openly with communities, protect natural resources, and cover the costs of their energy use. Benson’s plan calls for public hearings before projects move forward, allowing residents to ask questions and share concerns about proposed developments. It would also require transparency and disclosure reporting to prevent agreements between developers and government officials from excluding community members from the process. Another part of the proposal would require data center developers to demonstrate before construction that their projects would not negatively affect natural resources, including water and land. Benson also wants data centers to pay for the additional electricity they use rather than passing those costs on to residential and other consumers. Her proposal would prohibit data centers from receiving tax breaks. The plan also calls for union contracts to ensure data center projects create well-paying jobs for Michigan workers. Benson said companies that violate the proposed requirements would not be allowed to operate in Michigan. The proposal comes as data center development has become a growing concern for communities worried about energy demand, water consumption, environmental impacts, and the potential costs of large-scale facilities. Benson’s plan would establish requirements for how future data center projects are reviewed and approved, with an emphasis on community involvement and corporate accountability. During her one-on-one sit-down with Local 4 anchor Ty Steele, Benson said she supported a moratorium on new data centers until the state establishes safeguards to protect water and energy resources. Benson also said that companies should be required to pay for the energy they use and address noise pollution concerns. She proposed requiring community benefits agreements and creating an online portal where residents could track proposed and existing data center projects and provide input. Benson said the goal was to ensure communities benefit from development rather than simply absorbing its costs. More: Jocelyn Benson’s campaign promises as Michigan governor
