artigo.texto: Data center é o espaço físico que armazena toda a estrutura de computação necessária para o processamento, armazenamento e transmissão segura de dados digitais. Eles são importantes para a manutenção de serviços de internet e de ferramentas como a inteligência artificial, o que explica o rápido crescimento no número de data centers em todo o mundo. Dentro de um data center, é possível encontrar racks com elementos como switches, firewalls e servidores, bem como bancos de baterias, painéis elétricos e sistemas de refrigeração. Atualmente mais de 180 data centers estão em atividade no Brasil. Devido ao crescente uso da inteligência artificial, o país busca dar continuidade ao seu processo de desenvolvimento tecnológico por meio da atração de novos data centers. Para isso, criou uma medida conhecida como Redata, que foca na oferta de incentivos fiscais com contrapartidas. Contudo, há muitas críticas com relação a essa política por conta dos impactos ambientais dos data centers. Leia também: Por que tem se falado em uma bolha econômica em torno da IA? Data center é o espaço físico onde ficam as máquinas e equipamentos de computação que realizam o armazenamento, o processamento e a transmissão segura de dados digitais. São importantes porque mantêm o funcionamento dos serviços de internet e as ferramentas de inteligência artificial, cuja demanda cresceu de forma acelerada nos últimos anos. A capacidade instalada de data centers cresceu cinco vezes entre 2005 e 2025. O atual número de data centers no mundo passa de 13 mil, maioria dos quais está nos EUA. Dentro de um data center tem, entre outros: racks, onde ficam itens como painéis de conexão, servidores, firewalls e switches; banco de baterias e painéis de energia elétrica; sistemas de ventilação e de refrigeração; equipamentos para o controle de umidade. Três dos principais tipos de data centers são: data centers corporativos, que ficam no interior das próprias empresas; data centers de colocação, que são espaços compartilhados por várias companhias; data centers hiperescala, que são espaços de grande dimensão construídos exclusivamente para as operações de uma única empresa. A rápida difusão dos data centers tem gerado debates e críticas sobre sustentabilidade desse modelo de estabelecimento por conta do elevado consumo de energia e de água. Os data centers também geram poluição sonora e produzem ilhas de calor por conta da elevação da temperatura média do ar, causando alterações no microclima. O Brasil tem mais de 180 data centers, mas aprovou uma medida que promete isenções fiscais para a instalação de novas unidades no território nacional. Data center é um espaço físico onde ficam instaladas todas as máquinas e os equipamentos de computação responsáveis pelo armazenamento, processamento e transmissão segura de dados digitais de serviços em nuvem e de ferramentas como a inteligência artificial (IA). Em função da rápida modernização dos sistemas de propagação de informações e de comunicação que aconteceu nas últimas décadas, cresceu, na mesma proporção, a demanda por softwares e serviços de armazenamento em nuvem. Não obstante essas sejam redes que existem e se multiplicam no ciberespaço, elas demandam um outro tipo de rede, dessa vez, física, para se manter. Essa rede física é mantida em data centers. Os data centers são importantes porque eles mantêm o funcionamento dos serviços de internet que nós utilizamos todos os dias. Uma boa parte do nosso sistema moderno de comunicação depende diretamente de aplicações que são mantidas e aperfeiçoadas por meio desse tipo de infraestrutura. Segundo informações da Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA, em inglês) trazidas pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE)|1|, o número de usuários da internet aumentou em 78% somente entre 2015 e 2022, quando o tráfego global se expandiu aproximadamente seis vezes. Dentro do atual período técnico em que estamos inseridos, empresas, sistemas financeiros e mesmo governos desenvolveram uma alta dependência de ferramentas de TI para a sua gestão. Então, além de serem parte indissociável desse ecossistema de gerenciamento, os data centers são fundamentais para a garantia da eficácia e, sobretudo, da segurança no processamento e armazenamento de informações que, na maioria das vezes, são sensíveis e/ou confidenciais. Esses espaços físicos também são necessários para o funcionamento da inteligência artificial. As ferramentas de IA, entretanto, são bastante complexas e resultam em um trabalho mais intenso do que aquele desempenhado pelas máquinas que compõem os data centers convencionais. Dada a difusão acelerada das ferramentas de IA, que tem sido empregada tanto para atividades corriqueiras quanto para o gerenciamento de empresas e em setores estratégicos, como o energético, os data centers têm se multiplicado em um ritmo semelhante. Para evidenciar a importância dos data centers dentro do presente contexto tecnológico e informacional, basta analisarmos os dados que mostram a evolução da capacidade energética instalada nos data centers. No ano de 2005, essa capacidade ficava em torno de 20 GW, enquanto 20 anos mais tarde, em 2025, ela cresceu para 114,3 GW, segundo dados da IEA|2|. Essa capacidade corresponde a cerca de 13 mil data centers, a maioria dos quais fica nos Estados Unidos (5 mil), na Índia (348) e no Canadá (299)|3|. As seguintes estruturas e equipamentos são encontrados dentro de um data center: Racks, que é onde ficam todos os equipamentos utilizados para o processamento e armazenamento de dados, como patch panels (painel de conexões), switches, acesso remoto, firewalls, servidores, roteadores, fonte de alimentação de energia (UPS ou nobreak), unidades de distribuição de energia e sistemas de ventilação e refrigeração. Sistemas de ventilação e de refrigeração, como as unidades de ar-condicionado de precisão, que são próprias para data centers. artigo.texto: Elecom will launch a new cable-integrated 10,000mAh power bank in mid-November, featuring a semi-solid-state lithium-ion battery. It boasts high safety, a long lifespan, and wide temperature resistance for extreme cold and intense heat. The price is 7,480 yen. It will be available in three colors: Black, Shiro-chan (White x Black), and White. With a capacity of 10,000mAh, it features a lightweight design, weighing approximately 190g. A key feature is its integrated USB Type-C cable, allowing users to simply take it out of their bag and start charging immediately. Semi-solid-state lithium-ion batteries suppress electrolyte leakage by gelling the electrolyte, thereby enhancing chemical stability. Compared to the approximately 500 charge/discharge cycles of products using conventional lithium-ion batteries, this new battery boasts a cycle life of approximately 2,000 times, achieving about four times the lifespan of conventional models. Furthermore, it supports an operating temperature range of -15°C to 45°C during power supply, making it easy to use in cold regions or outdoors during summer. It also includes a "Health Monitor" that indicates battery status via LEDs, "Thermal Protection" for monitoring and controlling temperature, and multiple other protection functions. For charging, in addition to the integrated USB Type-C cable, it features one USB Type-C port and one USB-A port, allowing up to three devices to be charged simultaneously. It supports USB Power Delivery and PPS, supplying optimal power according to the connected device, thus enabling efficient charging of smartphones and tablets. When used alone, it supports a maximum output of 22.5W, while for multiple devices simultaneously, it distributes a total maximum of 21W. Furthermore, it supports pass-through charging, low-current mode, and "Omakase Charging" (auto-optimized charging), and is compatible with charging the Nintendo Switch 2, Nintendo Switch, and Nintendo Switch Lite.

artigo.texto: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 11. Kazakhstan's Kurultai has approved, in the first reading, amendments aimed at developing alternative energy sources and strengthening the resilience of the country's power system, the Kurultai press service announced. The bill was presented by Minister of Energy Yerlan Akkenzhenov and was drafted in line with President Kassym Jomart Tokayev's Nation Address on October 28 on strengthening the stability of the energy system. The proposed amendments introduce new mechanisms for developing the energy sector, aimed at improving power system reliability, attracting investment and expanding the use of alternative energy sources. One of the key provisions is the introduction of competitive auctions to select electricity storage system projects. To make these projects more attractive to investors, the bill proposes long-term payments for maintaining available capacity for up to 15 years. "Currently, the power system's need for flexible capacity is estimated at approximately 3 GW: around 2 GW is planned to be provided through renewable energy projects, while additional mechanisms are being developed to attract investment for the remaining 1 GW. To this end, competitive auctions for selecting energy storage system projects are proposed," Akkenzhenov said. The bill also proposes improving the mechanism for selling electricity under bilateral contracts. Power facilities that have supplied electricity under such contracts for at least 36 months will be eligible to switch to selling electricity to the Single Purchaser. This measure is expected to reduce the risk of losing sales outlets and improve the sustainability of investment projects. Another section of the amendments focuses on more efficient use of energy resources in heating and industry. In particular, the proposals envisage wider use of secondary energy resources, low-grade and waste heat, heat pumps, biomass, biogas and hydrogen. The bill also establishes a legal framework for developing hydrogen technologies, using energy generated by industrial processes and recovering energy through waste utilization. Overall, the proposed amendments are expected to introduce competitive mechanisms for developing energy storage systems, improve the investment appeal of projects, reduce electricity sales risks under bilateral contracts, and promote the wider use of modern energy technologies.

artigo.texto: CATL Builds an Ecosystem Around the Battery: Transit Deals, European Storage and an Aviation Niche Published on 11/11/2026 at 01:31 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL is pushing past the simple sale of battery cells. In a burst of announcements spanning public transport, home energy storage and electric aviation, the Chinese battery giant has sketched out a strategy in which the battery becomes the starting point for a wider set of services — swapping, servicing, recycling and grid interaction — rather than the end product itself. The most concrete piece of that puzzle arrived in the form of strategic cooperation agreements with four Chinese transit operators: Benxi Passenger Transport Group, Changzhou Transit Group, Guiyang Public Transport Group and Lanzhou Public Transport Group. According to media reports, the arrangements cover battery supply and exchange, customer service, citywide battery-swap networks, recycling, and vehicle-to-grid interaction. The breadth is the point. Rather than a one-off delivery notice, the deals tie a battery's deployment to its upkeep and its eventual disposal — a linked chain that only pays off if CATL can actually coordinate the various tasks in day-to-day operations. From the vehicle to the grid The larger idea running through the transit pacts is the coupling of mobility with energy supply. A swap network touches fleet operations; vehicle-to-grid interaction pulls the power system into the frame. That logic gains weight if the operators adopt these building blocks together and extract practical value from them. For investors, the question shifts accordingly: how much value can CATL create around a battery once it has been delivered? The answer hinges on the role the company genuinely takes on in swapping, servicing and recycling. The tighter those tasks can be woven together, the more convincing the strategic case for the package. The citywide approach matters in particular because it places the individual battery in a broader operational context. The test, ultimately, is execution at each transit operator. A related thread runs through CATL's home-storage ambitions. On 4 November, CATL, Ampace and Octopus Energy signed a memorandum of understanding to explore smart storage solutions for Europe, with the UK, France and Spain as the initial focus. Octopus Energy describes the plan as linking its software platform and electricity tariffs with the battery technology and hardware from CATL and Ampace. Here too the approach reaches beyond a single technical product: the collaboration would carry strategic weight for CATL if hardware, controls and household tariff design mesh sensibly. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? Storage at scale and a foothold in aviation The same theme recurs at utility scale. On 29 October, CATL gave the TENER+ energy storage system its global debut at All Energy Australia, signing memoranda with Hitachi Energy, EPEC Group and UNSW Sydney to implement large battery storage projects and their grid connections. Grid integration is thus a recurring concern across very different applications — a sign of a coherent strategic direction, provided CATL can successfully interlock its battery technology with its partners' contributions. Aviation is the newest frontier. On 3 November, CATL agreed to work with Blue Vector Intelligent Technology on a custom-built aviation battery for the latter's SKYLA V30 electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft. Blue Vector selected CATL as the exclusive battery partner for the model, so the arrangement covers both development of the specially adapted battery and CATL's sole-supplier role for that aircraft's battery needs. Buyback progress Alongside the deal flow, CATL disclosed the state of its share repurchase programme on 3 November. As of 31 October, the company had bought back a total of 19.6 million A-shares at a cost of RMB 5.36 billion, according to its own figures. CATL at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. What unites the transit agreements, the European storage memorandum and the Australian grid projects is the embedding of the battery in its surroundings — software and tariffs in the home, swapping, service and grid links in transport. That points to a plausible direction for CATL, so long as partners combine their respective contributions into offerings that work in practice. The yardstick for the stock is delivery on those connections: supply, operation and recycling coming together, and the agreed cooperation holding up in the everyday business of each partner. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no SoftBank registra prejuízo de US$ 7 bilhões após perdas com data centers nos EUA e queda das ações da Intel Publicado 10/11/2026 • 11:24 | Atualizado há 20 horas Nos bastidores da Nvidia: o primeiro dia de Jensen Huang de volta ao escritório após a revelação do caso extraconjugal Senador acusa Trump de defender o CEO da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, em detrimento da segurança nacional Caso envolvendo Jensen Huang amplia pressão sobre negócios da Nvidia na China Nvidia contrata escritório de advocacia Wachtell Lipton para liderar a investigação do caso Jensen Huang Laços da Nvidia com Trump entram na mira após relatos de que Jensen Huang foi alvo da inteligência chinesa KEY POINTS Foto: Divulgação O SoftBank registrou prejuízo líquido de 1,12 trilhão de ienes (US$ 7 bilhões) no segundo trimestre do ano fiscal, divulgado nesta terça-feira (10). O resultado foi pressionado por perdas relacionadas à aquisição de equipamentos para data centers de inteligência artificial (IA) nos Estados Unidos e pela desvalorização das ações da Intel. O conglomerado japonês também registrou uma perda de 597,2 bilhões de ienes (US$ 3,7 bilhões) nos seis meses encerrados em 30 de setembro, devido a mudanças nos planos de aquisição de equipamentos de geração de energia para projetos de data centers de IA nos EUA. O SoftBank afirmou que realizou investimentos antecipados para garantir o fornecimento de equipamentos de geração de energia para seus projetos de data centers de IA nos Estados Unidos, diante de preocupações com possíveis escassez e longos prazos de aquisição. Leia também: Por que a China barrou o negócio de US$ 5,4 bilhões do SoftBank? A disponibilidade de energia está se tornando uma das principais limitações para a expansão dos data centers de IA, à medida que as redes elétricas ficam sobrecarregadas com pedidos de grandes consumidores de energia, como essas instalações. Os pagamentos acumulados por equipamentos de geração de energia destinados aos projetos de data centers de IA nos EUA, incluindo o PORTS-Pike Technology Campus, no condado de Pike, em Ohio, totalizavam US$ 9,48 bilhões no fim de setembro. “Fizemos investimentos-ponte antecipadamente para garantir equipamentos de geração de energia, diante da expectativa de escassez”, afirmou um executivo do SoftBank durante a teleconferência de resultados da companhia. Veja o desempenho do SoftBank no segundo trimestre do ano fiscal: A receita avançou 13,3% no semestre encerrado em 30 de setembro, impulsionada pelo crescimento dos negócios de telecomunicações e computação em inteligência artificial. A empresa informou que o segmento SoftBank registrou aumento nas vendas em todas as suas operações, enquanto a receita da divisão de computação em IA também cresceu. O segmento Vision Fund passou a registrar prejuízo de 81,58 bilhões de ienes no segundo trimestre do ano fiscal, ante lucro de 2,38 trilhões de ienes no mesmo período do ano anterior. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC O Vision Fund 1 registrou perda de US$ 20 milhões em investimentos no trimestre, apesar de um ganho de US$ 1,3 bilhão com a ByteDance. O resultado foi influenciado pela queda das ações de empresas de capital aberto que integram seu portfólio, incluindo Coupang e Grab. Os fundos Vision Funds registraram ganhos de investimento de 85,45 bilhões de ienes, uma queda acentuada em relação aos 2,81 trilhões de ienes do mesmo período do ano anterior. O Vision Fund 2 apresentou ganhos de investimento de 89,26 bilhões de ienes, enquanto o Vision Fund 1 registrou perdas de 3,86 bilhões de ienes em seus investimentos. Até o fim de setembro, o investimento acumulado do SoftBank na OpenAI somava US$ 54,6 bilhões. O valor justo da participação era de US$ 99,6 bilhões, com ganho acumulado de US$ 45 bilhões, segundo a companhia. O SoftBank afirmou que uma possível elevação da avaliação da OpenAI após uma nova rodada de financiamento ainda não havia sido incorporada aos resultados, pois dependia de um anúncio oficial. A nova avaliação poderá ser refletida no terceiro trimestre do ano fiscal, com potencial para elevar o valor líquido dos ativos da companhia e melhorar sua relação entre dívida e valor dos ativos (loan-to-value, ou LTV). “ O ChatGPT tem sido continuamente uma arma da OpenAI, especialmente para os consumidores”, afirmou o executivo do SoftBank durante a teleconferência de resultados, ao destacar o crescimento da base de usuários do chatbot. Leia também: SoftBank registra lucro acima do esperado após ganho de US$ 8,2 bilhões com Intel As ações do conglomerado japonês fecharam em alta de 13,9% nesta terça-feira. O avanço ocorreu em meio à valorização de empresas asiáticas de tecnologia, incluindo Samsung Electronics e SK Hynix, após uma recuperação das ações do setor em Wall Street na noite anterior. Em relação aos investimentos em infraestrutura de IA, o SoftBank destacou um contrato de arrendamento de 20 anos com a OpenAI para oito gigawatts de capacidade de tecnologia da informação (TI) em um projeto de data center em Ohio. Sobre as preocupações com o consumo de água no data center planejado no Texas, o SoftBank afirmou que está adotando medidas para reduzir o uso do recurso por meio de um sistema de circuito fechado com resfriamento a ar. A companhia também mencionou planos de contratar trabalhadores e adquirir insumos localmente. Antes da divulgação dos resultados, o SoftBank Group anunciou, na segunda-feira (9), planos com a Grab e a empresa malaia PETROS para investir, em conjunto, US$ 1,85 bilhão em capital inicial no desenvolvimento de infraestrutura de inteligência artificial na Malásia. artigo.texto: Data center é o espaço físico que armazena toda a estrutura de computação necessária para o processamento, armazenamento e transmissão segura de dados digitais. Eles são importantes para a manutenção de serviços de internet e de ferramentas como a inteligência artificial, o que explica o rápido crescimento no número de data centers em todo o mundo. Dentro de um data center, é possível encontrar racks com elementos como switches, firewalls e servidores, bem como bancos de baterias, painéis elétricos e sistemas de refrigeração. Atualmente mais de 180 data centers estão em atividade no Brasil. Devido ao crescente uso da inteligência artificial, o país busca dar continuidade ao seu processo de desenvolvimento tecnológico por meio da atração de novos data centers. Para isso, criou uma medida conhecida como Redata, que foca na oferta de incentivos fiscais com contrapartidas. Contudo, há muitas críticas com relação a essa política por conta dos impactos ambientais dos data centers. Leia também: Por que tem se falado em uma bolha econômica em torno da IA? Tópicos deste artigo Resumo sobre datas centers - Data center é o espaço físico onde ficam as máquinas e equipamentos de computação que realizam o armazenamento, o processamento e a transmissão segura de dados digitais. - São importantes porque mantêm o funcionamento dos serviços de internet e as ferramentas de inteligência artificial, cuja demanda cresceu de forma acelerada nos últimos anos. - A capacidade instalada de data centers cresceu cinco vezes entre 2005 e 2025. O atual número de data centers no mundo passa de 13 mil, maioria dos quais está nos EUA. - Dentro de um data center tem, entre outros: - racks, onde ficam itens como painéis de conexão, servidores, firewalls e switches; - banco de baterias e painéis de energia elétrica; - sistemas de ventilação e de refrigeração; Anuncie aqui - equipamentos para o controle de umidade. - Três dos principais tipos de data centers são: - data centers corporativos, que ficam no interior das próprias empresas; - data centers de colocação, que são espaços compartilhados por várias companhias; - data centers hiperescala, que são espaços de grande dimensão construídos exclusivamente para as operações de uma única empresa. - A rápida difusão dos data centers tem gerado debates e críticas sobre sustentabilidade desse modelo de estabelecimento por conta do elevado consumo de energia e de água. - Os data centers também geram poluição sonora e produzem ilhas de calor por conta da elevação da temperatura média do ar, causando alterações no microclima. - O Brasil tem mais de 180 data centers, mas aprovou uma medida que promete isenções fiscais para a instalação de novas unidades no território nacional. Anuncie aqui O que é um data center? Data center é um espaço físico onde ficam instaladas todas as máquinas e os equipamentos de computação responsáveis pelo armazenamento, processamento e transmissão segura de dados digitais de serviços em nuvem e de ferramentas como a inteligência artificial (IA). Em função da rápida modernização dos sistemas de propagação de informações e de comunicação que aconteceu nas últimas décadas, cresceu, na mesma proporção, a demanda por softwares e serviços de armazenamento em nuvem. Não obstante essas sejam redes que existem e se multiplicam no ciberespaço, elas demandam um outro tipo de rede, dessa vez, física, para se manter. Essa rede física é mantida em data centers. Por que data centers são importantes? Os data centers são importantes porque eles mantêm o funcionamento dos serviços de internet que nós utilizamos todos os dias. Uma boa parte do nosso sistema moderno de comunicação depende diretamente de aplicações que são mantidas e aperfeiçoadas por meio desse tipo de infraestrutura. Segundo informações da Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA, em inglês) trazidas pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE)|1|, o número de usuários da internet aumentou em 78% somente entre 2015 e 2022, quando o tráfego global se expandiu aproximadamente seis vezes. Dentro do atual período técnico em que estamos inseridos, empresas, sistemas financeiros e mesmo governos desenvolveram uma alta dependência de ferramentas de TI para a sua gestão. Então, além de serem parte indissociável desse ecossistema de gerenciamento, os data centers são fundamentais para a garantia da eficácia e, sobretudo, da segurança no processamento e armazenamento de informações que, na maioria das vezes, são sensíveis e/ou confidenciais. Esses espaços físicos também são necessários para o funcionamento da inteligência artificial. As ferramentas de IA, entretanto, são bastante complexas e resultam em um trabalho mais intenso do que aquele desempenhado pelas máquinas que compõem os data centers convencionais. Dada a difusão acelerada das ferramentas de IA, que tem sido empregada tanto para atividades corriqueiras quanto para o gerenciamento de empresas e em setores estratégicos, como o energético, os data centers têm se multiplicado em um ritmo semelhante. Para evidenciar a importância dos data centers dentro do presente contexto tecnológico e informacional, basta analisarmos os dados que mostram a evolução da capacidade energética instalada nos data centers. No ano de 2005, essa capacidade ficava em torno de 20 GW, enquanto 20 anos mais tarde, em 2025, ela cresceu para 114,3 GW, segundo dados da IEA|2|. Essa capacidade corresponde a cerca de 13 mil data centers, a maioria dos quais fica nos Estados Unidos (5 mil), na Índia (348) e no Canadá (299)|3|. O que tem dentro de um data center? As seguintes estruturas e equipamentos são encontrados dentro de um data center: - Racks, que é onde ficam todos os equipamentos utilizados para o processamento e armazenamento de dados, como patch panels (painel de conexões), switches, acesso remoto, firewalls, servidores, roteadores, fonte de alimentação de energia (UPS ou nobreak), unidades de distribuição de energia e sistemas de ventilação e refrigeração. artigo.texto: A transitioning Congress finds itself in a pickle on AI data centers Table of Contents As Congress returns to Washington this week, the massive power demands of the AI boom have forced a reckoning over data center infrastructure. The Senate is preparing for a pivotal procedural vote on legislation that would speed approvals for energy projects while requiring large data centers to shoulder more of the costs they impose on the power grid. The bipartisan bill would add much-needed regulations on data centers, but, as some politicians believe, may also encourage more data center construction. Silicon Valley vs. a changed D.C. In the sweeping and history-making midterm elections last week, voters didn't just elect a new generation of Democratic lawmakers. They also sent a pretty unmistakable message to Big Tech, particularly the artificial intelligence industry: Enough with the data centers already. Or, more bluntly, "get out of town." Across the country, local communities are pushing to stop, restrict, or impose conditions on data center development. The election results reinforced that message, making clear that the AI gold rush is facing growing resistance. For the last two years, Silicon Valley has busied itself building more, building bigger and doing it ASAP. If a tech giant wanted to drop a warehouse-sized data center into a community, local governments often offered tax breaks and other incentives, then told residents it was harmless and would mean more jobs. Voters increasingly aren't buying it. Democrats now find themselves in a pickle. Many campaigned on restricting data center development, responding to voters concerned about electricity costs, water consumption, and the impact these enormous facilities have on their communities. Now, the aforementioned pending legislation forces a stark about-face — since, as Reuters reports, some Democrats believe provisions in the proposed bill could encourage the creation of more data centers. If that comes to pass, incoming lawmakers would need to explain why those campaign promises to halt data center construction no longer apply. Can data centers be built responsibly? There's a risk, too, in the new Democratic Congress pushing too forcefully for restrictions on AI, specifically on data centers. My well-seasoned brain believes AI companies will respond to restrictions not simply by complaining about the cost of doing business, but by slowing down the rollout of new technology. Some of that slowdown will be unavoidable. Without enough data centers, electricity, and computing capacity, companies cannot expand indefinitely. But some of it could be strategic. I suspect the message from Silicon Valley will be slightly PR-ish: If you don't want us building data centers, don't expect your ChatGPT, Claude, or Siri to keep getting faster, smarter, and more capable. That "hurry up and now" diagnosis for your sore knee might take a little longer. Picture AI as something other than a magical cloud floating above our heads. Every time you ask an AI assistant to write an email, generate an image, or summarize a document, powerful chips in actual buildings are cranking away, consuming tremendous amounts of electricity and water and pressuring local power grids. And all that power costs mega cash. Utility rates, grid upgrades, and higher electricity bills have turned an abstract technology debate into something much more personal. I don't blame communities for pushing back. Why should residents subsidize a multibillion-dollar technology company's expansion while wondering whether their electric bills will keep climbing? They're already fed up with rising gas and grocery prices and the cost of a new home. But there's another side to this costly coin that Democrats shouldn't ignore. Data centers can bring economic benefits, too, provided technology companies invest in the communities that host them. While data centers rarely employ local, low-skill workers directly, AI companies can bridge this gap by funding local infrastructure projects that immediately put the existing workforce to work. Furthermore, the resulting influx of permanent, high-salaried technicians injects new tax revenue into the community, triggering a powerful economic ripple effect for local restaurants and shops. Communities shouldn't have to choose between protecting residents and benefiting from technological investment. Companies that want to build in these towns should contribute meaningfully to their economic well-being. The risks of slowing down the AI gold rush Government intervention, even when well-intentioned, can also produce unintended consequences that ultimately hurt consumers. Just look at Europe. In 2024, Apple said it would hold back Apple Intelligence and other new features from EU customers, citing "regulatory uncertainties" tied to the Digital Markets Act. Regulators were trying to rein in Big Tech and protect competition. Whether you buy Apple's explanation or see it as a pressure tactic, European customers were left waiting while others got the shiny new toys. This doesn't mean all regulation is bad. It's a reminder that lawmakers cannot promise to put a tight leash on an industry without potentially creating bottlenecks in the products and services it provides. That's precisely the dilemma Democrats now face. If they make it too difficult or expensive to build data centers, AI companies will have fewer places to house the computing power necessary to expand their products. New features could take longer to arrive. More sophisticated applications could cost more. And I wouldn't be surprised if the industry makes sure consumers understand exactly who's responsible. The BYD Atto 2 EV has a full-LED light setup, panoramic sunroof, 17-inch tyres, rain-sensing wipers, heated steering, column-mounted drive selector, powered front row (six-way driver, four-way passenger), ambient lights, and a PM 2.5 filter. With a length of 4.3 metres, it places itself in the mid-size category. Other features include an 8.8-inch instrument cluster, 12.8-inch centre screen, USB-C ports (both 18W and 60W), 50W wireless charging pad, and wireless Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. Mechanically, the Atto 2 is powered by a BYD Blade LFP battery, with capacities of 45.1kWh and 64.8kWh. The smaller battery pack is paired with a 174bhp/290Nm motor, while the larger battery pack is paired with a 201bhp/310Nm motor. 0-100kmph comes in 7.9 seconds, and the SUV tops out at 160kmph. Charging speeds stand at 11kW AC (3-phase) and 160kW DC, the latter of which tops up the larger battery from 10-80 per cent in 25 minutes. Braking duties are handled by front ventilated and rear solid discs. As far as an India launch is concerned, the Atto 2 has not been officially announced yet. Image source: Rushlane

artigo.texto: O Conselho Gestor do Fundo para o Desenvolvimento Tecnológico das Telecomunicações (Funttel) aprovou a destinação de R$ 46,3 milhões para o desenvolvimento de uma plataforma inteligente de gerenciamento de data centers. O projeto batizado de Prisma terá duração de 36 meses e será executado pelo CPQD A iniciativa terá como base um convênio de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação com a Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep), entidade responsável pela administração dos recursos. Em linhas gerais, a intenção do projeto é usar Inteligência Artificial (IA) para identificar onde e como os dados devem ser processados em operações com diferentes infraestruturas computacionais, de modo a tornar os data centers mais eficientes, seguros e sustentáveis. Segundo o Ministério das Comunicações (MCom), a expectativa é de que a tecnologia também reduza o consumo de energia e a pegada de carbono, aumente a resiliência contra falhas no fornecimento de energia, eleve a proteção contra ataques cibernéticos, diminua os custos operacionais, acelere o acesso à informação e aumente a proteção de dados estratégicos. "Investir em tecnologia nacional é garantir que o Brasil tenha mais autonomia para proteger suas informações e desenvolver soluções para os desafios do futuro. Com o apoio do Funttel, estamos fortalecendo a inovação brasileira e criando condições para uma infraestrutura digital mais moderna, segura e sustentável, reduzindo nossa dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior", afirmou o ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, em nota. Data centers de borda O Prisma também deve estimular a expansão de data centers de borda (também chamados de minidata centers) pelo território nacional, com o objetivo de levar o processamento de dados para mais perto de onde são gerados e utilizados, o que reduz o tempo de resposta dos sistemas e melhora o desempenho de serviços digitais. A tecnologia deve beneficiar, sobretudo, setores como saúde, defesa, segurança pública, educação e telecomunicações. "Além de tornar mais rápidos o processamento e o acesso às informações, essa arquitetura permite maior controle sobre o dado que está na borda", destaca o diretor de Tecnologia e Inovação do CPQD, Gustavo Correa Lima.

artigo.texto: Data Center São Carlos pode receber R$ 2,2 bi São Carlos pode receber um investimento de R$ 2,2 bilhões para a instalação de um Data Center, conforme declaração do secretário João Muller nesta terça-feira, com exclusividade ao SÃO CARLOS AGORA. O anúncio aponta a existência de um grupo empresarial interessado em aportar os recursos no município. A informação foi divulgada em primeira mão e sinaliza um potencial avanço na infraestrutura digital da região. O que é um Data Center O Data Center é o “cérebro” físico da internet e da computação em nuvem, indispensável para operar redes sociais, bancos, serviços públicos digitais e ferramentas de inteligência artificial. Trata-se de uma instalação que concentra servidores e equipamentos de rede para processar e armazenar grandes volumes de dados. Sem essas estruturas, a oferta de serviços online e a transformação digital de empresas e governos seriam inviáveis. A chegada de um empreendimento desse porte coloca São Carlos em posição estratégica no setor de tecnologia. Investimento bilionário em negociação O secretário João Muller afirmou nesta terça-feira, com exclusividade ao SÃO CARLOS AGORA, que existe um grupo empresarial disposto a investir R$ 2,2 bilhões para instalar um Data Center em São Carlos. O valor representa um aporte significativo para a economia local, com potencial de gerar empregos diretos e indiretos durante a construção e a operação. A fonte não detalhou o nome do grupo nem o cronograma previsto para a concretização do projeto. A expectativa é que novas informações sejam divulgadas conforme as negociações avancem. Impactos na arrecadação municipal A implantação de um Data Center pode elevar a receita municipal por meio do ISS (Imposto Sobre Serviços), relacionado à construção e à operação, além de impulsionar o IPTU e, em alguns casos, a participação no ICMS, fortalecendo o orçamento público local. Esses tributos incidem sobre diferentes etapas do empreendimento, desde a obra civil até a prestação de serviços de hospedagem de dados. Para os cofres públicos, o incremento pode representar mais recursos para investimentos em áreas como saúde, educação e infraestrutura urbana. A administração municipal ainda não divulgou estimativas oficiais de arrecadação. Modernização da infraestrutura tecnológica A chegada de grandes operadoras exige melhorias nas redes de fibra óptica e nas subestações de energia elétrica, modernizando a infraestrutura tecnológica da região. Essas adequações beneficiam não apenas o Data Center, mas também empresas e moradores que dependem de conexão estável e energia de qualidade. O investimento em infraestrutura pode atrair outras empresas de tecnologia e serviços digitais, criando um ciclo virtuoso de desenvolvimento. A fonte não detalhou quais operadoras estariam envolvidas no processo. Desafios de energia e água Por outro lado, há um consumo intensivo de energia e água. Essas estruturas demandam grandes volumes de eletricidade para os servidores e de água para os sistemas de refrigeração, o que pode pressionar a rede local se não houver planejamento. Especialistas alertam para a necessidade de avaliar a capacidade das concessionárias e dos recursos hídricos antes da instalação. O poder público e o grupo investidor precisarão apresentar soluções sustentáveis para mitigar esses impactos. A fonte não detalhou medidas de eficiência energética ou hídrica previstas para o projeto. Perspectivas para o setor empresarial Para empresários e comerciantes da região noroeste paulista, o anúncio sinaliza oportunidades indiretas em serviços de apoio, como fornecimento de materiais, logística e manutenção especializada. A instalação de um Data Center pode aquecer a demanda por mão de obra qualificada e serviços técnicos, beneficiando pequenas e médias empresas locais. Entidades como ACSP, CDL e Sebrae poderão acompanhar o desdobramento do projeto e orientar seus associados sobre possíveis nichos de atuação. A concretização do investimento ainda depende de etapas formais e da confirmação do grupo empresarial. Perguntas Frequentes Qual é o valor do investimento previsto para o Data Center em São Carlos? O investimento previsto é de R$ 2,2 bilhões, conforme anunciado pelo secretário João Muller. Quais benefícios fiscais um Data Center pode trazer para São Carlos? A implantação pode elevar a receita municipal por meio do ISS, impulsionar o IPTU e, em alguns casos, aumentar a participação no ICMS. Quais são os possíveis impactos negativos da instalação de um Data Center em São Carlos? Há consumo intensivo de energia elétrica e água, o que pode pressionar a rede local se não houver planejamento adequado.

artigo.texto: Arctic data centers: Buy, Sell or Hold? Is the Arctic’s data center boom a smart investment for local communities, or will the costs outweigh the returns? At an Arctic Today-moderated panel during the recent Arctic AI Summit in Kirkenes, Norway, three experts delivered three very different verdicts: Buy, Sell and Hold. Justine Vanhalst, co-founder of Icelandic start-up Hringvarmi, which aims to turn data center waste heat into locally grown food, voted Buy, meaning Arctic people should welcome the centers. However, her vote came with conditions. Professor Lars Ailo Bongo of UiT, The Arctic University of Norway, and co-founder of the Sámi AI Lab at the Sámi University of Applied Science, delivered a resounding Sell, advising people to say no to building the centers in their backyards. Meanwhile, Mads Qvist Frederiksen, executive director of the Arctic Economic Council, opted for a Hold. These contrasting opinions show the underlying tension between the economic promise of major investment and the potential environmental and social costs for the Arctic communities involved. Why the Arctic and why now? AI is driving unprecedented global demand for computing infrastructure and Arctic countries offer an attractive value proposition for data center developers: naturally cold conditions for cooling, an abundance of open space for construction, and access to low-carbon electricity. Developers also choose the northern countries for their safety, political stability and reliable connectivity. However, negative environmental impacts are already being seen across the region. In Finland in September, Google plans to invest €13 billion in data center expansion, which according to their Finnish country manager would be the largest single investment in Finland’s history. By October, the project had hit a speed bump after more than 500 hectares of forest (about 740 football fields) were cleared without the correct environmental impact studies and approvals. In response, the Finnish police have now launched a criminal probe into the suspected breach. Hold: Not So Fast This kind of risk reward dilemma is familiar to Qvist Frederiksen, who was able to list myriad economic benefits for countries like Finland, not least that Google’s investment came with a forecasted €3.6 billion in annual GDP contributions for the construction phase. He also pointed to Greenland, where the government is actively seeking data center investment and exploring expanded hydropower capacity to attract developers. “For years, we’ve been screaming for investment,” he told the audience. “Now someone is coming in trying to invest. Do we want to say no?” Maybe not no, but not so fast. His instinct is to welcome direct investment while his HOLD verdict suggests a need for caution. Some investments bring substantial economic benefits, while others leave communities with higher energy costs and very few new jobs. Qvist Frederiksen referred to Bell Canada’s planned US$50 billion data center investment in Saskatchewan as a success case where investors are sourcing their own energy rather than drawing on existing community supplies and creating 4,500 high-quality jobs. (Although, as Bongo points out, in emissions terms, this is still a huge new CO2 source.) In contrast to Bell, Qvist Frederiksen cited the cryptocurrency mining facility in Norway that brought no meaningful benefits to the local community, while generating heavy noise pollution and higher electricity prices. BUY, but with conditions For Vanhalst, the opportunity lies in turning a costly byproduct of data centers into a valuable local resource. Or as she puts it, “turning data into dinner.” Her Icelandic startup, Hringvarmi, is developing modular farms that use excess heat from the centers to grow fresh produce, reducing food imports while creating jobs and new business opportunities. “We’re connecting all these sectors together,” Vanhalst told the audience. “We need the data centers, the municipalities and the local people who want fresh food. By using existing resources, we can create the right environment for local food production.” She pointed to a separate initiative in Akureyri, northern Iceland, where a data center is in discussions with the municipality about using waste heat to warm a swimming pool or keep a natural grass football playable through winter. However, her BUY verdict comes with conditions. “It’s more like BUY/HOLD,” she said. “It’s too simple to just say we have the Arctic, we have the energy, so let’s do it. We need to consider where the energy comes from, the land, the environment and whether the community supports the project.” For Vanhalst, realizing these benefits will depend on effective regulations, responsible energy use, and building local partnerships rather than simply hosting the infrastructure. Sell: Who really benefits? For Bongo, the central question is whether the Arctic risks becoming a supplier of energy and land for someone else’s digital economy. “Who stands to benefit from the Arctic’s land and energy resources?” he asked. “The wind farm might be owned by a German company, the data center by the British, and the main customer might be one of the big American tech companies. Then what does the local community get in return?” Bongo, co-founder of the Sámi AI Lab, pointed out that his AI lab’s electricity needs are equivalent to those of just one or two freezers, a stark contrast to the energy demands of large commercial data centers. He warned that expanding renewable energy production to power such facilities could place further pressure on Sámi lands, where development has already led to conflicts over Indigenous rights. He pointed to Norway’s Fosen wind farm controversy and the Norwegian Supreme Court ruling that wind energy development in this project violated Sámi reindeer herders’ fundamental human rights. “We cannot simply say that AI is so important, and that we need so much green energy that we can ignore human rights,” he said.

artigo.texto: On Monday, the Senate voted to advance a bipartisan bill aimed at easing the construction of new energy infrastructure. The bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), has a broad base of support, including from labor leaders who contend it will produce thousands of jobs and clean energy proponents who believe it could unlock wind and solar. Its sponsors are hoping to pass the bill before the current Congress ends in January. But the bill has also received vehement blowback from a growing coalition of anti-data center critics, who argue that it would accelerate the buildout of an industry that Americans resoundingly voted against in the midterm elections. BAAJA does address affordability concerns by forcing data centers to pay the full cost of the upgrades they trigger, and contains transmission reforms designed to modernize the grid. But it also strips back environmental protections and could lead to more data centers powered by gas and built on public lands. Hundreds of local and national organizations have signed letters urging Congress not to pass the bill as written, including the Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council. Conversely, many industry trade groups have been supportive of the bill, despite the fact that it would likely make building more expensive. On Sunday, Donald Trump urged the Senate to pass the bill on Truth Social, writing that “China will take any Data Center that we don’t want.” The bill represents the first major test for Democrats post-election, as they contend with how to deliver on affordability and many other issues in their sprawling coalition at the same time. “Everything about BAAJA goes against the spirit of voters this midterms, in which we saw voters turn out for candidates who directly oppose data centers,” says Allie Rosenbluth, U.S. campaigns manager at the environmental nonprofit Oil Change International. “This bill is a massive giveaway to the data center industry—and creates a backdoor for fossil fuels to enter the grid through data centers.” Read More: How AI Backlash Shaped the 2026 Midterms Gas and Fossil Fuels America’s data center boom has also been a gas boom. In the scramble to bring AI data centers online as fast as possible, many developers have built their own gas power plants instead of waiting to connect to the grid. Global Energy Monitor data reported by Wired show that U.S. gas projects powering data centers increased from roughly 4 gigawatts in early 2024 to 189 gigawatts in development by mid-2026. In some cases, these gas plants have worsened local pollution and exacerbated health issues like asthma, scientific researchers contend. BAAJA incentivizes a wide range of energy sources to come online faster, including solar and wind. Many experts are hopeful that the bill will accelerate the buildout of transmission lines that are essential for bringing clean energy online. But environmentalists worry that the first and foremost beneficiary of the bill won’t be clean energy sources but rather gas-powered data centers, because there is already a massive pipeline of proposed projects waiting for various approvals. Rosenbluth points to several gas-powered data centers that are currently plodding through the permitting process, including the Ports-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio and the STAK Energy Campus in Alaska. If BAAJA were to pass, she says, key environmental permits they are trying to obtain could be fast-tracked, potentially allowing them to come online much more quickly. Holly Bender, chief program officer of the Sierra Club, says that "based on their need for speed to power, the data center industry is driving a historic and alarming investment in gas and fossil fuels. There’s a lot in this bill that will make it easier and faster to build gas pipelines, while making it harder for communities to have a say.” Public and Tribal lands Another major concern from critics is that the bill will lead to many more data centers getting built on federally-owned land. The Trump administration has embraced this idea, and signed an executive order in July 2025 directing the Interior and Energy departments to make federal sites available for data centers and to streamline their environmental reviews. “We’re going to ‘mine, baby, mine’ so we can ‘build, baby, build’ because we’ve got to build AI data centers,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said in 2025. There are at least 17 active applications connected to data center campuses on public land, covering thousands of acres in Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, and other states, one recent study found. BAAJA’s permitting provisions could make those projects easier to advance and harder to stop, including limiting judges’ ability to halt construction due to environmental review. Additionally, some Tribal organizations and leaders have spoken out forcefully against the bill, with a coalition of Tribal leaders writing on Saturday that the bill would “gut the ability of Tribal Nations and the American public to identify and protect historic and cultural places threatened by federally connected projects—including data centers.” Potential benefits However, the bill’s advocates argue that it addresses several of the public’s most pressing data center concerns. The first is around affordability: The bill contains ratepayer protections which would require developers to pay for the added cost of transmission. One study estimates that data centers would pay approximately $55 billion in transmission charges over ten years—about $35 billion more than under current policy. The bill establishes protections to prevent households and businesses from being left with the bill for failed projects. “The day of data center freeloading ends when this bill passes,” Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, one of the bill’s Democratic sponsors, said last week. He added on Monday that passing the bill would set the stage for Democrats to work on substantial clean energy policies next year when they control bot

artigo.texto: LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI have each won an Innovation Award at the world's largest electronics and IT exhibition, "CES 2027." LG Energy Solution was recognized for a software technology that shortens the diagnostic time of used batteries to within 10 minutes, while Samsung SDI was acknowledged for its uninterruptible power supply (UPS) battery solution for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. According to the battery industry on the 10th, LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI have been named among the companies selected for the "CES 2027 Innovation Award" by the Consumer Technology Association (CTA). LG Energy Solution received the award in the Advanced Mobility category, while Samsung SDI won in the Enterprise Tech category. LG Energy Solution's winning entry is its software-based used battery diagnostic solution, "Re.Pulse." The technology involves applying specific current pulses to a battery to measure voltage changes and analyzing them with an AI-based proprietary model to evaluate the battery's state of health (SoH) and residual performance. Its most notable feature is reducing the battery diagnostic time from over seven hours to within 10 minutes. It also enables precise diagnosis down to the cell level within a battery pack, allowing for the repair or replacement of only the degraded parts. Another characteristic is its ability to link with existing battery charge/discharge testers or electric vehicle chargers without requiring separate dedicated equipment. Because it can perform diagnostics without removing the battery from the vehicle, it can be utilized in used battery energy storage systems (ESS) and electric vehicle maintenance and inspection centers. Based on diagnostic results, it can also contribute to increasing resource utilization and reducing carbon emissions by classifying batteries suitable for reuse, remanufacturing, or recycling. Following its award last year for the battery life enhancement technology "Better.Re," LG Energy Solution has won the CES Innovation Award with pure software technology for two consecutive years. Lee Sang-hoon, an official at LG Energy Solution, stated, "This award is a result of recognition for the distinctiveness of our battery diagnostic technology and software competitiveness." He added, "We will continue to advance our diagnostic and management technologies to enhance the utilization value of used batteries and strive to build a sustainable battery circular ecosystem." Samsung SDI made the Innovation Award list with its prismatic battery solution for UPS, "SDI U8A3-UPS." A UPS is a system that supplies emergency power to critical facilities such as data centers when unexpected power outages occur. Recently, it has gained attention as essential equipment for stable power supply as power demand at AI data centers surges. The SDI U8A3-UPS is a product featuring prismatic battery cells made of lithium manganate (LMO) material. It achieves ultra-high output and high energy density, improving space efficiency by 33% compared to existing products. Stable power supply is possible with fewer batteries. It also has the advantage of supplying auxiliary power when power demand spikes during AI computing processes, preventing server failures or data damage. Recently, it demonstrated fire safety by becoming the first in the world to meet all evaluation criteria in a large-scale indoor fire test conducted by UL Solutions, a global safety certification body. With this, Samsung SDI has set a record of winning awards for three consecutive years since its initial participation in CES 2025. Last year, its ultra-high output cylindrical battery "SDI 25U-Power" won the Best of Innovation Award, and its thermal runaway blocking technology "No TP" received an Innovation Award. A Samsung SDI official said, "This is a result of recognition for the innovativeness of core power solutions in the AI era." He added, "We will continue to lead the market with products that combine the performance and safety required by customers."

artigo.texto: asharkyu/Shutterstock Save for later Print Download Share LinkedIn Twitter The energy storage market is expanding at a speed that would have seemed impossible just a few years ago. Yet, government targets have not kept pace with the market's growth. Storage is no longer a peripheral technology whose deployment can be left until renewable generation is built. It is becoming a central part of how electricity systems will operate, how much value they can extract from renewable power and how reliably they can meet growing demand. With COP31 focused on accelerating electrification, the gap between storage deployment and government ambition raises questions about whether power systems can deliver on those commitments. Ember’s analysis of national 2030 storage targets shows how far countries have come and how far they still have to go. The combined ambition of countries and the EU has reached 822 gigawatts, nearly three times the 284 GW assessed when governments agreed the Global Energy Storage and Grids Pledge at COP29 in 2024. But that total remains 45% below the pledge’s 1,500 GW goal. More revealing still is where the increase has come from. China and the EU account for most of the increase in national storage targets worldwide. The global headline suggests a broad shift in ambition. The underlying picture is much more concentrated. Global Storage Ambition Rests on 2 Markets China has raised its 2030 storage ambition from 130 GW to 460 GW under its 15th Five-Year Plan. The target combines 300 GW of new-type energy storage, mostly lithium-ion batteries, with 160 GW of pumped hydro. The EU, meanwhile, established its first bloc-wide storage target at 200 GW in June 2026. These decisions are significant. China’s target reflects the need to integrate its rapidly expanding renewable capacity, while the EU’s agreement explicitly links storage to reducing gas demand and making better use of renewable electricity. But the concentration of ambition matters. Since COP29, only eight countries and the EU have increased or introduced 2030 storage targets. Many other major markets have made little change to their plans. The result is a global total that looks much stronger than the underlying policy shift. Two major economies have moved decisively, while much of the rest of the world has yet to follow. That matters because the energy transition is not being built in two markets alone. Countries are pursuing different combinations of solar, wind, electrification and grid investment. They will not all need identical storage technologies or deployment pathways. But they do need to understand what their own power systems require and plan accordingly. A global pledge is only as strong as the national plans on how to deliver it. The Market Is Already Moving Faster Than the Plans Annual storage additions reached a record 118 GW in 2025, 108 GW of them batteries, and installed capacity reached 430 GW by the end of the year. The pace of change is remarkable. It took four years for annual battery additions to rise from around 10 GW to 100 GW. Solar took nine years to cross the same threshold, while wind took 15 years. Falling costs have helped drive this expansion. Battery storage costs have declined by roughly 20% per year on average over the past decade, improving the economics of projects and opening up new opportunities for power systems. Current deployment also puts the shortfall in national targets into perspective. If annual additions remained at the 2025 level through to 2030, global installed storage capacity would reach around 1,020 GW. That would exceed the combined national targets by almost one-quarter. Reaching the 1,500 GW global pledge will require further growth. But our analysis suggests that the necessary acceleration is well within reach of recent market performance. Battery additions have grown at almost 80% a year since 2020. To reach the 1,200 GW of battery storage envisaged in the International Energy Agency’s net-zero scenario update, annual additions would need to grow at only about one-fifth of that rate. The market has already demonstrated that it can grow at extraordinary speed. The question is whether governments are planning for the power systems that this growth makes possible. Solar Policy Without Storage Planning Is Incomplete The consequences and benefits are clearest in solar markets. Solar power is generated mostly during the day, but electricity demand continues into the evening and overnight. Batteries can shift some of that daytime generation to periods when it is needed, reducing curtailment, easing pressure on grids and allowing existing renewable capacity to deliver more useful electricity. Storage and solar are therefore not separate policy choices. They are complementary parts of a power system. Building more solar without planning for flexibility risks leaving some of its potential untapped. Of the 20 largest solar markets by capacity in 2025, 12 have a 2030 storage target and eight do not. Some of these markets are already deploying storage at scale. The US has installed roughly 52 GW of utility-scale battery power capacity, while Germany has around 30 GWh of battery storage. Market signals can drive projects where the economics are attractive. But they do not necessarily ensure that the right amount and type of storage will be built in the right locations and on the right timelines. Nor do they guarantee that storage deployment will be coordinated with new generation, transmission infrastructure and changing patterns of demand. Credible targets can provide a direction around which these decisions are made. Storage Belongs at the Center of Energy Planning The stakes will grow as electricity takes on a larger role across transport, buildings and industry. The Global Electrification Pledge proposed by the COP31 presidency aims to raise electricity’s share of final energy demand from around 20% to 35% by 2035. artigo.texto: Battery storage opens evening electricity markets to solar: Ember November 11, 2026 | Electrification, News Battery storage is pushing solar power beyond daylight hours and into electricity markets long dominated by fossil fuels, according to a report from energy think tank Ember. The analysis, published August 12, finds solar and batteries already supplied roughly a quarter of evening electricity demand in California and Bulgaria during the first half of 2026. Globally, batteries expected to be installed this year could shift 34 per cent of new daily solar generation into evening hours, based on solar growth during the first six months. That compares with 18 per cent in 2025 and just 4 per cent in 2021. Ember cautions that the estimate is a theoretical ceiling. It assumes all the new batteries are used to shift solar electricity. Actual performance depends on how storage is operated and whether electricity market rules allow batteries to earn revenue from multiple services. The findings point to a new phase of solar expansion. Solar supplied just over 10 per cent of global electricity in the first half of 2026, nearly double its 5.6 per cent share three years earlier. On an average day, it met more than a quarter of demand between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m., before falling to almost nothing overnight. That concentration creates problems in markets already producing abundant midday solar electricity. Wholesale prices can turn negative, generators may be forced to curtail output, and returns on additional solar projects weaken. Batteries can store that electricity for later use, reducing waste and allowing solar to compete during evening demand peaks. In California, solar and batteries met more than a quarter of demand between 7 p.m. and 9 p.m. in the first half of 2026, up from 6.8 per cent in the same period of 2023. Bulgaria reached 24 per cent during those evening hours. In Chile, batteries helped solar meet more than 10 per cent of electricity demand through the evening and into midnight. “Solar’s role in global power systems can be far bigger than previously thought possible,” Ember analyst Kostantsa Rangelova said in the report. Deployment is accelerating. Ember cites projected global battery additions of 459 gigawatt-hours in 2026, a 50 per cent increase from 307 gigawatt-hours last year. But installing equipment is only part of the challenge. Batteries can earn money by shifting electricity between low-price and high-price hours, supporting grid stability and providing capacity when needed. Rules that let operators combine those revenue streams can improve utilisation. China illustrates the gap. Standalone batteries averaged 299 charge-discharge cycles in 2025, while batteries installed alongside generation averaged just 199. Ember compares that with international best practice of about 350 cycles annually. Storage also has limits. Today’s batteries primarily address daily fluctuations, leaving prolonged cloudy weather and seasonal shortages as continuing challenges. Ember says electricity systems will still need a complementary mix of wind, hydro, nuclear and longer-duration storage. The next stage of solar growth will depend increasingly on deploying batteries and integrating them into electricity markets, the report concludes. That makes market reform central to further expansion.

artigo.texto: Proposed 'data center' project could come to Greenville County A proposal is making its way through the Greenville County application process that looks to develop a building into a project resembling a data center The proposal The application, which was in front of the Greenville County Planning Commission in October, lists Steven Pearce of McGuireWoods Consulting for Robert Moser of Prime Storage as the applicant, and according to the application, developers have a portfolio of taking existing storage assets to develop a proposed "Inference Point." The proposed location is a Prime Storage location along Wade Hampton Boulevard next to a Texas Roadhouse and backing up to a residential street. The application goes on to say developers plan to take existing storage assets to develop that inference point, which is a low-latency use to assist with medical procedures. It claims a $100 million development would use 5 megawatts of power Developers claim this can all happen inside of the building without knocking it down. What is an 'Inference Point'? We researched Inference Point and found it was a trademarked project by Edge Inference, LLC, based in Saratoga Springs, New York. According to the website, the company has had several similar projects across the country. Their website says an inference point is a "Small piece of local infrastructure, inside a building that already stands, that works out AI answers for the people, hospitals, schools, and businesses around it. In an instant, because it is close" The website also says it serves a local community that is close to the physical location of the center, and answers are given instantly because, "they never leave town." The Inference Point website also claims the machines are quiet and use no city water. How much power does it use? Where they differ, according to the site, is that an Inference Point is a 'tenant in an existing building' and focuses on answering questions for nearby people instantly, not housing and storing data for worldwide customers. We also wanted to know how that power usage compares to similar proposals in the Upstate. Here is research from WYFF4 Reporter Alex Land. In Spartanburg, a data center along Tyger River Industrial Drive would use up to 65 megawatts. Another project at the former R.R. Donnelly Industrial property would also use around 65 megawatts. The project has passed through the Greenville Planning Commission with approval in October but still needs a final thumbs-up from the Greenville County Council. Councilmembers say the project is facing second reading on Nov. 17.

artigo.texto: In delivering the Benchmark Lifetime Achievement Award 2026 to CATL (HKG:3750) Chairman Robin Zeng, former recipient and long-time colleague Bob Galyen says Zeng has helped transform batteries from a niche technology into a global industry. Gaylen, CATL’s former CTO, credits him with bringing electrification to scale and positioning batteries at the heart of the modern economy. The award was delivered at Benchmark Week 2026 in Shanghai, held on 10–11 November at the Pudong Shangri-La. Zeng founded CATL in 2011, recognising that batteries would become an essential part of the global economy. Over the last 15 years, he has grown the company around that vision. Zeng was also named to the TIME100 Climate 2025 list for his leadership in business climate action. In 2023, he received a Nobel Sustainability Trust award recognising his contributions to transportation electrification and the energy transition. Galyen notes that Zeng recognised early on the need to electrify at scale and has since focused on making battery technology reliable, affordable, and available across income levels. Zeng points to five factors that matter for EVs: safety, performance, lifespan, cost, and environmental impact. That last factor extends to the company’s own operations, not just the impact of EV adoption. CATL says it achieved carbon neutrality across its core manufacturing operations in 2025 and aims to reach full value-chain carbon neutrality by 2035. A rising tide for the battery ecosystem In line with the event’s theme of collaboration across the battery value chain, Zeng says the industry can only achieve long-term success if it grows together. Rather than concentrating profits in one part of the supply chain, he believes value should be shared so that participants can continue investing, innovating, and scaling. Zeng likens the approach to ensuring everyone has enough oxygen to survive. A healthy industry, he says, relies on miners, processors, manufacturers, automakers, and technology providers all benefiting from growth. That philosophy extends beyond CATL. While acknowledging the geopolitical pressures affecting the industry and growing competition for control of battery supply chains, Zeng says no single country or business can dominate the energy transition alone. Achieving carbon neutrality requires nations and industries to work together, share expertise, and share the value created. Galyen agrees, noting the opportunities for communities and economies. He says global expertise is needed and that the West has much to learn from China in this area. CATL has put those principles into practice through partnerships around the world that allow participants to learn from each other. Innovation drives the next chapter For Zeng, the next phase of the battery industry will be driven by innovation. Since the early 2000s, falling prices and more efficient manufacturing have helped bring batteries and EVs into the mainstream. Zeng notes that long-term growth still depends on the industry’s ability to innovate, develop new technologies, and improve upon existing ones. He describes the battery sector as a “teenager”, with much more room to grow. As demand for electrification continues to rise, innovation across the supply chain remains a key challenge for industry leaders. AI can be a major enabler, Zeng notes, helping researchers identify new materials, accelerate laboratory work, and uncover opportunities for new battery technologies. Zeng believes that lithium-ion batteries will continue to play a dominant role, but sees growing opportunities for alternative chemistries such as sodium-ion, particularly in energy storage and urban transport. The end use will ultimately determine the most suitable chemistry, with producers matching batteries to each application and customer. Battery swapping is another innovation Zeng highlights, allowing users to access different batteries depending on their needs. Looking ahead, both Zeng and Galyen see opportunities in new materials, improved surface chemistry, and innovations such as low-cost graphene. As electrification expands, they expect the industry’s next breakthroughs to emerge through materials research and development, AI, and collaboration across industries and borders. Write to Amy Rotman at Mining.com.au Main image: Mining.com.au

artigo.texto: Lexus ES EV Takes Aim at South Korea's approximately $50,000 Segment — With a CATL Battery Again Toyota's premium brand Lexus has introduced electrified versions of its upper-midsize ES sedan in South Korea, rapidly reshaping the competitive landscape of the roughly 70 million won (approximately $52,000) EV market. This price band is the last stretch where automakers can maintain a luxury brand image while still qualifying for government subsidies, making it the segment where imported carmakers are racing to concentrate their new models. The catch: many of the leading EVs in this bracket run on batteries from China's CATL, leaving South Korea's three battery makers with even less room to maneuver. Lexus unveiled the fully redesigned eighth-generation ES in the South Korean market on the 13th of last month. Three powertrains were introduced together: the pure-electric ES350e and ES500e, and the hybrid ES350h. Since its global debut in 1989, the ES had been sold only with combustion and hybrid powertrains; the eighth generation marks the first time it has a pure-electric lineup. Lexus has discontinued combustion-engine models entirely for this generation. The pricing drew market attention. The entry-level Premium trim of the ES350e was set at 71.6 million won (approximately $53,000) — 1.3 million won (approximately $970) below the equivalent hybrid, the ES350h Premium at 72.9 million won (approximately $54,000). EVs typically cost more than combustion or hybrid models of the same class because of their expensive batteries, so this reversal is read as an intent to lift market share through price competitiveness. The ES500e Premium, a dual-motor all-wheel-drive variant, was priced in the 77 million won (approximately $57,000) range. Performance splits the two models' characters. The ES350e is a single-motor front-wheel-drive model with 478 km of range per charge and 227 horsepower. The ES500e is dual-motor all-wheel drive; range drops to 435 km but output rises to 347 horsepower. Note: Prices are for the South Korean market. With a lower-than-expected starting price, orders moved quickly. According to industry sources, cumulative orders for the new ES stand at about 5,000 units, including pre-orders taken over the past month. The electric ES350e and ES500e are said to account for roughly half. There is no shortage of rivals battling in the 70 million won band. Volvo's upper-midsize sedan ES90, Polestar's upper-midsize SUV Polestar 3 and BMW's midsize SUV iX3 all sit in the same range. Tesla's Model Y, which dominates South Korea's EV market, starts at 49.99 million won (approximately $37,000) for the rear-wheel-drive Premium, while the all-wheel-drive Model Y L Premium sells for 72.99 million won (approximately $54,000). Behind the rush of import brands into this price range is a restructuring of the subsidy system. EVs under 85 million won (approximately $63,000) currently qualify for subsidies, but the South Korean government plans to lower the threshold to under 80 million won (approximately $59,000) starting next year. Vehicles priced at 80 million won or more must carry green license plates when purchased as corporate cars. Drop below the 60 million won (approximately $45,000) range and the premium image fades; climb into the 80 million won range and you take on both the loss of subsidies and the license-plate regulation. That is why the 70 million won band — where brand value and practical benefits can be secured together — has emerged as effectively the only safe zone. The problem is that the heart of EVs in this segment is Chinese. The Lexus ES350e and ES500e, Volvo ES90 and Polestar 3 all carry CATL's LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries. The Model Y also uses LG Energy Solution's NCM (nickel cobalt manganese) batteries in its Long Range and Performance trims, but the cheaper rear-wheel-drive trim is fitted with CATL's LFP battery. The BMW iX3 runs on batteries from China's EVE Energy. CATL held the top spot in the global EV battery market with a 39.1% share in the January-September period this year. The reason automakers choose Chinese batteries is simple. The NCM batteries that South Korean companies focus on have high energy density and long range, but contain expensive raw materials such as cobalt and nickel. LFP batteries, by contrast, are based on iron and phosphorus, keeping procurement costs low. For automakers that must hold prices in the 70 million won range while preserving a premium image, cost reduction is a structural necessity. The sense of crisis in South Korea's battery industry goes further. The high-priced premium EV market has limited room to expand, and with Hyundai and Kia's EV sales stagnating, Chinese companies are encroaching on the South Korean market. "To make matters worse, Chinese EV makers such as BYD, followed by Zeekr and Xpeng, are entering South Korea one after another, further narrowing the ground for Hyundai and Kia," a battery industry official said. "The reason South Korean battery makers have recently been putting effort into the energy storage system (ESS) market is also the judgment that it will be difficult to reclaim leadership in the EV segment from Chinese companies for the time being." The implications for South Korea's three battery makers are significant. For LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On — which have been expanding their LFP lineups — the situation now requires head-on competition with Chinese companies in entry-level and mid-priced EVs where price competitiveness is decisive. If the Lexus ES EV proves a hit, the 70 million won market is expected to grow further, and battery makers that fail to secure an LFP supply chain in this segment may fall behind in the race for volume. Conversely, automakers are expected to further strengthen their 70 million won lineups starting next year, when the subsidy threshold drops below 80 million won, setting the stage for an even fiercer battle for battery orders in this price range.
