artigo.texto: Hagar Township has pumped the brakes on any proposals for data centers in the community. Township Supervisor Izzy DiMaggio tells us the board of trustees this week approved a one-year moratorium on any data centers while the matter is studied by the planning commission. “We want to take a hard look at this whole situation,” DiMaggio said. “So, what they did was they put a one year moratorium, and this was passed by the board. The planners prepared a one year moratorium on the construction of data centers in our township.” DiMaggio says the township planning commission sent the recommendation for a moratorium to the full township board. It’s also been approved by the Berrien County Planning Commission. “It’ll give them time — the planners — to study it and come up with an ordinance that probably will severely restrict any data centers.” DiMaggio says the concern is water and electricity usage by the large centers. The noise they generate is another issue. He doesn’t believe Hagar Township has the resources available to accommodate a large data center and says residents have been expressing concerns. Although he’s unaware of any proposal for a data center in Hagar Township and isn’t expecting one to be made, DiMaggio says hitting pause on any such construction will enable the township to better prepare itself for whatever’s coming.

artigo.texto: Google avança com centro de dados de 17 mil milhões A empresa prepara o seu primeiro centro de dados no Wyoming, mesmo depois de os eleitores norte-americanos terem rejeitado 40 das 41 propostas relacionadas com novas instalações. Neste artigo encontras: O Google vai avançar com um investimento de 17 mil milhões de dólares, cerca de 15,7 mil milhões de euros, numa conversão aproximada, para construir um centro de dados no Wyoming, nos Estados Unidos. A decisão surge numa altura em que a expansão da inteligência artificial enfrenta uma oposição crescente devido ao consumo de eletricidade, à utilização de água, ao ruído e ao impacto destas instalações nas comunidades locais. Google mantém plano apesar da reação política O projeto será desenvolvido em Laramie County com o apoio de quatro parceiros: Tallgrass Energy, Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power e Related Digital. A escolha do Wyoming é vista como favorável para a empresa. O estado apoiou maioritariamente Donald Trump nas eleições presidenciais de 2024, mas esse apoio político não elimina as preocupações das populações diretamente afetadas pelo centro de dados. Nas recentes eleições intercalares norte-americanas, candidatos críticos de novos centros de dados venceram disputas importantes no Texas e na Geórgia. No total, apenas uma das 41 medidas submetidas a votação acabou por beneficiar os interesses da indústria. O resultado mostra que a resistência aos centros de dados está a ganhar peso político nos Estados Unidos, precisamente quando as empresas tecnológicas tentam aumentar a capacidade necessária para serviços de inteligência artificial. Centro de dados terá capacidade energética de 702 MW O complexo deverá incluir uma instalação de células de combustível com 702 megawatts de capacidade. O sistema será fornecido pela Bloom Energy e contratado através da American Electric Power. As células vão produzir eletricidade a partir de gás natural. O projeto prevê ainda a captura e armazenamento de carbono, com o dióxido de carbono a ser transportado para armazenamento subterrâneo permanente num local operado pela Tallgrass Energy. O Google afirma que este acordo elevará para quase 1 gigawatt a sua capacidade contratada de captura de carbono nos Estados Unidos. A empresa também deverá recorrer a geradores a gás operados pela Tallgrass Energy e pela Black Hills Energy. Google promete reduzir consumo de água O consumo de água é uma das principais críticas dirigidas aos grandes centros de dados. Para limitar esse impacto, o Google planeia utilizar sistemas de arrefecimento a ar no Wyoming, em vez de soluções evaporativas que exigem grandes quantidades de água. A empresa comprometeu-se também a apoiar programas locais de reposição de recursos hídricos e garante que pagará integralmente a eletricidade utilizada pelo centro. Segundo o Google, a infraestrutura adicional diretamente causada pelo projeto será igualmente financiada pela empresa. A promessa pretende responder às preocupações sobre a pressão que o centro poderá colocar nas redes elétricas e nos serviços públicos. Impacto económico ainda gera dúvidas O Google estima que o investimento poderá gerar centenas de milhões de dólares em impostos sobre a propriedade para Laramie County e para o School District 1. A tecnológica promete ainda apoiar o ensino de ciência e tecnologia, a formação profissional, o empreendedorismo e as profissões técnicas no Wyoming. Apesar disso, os residentes querem respostas mais concretas sobre o número de empregos criados, os benefícios económicos permanentes e os efeitos acumulados de outros projetos semelhantes na região. Mais de 200 habitantes já participaram no processo de consulta. A construção do primeiro centro de dados do Google no Wyoming avança, mas terá de provar que os benefícios da inteligência artificial compensam os custos energéticos e ambientais para a comunidade. artigo.texto: In the 2026 midterm elections, people in at least 38 jurisdictions across the United States voted to limit or ban data centers. Data centers have existed in the U.S. for decades, but their numbers have increased rapidly in recent years to support the development of artificial intelligence. As the number of these facilities has grown, the public has become more aware of them and backlash against them has intensified. Pew Research Center has done several analyses about data centers in recent years. Here are some key facts from these studies. There were more than 3,000 operational data centers in the U.S. as of February 2026, with at least 1,500 others in development. Existing data centers tend to be clustered together: 87% are in urban areas and 89% are within 5 miles of another data center. However, data centers are increasingly coming to new areas of the country. Two-thirds of all planned data centers are in rural areas, and 39% are in counties that don’t currently have one. As of February, nine states had 100 or more operational data centers. Virginia had the most at 398, followed by Texas (296) and California (277). Virginia also had 287 planned data centers – far more than any other state. Loudoun County in Northern Virginia is known as “Data Center Alley” because of its high density of data centers. Around four-in-ten U.S. adults (42%) lived within 5 miles of an existing or planned data center as of February. This included 38% who lived within 5 miles of an operational data center and 4% who lived within that distance of a planned one. Americans have become more pessimistic about data centers’ impact on a range of things, according to a summer 2026 survey. We asked U.S. adults whether they think data centers are mostly good, mostly bad, or neither good nor bad for: - The environment - Home energy costs - People’s quality of life nearby - Local jobs - Local tax revenue About half or more said data centers are mostly bad for the environment, home energy costs and neighbors’ quality of life – up substantially since January. Americans’ views of the impact of data centers on local jobs and local tax revenue were more mixed. Similar shares – between 21% and 24% – said that data centers are mostly good and mostly bad for these things. Still, the public became more likely between January and August to say data centers are mostly bad for each of these things. As of the summer survey, Americans who lived near a data center and those who didn’t live near one had similar views of the facilities and their impacts. Six-in-ten U.S. adults said this past summer that they would be not too or not at all comfortable with a new data center operating in their area. Just 7% said they’d be extremely or very comfortable with this, and 19% said they’d be somewhat comfortable. Even though data centers are currently concentrated in urban areas, the public’s discomfort with them cuts across community types. Majorities of urban, suburban and rural Americans said they would not be comfortable with a new data center in their area. More Americans said in a fall 2026 survey that they dislike than like political leaders who support building data centers locally. About six-in-ten U.S. adults (58%) said they dislike these leaders, compared with 9% who said they like them. Another 32% said they neither like nor dislike such leaders. Related: On Facebook and Instagram, Political Ads Are Increasingly Critical of Data Centers Some Americans blame data centers for their rising home energy costs, according to a March survey. Most Americans said their home energy costs had gone up in the last few years. Among those who said this, about two-thirds pointed to data centers using more energy as a major or minor reason why. Another 26% said they weren’t sure whether data centers were a reason for this, and 9% ruled out data centers as a contributing factor. Americans were most likely to blame their rising energy costs on utility companies wanting to make more money. More than eight-in-ten (85%) of those who said their energy costs had increased said this was a major or minor reason why. Still, data centers were a more common source of blame than government regulations or Americans’ own increased energy use. Across our surveys, Democrats and Republicans alike tend to have more negative than positive views of data centers. (In this analysis, Democrats and Republicans include those who lean to each party.) For example, both Democrats and Republicans were more likely as of August to have negative than positive views of data centers’ impact on the environment, home energy costs and people’s quality of life nearby. (However, they differed on whether data centers are mostly good or mostly bad for local jobs and local tax revenue.) In the same survey, 68% of Democrats and 54% of Republicans said they would be not too or not at all comfortable with a new data center in their area. Just 4% of Democrats and 10% of Republicans said they’d be extremely or very comfortable with this. In our fall survey, Democrats were more likely than Republicans to disapprove of leaders who support data centers (69% vs. 49%). Still, people in both parties were much more likely to say they dislike than like such leaders, though sizable shares also said they neither like nor dislike them. In addition, similar shares in both parties pointed to data centers as a major reason for their rising home energy costs in our March survey. Democrats and Republicans differed on some other potential reasons, including government regulations and extreme weather events. The amount of electricity that U.S. data centers used increased significantly from 2020 to 2024, according to an October 2025 analysis of data from the International Energy Agency. In 2020, U.S. data centers used 108 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity in total, and that increased to 183 TWh in 2024. Their electricity use is projected to grow to 426 TWh in 2030. artigo.texto: On November 5, 2026, OpenAI published a National Community Compact, a set of public promises for the data centers it plans to build across the United States. The timing and the vocabulary tell the story. As TechRadar reported, the company wants to build more AI infrastructure while Americans are increasingly saying no, and The Information has tracked the same tension. The OpenAI data center problem is no longer a zoning footnote. It is a political fight. The compact commits OpenAI to pay the full cost of electricity and grid infrastructure for campuses it owns and operates. It promises community input, published construction plans, no nondisclosure agreements with public officials at future sites, and a water plan plus a noise study for every location. It also introduces a new label. OpenAI now wants to call its data centers “compute campuses.” Is that enough? Our read is that the pledges are real and the money commitments matter, but a rename and a communications push cannot settle a dispute about power bills, water and who decides. Local resistance was already measurable before the announcement, as we covered when voters put the AI data center boom on notice. This analysis walks through what OpenAI confirmed, what it left open, what the market is pricing in and where the fight probably goes next. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What the National Community Compact Actually Promises Start with what OpenAI itself confirmed. The National Community Compact dates to November 5, 2026, and it frames a set of commitments for data-center campuses that OpenAI owns and operates. That scope matters. A pledge covering owned-and-operated sites says nothing by itself about facilities run by partners or landlords, and a large share of AI capacity gets built through such arrangements. The confirmed list is short and concrete. OpenAI says it will pay the full cost of electricity and grid infrastructure for those campuses. It says it will solicit community input and publish construction plans. It says it will not use nondisclosure agreements with public officials for future sites. And it says each site will come with a water plan and a noise study. Each item answers a specific complaint that has dogged hyperscale builds. Residents have objected that power costs get shifted onto household bills. Councils have complained that deals were negotiated in secret. Neighbors have raised noise and water draw. By addressing all three, OpenAI shows it has read the objections correctly. The open question is whether a corporate pledge can substitute for binding local rules. The company also stated that it will keep pursuing U.S. data-center expansion despite the heightened political scrutiny. That sentence is the real context for everything else. The compact is not a retreat. It is a plan to keep building under new terms, which is why critics and supporters will both read it as a negotiating position rather than a final settlement. The Pay-Its-Own-Way Pledge on Power and Grid Costs The headline promise of the new OpenAI data center policy is financial. OpenAI says it will cover the full cost of electricity and grid infrastructure for the campuses it owns and operates. CNBC framed the move as a response to the election, reporting that OpenAI would pay for data center power after the vote showed public concern about AI. Why lead with power? Electricity is the most politically portable grievance. A voter who never sees a server rack still sees a utility bill. When a large new load connects to a regional grid, the fear is that upgrade costs spread across all ratepayers. A pledge to carry those costs directly tells that voter the bill will not land on their kitchen table. The pledge has limits that readers should keep in view. It applies to campuses OpenAI owns and operates. It is a company commitment, not a tariff approved by a state regulator. And the fact sheet from the announcement does not describe how compliance would be verified or what happens if a project is scaled back. Those details decide whether the promise protects ratepayers or merely reassures them. Still, the commitment is a meaningful concession. Paying the full grid bill raises OpenAI’s cost of building each campus, and that cost sits on top of an already heavy capital program. Few companies volunteer to raise their own cost of expansion unless they believe the political price of not doing so is higher. Why OpenAI Now Says Compute Campuses The second headline item is vocabulary. OpenAI plans to call its data centers “compute campuses.” An OpenAI spokesperson explained the choice this way: “Compute campuses better describes the scale and role of the infrastructure we’re building for AI.” The word campus borrows from universities and corporate parks, places that suggest jobs, landscaping and civic presence. The phrase data center, by contrast, has picked up associations with humming warehouses, diesel backup generators and thin payrolls. Rebranding is an old public-relations move, and this one is easy to read. How the press received the rename Reception has been skeptical. Business Insider’s headline on the topic put it bluntly: good luck trying to rebrand data centers. The headline signals what many readers already suspect, that swapping one noun for another is the oldest trick in the brand playbook. The comparison is fair as far as it goes, but it also understates one point. Words do shape how a project gets described in a council meeting. If officials and local press adopt the new phrase, it changes the first impression of a proposal. The catch is that the first impression lasts only until the first question about power, water or noise. After that, the substance of the answers does the work. Altman, Brockman and Friar on the Backlash OpenAI’s senior executives have addressed the resistance directly, and their remarks reveal how the company diagnoses the problem.

artigo.texto: City of Eagan sues data center company Eagan Capital over "temporary chillers" The City of Eagan is suing Eagan Capital, a data center company in business along Pilot Knob Road, alleging they've been operating "temporary chillers" without proper permits. This comes months after Eagan Capital sued the city over a data center moratorium, calling it "unlawful." This latest lawsuit focuses on "chillers," which cool the data center and prevent overheating. During a city council meeting on Nov. 2, Mayor Mike Maguire announced the legal action and claimed the company was operating "without the required permits and approvals". The court document shows aerial pictures from 2025 showing no chillers on the property and from 2026 showing the chillers in place. In May, a representative for Eagan Capital told the council the company didn't think they needed a permit for installing the chillers but applied for one as soon as they were notified. The representative also said Eagan Capital designed a sound barrier around them. The city denied an interim use permit and later denied an application for a mechanical permit for permanent chillers in part because "data centers are not a permitted principal use in the Research and Development zoning district," the lawsuit explains. "There is a neighborhood just north of that facility in the Lawn Oak and Pilot Knob area that has waited a long time for this process to take place," said Maguire. "We appreciate the patience of that neighborhood." The city also alleges in the lawsuit, despite the sound barrier, that noise levels are beyond code. Denn lives across the street from the facility and hopes the court rules in favor of the city. He told WCCO the noise from the center is constant. "It's just a dull roar all the time, very uncomfortable," Denn said. "We have a patio that is down the hill from the chillers and they just make a lot of noise 24/7; [it] never goes away."

artigo.texto: Standalone four-hour system adds 600 MWh of contracted storage capacity WASHINGTON, November 10, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Lydian Energy ("Lydian"), an Excelsior Energy Capital-backed developer, owner, and operator of energy infrastructure projects, today announced that its Faraday battery energy storage system (BESS) in Utah County, Utah, has reached commercial operation. The 150 MW/600 MWh project began operating on September 18, 2026. Faraday is contracted via a Schedule 34 contract in support of Meta's Eagle Mountain data center operations. A standalone, four-hour lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) battery system, Faraday BESS delivers 600 MWh of contracted storage capacity to PacifiCorp under a long-term energy storage agreement, supporting grid reliability in Utah. The project is situated on an approximately eight-acre site adjacent to the 525 MW Faraday solar facility and shares that facility's substation and interconnection, allowing Lydian to add storage using existing infrastructure. Lydian took Faraday BESS from mobilization to commercial operation in approximately 10 months. Faraday BESS is expected to pay approximately $9 million in property tax over the course of the project life. "Faraday BESS shows what a mature platform like Lydian's can deliver," said Kim Smith, Chief Operating Officer of Lydian. "Bringing it online on an extremely tight timeline took close coordination across our own team and our supply chain, construction, and financing partners, from acquisition through commissioning. When a wildfire threatened the area in June, our team put safety first while keeping the project on track. Faraday BESS enhances PacifiCorp's reliable, contracted capacity for Utah customers." "Storage is an essential part of a resilient grid. It gives utilities the flexibility to respond when conditions change, from extreme weather to unexpected outage," said Amanda Yang, Director of Clean and Renewable Energy at Meta. "Our investments in new energy resources are helping projects like Faraday BESS reach the grid, and that's a role we want to keep playing as we support our Eagle Mountain Data Center." "Excelsior backed Lydian because we recognized that a disciplined, execution-driven team could build a leading energy infrastructure platform," said Chris Moakley, Managing Partner at Excelsior Energy Capital and Chair of the Board of Lydian Energy. "As demand for reliable, domestically produced power continues to grow, storage projects like Faraday BESS will play a larger role in keeping the grid dependable."

artigo.texto: In 2020, Virginia passed the Clean Energy Act to combat the disproportionate amount of carbon pollution the state's energy sector produces: an estimated third of Virginia's total carbon pollution. The main goal of the Act was to see energy reach net-zero emissions by 2050. Dominion Energy, one of Virginia's primary electric utility companies, has undertaken renewable projects in accordance with the Act, including the country’s largest offshore wind farm. Coincidentally, Dominion has not stopped investing in fossil fuels, as shown by its development of a gas plant in Chesterfield County and ongoing plans to develop one in Cumberland County. In a quote shared with WHRO’s Mallory Noe-Payne, Jeremy Slayton, a Dominion spokesperson, explained how “[O]n the hottest and coldest days of the year, when people are running their air conditioning, they’re running their heater, and that demand goes up and up and up.” Slayton also added, “if we can’t meet that demand, that means there will be blackouts”. This rhetoric not only misplaces blame on the average homeowner but also establishes the basis for Dominion’s plans to develop up to eight new gas plants within the next decade. These will be known as peaker plants, which are used selectively when energy demand is exhausted within Dominion’s pre-established grid. There is a caveat to the purpose of peaker plants, however, and that is their main purpose as energy sources for data centers. On Aug. 27, Prince Edward County hosted a public meeting with AVAIO Digital, a company planning to develop a data center on the 280 acres of Hit Park, located just three miles from Longwood’s campus. AVAIO is in the early stages of planning but has already established data centers in Appomattox and Caroline counties, as well as Arkansas, California and Mississippi. As listed on their website, the company is committed to cleaner, more sustainable data centers. Instead of using an influx of water to cool equipment, they use a closed-loop system wherein the water does not evaporate and is not discharged. The center is expected to require only 30,000 gallons of water per day compared to the average data center’s three to five million gallons per day, according to the Virginia Conservation Network. The largest disadvantage to such a system is that it will also need an estimated 300 megawatts of energy, which would require further development to strengthen the site’s connection to Dominion’s power grid, as Hit Park currently lacks necessary power access. AVAIO addressed the upfront costs associated with data centers, informing the community that they would pay all of the expected monetary costs of development as well as minimize the effects on the environment. The company detailed plans to uplift local conservation efforts and offset their carbon footprint to reach net zero. They attempted to make their plans palatable by noting data centers have been around since streaming and the internet but failed to reflect on the recent acceleration in data center development being due to advancements in generative AI. AVAIO also assured attendees they would be paying more than their fair share to Dominion but again failed to address the stress data centers place on energy grids—stress that will lead to the average person paying the price. More information about AVAIO’s plans is organized on Prince Edward County’s FAQ webpage.

artigo.texto: Data centers go 0-for-21 on the ballot By Nick Evans/Ohio Capital Journal Ohio voters sharply rejected data centers in this year’s election. Around Ohio, 18 communities voted on whether to curb or ban data center developments. In all 18 communities, voters decided that, yes, that would be a good idea. In most, the results were resounding — like Harlem Globetrotters vs. Washington Generals resounding. City leaders in Wilmington, the county seat of Clinton County, asked voters to rezone four parcels to allow data center development. Roughly 80 percent of voters rejected all four. In the Lake County Village of Perry, more than 87 percent of voters backed an initiative requiring data centers that accept tax incentives to take out a bond, operating kind of like an insurance policy, to back up their promises of local tax revenue. Voters in Piqua prohibited data centers within city limits by a 2-to-1 margin and didn’t stop there. They also recalled three city commissioners — including the mayor and vice-mayor — for approving a Meta data center in November last year. From Conneaut in far northeastern Ashtabula County to Trenton in Southwestern Butler County, nine communities passed initiatives modeled on the statewide data center moratorium Conserve Ohio organizers are trying to put on the ballot in 2027. That initiative would amend the state constitution to prohibit any data center drawing more than 25 megawatts a month. In a press release, Conserve Ohio congratulated communities who voted against data center development, and warned elected officials that “You cannot look away now.” “The above election results demonstrate that when communities have a say regarding the construction of a hyperscale data center in their local area, they overwhelmingly say no,” the group wrote. “Your oath is invoked. Stop the self-dealing, corporate fealty, and greed. Represent and serve the people who elected you.” Conserve Ohio urged Ohio citizens to push state lawmakers to pass a 12-month moratorium on any data center development in Ohio during the lame duck session between now and the end of the year. Upper Sandusky Angela Huffman is a sixth-generation farmer in northwest Ohio, and she heads up the national watchdog group Farm Action, which focuses on corporate consolidation in the food and agriculture sector. She explained data centers came onto their radar about a year ago, because of concerns about their impact on farmland. “And then lo and behold,” Huffman said, “I read in the newspaper back in June of this year that a data center, a nearly $1 billion data center, was proposed here right outside Upper Sandusky, which is about 10 miles from my farm.” Upper Sandusky is the county seat of Wyandot County, but it’s a small city with a population of less than 7,000 residents. In June, the company Smartland Energy proposed building a 150-megawatt natural gas plant on a 46-acre parcel. The idea was to build the powerplant first and then sell the power directly to a data center client on an adjacent 100-acre parcel. Smartland emphasized it “would not build, own or run” the data center, and that the eventual end-user would still need city approval and hadn’t been pre-selected. Huffman and other organizers began collecting signatures to oppose the project, and unlike many petition drives, she said their job was relatively easy. “Really our challenge was just finding ways to get in front of people,” she said. “They already knew about the issue. They were already concerned about data centers. So fortunately, we didn’t have to first educate or raise awareness and educate about what the problem was. They already knew. We just had to get their names on these petitions in time.” Huffman noted construction of a Louis Dreyfus Company soybean processing plant was already stretching local infrastructure, and a data center adding to the strain was a daunting prospect. When Upper Sandusky voters went into the booth last Tuesday, nearly 77 percent of them approved a city charter amendment banning data centers within city limits. Looking forward In a Facebook post last Thursday, Smartland Energy seemingly acknowledged its project doesn’t have a future in Upper Sandusky. The company thanked the community and reiterated its belief in their proposal. “At the same time,” it stated, “we value and respect the democratic process and the outcome of the charter amendment vote.” “Our team will take some time to come together, reflect on this process, and discuss the outcome,” Smartland added. “If there is ever anything further to share, this will be the first place we communicate it.” The drubbing data centers took in Ohio last Tuesday didn’t stop at the state line. Around the country, 47 initiatives were on the ballot to restrict data centers. Election officials are still counting votes for two of those contests, but according to the website Data Centers on the Ballot, 44 jurisdictions rejected data centers and just one welcomed them – that one was in Harwood, North Dakota (population 940). The day after the election, data center industry group Infrastructure for America released what it called a “good actor pledge”. It’s members, including Compass, Digital Realty, QTS and Vantage, committed to operate transparently, invest in their communities, and not be a drain on local power and water infrastructure. Ohio Capital Journal sent an email to the Data Center Coalition seeking comment about Ohio’s results, but got no response. artigo.texto: [SMM PV Flash] China's first commercial-grade pure solar-powered drone successfully completed its maiden flight, with a maximum driving range of 30 hours and vehicle-mounted takeoff capability. A reporter learned from the 11th Academy of China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation that on November 11, 2026, the “Light Cavalry” small and medium-sized solar-powered UAV, independently developed by China, completed its maiden flight at an airport in northwestern China. As a pure electric aircraft powered solely by solar energy, the “Light Cavalry” offers core advantages such as long endurance, rapid deployment, and easy support. The aircraft is 3.2 meters long with a wingspan of 8 meters and a maximum designed endurance of 30 hours. Through modular design, it can be quickly adapted to various mission payloads, including communications and remote sensing. The aircraft can be launched from a vehicle, with ground preparation taking only 20 minutes, giving it rapid deployment capability.

artigo.texto: Leilão de baterias atrai mais de 6 mil projetos e movimenta setor elétrico BNDES destinará R$ 30 bilhões a empreendimentos com componentes nacionais, em certame que marca a entrada do armazenamento em larga escala no sistema brasileiro Atualizado Pela primeira vez, o sistema elétrico brasileiro está em via de investir bilhões de reais em tecnologias para armazenamento de energia. Com isso, se insere na tendência global. Apenas no segmento de baterias, em 2025 a capacidade instalada no mundo atingiu 108 GW (gigawatts), volume 40% superior ao de 2024 e 11 vezes maior que o de 2021, segundo a Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA, na sigla em inglês). O movimento foi impulsionado pela China, Estados Unidos e Europa. “Baterias são a tecnologia que mais cresce no mundo”, diz Donato Filho, CEO da consultoria Volt Robotics. O Brasil, devido à matriz majoritariamente hidráulica, também conta com as hidrelétricas reversíveis (com dois reservatórios). No entanto, esse mercado ainda é incipiente. Somente no fim de setembro, portaria do Ministério de Minas e Energia as incluiu nos leilões para contratação de reserva de capacidade a serem realizados em 2027, 2028 e 2029. As baterias, no entanto, já têm leilão marcado para o início de dezembro de 2026. Segundo o Plano Decenal de Expansão da Energia (PDE) 2036, elaborado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) e em consulta pública até o fechamento desta edição, ao final deste período o país deverá contar com 9,2 GW em capacidade de armazenamento. Deste total, 7,2 GW em baterias e 2 GW em hidrelétricas reversíveis. A função do armazenamento é acumular energia elétrica em momentos em que há excesso de produção para utilizá-la em períodos de escassez. Como registra o PDE 2035, “as tecnologias de armazenamento constituem um recurso estratégico para o provimento de capacidade e para a ampliação da flexibilidade operativa do sistema”. Para o período, o PDE estima uma expansão de 100 GW na capacidade instalada do país, totalizando 359 GW. Essa expansão viria da construção de usinas convencionais e de soluções de armazenamento. A diferença entre as hidrelétricas reversíveis e sistemas de baterias, também chamados de BESS (batery energy storage system), é que as primeiras demandam de sete a oito anos para entrar em operação, só podem ser erguidas em locais onde há reservatórios, são mais lentas para ligar e desligar, podem acumular energia por muitas horas e demoram também horas para descarregar essa mesma energia. Além disso, contribuem para o abastecimento em períodos de estiagem. Já os BESS são mais ágeis: podem ser erguidos em um a dois anos, acumulam energia em poucas horas e a descarregam em períodos de tempo mais curtos, como quatro a oito horas. Além de beneficiar a potência, tornam a operação do sistema mais flexível. Por isso, os BESS são particularmente adequados a parques eólicos e solares, que contam com excesso de produção quando o vento sopra e o sol está a pino, mas sofrem com a escassez de insumo nos outros períodos. Isso provoca dois problemas: excesso ou escassez de energia. As duas situações são perniciosas, pois podem provocar apagões de energia e problemas de variação de tensão e de frequência. Isso obriga o Operador Nacional do Sistema (ONS) a determinar o corte da produção das renováveis quando há excesso (curtailment) ou aumentar a produção das térmicas e das hidrelétricas quando há escassez, a um preço maior. A questão é acentuada pelo comportamento do consumo: menor durante o dia, quando a produção é farta, e maior no início da noite, quando há escassez. “O problema é que esses cortes não são ressarcidos. Nós temos contratos, não recebemos o que não geramos e, às vezes, somos até multados”, diz Rodrigo Sauaia, CEO da Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar), referindo-se ao curtailment. “Temos que colocar o consumidor como protagonista e induzi-lo a mudar o horário de carga”, afirma Luiz Eduardo Barata Ferreira, presidente da Frente Nacional dos Consumidores de Energia (FNCE). A expansão dos BESS tem sido beneficiada pela queda nos preços, que a partir de 2010 recuaram de mais de US$ 1.000/kWh (kilowatt/hora) para uma média global de US$ 108/kWh, conta Sauaia. Por isso, eles já são utilizados em projetos de média tensão, como indústrias, comércios e hospitais em substituição aos geradores convencionais. “Estamos vivendo uma onda que chega a 1 GW em projetos de menor porte e carga de média tensão”, diz Markus Vlasits, presidente da Associação Brasileira de Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae). A exceção é a subestação de Registro (SP), da ISA Energia Brasil, primeiro BESS de grande porte no Brasil, inaugurado em 2022, com 90 MW de potência e 60 MWh de energia. Agora, o setor elétrico prepara-se para introduzir os BESS no Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Pela primeira vez na história, em dezembro eles serão objeto de leilão específico organizado pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e pela Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE) para reserva de capacidade (LRCAP - Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade) na forma de potência. Isto significa que os projetos vencedores serão acoplados a subestações ligadas às linhas de transmissão de alta tensão do SIN, aumentando a potência e dotando o sistema de maior flexibilidade operacional. O leilão foi dividido em duas etapas. A primeira, no dia 2 de dezembro, para projetos com componentes nacionais. A segunda, no dia 4 de dezembro, para equipamentos nacionais e estrangeiros. Os primeiros contarão com financiamento de R$ 30 bilhões do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES), via Finame. Para os demais, o financiamento ainda está indefinido. Mas, como diz Donato Filho, “no momento há muitos recursos externos para projetos ligados à energia renovável”. “O acesso ao financiamento do Finame, associado a critérios de conteúdo local, pode fazer do leilão de baterias também um instrumento de política industrial. artigo.texto: This signal was most prominent in Texas, where Gina Hinojosa, a relatively unknown state legislator, campaigned heavily in opposition to these projects and toppled Greg Abbott, a three-term incumbent governor. Abbott had embraced the data-center boom and only called a pause in August amid alarming poll numbers. The problem is the U.S. needs to keep building data centers, which house thousands of computer servers, to process the clicks and taps that underpin modern life and to harness the productivity gains of an artificial intelligence revolution that is already taking hold in the economy. Productivity gains are what drive wage increases without spurring inflation and are the basis for the high U.S. living standards compared with the rest of the world. The consequence of the election should not be the demonization of data centers but the opportunity to build them with community concerns in mind. What shouldn’t be lost amid all the noise is that data-center construction is booming despite the mounting opposition that morphed into a bipartisan issue and left few politicians to defend these crucial projects — not even the governor of business-friendly Texas. Two suppliers closely tied to data centers, Vertiv Holdings Co. and Amphenol Corp., both reported that third-quarter orders doubled from a year ago, with no visible cracks in demand. The value of U.S. data-center construction jumped 90 percent in September from a year earlier, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. Data-center construction won’t stop, but the results of the midterm election give communities the upper hand in negotiating where and how they will be built, tempering the mad dash to put up these projects and halting some of the community-unfriendly solutions, such as deploying loud jet-aircraft engines as a quick way to generate off-grid electricity. The builders of data centers will be wise to heed the message that they must be more transparent on how these projects will use energy, consume water and create noise. More scrutiny of large projects is welcome to head off abuses that could take place if developers had free rein to build these facilities. Unfortunately, politicians latched on to the public’s concern and then amplified it into irrational fear that now has people discussing these projects as if they were nuclear waste dumps. The opposition has been fueled by the simplistic sound bites, and even disinformation, that flood the social media where many people obtain their news. The biggest obstacle for data centers is access to vast amounts of uninterrupted power supply, which has sparked fear that residential electricity bills will skyrocket. The answer is straightforward: Generate more electricity and shield households from cost increases. More than 200 companies, including the largest power producers and hyperscalers, signed a Ratepayer Protection Pledge at the White House in March, which, among other things, promised that data-center power needs wouldn’t push up residential rates. These promises aren’t mandatory, but the backlash should be fierce if they’re broken. Early signs are encouraging. In a deal to expand Google’s data-center campus in West Memphis, Arkansas, Entergy Corp. plans to add capacity to the grid that it says will result in $500 million of savings for customers beginning in 2028. In addition, Google pledged $25 million over five years for the local community, including workforce training. Similarly, Duke Energy Corp. last month reached a deal with several of the largest tech companies that will protect customers in North Carolina from some data-center costs, including infrastructure such as substations and transmission lines. Water use is often cited by opponents of data centers as a serious drawback, but this has been blown out of proportion. Data centers don’t use nearly as much water as traditional industries including agriculture, chemicals or food and beverages. Besides, recycling technology can reduce data-center water use to negligible amounts. This is where good governance can locate a project away from residential neighborhoods and insist on robust water recycling. Oracle Corp. is using closed-loop cooling technology that doesn’t require continuous water supply for data centers it’s building in Michigan, New Mexico, Texas and Wisconsin. Acoustic panels could help mitigate the low humming noise that opponents cite. The benefits of data centers have been lost in the overheated rhetoric of the midterms. These facilities generate local tax revenue and have a relatively light environmental footprint and social impact. They don’t pollute as much as traditional heavy industries, such as steel, glass or chemicals. They don’t generate heavy truck traffic like typical industrial plants and warehouses do. Most people and politicians support manufacturing more goods in the U.S. Those plants use electricity, consume water, make noise and create more traffic — all of which create local challenges that can be overcome. Should we just throw up our hands and quit making goods altogether? That would be irrational and unwise. The data-center boom will continue because AI has unleashed unprecedented demand that needs to be met. These facilities form the infrastructure backbone of our modern lives and, just as the water faucet and light switch are expected to work, it’s easy to take that for granted. Done right, these facilities will drive the digital revolution while most communities won’t even know they’re there, humming along 24/7 and processing every tap and click. ©2026 Bloomberg L.P. He was previously a Bloomberg News reporter covering logistics, manufacturing and private aviation. artigo.texto: Residents of Sutton expressed shock and outrage this week when they learned one of Robert Kraft’s companies had proposed building a massive data center complex in their small town 10 miles south of Worcester. But the idea was first discussed in public over a year ago when Sutton’s Select Board was encouraging a packaging company owned by the Kraft Group to develop a large parcel of land it owns on the north side of town, according to videos of public town Select Board meetings reviewed by the Globe. It’s not clear when the Krafts took up the idea, which was discussed Tuesday at a Select Board meeting. In December, a Kraft representative at a Select Board meeting said they had not formally presented any plan to Sutton officials. But there’s no doubt its $16 billion data center plan — potentially one of the largest in the country — has crashed headlong into the powerful political backlash nationwide against the energy-hungry facilities used to develop and run artificial intelligence systems. The Kraft Group did not respond Wednesday to requests for comment. The 383-acre parcel has been used for industrial purposes since the 1930s, according to town filings with the Worcester County Register of Deeds. Before the Krafts owned it, it housed a cement factory and a gravel pit. In 2022, Sutton had given the Kraft company, Unified Global Packaging Group, a tax incentive deal to build a huge warehouse on part of a 383-acre parcel it bought for $9.5 million in 2020. But by 2025, Unified told the town it couldn’t find a tenant for a warehouse and it would have to reboot its plans. At a meeting in March of last year, then-Select Board member Normand Champigny floated some advice on attracting a new major tenant — a data center. He had a modest-size one in mind, known as a co-location facility, or colo. In the meeting video, he said they’re not like the giants: “When I think of [a big tenant], I think of, for instance, a colo like Amazon Web Services.” Amazon’s cloud computing and AI unit lease data centers all over the world. Representatives of the Kraft Group and Unified present at the meeting did not react to the suggestion at the time, according to the video. Another 18 months later, however, they embraced the idea of installing not just a co-location data center, but a massive, AI-capable data campus that would rank as one of the largest in the entire country. Earlier in the meeting, Champigny also suggested the Kraft family should leverage its network of connections to find a tenant for the lot. “I know Jon Kraft is very engaged,” he said, referring to Robert Kraft’s son Jonathan Kraft, who is president of the Kraft Group. To that, the Kraft representative told town officials they were “leveraging those relationships all the time.” Champigny, who is no longer on the board, made his suggestion well before the major backlash against data centers erupted this year. But he foresaw at the time one concern residents might ultimately have: There would be a “a water constraint” because the centers require so much water for cooling. Still, he’d heard that using recycled water “could be the answer.” The current Kraft proposal includes the idea of using recycled water to avoid tapping town supplies. That didn’t mollify Sutton residents who appeared in droves at a Select Board meeting to oppose the new Kraft proposal on Tuesday night. “A facility of this scale would require vastly substantial quantities of water,” said Jessica Herbert, who grew up in Sutton and now resides in neighboring Millbury. Herbert said even if the water will be recycled from waste water, that raises questions over treatment and environmental harm. Reached on Wednesday, Champigny told the Globe he never imagined a data center of the size proposed by the Kraft Group. Co-location facilities are much smaller, he noted, than “the monstrosity” of an AI data center. His first preference for the property would be a sports complex, maybe with tennis courts, soccer fields, and restaurants, he said, modeled after Patriot Place in Foxborough. Ultimately, Sutton residents will get to weigh in, he said. “Town Meeting is their meeting,” he said. “That’s going to have the final say.” Regardless of Champigny’s intentions, whispers of a data center project loomed over the town and persisted throughout the months that followed. At a Select Board meeting on Dec. 9, 2025, members of the public expressed their disdain for a data center — although there was no official proposal on the table. At that meeting, Select Board member Jesse Limanek implied that some data center concept might be in the works but didn’t offer details. “As far as I know, the only ones who received that information were members of our board,” he said cryptically. “If that information somehow got out into the public and it’s incorrect, unfortunately that meant, you know, one of your elected officials shared information that they received in confidence,” he told attendees, according to video of the meeting. At that same meeting, Matthew Piekarski, the Kraft Group representative, said of the rumors: “We have not formally presented anything to the town. We haven’t talked to the town with regards to any specific opportunities within Lot 1 itself.” Limanek has not responded to requests for comment from the Globe. Representatives from Unified were present at that meeting as well. Len McAleer, Unified’s chief operating officer, reiterated at the December meeting that any project built on the empty lot would have to be in “the best interest of the town.” “Data center, no data center, whatever it happens to be, we’re going to put in that area what is in the best interest of the town and us,” McAleer said at the meeting. This week, Town Manager Austin J. Cyganiewicz told the Globe that he first officially heard of the mega-data-center proposal in late October. artigo.texto: AMD pronta para expansão de data centers na América Latina Região representa menos de 2% do mercado mundial de servidores, mas quase 8% dos gastos com nuvem, segundo executivo da fabricante. A AMD prevê uma expansão dos investimentos em data centers na América Latina, impulsionada pela demanda por IA e pela necessidade de manter determinadas cargas de trabalho em infraestrutura local. Segundo Nicolás Cánovas, líder da fabricante para a região, a América Latina representa menos de 2% do mercado mundial de servidores, mas responde por quase 8% dos gastos globais com serviços de nuvem. Os indicadores foram apresentados durante o AMD Partner Summit 2026, realizado entre 9 e 11 de novembro, na região de São Paulo. O encontro reúne representantes de cerca de 70 empresas parceiras e marca os 30 anos de atuação da companhia no Brasil. Para Cánovas, a diferença entre os dois indicadores mostra que a região expandiu sua capacidade computacional principalmente pela contratação de serviços de nuvem, sem desenvolver infraestrutura local na mesma proporção. “A América Latina, além de continuar crescendo como uma região focada em nuvem, terá que desenvolver seus próprios data centers para hospedar as cargas de trabalho e as informações sensíveis”, afirmou. Segundo o executivo, a tendência é de maior utilização de arquiteturas híbridas, que combinam serviços de nuvem e servidores próprios conforme os requisitos de cada aplicação. Os percentuais apresentados por Cánovas não vieram acompanhados do detalhamento das bases estatísticas utilizadas. Atualmente, a AMD registra crescimento das vendas para infraestrutura de processamento. No terceiro trimestre de 2026, a receita global da fabricante alcançou US$ 13,4 bilhões, alta anual de 45%. O segmento de data centers respondeu por US$ 8,5 bilhões, crescimento de 97% em relação ao mesmo período de 2025, impulsionado pelas vendas de processadores EPYC e aceleradores Instinct. Energia e Redata entram na avaliação dos investimentos A disponibilidade de energia, os custos operacionais e as condições regulatórias estão entre os fatores apontados pela AMD para a expansão da infraestrutura computacional na América Latina. Cánovas afirmou que as restrições de espaço físico e de acesso à energia em mercados como Estados Unidos e Europa contribuem para ampliar o interesse pela região. O executivo destacou a importância de políticas públicas, marcos regulatórios e oferta de energia limpa para viabilizar novos projetos. Questionado sobre o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata), Sergio Santos, diretor-geral da AMD Brasil, manifestou apoio a iniciativas de incentivo à produção local e à atração de tecnologia. “Qualquer programa do governo que incentive a produção local e traga mais tecnologia para o país é sempre bem-vindo”, declarou. Santos também apontou a composição da matriz energética brasileira como um fator considerado nas decisões de investimento e afirmou esperar que projetos em discussão comecem a se materializar em 2027. AMD quadruplica eficiência energética em IA A necessidade de ampliar o processamento sem aumentar proporcionalmente o consumo de eletricidade também orienta o desenvolvimento de produtos da AMD. Em comunicado divulgado em agosto, a fabricante informou ter alcançado, até meados de 2026, uma melhora estimada de quatro vezes na eficiência energética de seus sistemas de IA em relação a 2024. O resultado superou a meta intermediária de três vezes estabelecida para o período. A companhia trabalha com o objetivo de ampliar em 20 vezes a eficiência energética de sistemas de IA em nível de rack até 2030, considerando cargas de treinamento e inferência e utilizando 2024 como referência. Nas projeções apresentadas pela AMD, dois racks de sua futura arquitetura poderão oferecer capacidade computacional equivalente à de 570 racks de referência de 2024. Para a carga de treinamento utilizada no estudo, a fabricante estima uma redução de 20 vezes no consumo elétrico durante o uso e de até 28 vezes na intensidade de carbono. A estratégia envolve mudanças nos processadores, nas memórias, nas interconexões, no software e na arquitetura dos sistemas. Durante o Partner Summit, Santos relacionou a evolução dos processadores à possibilidade de modernizar instalações existentes e liberar capacidade elétrica para novas aplicações de IA. Segundo o executivo, dependendo da carga de trabalho, as soluções da AMD permitem consolidar até 11 servidores antigos em um único equipamento. No ano anterior, a relação apresentada pela fabricante era de sete para um. “Dependendo da carga de trabalho utilizada por uma empresa ou por um hyperescaler, podemos fazer uma consolidação de até 11 para um”, afirmou. Santos explicou que o aumento da densidade de processamento pode reduzir a quantidade de equipamentos necessários, a ocupação física e os custos de refrigeração. A companhia também considera métricas como desempenho por watt, desempenho por dólar e custos de licenciamento nas avaliações de infraestrutura. AMD amplia participação e rede de canais no Brasil Além dos investimentos em infraestrutura, a AMD está expandindo sua atuação no mercado corporativo brasileiro, especialmente entre pequenas e médias empresas. Segundo Santos, a companhia contratou mais de 12 profissionais para reforçar sua equipe de canais e ampliou seu programa de parceiros comerciais, buscando maior integração com as redes de distribuição de fabricantes como HP, Dell e Lenovo. A estratégia está associada à adoção de IA pelas empresas, incluindo aplicações executadas em servidores e computadores com processamento local. “A IA vai muito além do nosso chip. Ela faz parte do ecossistema”, afirmou Santos. O executivo destacou que a comercialização dessas soluções exige que revendedores e integradores ofereçam serviços de implementação, segurança e suporte técnico, além do fornecimento de equipamentos. “Se você vende apenas a caixa, qualquer cliente pode procurar na internet e comprar mais

artigo.texto: BYD’s new EV may be about the size of a Toyota Camry, but it’s playing in a whole different league when it comes to technology. BYD debuts new Cloud Carriage body control system BYD launched the second-generation Seal 07 last week, calling it “the new choice for a class-leading luxury experience.” It’s available in battery electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with prices starting at 139,900 yuan (about $21,000) for the plug-in hybrid and 149,900 yuan (around $22,500) for the fully electric version. Both versions measure 5,080 mm long, 1,960 mm wide, and 1,495 mm high, with a 2,960 mm wheelbase, which is slightly longer than the Toyota Camry. Don’t let the price fool you, however, the vehicle is packed with BYD’s latest breakthrough technology. The new Seal 07 EV uses a 76.7 kWh second-generation BYD Blade LFP battery that provides a CLTC range of up to 481 miles (775 km). Thanks to the second-gen Blade Batteries and BYD’s Flash Charging technology, the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 70% in just five minutes. A full recharge, or going from 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes. The Seal 07 is also BYD’s first vehicle to debut with its new Disus-M Intelligent Magnetorheological Body Control System. The setup features a front double-wishbone suspension and an enhanced rear five-link suspension. It works alongside BYD’s road-surface sensors that use LiDAR, plus its iTAC 2.0 Intelligent Torque Adaptation System. Zhang Zhuo, the general manager of BYD’s Ocean sales division, offered a better look at how the system works in real life in the video shown above. BYD said the system provides ultra-fast response times down to the millisecond. The advanced suspension system adjusts damping force across a wide range of 100 to 10,000 Nm. It’s equipped on the all-electric Flagship Seal 07 variant, while lower-priced versions have the Disus-C intelligent body control system. The top-spec EV model with the Disus-M setup starts at 172,900 yuan ($26,000). Still, not too bad for what you get. Inside, the new Seal 07 adopts BYD’s new interior design, including a 15.6″ floating center infotainment screen, a 10.25″ instrument cluster, and two rear passenger entertainment screens. BYD added a few premium extras, including a built-in 6.8L smart refrigerator, zero gravity seats, and driver headrest audio. Top comment by Dan B Quite impressive for sure. What's more impressive is that GM/Cadillac first offered magnetic ride control back in 2002 (a full 24 years ago!!). It may not have been quite as advanced as this system in 2026, but still one of the most advanced suspension systems offered to date for a line of vehicles. I really want this car!! I truly hope BYD will be able to sell this in the USA soon. The Seal 07 also debuts BYD’s Smart Ecosystem 2.0, including “Diva,” a smartwatch that lets drivers interact with the vehicle and manage functions remotely. Higher-priced versions are available with BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system, which includes a roof-mounted LiDAR. The setup provides safety and convenience features like Navigation on Autopilot in the city and on highways, plus full-scenario intelligent parking. For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super trade-in price” special, starting at 145,900 yuan ($22,000) for the new Seal 07 EV and 135,900 yuan ($20,500) for the PHEV version.

artigo.texto: Captona, a North American energy transition investment firm, has partnered with Sunrun to finance 9,400 residential solar and storage projects across more than 20 US states. The preferred equity investment covers 74 MW of solar generation and 110 MWh of battery storage. Sunrun said the project-level financing structure is designed to facilitate tax credit monetization and senior debt placements. Earlier this month, Sunrun expanded its distributed power plant in Puerto Rico to more than 60,000 customers. It now represents nearly 70,000 home batteries capable of delivering 45 MW of dispatchable power for up to four hours to support grid stability. Philippines-based renewable energy developer RASLAG Liwayway has secured a Certificate of Authority (COA) from the Department of Energy (DOE) for its proposed 98.24 MW AC/132.034 MW DC solar power project integrated with 25 MW/120.38 MWh of BESS. The project is located in Nueva Ecija, Philippines. It will be developed in two phases, each combining approximately 67.09 MW DC/49.92 MW AC of solar capacity with a 12.5 MW/60.19 MWh BESS. The COA follows an assessment of the project's technical and financial feasibility and marks a step toward implementation, RASLAG said. Denmark’s European Energy has agreed to sell a 50% stake in its 323 MW solar portfolio in the country to pension investment companies administered by Danish pension provider Sampension. The portfolio comprises the operational 148 MW Glejbjerg and 175 MW Holsted solar parks in Vejen, along with a planned 87 MW/351 MWh BESS. The transaction will strengthen the existing partnership between the companies, says European Energy, which also includes joint investments in Latvia and Greece. The deal is expected to close in December 2026. UK-based independent power producer (IPP) Elgin has acquired its sixth project in Italy, a planned 72 MW facility in Belvedere di Aquileia, Udine, in the Friuli Venezia Giulia region. The project will combine a 57 MW agrivoltaic plant with a 15 MW BESS, with an estimated construction cost of €46 million. The facility will use elevated solar modules and monitoring technologies to enable electricity generation alongside continued agricultural activities. Elgin said the acquisition supports its goal of developing more than 3 GW of renewable energy projects in Italy by 2030. UK-based project developer Ampeak Energy has completed the delivery of all batteries and key components for its 240 MWh Afon Wysg 1 (AW1) BESS project in Wales. Located at Uskmouth Sustainable Energy Park, the project includes 55 battery units supplied by e-STORAGE, a subsidiary of Canadian Solar, along with 36 inverters and associated grid infrastructure. It is expected to be energized in November 2026 and enter commercial operation in Q1 2027. Ampeak also plans to expand the project to 480 MWh. Jinko ESS, the energy storage arm of Chinese solar manufacturer JinkoSolar, has delivered BESS with a combined capacity of approximately 65 MW/260 MWh across Australia. These projects are located in Victoria, New South Wales, and South Australia. The projects include standalone battery systems and solar-plus-storage installations. Jinko ESS has supplied its flagship SunTera G2 liquid-cooled battery systems and served as the BESS integrator, while Spain-based Ingeteam provided the power conversion systems. Jinko ESS said it has delivered more than 600 MWh of storage capacity in Australia. Revolta AG, a German technology startup developing battery systems and power electronics, has installed and commissioned its first 10 kWh sodium-ion home battery storage system at a customer site in Germany. The system, near Aschaffenburg, comprises five battery modules. It is installed at a property that already houses around 20 kW solar PV system and a small hydroelectric power plant. Revolta says the installation marks the commercial launch of its residential sodium-ion storage solution. It plans to commission additional systems at selected customer sites across Germany in the coming weeks. Revolta is the recipient of funding from the State of Hesse under the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) to develop sodium-ion AC battery for households, even those without rooftop solar. This includes rental apartments. Spanish renewable energy company Umbrella Global Energy has expanded its contract with ceramics manufacturer Pamesa Grupo Empresarial by €11.6 million to extend the Pamesa Net Zero project in Spain. The expansion will add 6.71 MW of solar PV capacity and 51 MWh of BESS across Pamesa’s additional industrial sites and existing facilities. The project integrates solar generation, battery storage and intelligent energy management technology supplied through Umbrella subsidiaries IM2 Energía Solar and Turbo Energy. The expansion builds on an initial €73.6 million contract signed in 2025, covering 80.56 MW of solar generation and 366.84 MWh of storage. Alinta Energy, an Australian energy retailer and power generator, has commissioned its 100 MW/200 MWh Wagerup BESS project in Western Australia. The facility has been operating commercially since September 2026. Alinta said the project faced challenging site conditions that required design changes, including raising the battery platform and constructing retaining infrastructure. It adds storage capacity to Alinta Energy's generation portfolio.

artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Modine inicia a produção de chillers no Texas para data centers de IA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google A Modine anunciou o início da produção comercial em 11 de novembro de 2026, em uma nova fábrica de chillers da Airedale, com 682.000 pés quadrados, em Grand Prairie, Texas, ampliando a capacidade de fabricação nos Estados Unidos de equipamentos para refrigeração de data centers. A unidade, construída especificamente para esse fim, é dedicada à fabricação de chillers de 2 MW e 3 MW com resfriamento livre. A capacidade adicional é voltada a provedores de nuvem em hiperescala, operadores de colocation e ambientes de computação de IA de alta densidade. O presidente e CEO Neil D. Brinker descreveu o lançamento como um marco no plano de expansão da capacidade da Modine nos Estados Unidos e afirmou que instalar capacidade perto dos clientes tem o objetivo de apoiar a entrega de sistemas de refrigeração projetados sob medida. Ampliação gradual da produção em Grand Prairie A linha de produção inicial está em operação. A Modine tem como meta colocar quatro linhas em operação até o fim do atual ano fiscal, condicionada ao comissionamento dos equipamentos, à preparação da força de trabalho e a outras considerações operacionais. Atualmente, a unidade opera em um turno, com planos de ampliar sistematicamente a operação para três turnos. A Modine espera que Grand Prairie se torne a maior unidade de fabricação de chillers da Airedale em sua rede global. Os chillers fazem parte de um portfólio mais amplo da Airedale, que inclui resfriadores secos, unidades de distribuição de líquido refrigerante e controles inteligentes. Segundo a Modine, os sistemas são projetados para atender a demandas térmicas complexas e de alta densidade, maximizando a eficiência energética e hídrica. Investimento na capacidade dos Estados Unidos por trás da unidade A Modine anunciou o investimento de US$ 100 milhões em 29 de julho de 2025, prevendo então que os recursos seriam aplicados nos 12 a 18 meses seguintes para ampliar a capacidade de fabricação de produtos de refrigeração de data centers na América do Norte. O plano abrangia uma nova unidade na região de Dallas, a expansão da fábrica em Grenada, Mississippi, e a possível reutilização de unidades existentes da Performance Technologies em Franklin, Wisconsin, e Jefferson City, Missouri. O plano também incluía melhorias nas capacidades de engenharia, desenvolvimento de produtos e testes, além da criação de novos empregos e do apoio à realocação e à requalificação de funcionários existentes. Eric McGinnis, então presidente do segmento Climate Solutions da Modine, descreveu a expansão como uma estratégia de produção local para atendimento local, concentrada nas regiões onde a Modine observava a maior demanda. Planos para a unidade de Grand Prairie e para o emprego A cidade de Grand Prairie anunciou a escolha do local pela Modine em 14 de outubro de 2025, identificando o endereço 2100 Refuge Way como a localização e projetando a criação de mais de 1.000 novos empregos, com remuneração anual média de US$ 66.760. A Modine mencionou a localização na região de Dallas–Fort Worth, a infraestrutura de transporte, a proximidade do Aeroporto Internacional de DFW, o acesso a uma força de trabalho qualificada, apoiado por programas regionais de treinamento, e a colaboração com funcionários da prefeitura. O cronograma original da cidade previa o início das obras no quarto trimestre de 2025 e o começo das operações no primeiro trimestre de 2026. O início da produção anunciado ocorreu depois dessa previsão operacional inicial. No mesmo anúncio de investimento, Brinker definiu como meta da administração que a receita total de data centers se aproximasse de US$ 2 bilhões no ano fiscal de 2028. Grand Prairie transforma parte desse programa em capacidade operacional; a dimensão de sua contribuição no curto prazo para essa meta depende agora da conclusão de uma ampliação condicionada ao comissionamento dos equipamentos e à preparação da força de trabalho.

Há dois anos, escrevi nesta coluna sobre a pegada de carbono das baterias de íons de lítio. O título Pegada de carbono das baterias – parte 1: do 8 ao 80 era uma provocação para mostrar como diferentes estudos podiam chegar a resultados muito diferentes para uma mesma tecnologia, dependendo das premissas adotadas e, principalmente, dos dados utilizados. Naquele momento, um dos pontos que mais me chamou a atenção estava no grafite utilizado nas baterias. Quem acompanha as discussões sobre veículos elétricos provavelmente já se acostumou a ouvir que a bateria é o grande vilão ambiental do carro elétrico. A afirmação é simplista e há uma questão interessante por trás dela. Quanto realmente sabemos sobre as emissões associadas à fabricação das baterias? A resposta depende muito da qualidade dos inventários utilizados nas avaliações de ciclo de vida. Em 2024, esta coluna já havia destacado diferenças expressivas nos dados disponíveis para a produção de grafite. Um dos problemas estava relacionado à produção de grafite sintético em rotas industriais amplamente utilizadas na China, entre elas o processo Acheson. A produção exige temperaturas muito elevadas e grande consumo de eletricidade. Além disso, os cadinhos de grafite utilizados no processo sofrem desgaste e precisam ser substituídos. Quando esse material não é corretamente contabilizado, uma parcela relevante das emissões simplesmente desaparece do cálculo. Naquele artigo, mostrei que algumas bases de dados utilizadas em avaliações de ciclo de vida apresentavam valores de emissões para o grafite muito inferiores aos encontrados quando o processo industrial era representado de maneira mais completa. Era uma questão metodológica, mas com consequências práticas. Se o inventário de um dos principais materiais da bateria está errado, a pegada de carbono atribuída à bateria também estará. Na época, era razoável tratar o assunto como uma hipótese que precisava de melhores dados. Agora, esses dados começam a surgir e permitem avaliar com mais segurança o peso do grafite na pegada de carbono das baterias. Um estudo publicado por pesquisadores alemães no Journal of Energy Storage (PUSHPENDRA et al, 2026) utilizou dados industriais primários, revisitando justamente o problema do grafite. O resultado é relevante porque mostra que a escolha do inventário utilizado na avaliação pode alterar significativamente a pegada de carbono atribuída à bateria. Em uma célula NMC622 analisada pelos pesquisadores, composta por níquel, manganês e cobalto na proporção 6:2:2, a pegada de carbono passou de aproximadamente 58 para 93 kgCO₂e/kWh quando os dados de grafite foram atualizados com dados industriais primários. Um aumento de cerca de 60%. Embora o estudo tenha sido conduzido com uma célula do tipo níquel-manganês-cobalto, suas conclusões são relevantes também para as baterias LFP (lítio-ferro-fosfato), hoje amplamente utilizadas em veículos elétricos e sistemas de armazenamento estacionário. Isso porque ambas as tecnologias utilizam predominantemente grafite no ânodo. Em outras palavras, mesmo quando se eliminam metais críticos como níquel e cobalto do cátodo, a origem e o processo produtivo do grafite continuam exercendo influência decisiva sobre a pegada de carbono da bateria. Observe ainda que não se trata de uma diferença marginal. É o tipo de alteração que pode mudar a conclusão de uma análise de ciclo de vida. O resultado também não apareceu do nada. Um estudo publicado por CARRÈRE et al. (2024) no mesmo periódico já havia identificado forte subestimação nos dados disponíveis para o grafite sintético de grau-bateria. Outros trabalhos publicados nos últimos anos chegaram a conclusões semelhantes, apontando que os inventários utilizados em muitas avaliações ainda dependem de dados antigos, secundários ou que não representam adequadamente as rotas industriais atuais. O que isso tudo significa? Frequentemente, vemos números sobre “uma bateria emite determinada quantidade de CO₂ por kWh”, “um veículo elétrico compensa sua fabricação depois de tantos quilômetros” ou “determinado modelo apresenta determinada vantagem sobre um veículo a combustão”. Nada disso é tão simples. O grafite é um bom exemplo de como uma variável aparentemente secundária pode alterar o resultado final. Por isso, quando se pretende calcular a pegada de carbono de uma bateria, escolher um número médio da literatura e simplesmente multiplicá-lo pela capacidade em kWh pode produzir uma falsa sensação de precisão. Uma bateria de 50 kWh não carrega consigo uma etiqueta dizendo quantas toneladas de CO₂ foram emitidas para fabricá-la. Esse número precisa ser construído a partir da cadeia de produção. Se queremos comparar tecnologias de propulsão, precisamos comparar sistemas completos. O veículo elétrico tem emissões associadas à mineração, ao processamento de materiais, à fabricação da bateria, à geração de eletricidade e ao uso. O veículo a combustão tem sua própria cadeia de petróleo, refino, distribuição e combustão. Quando utiliza biocombustíveis, entram também na conta as emissões e remoções associadas à produção de biomassa, ao processamento industrial e à logística envolvida. Híbridos acrescentam uma combinação adicional de componentes, combustíveis e fontes de energia. A pergunta relevante não é qual tecnologia parece mais limpa. É qual delas apresenta menor impacto quando colocamos todas as etapas na conta. E, para responder, precisamos de bons dados. Meu artigo de 2024 não pretendia dizer que todas as baterias tinham uma determinada pegada de carbono. A questão era justamente a incerteza. artigo.texto: BMW Group has contracted Samsung SDI in Europe and LG Energy Solution (LGES) in the US as additional cell suppliers for its Gen6 high-voltage batteries. Following the nominations, the car maker will receive European-produced cells from CATL, EVE Energy, and Samsung SDI, whilst LGES will deliver cells within the US. The appointments follow the company's "local for local" principle, whereby components are acquired close to vehicle assembly locations wherever possible. Both manufacturers will supply BMW Group from their established regional plants beginning in the late 2020s. BMW stated that targeted localisation across Europe, Asia, and North America reduces transit distances and bolsters supply security, while a globally diversified network supports flexibility and resilience. Assembly of the Gen6 high-voltage batteries will take place at five newly constructed facilities adjacent to vehicle plants in Debrecen, Hungary; Shenyang, China; Woodruff, US; San Luis Potosí, Mexico; and Irlbach-Straßkirchen in Lower Bavaria, Germany. Series production of the batteries commenced in Shenyang last month. Following Debrecen and Irlbach-Straßkirchen, Shenyang is the third location in the new global production network for Gen6 battery technology. BMW added that localising industrial value creation remains highly complex, particularly for cell production, requiring heavy investment and supply arrangements with global technology leaders willing to set up operations locally. It added that fostering regional battery ecosystems over the long term depends on feasible political regulations and attractive local conditions for the necessary industrialisation periods. The group also retains internal development, production, and recycling capabilities at three Bavarian competence centres. The Battery Cell Competence Centre in Munich investigates new cell technologies, whereas the Cell Manufacturing Competence Centre in Parsdorf tests near-series cells and evaluates high-quality, resource-efficient production. In Salching, German circular economy service provider Encory will construct and operate the Cell Recycling Competence Centre, recovering raw materials using BMW's direct recycling method to reintegrate into production. BMW purchasing and supplier network management board member Nicolai Martin said: "We aim to ensure our products' global competitiveness and to be successful in different markets. To achieve this, we operate as locally as possible in our value chains, leveraging the potential of our global procurement markets. Through our battery cell partnerships, we are actively strengthening value creation in Europe and the US." "BMW Group adds Samsung SDI and LGES as battery suppliers" was originally created and published by Just Auto, a GlobalData owned brand.
