artigo.texto: SAN JOSE, Calif., Nov. 11, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- QuantumScape Corporation (NASDAQ: QS), a global leader in solid-state lithium-metal battery technology, today announced Osprey: its next-generation open platform for all-solid-state batteries. Osprey cells have delivered the world’s first public data demonstrating a sulfide-based cathode cycling 1,000 times under just one atmosphere of pressure - an unmatched capability that is necessary for automotive solid-state batteries. Osprey pairs the QS proprietary ceramic separator and anode-free lithium-metal design with a solid cathode, creating an all-solid-state cell. Osprey builds on the company’s QSE platform, and opens new licensing and co-development options for current QS customers and expanding its offering to developers of sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries. QS technology has demonstrated an enhanced safety profile compared to conventional lithium-ion cells, along with low operating pressure and excellent energy retention. Osprey’s all-solid cathode, paired with the proprietary QS ceramic separator, enables additional performance benefits, including faster charging, operation across a wider range of temperatures, and projected energy densities up to ~1,100 Wh/L. In early testing, Osprey cells have demonstrated: - Cycle life: 1,000 full charge cycles with ~80% capacity retention under gold-standard testing conditions - Fast charging: 10% to 80% in five-minutes - Low pressure: Requires only one atmosphere of pressure - Cold-weather performance: Operational to less than -20 °C (-4 °F) More information, including test results and conditions, can be found in a new white paper. The battery industry has long pursued all-solid-state batteries using sulfide-based electrolytes, but this has yet to result in a commercially viable technology. Sulfides can react with lithium metal, which shortens battery life, and they typically need to be held under high pressure to operate, which is impractical for vehicles and many other applications. Osprey is conceived as an open platform capable of working with a range of cathode chemistries. QS has tested Osprey with all-solid cathodes developed both in-house and by its automotive customers, laying the groundwork for multiple technology pathways for solid-state battery development. "Osprey is the result of years of frontier R&D efforts, and we’re excited to share it publicly for the first time,” said Dr. Siva Sivaram, president and CEO of QS. "The industry has invested heavily in sulfide-based batteries but keeps hitting the same fundamental limits. As the data shows, Osprey can address these limitations. We believe Osprey can unlock the full potential of all-solid-state batteries, and our goal is to make it the leading platform for solid-state battery development.” QS is already working with partners across the automotive industry on development using the Osprey platform. Cells based on the company’s QSE platform are shipping to customers today, and Osprey represents its long-term technology solution for all-solid-state battery development. About QuantumScape Corporation QuantumScape is on a mission to revolutionize energy storage to enable a sustainable future. The company’s next-generation solid-state lithium-metal battery technology is designed to enable greater energy density, faster charging and enhanced safety to support the transition away from legacy energy sources toward a lower carbon future. For more information, visit www.quantumscape.com. artigo.texto: Microsoft President Brad Smith talks data centers, Millionaires Tax WASHINGTON STATE — Microsoft President Brad Smith acknowledged tech companies will need to brace for further legislation to limit data centers, amid a growing wave of pushback against the facilities. In his first comments since Election Day, Smith addressed the fact that 40 of 41 local ballot measures across the country were approved to limit data centers. “We are going to see more legislation. We're going to see state legislation across the country. We're going to see federal legislation across the country. I don't know how many of those bills will pass, but I think at some level, the best thing for our industry to recognize is usually to give people confidence that things will be done in a responsible way,” Smith said in an interview on the Microsoft campus in Redmond on Monday morning. “Everyone who wants to build a data center has to do it responsibly. I think that's the message.” Smith says the company’s internal polling suggests 15% of the public wants to build data centers, another 15% don’t want them built at all, and 70% say they want them built responsibly. Smith points to the story in Quincy, Washington, where Microsoft broke ground on a new data center and tax revenue in Grant County skyrocketed, leading to the construction of a new school, hospital, police station and fire station. “The poverty rate’s been cut in half. The property taxes that people pay have fallen, but property tax revenue has grown 12-fold, basically because of data centers,” he said. “When we started 20 years ago, Quincy, Washington, had one traffic light. Now it has two. There are ways to do this.” Smith and Microsoft also dipped their toes into the state elections, funding a political action committee called “Washington Needs to Compete." Smith had sounded alarm bells prior to the vote, suggesting a payroll tax in the future would be like “waving a flag” asking businesses to move jobs out of state. The PAC aired ads during Seahawks games but stopped short of taking a position on the Millionaires Tax, and Gov. Bob Ferguson was reportedly upset about it all. On Monday, Smith said, “The public has voted, it's offered its point of view, and that tax has been upheld, and barring a change from the Supreme Court, we should all assume it's going to become part of Washington state law as we go forward.” “I think everybody in the state worries about affordability. We do. Our employees do. Everybody does. We also need to recognize that when taxes rise on businesses, businesses inevitably pass those costs on to consumers, and so ongoing tax increases are making the state less affordable,” he added. As for his relationship with Ferguson, Smith said, “We have long worked with Bob Ferguson. We work with him as attorney general. We work with him as governor. I think the state is fortunate to have him as a governor. I look forward to working to support him. I especially look forward to working with him and our leaders in Olympia. Let's go forward in a way that really focuses on budget stability, affordability for our people, the creation of new businesses and jobs for our economy.” Ferguson, along with Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, has indicated the payroll tax is off the table with the approval of the Millionaires Tax.

artigo.texto: Reno pauses new data center approvals as officials weigh water, power rules RENO, Nev. — Reno’s decision to pause new data center approvals has intensified questions about how much water and power the facilities could require — and which agencies actually have the authority to decide whether more can be built. RELATED: No new data centers in Reno: Council adopts temporary moratorium, starts drafting rules Data centers are large facilities that house computer servers and related equipment that support internet services, cloud computing and artificial intelligence. Centra, the company building a data center off Keystone Avenue, describes its facilities as “engineered from day one to support modern digital services and AI workloads.” As the region weighs what rules should apply to future projects, the Truckee Meadows Regional Planning Agency is studying how data centers could affect Northern Nevada. Jeremey Smith, the agency’s director of regional planning, said the agency’s role is not to approve or deny projects, but to provide research and recommendations. “In the data center conversation specifically, our role is to research, provide factual information about data centers and growth in the region of data centers,” Smith said. “And we were asked to come up with recommendations and best practices.” Smith said data centers are tied to growing technology use. “We’re working as a society and we’re using our phones, we’re use more computers,” he said. “It’s underpinning the digital economy, if you will.” One concern highlighted in the research is electricity demand. “The power demand is unprecedented for data centers. I mean, it’s huge,” Smith said. RELATED: NV Energy’s new long-term plan highlights massive power demand tied to data centers NV Energy said the potential demand tied to data center proposals in Nevada totals 22,000 megawatts — roughly enough to power 20 million average U.S. homes at once. Jeff Brigger, NV Energy’s vice president of business development, said the utility is required to serve customers. He also said data center developers would be responsible for major upfront costs tied to the infrastructure needed to supply them. “They also would pay upfront costs for the transmission infrastructure that we need to build to serve them essentially, growth pays for growth,” Brigger said. Water is another major issue. The Truckee Meadows Water Authority plans for the region’s water needs, and about 80% to 85% of the water it provides comes from the Truckee River — a key reason residents have been asking how much water additional data centers could use. Danny Rotter of TMWA said the data centers currently in progress account for a relatively small amount of water use. “The six data centers that we have underway right now use only about 22 acre-feet, or about 50 to 60 homes’ worth of water,” Rotter said. While public utilities provide information and plan for the resources a data center would need, local leaders use those plans when making final decisions about whether projects can move forward. Newly elected Mayor Kate Marshall said she opposes placing data centers in Reno neighborhoods, including the Keystone Avenue area. “Data centers don’t belong in our town. They don’t belonging in your neighborhood. They don’t belong near your child’s school or next to your grocery store. And they certainly didn’t belong on Keystone Avenue,” Marshall said. Reno’s moratorium on new data centers runs through Aug. 31, 2027 — or until the city adopts regulations and rules for approving new data centers

artigo.texto: The dust from last week's rout of AI-related stocks is settling. But the damage is done. Confidence in these companies' foreseeable futures is weakened. Even names outside the heart of artificial intelligence mania have been upended. Take GE Vernova (NYSE: GEV), for instance, which simply makes power-generating equipment used by some AI data center owners. Shares of this industrial outfit are down 25% since their early October high, with much of this setback materializing just this month following concerning quarterly reports from Alphabet and Nvidia. There may be some degree of misunderstanding regarding GE Vernova's business, however, that needs to be clarified. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » An important detail You may be aware that GE Vernova manufactures a number of power-related solutions, ranging from transformers to wind turbines to hydropower equipment. But its leading product line right now is natural gas turbines, accounting for most of last quarter's $6.1 billion in revenue from its power division, which was nearly half of its total top line of $12.6 billion. Sales of this arm's wares improved 25% year over year, while orders for future deliveries of power equipment -- still mostly natural gas turbines -- jumped 178% to $21.8 billion. Yes, artificial intelligence data centers are now using gas turbines as secondary or even primary power sources, and yes, some data center owners and operators are purchasing this equipment from GE Vernova. That's why its stock's been so vulnerable to worries of a sudden slowdown in AI's anticipated growth. Just don't lose perspective on the matter. As CEO Scott Strazik said of Vernova's power division in last month's third-quarter conference call, "Demand also remains diverse, with approximately 100 customers in 25 different countries, of which approximately 80% are traditional customers and 20% are for data centers." In other words, GE Vernova isn't nearly as vulnerable to a contraction in artificial intelligence capital spending as the stock's recent sell-off suggests. Tailwind outside of AI There's some nuance to consider. While most of GE Vernova's gas turbine buyers are more traditional institutions like utility companies, many of these buyers are still purchasing this equipment to provide electricity to data centers. As Goldman Sachs notes, data center demand for power alone is set to more than double between last year and the end of 2027.

artigo.texto: O Acre deu um importante passo em direção à certificação internacional de seus créditos de carbono. Na terça-feira, 10, em Antalya, na Turquia, a governadora Mailza Assis participou de uma reunião com a ART Trees, entidade responsável pela validação de projetos de carbono, para discutir o progresso da auditoria necessária ao reconhecimento dos créditos jurisdicionais do estado. A reunião ocorreu durante a 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP31). O encontro é um desdobramento das articulações realizadas em junho, durante a Semana de Ação Climática em Londres, onde Mailza se encontrou com Mary Grady, presidente da ART Trees. Também participaram da reunião Neide de Lima, presidente do Instituto de Mudanças Climáticas e Regulação de Serviços Ambientais (IMC), Victor Hugo Rondon, consultor internacional de mercados de carbono, Madson Cameli, chefe de gabinete, e Lúcia Madrid, diretora associada da ART. O principal objetivo da reunião foi atualizar o status da auditoria e alinhar procedimentos para avançar na certificação. O reconhecimento internacional permitirá ao Acre registrar créditos de carbono jurisdicionais, facilitando futuras negociações no mercado internacional. Mailza expressou sua gratidão pela disponibilidade da ART e reiterou o compromisso do governo em concluir o processo, afirmando que “estamos colocando um grande esforço, por meio do IMC, para concluir esse processo, que será muito importante para o desenvolvimento do Acre.” A auditoria está sendo conduzida por uma empresa independente que segue os critérios do padrão internacional ART Trees, que estabelece normas para a contabilização e verificação de reduções de emissões decorrentes do desmatamento e degradação florestal. Neide Lima destacou a importância de cumprir todos os requisitos previstos para a conclusão satisfatória da etapa, com o Acre atualmente na oitava de 11 etapas do processo de certificação. Entre os próximos passos, estão a finalização das verificações técnicas e a submissão dos resultados ao conselho deliberativo da ART. Uma nova fase da auditoria está prevista para o primeiro trimestre de 2027, quando auditores visitarão comunidades no Acre para realizar verificações. Neide também ressaltou a dimensão social do processo, enfatizando que os recursos obtidos com a comercialização dos créditos devem contribuir para o desenvolvimento das comunidades locais. Victor Hugo Rondon sublinhou a necessidade de assegurar que todas as exigências internacionais sejam cumpridas, levando em conta as prioridades sociais e ambientais do governo acreano. A Companhia de Desenvolvimento de Serviços Ambientais (CDSA) também será envolvida nas próximas etapas, especialmente nas estratégias relacionadas às negociações dos créditos certificados. O governo do Acre espera que a certificação abra oportunidades para atrair investimentos em agricultura familiar, extrativismo sustentável e iniciativas de preservação ambiental. A certificação envolve uma avaliação independente para assegurar que os resultados ambientais atendam aos requisitos estabelecidos, com cada crédito de carbono representando uma tonelada de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO₂e) cuja emissão foi reduzida ou removida. O IMC continua promovendo agendas estratégicas durante a COP31, defendendo a valorização das comunidades e apresentando projetos de desenvolvimento sustentável para ampliar o diálogo com governos, investidores e instituições internacionais. artigo.texto: Normally this newsletter is dedicated to local San Diego issues. But allow me, for a moment, to fixate on members of Congress. They’re actually doing something – though how good it will be, on the whole, is up for debate. A contingent of Democrats and Republicans just wrote the country’s biggest set of permitting reforms in years, and they’re trying to pass it before Democrats take over, following the “blue wave” midterm elections. The reforms would accelerate permitting for energy and transmission projects while also limiting environmental review, and put the onus on data center developers to pay for all their own energy costs. The Senate got enough votes Monday to limit debate on the so-called BAAJA or Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act and move it forward for a final vote. The bill could have big implications for the data center proposed on U.S. Navy land near downtown San Diego. This 400-plus-page law would force data centers, rather than taxpayers, to pay for all their costs – both the power and the upgrades to the local power grid to keep it running. While California lawmakers passed similar laws on data centers this last session, they don’t apply to San Diego’s proposed project. The state doesn’t have jurisdiction over land owned by the U.S. Navy. For that reason, among others, San Diego Rep. Scott Peters, along with clean energy proponents and developers and labor leaders, urged fellow Democrats to support the bill generated by the currently Republican-controlled Congress. “Democrats say they want to lower utility costs and combat climate change. Research shows the bipartisan permitting package would do both,” Peters told Politico recently. If you’d like to go deeper, David Roberts, a clean energy journalist and host of the Volts podcast, spent two hours unpacking its main reforms, chief among them allowing both electric transmission lines (the biggest powerlines carrying energy across state lines) and natural gas pipelines to be built much faster. Electricity demand by Americans had been stagnant until the recent business of building data centers to fuel artificial intelligence coupled with electrification of cars and buildings exploded. But it takes 10 to 15 years to actually build a new transmission line, the highways of the power grid that can carry power from state to state. Whole regions of the country are beginning to hit their limit in terms of how much power they can get to customers during heat waves, for example. The culprit? Many backers of the bill say it’s long, arduous permitting processes making it difficult to expand energy grid infrastructure. Without transmission lines, it’s a lot harder to bring new clean energy projects online, dispatch their power to places that need it and really transition the grid off of fossil fuels. The kicker is, BAAJA also makes it easier to build things like natural gas pipelines which are not good for the climate. (That’s because natural gas is a fossil fuel burning as almost pure methane, a huge climate heater-upper). But that’s how lawmakers were able to make this a bipartisan deal. In any good compromise, neither side is happy. The bet, as Roberts put it, is that both energy sources (Republicans favoring fossil fuels and Democrats favoring clean energy) would be on more equal footing to compete for energy proliferation. To speed up their permitting, both would get to bypass, in large part, the National Environmental Protection Act, which requires an analysis of a project’s environmental impacts. (Projects would still be subject to laws like the Clean Water Act, however.) Environmental groups like the Center for Biological Diversity have decried this law for that reason. Daniel Palken, Roberts’ guest who works for the oil-exec-owned Arnold Ventures, says that if this bill passes, it would allow a fair amount more drilling for oil and gas especially on federal land. The Rhodium Group, an independent research think tank based in New York City, did a bunch of modeling on what the outcome of the bill reforms might be – and the conclusion was to take some bad with the good. The researchers’ paper said that the bill would allow for up to 249 gigawatts of clean resources to be built through 2040 – a 50 percent increase to average U.S. electricity demand now. Liquified natural gas production, mainly to be exported outside the U.S., would increase by up to 15 percent. They estimate that tradeoff, in the best case scenario for the climate, would reduce economy-wide greenhouse gas emissions by 149 million metric tons by 2040. That’s like taking 32 million cars off the road for one year. But it’s not as astounding as it sounds. Humanity as a whole needs to reduce greenhouse gas emission by 1,350 billion metric tons to have a 50 percent shot at reducing global warming by 2 degrees Celsius – a level of warming the United Nations predicts will still cause near total destruction of the world’s coral reefs and intensify drought, sea level rise and extreme heat on millions. The U.S. is the biggest emitter, especially if you include our offshoring of much of our manufacturing demand. But it’s a start, I guess. In Other News - Rep. artigo.texto: Could tech giants eye Florida for data centers after midterms? AUBURNDALE, Fla. - A fierce political and environmental clash is brewing in Auburndale, where more than 1,000 residents mobilized against a proposed hyperscale data center amid fears that nationwide tech restrictions will drive massive industrial projects to Florida. Auburndale data center pushback What we know: More than 1,000 residents packed a public workshop Tuesday night to fight a proposed data center. Community members sounded alarms over persistent noise, environmental pollution, and declining property values. Midterm elections and data centers The backstory: Tech companies face tightening rules across the country following the recent midterm elections. Democratic governors in Texas, Georgia, and New Mexico plan to impose strict moratoriums and regulations on the sector. Florida emerged as an outlier after Republican Rep. Byron Donalds narrowly defeated Democrat David Jolly in the gubernatorial race with millions in tech industry backing. Donalds shifted his tone during the campaign from fully pro-business to remaining open to development while adopting caveats and restrictions. Florida remains highly attractive to developers because tech firms already operate across the state, alongside an existing multinational talent pool. The state also possesses robust power grids and extensive fiber-optic infrastructure that help hyperscale facilities manage extreme cooling demands. Shifting tech industry landscape What we don't know: Officials have not yet confirmed whether municipal leaders will approve or block the facility's construction permits. State authorities have not detailed how proposed statewide caveats will interact with local zoning ordinances. Balancing economy and community What they're saying: AI strategist Dr. Jill Schiefelbein emphasized that data center expansion transcends partisan labels. "When it comes to data centers, I don’t think this is a red state versus blue state issue at all," Schiefelbein said. "I think there are much more nuanced perspectives that go into it. Will companies be looking at Florida? Yes, 100 percent they will be. But will it become the next hotbed for data centers? Only time will tell." Schiefelbein added that state officials face a precarious balancing act between regional investment and neighborhood preservation. "I think there will be a fine line the government will have to walk between being pro-business—because there are some massive economic gains that can be realized by the state when you have tech and data centers move in—versus what the short, medium, and long-term consequences are for the everyday resident," Schiefelbein said. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from FOX 13 reporter Carla Bayron, who attended the public workshop and interviewed AI strategist Dr. Jill Schiefelbein, as well as public election statements from gubernatorial candidates.

artigo.texto: - A new global network launching at COP31 aims to channel more carbon market investment towards climate projects, particularly in developing countries. - Carbon pricing is expanding, but fragmented markets, inconsistent standards and concerns over credit quality are limiting the potential to mobilize finance. - Convened by UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the Network will bring together exchanges, financial institutions and other market actors to improve transparency, strengthen trust and facilitate cross-border transactions. A new global network will launch at the UN climate summit COP31 on 12 November in Antalya, Türkiye, aiming to tackle fragmentation in carbon markets and help channel more investment into climate projects, particularly in developing countries. Convened by UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the Global Carbon Market Network will seek to strengthen links between carbon and capital markets, improve transparency and credibility, and facilitate cross-border transactions. Carbon markets remain fragmented across different standards, registries and trading systems. Concerns over credit quality, transparency and double counting have weakened confidence and constrained market development, particularly in developing economies. Ahead of the official launch, UNCTAD Acting Secretary-General Pedro Manuel Moreno expressed hope that the Network would help make carbon pricing a more effective tool for for reducing emissions and mobilizing climate finance for developing countries. Connecting fragmented carbon markets “Carbon markets can play a role in putting a price on emissions and mobilizing finance for climate action, but their effectiveness depends on trust, integrity and functioning market infrastructure,” said Nan Li Collins, UNCTAD’s Director of Investment and Enterprise and Chair of the UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges Initiative. The Network will promote cooperation among exchanges and market institutions, including technical work on market integrity, measuring and verifying emissions reductions, and digital technologies to improve transparency and reduce transaction costs. Why it matters now Carbon pricing is expanding. Emissions trading systems and carbon taxes now cover nearly 30% of global greenhouse gas emissions and generated more than $107 billion in public revenue in 2025. The UNCTAD-convened Network will not create a new carbon market or standard. Instead, it aims to connect existing markets and initiatives, including voluntary and compliance markets. Voluntary carbon markets have particular potential to channel private investment across borders. UNCTAD research shows that most voluntary carbon credits are generated by projects in developing countries and sold to buyers in developed countries. Stronger links between markets could help build confidence in these transactions and expand financing for projects that reduce or remove emissions in developing countries. Who is participating and what’s next? The Network’s initial activities include capacity-building programmes, market-practice benchmarking, a global synthesis report on the state of carbon markets, and engagement with emissions trading system regulators on technical and interoperability issues. Founding members span Africa, Asia, the Middle East, Europe and Latin America. They include: Astana International Financial Centre Authority, Capacity Building Alliance for Sustainable Investment, Casablanca Finance City (Morocco), Climate Impact X (Singapore), Colombian Association of Carbon Market Actors (ASOCARBONO), Financial Services Development Council (Hong Kong, China), Global Carbon Council (Qatar), Indonesia Stock Exchange, Johannesburg Stock Exchange, Macao International Carbon Emission Exchange, Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority, UK Carbon Market Forum, Verra, and Voluntary Carbon Market Company (Saudi Arabia).

artigo.texto: Trump '100%' backs bill to make data centers pay more, potentially lowering electricity costs President Trump says the White House is "100% behind" a bipartisan bill that could reduce electricity bills by requiring data centers to pay more for energy infrastructure. Trump '100%' backs bill to make data centers pay more, potentially lowering electricity costs President Trump says the White House is "100% behind" a bipartisan bill that could reduce electricity bills by requiring data centers to pay more for energy infrastructure. President Donald Trump said Monday he is fully behind bipartisan legislation that could lower Americans' electricity bills by requiring large data centers to shoulder more of the costs of expanding the nation's electrical grid. "We are behind it 100%," Trump told reporters when asked about the legislation. Congress is considering the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act as electricity demand grows rapidly across the country, driven in part by the explosion of artificial intelligence and data centers. The legislation would speed up federal approval of energy infrastructure projects while requiring large data centers to contribute more toward the costs of expanding the electrical grid. An analysis by Grid Strategies estimates that, under the legislation, data centers would pay an additional $35 billion toward transmission infrastructure over the next decade, compared with what they would otherwise pay under current policies. A separate analysis from Rhodium Group estimates the bill could save the average American household between $50 and $78 a year on electricity by 2040, compared with what households would otherwise pay without the legislation. Both analyses examined an earlier version of the bill, before lawmakers released amendments Saturday. The savings are projections, not guaranteed reductions from today's electricity bills. "This bill has specific provisions related to data centers where they pay more. In fact, they pay more than their fair share. Intentionally to enable them to pay for more of the grid and then other rate payers, you and me. And homes and businesses. We would all pay relatively less," said Rob Gramlich, president of Grid Strategies. How the legislation would work Energy experts say the country faces an infrastructure bottleneck as electricity demand grows. Building the power plants and transmission lines needed to keep up can take years, with federal permitting among the obstacles. The legislation aims to speed up that process by setting stricter deadlines for environmental reviews and making it easier to approve new transmission lines. It would also give states additional options to require data centers to pay more than the cost of serving them and use the additional revenue to reduce electricity costs for other customers. States including Virginia, Ohio and Florida have already approved special electricity rate structures designed to make large power users shoulder more of the infrastructure costs associated with serving them. Why the bill faces opposition The legislation would also make it easier to approve fossil fuel projects, drawing opposition from environmental groups. Critics warn it could weaken federal safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge new projects. The bill was negotiated by four senators: Republicans Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah, and Democrats Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island. The four lawmakers released amendments Saturday aimed at addressing some of those concerns, including strengthening consultation with Native American tribes and giving states more opportunities to weigh in on proposed projects. Major industry groups representing renewable energy developers and oil and gas companies support the legislation. The bill also includes a provision that Whitehouse says would prevent the Trump administration from continuing to pay offshore wind developers to abandon their projects. The administration has spent nearly $4 billion on such settlements, according to the Associated Press. Despite endorsing the legislation, Trump continued criticizing wind energy Monday, telling reporters that "wind turbines are a major loser." Will Congress pass it? The bill's future remains uncertain despite bipartisan support and the president's endorsement. Some Democrats helped write the legislation and want it passed now, while others, including House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, are pushing for changes. Jeffries' office said last week that the legislation "falls short" in several areas. The debate comes just days after Democrats won control of Congress, giving them more leverage to negotiate energy legislation when the new Congress takes office in January. The Senate scheduled a procedural vote for Monday evening on whether to advance a legislative vehicle for the permitting proposal. The vote requires 60 senators to move forward and would not constitute final passage of the legislation.

artigo.texto: Letter: Hearing on Proposed Data Center Ban Nov. 12 I am writing to make residents aware of two important opportunities to make their voice heard in the next week. Ban Data Centers – Hearing on Thursday, November 12th at 7:00 p.m. Zoom Link At our Town Council meeting on Oct 5, we voted to refer a zoning bylaw amendment to the Planning Board and the Council’s Community Resources Committee that would ban data centers in all zones in Amherst. This zoning amendment had a total of nine council sponsors (over half of the council, myself included) because we recognize the harmful impacts of data centers on host communities. Please see this document compiled by Amherst for the People for more information, including information specifically relevant to the Amherst context. At the Planning Board/CRC hearing held on Oct. 22, members of the Planning Board and CRC discussed the possibility of recommending that this amendment be converted into a moratorium on data centers, which would allow the town time to study and create regulations around data centers. If you are against data centers in Amherst, please attend the next hearing at the Planning Board/CRC to let them know that we want a ban only. Here are some key points: - We don’t need to waste town staff time on studying how to regulate data centers, because we don’t want them in our community. - The measure that was brought to the Planning Board and CRC to study was a ban – and it was supported by over half of the council because the people we represent also don’t want data centers in our community. FY28 Budget Hearing – Monday, Nov. 16, 6:30 p.m. (Town Hall or Zoom) On Monday, November 16th, the Town Council will hold a public forum on the budget for next year. It is essential that residents weigh in on their priorities now, because the Finance Committee is working on budget guidelines that the Council will vote on in early December. The Finance Committee and Town Manager always increase each department’s budget by the same percentage, which has led to major budget cuts in our schools and the chronic underfunding of CRESS, our civilian responders – among other issues. Please attend the budget hearing to make your voice heard. Equality is not the same as equity. The finance committee and the council should carefully consider the needs of each department when creating the budget guidelines. It’s really important to understand that if residents don’t speak out and impact the budget guidelines now, it will be very hard if not impossible to make any changes next year – even if the percent increase voted for the schools and other key departments lead to cuts. If you have any questions or concerns, please feel free to contact me directly at canomartina@amherstma.gov Amber Cano-Martin Amber Cano-Martin is an Amherst Town Councilor representing District 2.

artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA PSI detalha a receita de seus data centers por trás de suas ambições de pesquisa em IA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google A TechCrunch informou em 10 de novembro de 2026 que a Physical Superintelligence obtém sua receita atual usando suas ferramentas para otimizar data centers, enquanto busca construir, no longo prazo, um negócio baseado na descoberta de fenômenos físicos com auxílio de IA. O CEO Matt Pines descreveu o objetivo como transformar avanços da física teórica em tecnologias concretas. Os data centers são o primeiro campo de provas dessa abordagem, onde os sistemas de pesquisa em IA da PSI, que ela chama de físicos virtuais, podem atuar em sistemas físicos reais sujeitos a restrições operacionais mensuráveis. A PSI é uma empresa de benefício público, com segurança, verificação, desenvolvimento responsável e amplo benefício público estabelecidos em seu estatuto. Em sua página da empresa, informa ter mais de 25 pesquisadores e engenheiros e ter captado mais de US$ 58 milhões, em uma rodada liderada pela Breakthrough Energy Ventures. Data centers como campo de provas comercial O trabalho atual de otimização simula calor, energia, água e som, relacionando o desempenho das instalações e seu impacto nas comunidades à física de cada local. Em sua página sobre sua visão, a PSI afirma que constrói modelos de alta fidelidade de instalações em operação para que os físicos virtuais possam examinar o sistema por completo, identificar restrições ocultas e testar intervenções. Os resultados pretendidos incluem maior densidade computacional, uso mais eficiente da energia, melhor gestão térmica e maior eficiência de capital. As campanhas comerciais também fornecem subsídios para a pesquisa. Segundo a PSI, instalações em operação impõem restrições que não seriam propostas em simulações, e cada campanha treina os físicos virtuais usados nas campanhas seguintes. Assim, o negócio de data centers cumpre duas funções: gerar receita no presente e fornecer restrições práticas que ajudam a aprimorar o sistema de pesquisa. Um sistema de pesquisa baseado em verificação Pines descreveu um sistema de pesquisa eficaz como uma combinação de estruturas de software em torno de modelos, ferramentas, sistemas de memória e infraestrutura de simulação, que permite explorar um problema em amplitude e profundidade, considerando uma ampla variedade de alternativas. A PSI formaliza esse processo como uma Campanha Autônoma, um esforço contínuo que vai da definição do problema à formulação de hipóteses, verificação, experimentação, engenharia e implantação. Cada campanha tem marcos mensuráveis, etapas rigorosas de verificação e um caminho para a aplicação, enquanto os pesquisadores humanos escolhem as missões e os critérios de sucesso. A arquitetura separa a geração de candidatos da verificação. Entre as verificações estão as leis de conservação, a simetria, a consistência dimensional, a demonstração formal, a simulação, os gêmeos digitais — contrapartes virtuais de sistemas físicos — e as medições físicas. A PSI afirma que os verificadores que certificam um resultado também podem se tornar funções de recompensa, ou sinais de treinamento, para os físicos virtuais usados posteriormente, vinculando diretamente a avaliação ao aprimoramento do sistema. O anúncio de pesquisa de 6 de novembro de 2026 da PSI fornece um exemplo. A empresa afirmou que seu sistema desenvolvido internamente, executando um modelo da Anthropic que ainda não era público na época, produziu uma demonstração completa da conjectura de Aaronson–Ambainis no terceiro dia de uma execução; o Lean, um assistente de demonstração que verifica cada etapa, aceitou o resultado e, posteriormente, aceitou uma versão final após duas melhorias. Em aberto desde 2008, a conjectura trata das situações em que computadores quânticos podem ser exponencialmente mais rápidos do que computadores convencionais ao processar entradas aleatórias. David Turturean liderou o trabalho com acesso antecipado ao Claude Fable 5.2, que a Anthropic apresentou publicamente em 9 de novembro de 2026. A validação física continua sendo o teste comercial A demonstração também ilustra um limite à comercialização. A matemática e a ciência da computação podem expressar resultados em código validado, mas a física e as ciências da vida ainda exigem contato experimental com a natureza. Pines disse que a PSI está trabalhando em formas eficientes de validar resultados computacionais por meio de experimentos, resumindo a diferença com a observação de que “a natureza também tem voz nos seus modelos da realidade”. Pines também disse que a física teórica ainda não é, em sua maior parte, domínio das máquinas, apesar de ter apresentado aos investidores, de seis a nove meses antes, uma tese mais contundente, embora condicional. Essa ressalva é importante para os negócios da PSI: sua receita atual depende da otimização de instalações, enquanto sua ambição mais ampla exige descobertas validadas que possam se tornar dispositivos ou outras tecnologias. Pines relacionou um fato da natureza validado à possibilidade de construir um dispositivo com capacidades antes indisponíveis. Para a PSI, portanto, a questão comercial é saber se seu processo de geração e verificação pode produzir repetidamente resultados confirmados por experimentos, permitindo que o mesmo sistema de pesquisa passe da otimização da infraestrutura de IA à criação de tecnologias baseadas em nova física.

artigo.texto: A new global network will launch at the UN climate summit COP31 on 12 November in Antalya, Türkiye, aiming to tackle fragmentation in carbon markets and help channel more investment into climate projects, particularly in developing countries. Convened by UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the Global Carbon Market Network will seek to strengthen links between carbon and capital markets, improve transparency and credibility, and facilitate cross-border transactions. Carbon markets remain fragmented across different standards, registries and trading systems. Concerns over credit quality, transparency and double counting have weakened confidence and constrained market development, particularly in developing economies. Ahead of the official launch, UNCTAD Acting Secretary-General Pedro Manuel Moreno expressed hope that the Network would help make carbon pricing a more effective tool for reducing emissions and mobilizing climate finance for developing countries. Connecting fragmented carbon markets “Carbon markets can play a role in putting a price on emissions and mobilizing finance for climate action, but their effectiveness depends on trust, integrity and functioning market infrastructure,” said Nan Li Collins, UNCTAD’s Director of Investment and Enterprise and Chair of the UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges Initiative. The Network will promote cooperation among exchanges and market institutions, including technical work on market integrity, measuring and verifying emissions reductions, and digital technologies to improve transparency and reduce transaction costs. Why it matters now Carbon pricing is expanding. Emissions trading systems and carbon taxes now cover nearly 30% of global greenhouse gas emissions and generated more than $107 billion in public revenue in 2025. The UNCTAD-convened Network will not create a new carbon market or standard. Instead, it aims to connect existing markets and initiatives, including voluntary and compliance markets. Voluntary carbon markets have particular potential to channel private investment across borders. UNCTAD research shows that most voluntary carbon credits are generated by projects in developing countries and sold to buyers in developed countries. Stronger links between markets could help build confidence in these transactions and expand financing for projects that reduce or remove emissions in developing countries. Who is participating and what’s next? The Network’s initial activities include capacity-building programmes, market-practice benchmarking, a global synthesis report on the state of carbon markets, and engagement with emissions trading system regulators on technical and interoperability issues. Founding members span Africa, Asia, the Middle East, Europe and Latin America.

artigo.texto: West Sedgwick County group raises concerns about data center size, location Planning committee to discuss data centers in Wichita Thursday WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH) - The group ‘Renwick Area Against Data Centers in West Sedgwick County’ says its name is not the full story. “We are not anti-technology,” said Kaitlyn Gruenbacher, a member of the group. “We are not anti-data center. However, we do have some issues with these hyper-scale sites that they think are appropriate to put anywhere in the county.” Gruenbacher says they just want the data centers to be right for Sedgwick County. “This is laying the groundwork for how we’re going to see data centers in our community, if we want to see data centers in our community,” Gruenbacher said. The two main issues the group has are location and size. Right now, data centers can be placed anywhere, and there are no limits on their sizes. “Neighbors talk to neighbors, and we honestly were just trying to understand what was happening,” Gruenbacher said. Currently, a moratorium against data centers is in place in Sedgwick County. However, that does not bring comfort to Gruenbacher. “The moratorium right now only goes through December,” Gruenbacher said, “The moratorium also can be extended or it can be removed at any time, so it could end as soon as the commissioners feel that they have enough information.” On Thursday, the Advanced Plans Committee, a subcommittee of the Wichita-Sedgwick County Metropolitan Area Planning Commission, is meeting to discuss data centers. Gruenbacher is hoping the committee listens to the people. “I think best case scenario for the meeting tomorrow is that advanced plans chooses to listen to the public, and really take that feedback and show that they can take that guidence,” Gruenbacher said. The Advanced Plans Committee meeting will take place at 10 a.m. on Thursday in the Ronald Reagan Building, 271 W. 3rd Street, in downtown Wichita. Copyright 2026 KWCH. All rights reserved. artigo.texto: Trending A proposed natural-gas fired, electrical generating station in Oliver County would offer numerous economic benefits in the region, according to a project spokesperson who presented at the Minot Area Chamber EDC's Energy Committee meeting in Minot Monday, Nov. 9. Base Electron's proposed Missouri Bend Energy Center will be a 1,200-megawatt, natural gas-driven facility designed to support the electrical needs of a nearby data center, said Tyler Hamman, the company's vice president of Community Engagement and External Affairs. The generation plant will be somewhat larger than the state's current largest generating facility, lignite-fueled Coal Creek Station near Underwood, which is just over 1,100 megawatts. Another natural gas facility, Basin Electric's approximately 1,490-megawatt Bison Generation Station, is under construction in Williams County. Base Electron is working on permitting through the county and will be filing for permits with the North Dakota Public Service Commission and North Dakota Department of Environmental Quality. The hope is to break ground next spring, Hamman said. Operational startup could happen in the second half of 2030. Base Electron, headquartered in Plano, Texas, is an independent power producer, incorporated in December 2025. The company formed specifically to provide power generation for large industrial loads, particularly data centers. "We have the same co-founders as Applied Digital, but we're organized as a separate company," Hamman said. Base Electron's first anchor project is the proposed Applied Digital data center in Oliver County. The company plans to build a $2.4 billion steam turbine electrical plant in association with a long-term power purchase agreement with Applied Digital. "Those dollars are going to recycle several times throughout the community by the time it's all said and done. So, pretty significant investment for the region, a lot of construction jobs," Hamman said. "We're guessing it's probably going to be about 300 (workers) on an average rolling basis throughout the construction period, but we hope to get about 1,000 on site for a short period of time in 2028. Sixty to 70 full-time jobs once we finish operations. So, those will be anything from technicians, maintenance, operators, welders, boiler workers, etc. "And then, of course, you're going to have seasonal and cyclical maintenance every few years," he added. "That will bring 100 to 200 workers at a time during those periods." In addition, the project will generate both property taxes and an electrical generation tax. The use of natural gas will help sustain that piece of the energy industry while generating additional taxes, Hamman said. Base Electron has a natural gas agreement with WBI Energy, which plans to construct the Bakken East Pipeline to run about 350 miles from near Watford City to near Fargo. Hamman noted North Dakota has a large gas production industry that creates opportunity for a low-cost and secure supply of fuel to feed power facilities. Use of that natural gas helps address reliability concerns within the transmission grid, he said. Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO), the region's transmission organization, predicts the need for 15-20 gigawatts of power by 2035, creating opportunity for new power generation, Hamman said. "We've set ourselves up to capitalize on the energy infrastructure and the investment environment in North Dakota to utilize produced gas and meet the need for reliability," he said of Basin Electron. Hamman said the company chose a location enabling it to access transmission infrastructure already in place. Missouri Bend Energy Center will connect into an existing 345 kV power line. Base Electron acquired 312 acres, much of it to be used during the construction period. The operational footprint will be 30-50 acres, Hamman said. Applied Digital's data center will be about a mile north and will be served by the local utility. "But we're basically providing that power as a capacity backstop to the grid," Hamman said. Base Electron estimates a need for about a million and a half gallons of water a day. The intent is to draw water from Nelson Lake, located about eight miles from the proposed plant and fed by the Missouri River. If that option is not available, the draw would come directly from the Missouri River, 16 miles away. The usage represents a fraction of a percent of Missouri River flows, Hamman said. "We're using air cool condensing, which significantly reduces your water demand," he said. "There'll be a lot of recycling of the water." The proposed construction would come at a time when other regional construction will be happening on the Applied Digital data center, the River Run Energy Center gas-powered plant and data center campus in Mercer County and the Garrison spillway. It could result in a demand for 10,000 construction workers in a confined region in a short period of time, but Hamman said trade unions are confident they can provide the workers.

artigo.texto: Cincinnati council hears study on how to regulate data centers CINCINNATI (WXIX) - The City of Cincinnati is considering how to regulate data centers. A presentation Tuesday in council gave an overview of how data centers could be installed in the city. The city ordered a study to help guide council as members consider how to handle data centers if more are brought into the city. What the study found The Department of City Planning and Engagement representatives acknowledged that data centers may be a piece of important infrastructure, but not everyone wants them around. “We all use the internet. We use social media, we do Google search ... All of that uses data from data centers, so if we want to do that, we need data centers,” Councilman Mark Jeffreys said. About 400 people provided the city with feedback on the issue. “The primary message that we received from community members was a strong desire to see the zoning code prohibit data centers as a land use,” said Sophia Ferries-Rowe with the Cincinnati Department of City Planning and Engagement. The department said 28 data centers currently operate within the Greater Cincinnati area, with nine directly in the city. If more arrive, residents are concerned about increased heat, noise, energy bills and water utility bills, the study found. The study also found that more data centers could create jobs and help support local infrastructure, but they may have negative environmental impacts on carbon emissions. RELATED | Data centers multiply across Ohio, raising questions about costs and benefits Water use and costs “Why should citizens and property owners pay higher water bills to protect a billion dollar company?” Stephan Pryor said. Representatives with the Metropolitan Sewer District and Greater Cincinnati Water Works suggested that existing regulations already control how companies use water. They said the city could implement a reuse system that would allow water that is not fully treated to be rerouted directly to data centers and other uses not related to drinking water. They told Councilman Evan Nolan that it would require new infrastructure. “That could be expensive,” Nolan said. “Could be, yes, but other places in the country have had private investment,” said Scott Bessler, with the Metropolitan Sewer District. PREVIOUSLY | Cincinnati considers temporary halt on new data centers Next steps As the study continues, local leaders still have questions about how much energy and water current data centers use before setting any guidelines. “We need to put a cost associated with those, and if another data center is proposed to be built, we need to know what that cost is so we can offset it. It shouldn’t be on ratepayers,” Jeffreys said. The next step is more research, and city departments will put forth recommendations for the zoning rules. Another public engagement session will follow, and the recommendations will be refined before going before council. See a spelling or grammatical error in our story? Please click here to report it. artigo.texto: Cabinet tackles grid congestion with large-scale energy storage The Dutch government wants to expand energy storage to ease pressure on the country’s overloaded electricity grid. Published on November 9, 2026 According to the government, more energy storage is needed to ensure that renewable electricity remains available when there is little wind or solar power being generated. It therefore aims to increase battery storage capacity in the Netherlands to 110 gigawatt-hours (GWh) by 2040, more than 50 times the level at the end of 2025. The expansion should also help reduce pressure on the electricity grid. Climate and Energy Minister Stientje van Veldhoven and State Secretary Jo-Annes de Bat announced the plans in a letter to the Dutch House of Representatives. To make the expansion possible, the government has reached agreements with grid operators, industry association Energy Storage NL, regional and local authorities, and the Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM). These agreements are set out in a joint Energy Storage Policy Agenda. Batteries to ease pressure on the grid The expansion is intended, among other things, to reduce pressure on the electricity grid. In many parts of the Netherlands, the grid is so congested that businesses and households have to wait for a new or upgraded connection. This is also holding back the construction of new homes. By storing electricity when demand is low and making it available during peak periods, batteries can help relieve pressure on the grid. According to the government, grid-friendly energy storage could also reduce the need for investments in expanding the electricity grid. Faster permitting The 25 action points include measures to speed up the permitting process for large-scale battery projects. Grid operators, the energy storage sector and regional authorities will need to work more closely together to achieve this. The parties are also working on agreements concerning the conditions and compensation for energy storage. One example is the use of flexible grid contracts, under which large batteries are connected subject to conditions that take into account the available capacity on the electricity grid. Compensation for households Large-scale batteries are not the only way to help stabilise the electricity grid. Households can also receive compensation if they help manage peak demand using their home batteries, heat pumps or electric vehicle chargers. Since November 1, households in the provinces of Gelderland, Utrecht, Flevoland and North Brabant have been able to participate in the scheme through a number of energy suppliers. The scheme is expected to be extended to the rest of the Netherlands in 2027.

artigo.texto: Quanta Services is growing faster than expected, driven by demand for power infrastructure, data centers and renewable energy. CEO Duke Austin sees potential for growth in the 20% range next year, while leaving the company's longer-term targets unchanged. Data centers and related projects account for roughly 10% to 15% of the business, and Quanta's revenue per megawatt on data center work has increased to about $4 million to $6 million as customers award it more work at each site. Quanta is investing in equipment manufacturing and supply to ease project bottlenecks, but that spending could weigh on free cash flow over the next couple of years. The company is also pursuing generation projects, with some work expected to begin in 2027. Vertiv's UIG Deal Targets the Next Big Constraint in AI Data Centers Quanta Services (NYSE:PWR) is growing faster than management anticipated at its March analyst day, driven by demand for power infrastructure and technology-related construction, CEO Duke Austin said at the Baird 2026 Global Industrial Conference. Austin said the company was ahead of the five-year plan it outlined at the event, which included a target for 15% to 20% compound annual growth in adjusted earnings per share. He said demand for power and computing capacity had developed more quickly than expected, while renewable energy work had remained stronger than anticipated. Data Center Delays Create Opportunity in These 3 Stocks "It's broad-based growth, faster than we thought," Austin said, pointing in particular to expansion in mechanical, electrical and plumbing, or MEP, work. Austin said Quanta expects to grow next year and sees an opportunity for growth in the 20% range, with potential to grow faster. He did not revise the company's longer-term targets at the conference. 3 Stocks Cashing In on AI While Everyone Watches NVIDIA Quanta serves utilities and large power users, including technology customers. Austin said the company self-performs about 85% of its work, has 95,000 employees and generates $41 billion in revenue. He said data centers and related work, including chip and Tesla projects, represent roughly 10% to 15% of the business. Electricians can move among data centers, pharmaceutical facilities and other projects, giving Quanta flexibility if demand shifts, he said. Austin said Quanta's revenue capture on data center work had risen to approximately $4 million to $6 million per megawatt from $3 million to $5 million, as customers ask the company to take on more work at each site. He expects that share to continue expanding. On transmission projects, Austin said Quanta had not yet started field work on 765-kilovolt lines and probably would not begin until sometime next year. He said the company's existing business was growing without that contribution. Supply Chain and Generation Investments Quanta has expanded into manufacturing and supply of equipment to keep projects moving when materials are scarce, Austin said. Its investments include transformers, circuit breakers and poles. The company formed a breaker joint venture with Hyosung HICO and acquired a pole manufacturer during the quarter, he said. Austin also discussed Quanta's fossil-fuel generation business, including a combined-cycle power plant program with NiSource. He said Quanta structured the work to manage risk and target a margin profile consistent with the segment, which he described as approximately 10% to 12%. Some generation work will start in 2027, Austin said, adding that other customers have expressed interest. He expects the business to become a meaningful platform, though not Quanta's largest segment. Cash Flow and Capital Deployment CFO Jayshree Desai said growth in renewables, MEP and engineering, procurement and construction work can support a more favorable free-cash-flow profile because those activities generally have more favorable working-capital characteristics than Quanta's typical utility master service agreement work. Desai cautioned that spending to expand transformer, breaker and offsite manufacturing facilities could pressure free cash flow over the next couple of years. The mix and growth rate of the company's businesses will influence the outcome, she said. Austin said Quanta could deploy capital through acquisitions or by buying back stock if the share price becomes disconnected from the business. He also expressed confidence in demand beyond the near term, saying he felt good about the outlook through 2029. About Quanta Services (NYSE:PWR) Quanta Services, Inc. provides specialized contracting and infrastructure services to the electric power, energy and communications industries. Its work spans the planning, design, construction, repair and maintenance of essential infrastructure. The company's services include electric transmission and distribution lines, substations, renewable energy facilities, natural gas and pipeline systems, and communications networks. Quanta supports projects across the infrastructure lifecycle, from initial development and construction to ongoing upgrades and maintenance. artigo.texto: COLUMBUS, Ohio — The push against data centers has been well-documented. One independent tracker counts nearly 150 data center moratoriums in place all across the state. Opponents are concerned about a wide variety of issues, including the impact the centers have on the environment and their utility bills. At the same time, supporters point to the fact that those data centers are bringing billions of dollars in investment and new opportunities for construction workers. As data centers continue to expand across Ohio, so does the demand for the workers needed to build them. “We’ve got in-house architecture and engineering, licensed and stamped in all 50 states,” said Will Goodin, vice president of project development for Terrapin Construction Group. Terrapin Construction Group designs data centers across the country with four separate projects currently in Ohio. “And that’s inclusive of mechanical, electrical, plumbing as well as engineering, civil, so site work and structural work as well,” Goodin said. He said the growing number of data center projects is creating more business for his company, making over $100 million from design, construction and procurement of HVAC equipment this year, and they’re on track to triple that next year. “We’ve seen a huge uptick in not only design but also a lot of pre-construction, a lot of construction specifically in the data center asset class,” Goodin said. And it’s not just the construction crews. Goodin said demand for the specialized equipment needed to build these facilities is also high, with some supplies taking months to arrive. “There’s huge lead times depending on the types of equipment that you’re looking to source for your project. Anywhere from 18- to 50-plus weeks for any number of transfer switches, switch gears, chillers, things of that nature,” Goodin said. That demand creates opportunities for a wide range of skilled trades, including electricians, mechanical contractors, framers and carpenters. Goodin said the steady pipeline of projects is providing job security for his company and the subcontractors it relies on. But he recognizes the industry is not without controversy. “Depending on who you ask, it’s kind of a loaded, complicated issue but we’re very excited to be a resource for folks who are looking to get into this business and are expanding their current operations,” Goodin said. Across Ohio, communities are pushing back against data center development. As more communities consider putting development on pause, the question becomes: How many jobs do these facilities actually create once construction is over? Case Western Reserve University Economics Professor Jonathan Ernest said the initial construction phase can provide a significant employment boost. But he said once it’s built, that changes. “There are fewer people onsite for the longterm with lots of jobs in an area. So we’re not likely to get entire cities that are built around the one plant that everyone works at we’re not likely to get that with data centers because they don’t need that many capacity of people on site for the long run,” said Ernest. So, while the construction boom is creating opportunities for Ohio’s skilled trades, Ernest said communities should take a closer look at what those projects will mean for the local workforce once the facilities are up and running. According to the U.S. Data Center Map, there are 26 data centers currently being constructed, with another 54 in the planning phase.

artigo.texto: Eletronet investe R$ 25 milhões em novo data center em São Paulo Com obras iniciadas, ELET1 terá 90 racks e potência inicial de 0,5 MW; lançamento está previsto para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. A Eletronet, empresa da Axia Energia (antiga Eletrobras), anunciou investimento de R$ 25 milhões na construção de um novo data center em São Paulo. Batizada de ELET1, a unidade terá 350 m², capacidade para cerca de 90 racks e potência inicial de 0,5 MW. As obras já começaram, e o lançamento está previsto para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. O projeto prevê uma segunda fase de expansão, na qual a potência poderá chegar a 1 MW, cujo prazo de entrega ainda não foi definido. A instalação ampliará a oferta de serviços de colocation, conectividade e interconexão, com atendimento a provedores de nuvem, operadoras de telecomunicações, provedores de internet (ISPs) e hyperscalers. Interconexão e migração da infraestrutura O ELET1 abrigará o ponto de interconexão (PIX) da Eletronet no IX.br São Paulo. Segundo a empresa, a unidade ficará em uma região com concentração de redes de telecomunicações e provedores de conteúdo. O projeto também contempla a migração da infraestrutura instalada no atual data center da companhia em São Paulo. A Eletronet afirma que a transferência será planejada para preservar a continuidade dos serviços. “Estamos ampliando nossa estrutura para atender às necessidades dos clientes que já utilizam nossos serviços e abrir novas oportunidades de negócios, em um contexto no qual a hiperconectividade e a disponibilidade se tornam cada vez mais essenciais”, afirma Rogerio Garchet, CEO da Eletronet (na foto acima). Segundo o executivo, o investimento acompanha o avanço de aplicações em nuvem, inteligência artificial, streaming e serviços digitais, que demandam suporte a volumes crescentes de dados. Energia e redundância Entre os recursos previstos para o ELET1 estão dois geradores redundantes de 500 kVA, dupla entrada de rede, backbone DWDM protegido, sistema de gerenciamento predial (BMS) e monitoramento contínuo. A unidade também contará com um Centro de Operações de Rede (NOC) de contingência. “Mais capacidade precisa vir acompanhada de eficiência, resiliência e previsibilidade operacional. Por isso, o ELET1 foi concebido com uma arquitetura que otimiza o uso dos recursos e oferece mais flexibilidade à operação”, afirma Emerson Hioki, diretor de tecnologia da Eletronet. (Com assessoria de imprensa)

artigo.texto: Confira o resumo que a OESTE.IA, a IA da Revista Oeste, fez pra você A Noruega decidiu suspender temporariamente novas reservas de conexão de data centers à rede elétrica para avaliar a crescente demanda de energia dessas instalações, impulsionada pela expansão da inteligência artificial. A medida foi anunciada pela operadora do sistema elétrico, Statnett, nesta segunda-feira, 9, e deve durar até, no máximo, 1º de agosto de 2027. A Noruega vai suspender temporariamente novas reservas de conexão de data centers à rede elétrica. A decisão busca avaliar como o país vai lidar com a demanda de energia dessas instalações, que vem crescendo com a expansão da inteligência artificial (IA). A operadora do sistema elétrico norueguês, Statnett, anunciou a medida nesta segunda-feira, 9, em comunicado. A previsão é que a suspensão termine, no máximo, em 1º de agosto de 2027. Receba nossas atualizações Leia também: “Nvidia investiga suspeita de espionagem envolvendo CEO“ A construção de data centers avança em diversos países. Empresas de tecnologia investem centenas de bilhões de dólares em estruturas destinadas à operação e ao treinamento de sistemas de inteligência artificial. A expansão, contudo, também provoca resistência de comunidades nos Estados Unidos e na Europa, principalmente por causa da demanda por terrenos e eletricidade e do possível aumento das tarifas de energia. O ministro da Digitalização da Noruega, Torgeir Micaelsen, defendeu o controle sobre a expansão dessas instalações. “Queremos data centers na Noruega, mas não podemos aceitar todos os tipos de data centers”, afirmou a jornalistas nesta segunda-feira. “Portanto, precisamos controlar o crescimento e garantir que a Noruega receba os data centers de que realmente necessita, aqueles que proporcionam os maiores benefícios para a sociedade.” Demanda supera o consumo máximo do país Segundo dados da Statnett, os data centers já conectados à rede norueguesa somam 800 megawatts (MW) de capacidade. Outros 4.200 MW têm reserva de conexão, enquanto 9.100 MW aguardam na fila por capacidade. Além desses pedidos, empresas solicitaram conexão para mais 18 mil MW. Com isso, a demanda total à espera de acesso chega a 27.100 MW. O volume supera o consumo máximo de energia da Noruega, que fica pouco acima de 25 mil MW. Os números ajudam a dimensionar a pressão que os novos empreendimentos podem exercer sobre o sistema elétrico do país. Um relatório recente do Conselho Norueguês de Tecnologia também questionou os benefícios econômicos dessas instalações. Segundo o documento, os data centers geram poucos empregos permanentes depois da conclusão das obras. O conselho informou ainda que 90% dessas estruturas pertencem a empresas estrangeiras. + Entenda mais de Mundo em Oeste

artigo.texto: Data centers may be willing to be double charged for grid infrastructure, so long as those costs are paired with policy that makes it easier to build in the U.S. Tucked inside the Senate’s bipartisan permitting reform bill are provisions that would upend decades of federal power rules by directing data centers and crypto miners to pay for both the new transmission lines needed to serve them, as well as the cost of using the existing grid. Historically, charging a customer twice for the same capacity was considered an illegal practice. But that could change, as data centers disproportionately drive up demand for electricity across the U.S. and hyperscalers promise not to saddle other customers with the bill. The shift reflects a fraught moment in the race to power artificial intelligence, especially heading into the midterm elections next week. Energy affordability is top of mind for many voters across the U.S., whose opinion of data centers has soured dramatically this year, according to the latest polling by POLITICO. Half of Americans now oppose data centers being built within three miles of their home, up from 28% in January. Their concerns are rooted in rising utility bills, water use, air pollution, and AI’s impact on jobs and the broader economy. Controversial projects are affecting local races, including in states like New Mexico, Utah, and Wisconsin. “I think the data center industry will take this deal because they’ve already acknowledged that they need to cover their costs,” Tyson Slocum, director of Public Citizen’s energy program, told Latitude Media. “And at the end of the day, the bill will make it a lot easier to build the gas and renewable infrastructure needed to serve data centers.” President Donald Trump, a vocal supporter of data centers that underpin the global AI race, who says the U.S. needs to win against China, launched a voluntary ratepayer protection pledge in March. Tech giants, AI labs, and major utilities signed it, with the tech companies promising to either build or buy generation to power new data centers and pay for any new grid infrastructure to serve them. Trading extra cash for speed The Senate permitting deal, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, aims to actually enforce that pledge. And so far, at least two industry groups that represent companies including Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft have endorsed the legislation: the Corporate Energy Buyers Association and the Electricity Customer Alliance. However, the Data Center Coalition has not endorsed the bill. The group told Latitude Media in a statement that it’s still reviewing the legislation with its members. Amazon, Google, and Meta didn’t respond to a request for comment. Microsoft declined to comment. CEBA in a statement described BAAJA as a “generational opportunity” to build out U.S. energy through faster infrastructure permitting and improved transmission planning. Jeff Dennis, executive director of ECA — which represents tech companies and residential and industrial customers — said BAAJA strikes a balance between encouraging the build out of larger transmission lines in a more financially disciplined way, while setting the stage for long-term affordability. He noted that data center developers have already said they expect to pay their own costs, and then some. “They are willing to pay more than their own costs to make sure other customers are treated fairly,” Dennis said. BAAJA would require the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to rewrite a 1994 policy that allowed electricity customers to pay either the “embedded” costs of the existing grid, or the “incremental” cost of its expansion — not both. Instead, computational loads larger than 20 megawatts would be forced to pay both. States could charge a “surplus” on top of that, in order to lower other customers’ utility bills, and discriminate against data centers by treating them as a “less favorable” customer class to other large industrial, manufacturing, or commercial loads. The bill also would mandate that utilities hold data centers liable for capital costs, even if they exit agreements early for any reason, to make sure ratepayers aren’t left on the hook. Dennis said a final bill must ensure that data centers aren’t forced to shoulder so much of the costs that they ultimately decide to build off-grid. Some projects are already going that route, including those backed by Microsoft and Amazon, mainly powered by gas turbines and engines and backup diesel generators. “That could pose negative impacts to customers and removes a lot of investment in the grid we all rely on,” he said. A Senate aide told Latitude Media that key negotiators are working on a managers’ amendment to BAAJA, although it’s unclear whether it would revise the ratepayer protection section of the bill. Nidhi Thakar, CEBA’s senior vice president for policy, said the group supports BAAJA in its current form, but acknowledged there is some concern among its data center members about how much they’ll be forced to pay. “A lot of this will have to get worked out in a FERC rulemaking,” Thakar said. “That is where the deep details on how to allocate costs for new transmission lines will occur. So that rulemaking will be very critical.” The Senate is set to vote on the permitting bill on Nov. 9, the week after the midterm elections.
