artigo.texto: As Toyota's luxury brand Lexus rolls out electric versions of its midsize-plus ES sedan, competition is heating up in Korea's 70 million won EV segment. The 70 million won range is expected to see fast-growing demand because it preserves a premium image while still qualifying for subsidies. But most of the key models at this price point, including the ES EVs, are equipped with batteries from China's CATL, leaving Korean battery makers on the sidelines. According to the auto industry on the 10th, Lexus on the 13th of last month launched the all-electric ES350e and ES500e and the hybrid ES350h as part of the new eighth-generation ES in the Korean market. The ES is a core Lexus model that made its global debut in 1989. The new ES is the fully redesigned eighth generation, the first full change in eight years since 2018. Until now, the ES was sold only with internal-combustion and hybrid powertrains, but starting with this eighth generation Lexus has dropped the combustion-engine model and added an EV. The entry-level Premium trim of the ES350e is priced at 71.6 million won. That is 1.3 million won cheaper than the ES350h Premium trim at 72.9 million won. Because EVs carry costly batteries, they are often pricier than comparable combustion or hybrid models. Lexus appears to have set the EV's starting price below the hybrid to quickly gain share on price competitiveness. Lexus also priced the higher-spec ES500e Premium in the 77 million won range. The ES350e is a front-wheel-drive model with a single motor, while the ES500e is all-wheel drive with dual motors. The ES500e's range is 435 km per charge, shorter than the ES350e's 478 km, but it outmuscles the ES350e with 347 horsepower versus 227 horsepower. After Lexus priced the new ES EVs in the lower-than-expected 70 million won range, domestic consumer interest surged. Industry sources say total orders for the new ES, including one month of preorders, have reached about 5,000 units. EVs—the ES350e and ES500e—account for roughly half. Rivals starting in the 70 million won range include Volvo's midsize-plus ES90 sedan, Polestar's midsize-plus SUV Polestar 3, and BMW's midsize SUV iX3. Tesla's midsize SUV Model Y, which dominates the Korean market, starts at 49.99 million won for the base rear-wheel-drive Premium, while the all-wheel-drive Model Y L Premium sells for 72.99 million won. Automakers are clustering new models in the 70 million won bracket because policy changes on subsidies are seen as boosting demand at this price point. Currently, EVs priced under 85 million won qualify for subsidies, but the government plans to lower the threshold to under 80 million won starting next year. In addition, vehicles priced 80 million won or more must carry green license plates if purchased as corporate cars. Price a car in the 60 million won range or lower and its premium image fades; move into the 80 million won range and you risk losing subsidies and being required to use green plates, among other drawbacks. As a result, import brands are concentrating on the 70 million won segment to protect brand value while reaping multiple practical benefits. The problem is that batteries in EVs priced in the 70 million won range are effectively dominated by China's CATL. CATL is the world's No. 1 supplier, with a 39.1% cumulative share of the global EV battery market from January through September this year. The Lexus ES350e and ES500e, Volvo ES90, and Polestar 3 all use CATL's LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries. For the Model Y, the Long Range and Performance trims use LG Energy Solution's NCM batteries, but the cheaper rear-wheel-drive trim also uses CATL's LFP battery. The BMW iX3 is equipped with batteries from China's EVE Energy. Automakers are largely sourcing batteries from CATL and other Chinese makers because they are relatively inexpensive. NCM batteries, the mainstay of Korean suppliers such as LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI, offer higher energy density and longer range but cost more due to pricey cobalt and nickel. LFP batteries, by contrast, use iron and phosphorus as main materials and can be procured at lower cost. Battery industry officials worry that LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and SK On—the three Korean players—will keep losing share at home to Chinese batteries. The high-end premium EV segment has limited room to expand, and domestic automakers such as Hyundai Motor are struggling to grow EV sales. "To make matters worse, after BYD, Chinese EV makers such as Zeekr and Xpeng are entering Korea one after another, further squeezing Hyundai Motor and Kia," a battery industry source said. "Korean battery makers' recent focus on the energy storage system (ESS) market also reflects their judgment that it will be hard to win back EV leadership from Chinese companies anytime soon."

artigo.texto: Lubbock residents urge council to pass data center moratorium City council hosts first public hearing over proposed 90-day moratorium LUBBOCK, Texas (KCBD) - Residents urged the Lubbock City Council to pass a 90-day data center moratorium during the first of two public hearings on the proposal. The proposed moratorium followed a successful citizen petition organized through SAVE Lubbock this past summer. Residents raise concerns Fabian Mata, a north Lubbock resident, told city council Tuesday afternoon he does not trust the city to enforce its ordinances. “We don’t trust you when you say you’re going to put 1,000, 2,000, 5,000 feet [setback] in the data centers in north Lubbock because you don’t enforce any of the ordinances,” Mata said. Natalie Miller of the North and East Lubbock Coalition said while the moratorium proposal isn’t exactly what citizens asked for, she hopes council respects their wishes. “Citizens of Lubbock asked for 18 months. There was a compromise for 90 days, and that’s what the law would allow for. And so, we accepted that answer, and now we’re just asking to simply honor that,” Miller said. Zoning recommendations At its meeting last week, the Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended that Lubbock require specific zoning for AI factories. The proposed rules would address landscaping, setbacks, noise and pollution limits, and data center decommissioning. Stephen Sanders of SAVE Lubbock said residents should be heard. “We don’t want a data center in those communities at all. But if we have to have one, it needs to be 1,000 foot setback,” Sanders said. The commission’s recommendations for large-scale data centers are scheduled to come before the council Dec. 1. Some residents said a moratorium would come too late because the Lubbock Economic Development Alliance has already approved a new data center inside city limits. That facility is smaller than the large-scale data centers the city is considering regulating. “We had no opportunity to say no because LEDA and you all had already spoken about it,” Stephanie Smith said. The second public hearing on the moratorium is set for Dec. 10, when council will have its first opportunity to vote on it. “Usually it’s the industry comes in first and then we study. We’re just saying let’s study this first, right?” Miller said. Copyright 2026 KCBD. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: In the final days of Joe Biden’s administration, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) filed a lawsuit alleging PepsiCo violated the Robinson-Patman Act. This largely dormant New Deal-era antitrust law prohibits wholesalers from giving large retailers preferential prices disproportionate to sales volume. Donald Trump’s second administration dropped the case soon after taking office, but a watchdog group, the Institute for Local Self-Reliance, petitioned the Southern District of New York court to unseal the Biden-era complaint in late 2025, and the court did. The details that emerged were explosive. Drawing on a trove of internal PepsiCo emails and other documents, Biden’s FTC accused the company of forging a secret pact with Walmart to ensure the big-box giant had unbeatable retail prices on PepsiCo products. PepsiCo allegedly did this by monitoring retail prices for its products and raising wholesale prices on retailers whose PepsiCo prices were too close to Walmart’s. As the Monthly reported in January, the alleged conduct carried profound implications for food pricing and affordability. Conventional wisdom holds that Walmart’s low prices reflect volume discounts and economies of scale used by the Bentonville, Arkansas-based retailer—America’s largest employer and largest grocery retailer by sales. But the PepsiCo suit, brought by the FTC under its then-Chair Lina Khan, presented evidence of the opposite of efficiency: PepsiCo’s painstaking micromanagement of prices to protect its most powerful buyer. For consumers, this raises the possibility that Walmart’s market power does not, at least in this case, discipline prices downward, but inflates them across the market. (Since the Trump administration dropped the suit, PepsiCo did not get to make its case in court, although it said in a statement at the time that it “has always and will continue to provide all customers with fair, competitive, and non-discriminatory pricing, discounts and promotional value.”) But before the FTC suit regarding PepsiCo was filed in January 2025, private plaintiff antitrust suits against Walmart and battery maker Energizer had already been underway for two years. These cases, which have received scant media attention, provide another set of allegations that Walmart may be influencing its suppliers’ pricing decisions in ways that harm consumers. Reached for comment, Walmart and Energizer did not respond. The plaintiffs in these suits, which include both smaller retailers and consumers, allege that Walmart pressured Energizer to monitor sellers’ prices to ensure they didn’t underprice Walmart’s. If they did, Energizer would discipline the sellers by raising their wholesale prices or limiting access to products. The plaintiffs allege the scheme is evidenced by price increases between 2019 and 2023 that exceeded what a normally competitive market would see, as well as internal corporate correspondence and pricing records describing the pressure Energizer allegedly faced from Walmart to hike prices on smaller retailers. The internal records and correspondence described in the legal filings seem to show that as early as January 2018, Energizer had allegedly developed an internal team, Project Atlas, to police customers who sold batteries below Walmart’s rate. One of the plaintiffs, a discount battery reseller called Portable Power, employed pricing strategies that were considered “disruptive,” according to an Energizer manager. To “resolve” the issue in Walmart’s favor, Energizer raised wholesale prices for headlamps on Portable Power by 50 to 85 percent as early as November 2018, telling the California-based reseller the increase aligned with internal pricing policy. This was the first of many Energizer moves to discipline Portable Power’s pricing, according to the reseller’s amended complaint. In the second quarter of 2019, Energizer again raised the wholesale prices of certain products—Max Alkaline and Ultimate Lithium batteries—by 8 percent for all its non-Walmart customers. The plaintiffs say this allowed Walmart to raise retail prices for the same Energizer products by an even greater margin—nearly 40 percent by the first quarter of 2020—while still maintaining price leadership. In January 2021, an Energizer sales representative forwarded an email from the company’s Project Atlas team to Portable Power’s CEO, Richard Petretti, informing the battery reseller that it was “in violation” of Energizer’s “pricing policies.” Energizer then hiked the prices it charged Portable Power and, according to the amended complaint, “told Portable Power the minimum price it had to charge—Walmart’s price—to avoid being terminated as a distributor.” Portable Power refused, and on February 1st, the Energizer sales representative warned Portable Power that it could no longer distribute certain Energizer products. When Portable Power’s CEO discussed the decision with the representative later that day by phone, the complaint alleges, the representative told him that “this is 1000% about Walmart and wanting the best price.” Energizer has filed counterclaims in the same lawsuit against Portable Power, accusing the company of illegally obtaining “trade secrets” from Energizer employees to bring and support the litigation. The two cases, PepsiCo and Energizer, show that Walmart’s business is “based on exercising market power over suppliers,” says Ron Knox, a senior researcher and policy advocate at the Institute for Local Self-Reliance. Indeed, other signs have emerged. As far back as 2017, Walmart reportedly demanded that prices from large consumer-goods companies selling through the retailer be 15 percent lower than competitors’ prices 80 percent of the time. Whether Walmart illegally pushed suppliers to raise prices on its rivals has not been adjudicated. The PepsiCo case is dismissed. artigo.texto: OKLAHOMA CITY – The Oklahoma City Council voted unanimously Tuesday to extend its existing moratorium on approvals for new large-scale data center projects through December 2027, continuing a pause that’s been in effect since April of this year. The moratorium officially blocks planning, zoning, and expansion applications for any data center exceeding 75 megawatts of electrical load, effectively halting any new “hyperscale” data center projects while City officials continue examining questions of potential utility strain, environmental impact, and noise pollution. “City staff will be researching best practices and working with a consultant and community stakeholders to update the zoning code, including the creation of a specific use unit for data centers,” Planning Director Geoff Butler said in a press statement. “Extending the temporary moratorium will give City Council time to evaluate the full scope of the potential impacts and determine appropriate regulations.” Some exemptions, including newly approved hyperscale data center The new extension comes hot on the heels of last month’s City Council approval of the city’s first hyperscale data center development, a 500 megawatt, multi-site mega-project planned by Beltline Energy on the far westerns edges of OKC, at NW 23rd St. and Frisco Rd., overlapping with parts of Yukon. That project was specifically exempted from the moratorium, as it had already been approved by Planning Commission and had entered the development pipeline before April’s vote to pause further data center approvals. The Beltline development was joined by two other projects that were retroactively exempted from the moratorium – the Scale Datacenters facility on the Expand Energy (formerly Chesapeake) campus, serving Cerebras AI, and the 7725 Connect development on W. Reno, housing the Rack59 Data Center. Both of those data centers fall well below the 75 megawatt usage threshold for the moratorium, however, and with no official large-scale expansion plans outlined, it remains unclear as to why they were exempted by name. Moratorium could be lifted with new Zoning Code The moratorium could also be lifted before December 2027 if the City of OKC’s impending Zoning Code overhaul outlines firm new regulations for data center operations in the city limits. “If there is a situation where we have a revised ordinance ready to accept applications, the moratorium could end earlier than the end of 2027,” Mayor David Holt clarified in discussion with City Manager Craig Freeman from the dais at Tuesday’s meeting. “But that’s not guaranteed.” Holt explained that the moratorium could, in fact, continue even after the approval of a new Zoning Code, if the council and City consultants determine that more study is still needed. “If we decided, as a policy matter, that even with the adoption, we still wanted to maintain this expectation,” he said, “we certainly could, in the new ordinance, say ‘this moratorium still lasts through 2027.’” Brett Fieldcamp is the owner and Editor in Chief of Oklahoma City Free Press. He has been covering arts, entertainment, news, housing, and culture in Oklahoma for nearly two decades and served as Arts & Entertainment Editor before purchasing the company from founder Brett Dickerson in 2026. artigo.texto: A melhoria dos mecanismos de gestão de emissões abre caminho para um mercado de carbono. Alterar a Lei de Proteção Ambiental e aprimorar as regulamentações sobre emissões criará um arcabouço legal sincronizado e transparente, ajudando o mercado de carbono nacional a operar com mais eficácia. Aprimorar as instituições e padronizar a gestão de emissões. A transição verde impõe novas exigências à gestão estatal e às atividades produtivas e empresariais. À medida que as normas ambientais se tornam cada vez mais uma condição para o acesso ao mercado, a redução das emissões não é apenas uma responsabilidade a cumprir, mas também está diretamente ligada à competitividade das empresas. A Conclusão nº 75-KL/TW, de 28 de julho de 2026, do 14º Comitê Central do Partido Comunista do Vietnã, identifica a proteção ambiental, a adaptação às mudanças climáticas e a transição verde como a base e a força motriz para a inovação de modelos de desenvolvimento, a melhoria da qualidade do crescimento e o aumento da competitividade da economia . A conclusão estabelece uma meta para 2030: a economia verde representará 10% do PIB, a proporção de energia renovável no fornecimento total de energia primária atingirá pelo menos 26,1% e as emissões nacionais de gases de efeito estufa serão reduzidas em pelo menos 9% em comparação com o cenário sem intervenção. Para alcançar esses objetivos, é crucial aperfeiçoar a estrutura institucional e os instrumentos econômicos para a redução de emissões. Em consonância com essa direção, o Ministério da Agricultura e do Meio Ambiente está elaborando um projeto de lei revisado e emendado sobre a Proteção Ambiental para institucionalizar novas políticas, remover obstáculos à aplicação da lei , promover a descentralização e a delegação de poderes e reduzir os procedimentos administrativos. Notavelmente, o projeto adiciona regulamentações ao mercado interno de carbono de forma transparente e aberta, em consonância com as práticas internacionais. Paralelamente à alteração da Lei, o Ministério da Agricultura e do Meio Ambiente está elaborando um Decreto que detalha diversas disposições da Lei de Proteção Ambiental relativas à resposta às mudanças climáticas, esclarecendo especificamente as normas sobre gestão de emissões e funcionamento do mercado de carbono. O projeto concentra-se em quatro grupos principais de políticas: adaptação às mudanças climáticas, gestão de emissões de gases de efeito estufa, desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono e proteção da camada de ozônio. Especificamente, instalações com emissões superiores a 3.000 toneladas de CO2 equivalente por ano estão sujeitas a requisitos de inventário. Diversas instalações nos setores de energia, indústria, transporte, comércio e tratamento de resíduos também devem realizar inventários se atenderem aos critérios especificados. Na oficina de consulta sobre o projeto de Decreto, realizada em 10 de novembro, diversos ministérios, setores, associações e empresas contribuíram com opiniões para aprimorar a regulamentação, de modo a alinhá-la melhor às práticas de produção e negócios. Representantes do Ministério da Indústria e Comércio afirmaram que, por meio do programa piloto de alocação de cotas para usinas termelétricas, siderúrgicas e cimenteiras, é necessário um maior rigor na padronização dos dados de entrada, dos métodos de cálculo e dos procedimentos de avaliação. O Ministério recomendou uma avaliação completa dos resultados do piloto, o aprimoramento do banco de dados, a definição de prazos de implementação e o esclarecimento da autoridade e dos recursos necessários para a execução do projeto. Você também pode gostar Representantes do Grupo de Eletricidade do Vietnã ( EVN ) solicitaram esclarecimentos sobre os limites das fontes de emissão, o escopo das emissões diretas e indiretas, especialmente para usinas hidrelétricas e instalações de geração de energia em ilhas. A distinção entre instalações obrigadas a realizar inventários e aquelas com cotas alocadas também precisa ser claramente definida para evitar procedimentos desnecessários. Em relação ao método de alocação de cotas, um representante do Grupo Hoa Phat sugeriu que a indústria siderúrgica precisa diferenciar entre as tecnologias de alto-forno e forno elétrico. Para complexos integrados, o limite de emissão deve corresponder à produção de aço bruto, considerando também soluções para o aproveitamento do calor e dos gases residuais a fim de reduzir as emissões. Em relação ao setor elétrico, a EVN e representantes do Ministério da Indústria e Comércio propuseram a inclusão de uma disposição para o ajuste de cotas quando as usinas termelétricas precisarem aumentar a produção para atender às demandas de despacho e garantir a segurança energética nacional. Este é um fator que precisa ser considerado para assegurar que o mecanismo de gestão de emissões seja consistente com as necessidades operacionais do sistema elétrico e com a produção real. Os delegados também sugeriram a disponibilização pública das fontes de dados, coeficientes e métodos de alocação para que as empresas possam verificá-los e compará-los; e a inclusão de um mecanismo para feedback e resolução de reclamações quando surgirem discrepâncias. Em relação ao mercado de carbono, as principais áreas de preocupação incluem os padrões de crédito de carbono, os regulamentos de leilão, a compensação e a prevenção da dupla contagem para os mesmos resultados de redução de emissões. Representantes do setor florestal propuseram uma distinção clara entre emissão duplicada de créditos de carbono, uso duplicado e declarações duplicadas; e o estabelecimento de um mecanismo de contingência para o risco de reversão dos resultados de redução de emissões devido a incêndios florestais e desastres naturais. artigo.texto: Improving emission management mechanisms paves the way for a carbon market. Amending the Environmental Protection Law and improving regulations on emissions will create a synchronized and transparent legal framework, helping the domestic carbon market operate more effectively. Improving institutions and standardizing emission management. The green transition is placing new demands on state management and production and business activities. As environmental standards increasingly become a condition for market access, reducing emissions is not only a responsibility to comply with but is also directly linked to the competitiveness of businesses. Conclusion No. 75-KL/TW dated July 28, 2026, of the 14th Central Committee of the Communist Party of Vietnam identifies environmental protection, adaptation to climate change, and green transition as the foundation and driving force for innovating development models, improving the quality of growth, and enhancing the competitiveness of the economy . The conclusion sets a target for 2030: the green economy will account for 10% of GDP, the proportion of renewable energy in the total primary energy supply will reach at least 26.1%, and national greenhouse gas emissions will be reduced by at least 9% compared to the business-as-usual scenario. To realize these goals, perfecting the institutional framework and economic tools for emission reduction is crucial. In line with this direction, the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment is developing a draft revised and amended Law on Environmental Protection to institutionalize new policies, remove obstacles in law enforcement, promote decentralization and delegation of power, and reduce administrative procedures. Notably, the draft adds regulations on the domestic carbon market in a transparent and open manner, consistent with international practices. Alongside the amendment of the Law, the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment is drafting a Decree detailing several provisions of the Law on Environmental Protection regarding climate change response, specifically clarifying regulations on emission management and carbon market operation. The draft focuses on four main policy groups: adaptation to climate change, greenhouse gas emission management, carbon market development, and ozone layer protection. Specifically, facilities with emissions exceeding 3,000 tons of CO2 equivalent per year are subject to inventory requirements. Several facilities in the energy, industrial, transportation, trade, and waste treatment sectors must also conduct inventories if they meet the specified criteria. At the consultation workshop on the draft Decree on November 10th, many ministries, sectors, associations, and businesses contributed opinions to improve the regulations in a way that is more aligned with production and business practices. Representatives from the Ministry of Industry and Trade stated that, through the pilot program of allocating quotas to thermal power plants, steel and cement production facilities, further standardization of input data, calculation methods, and appraisal procedures is needed. The Ministry recommended a full evaluation of the pilot results, improvement of the database, consideration of implementation timelines, and clarification of the authority and resources for implementation. You may also like Representatives from the Vietnam Electricity Group ( EVN ) requested clarification on the boundaries of emission sources, the scope of direct and indirect emissions, especially for hydropower plants and power generation facilities on islands. The distinction between facilities obligated to conduct inventories and those allocated quotas also needs to be clearly defined to avoid unnecessary procedures. Regarding the quota allocation method, a representative from Hoa Phat Group suggested that the steel industry needs to differentiate between blast furnace and electric furnace technologies. For integrated complexes, the emission threshold should correspond to crude steel production, while also considering solutions for utilizing waste heat and gases to reduce emissions. Regarding the electricity sector, EVN and representatives from the Ministry of Industry and Trade proposed adding a provision for adjusting quotas when thermal power plants need to increase production to meet dispatching requirements and ensure national energy security. This is a factor that needs to be considered to ensure that the emission management mechanism is consistent with the operational requirements of the power system and actual production. The delegates also suggested making the data sources, coefficients, and allocation methods publicly available so that businesses can verify and compare them; and adding a mechanism for feedback and resolution of complaints when discrepancies arise. Regarding the carbon market, key areas of concern include carbon credit standards, auction regulations, offsetting, and prevention of double counting for the same emission reduction results. Representatives from the forestry sector proposed clearly distinguishing between duplicate carbon credit issuance, duplicate use, and duplicate declarations; and establishing a contingency mechanism for the risk of reversing emission reduction results due to forest fires and natural disasters. artigo.texto: Huawei Luterra S2 All-in-One Residential Energy Storage System Huawei has introduced the Luterra S2, a residential energy storage package that integrates a hybrid inverter, lithium iron phosphate batteries and AI-driven energy management into one system. Single-phase hybrid inverter options span 3 kW to 10 kW, while three-phase versions range from 5 kW to 20 kW. As many as three 20 kW inverters may be paralleled, yielding a combined maximum output of 60 kW. The LFP battery modules offer nominal capacities of 5.02 kWh and 7.03 kWh, corresponding to usable capacities of 4.9 kWh and 6.9 kWh. Rated charge and discharge power stands at 2.5 kW and 3 kW for the smaller module, versus 3.5 kW and 4 kW for the larger one. Ten-second peak discharge reaches 5 kW and 7 kW respectively. Dimensions are 590 mm x 255 mm x 290 mm for both modules, which weigh 46 kg and 57 kg. Across interconnected systems, the modular design accommodates as many as 48 battery packs, reaching a maximum nominal storage capacity of 336 kWh with the 7.03 kWh modules. Huawei stated that the batteries come with integrated energy optimizers and are engineered for more than 15 years of service. The company claims lifetime usable energy throughput of up to 5 MWh for every kWh of battery capacity. Inverter and Backup Specifications Silicon carbide power electronics and active neutral-point-clamped topology are used in the inverters. Per Huawei's preliminary specifications, single-phase models reach 98.6% maximum efficiency, while three-phase units reach 99%. Maximum PV input voltage is 600 V and 1,100 V respectively, with as many as three maximum power point trackers and up to 18 A of input current per tracker. Three-phase models accept up to 40 kWp of PV input power. In backup applications, switchover takes under 10 milliseconds, and continuous off-grid loads of up to 20 kW are supported. According to the preliminary specifications, the 20 kW three-phase inverter can supply peak backup output of up to 40 kW for 10 seconds. Cooling is passive, with no external fans, and claimed operating noise stays below 29 dB. The system runs at ambient temperatures between -25 C and 60 C and carries an IP66-rated enclosure with corrosion protection up to C5-M. Energy Management and Connectivity Huawei's AI Energy Management 2.0 platform draws on weather forecasts, electricity tariffs, household consumption data and battery status to optimize energy flows among PV installations, storage, electric vehicle chargers and heat pumps. Participation in virtual power plants is also supported. Connectivity options include EEBUS, SG Ready, OCPP and Modbus TCP. Additional software features include an AI-based assistant for homeowners, 3D modeling tools for installers and remote diagnostics. Cell-level thermal isolation, pressure relief and smoke evacuation channels are built into the battery system, together with continuous temperature monitoring of AC and DC terminals. Huawei said TUV Rheinland safety testing has been completed, covering thermal runaway, fire exposure and hydrogen explosion tests. The company also reported UL 9540A validation and compliance with IEC 63027 requirements for arc-fault protection. Pricing and market availability details have not been disclosed by Huawei. artigo.texto: Hyperscale Data, Inc. Announces Intent to Launch Exchange Offer to Acquire Up to $50,000,000 of Outstanding Shares for Cash and New Preferred Shares Company Moves to Address Significant Gap Between Market Value and Balance Sheet Strength LAS VEGAS , Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hyperscale Data, Inc. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced that it intends to commence an exchange offer to purchase up to 192,307,692 shares of its Class A Common Stock, $0.001 par value per share ("Common Stock") in exchange for units (the "Units") consisting of (a) $2.00 in cash and (b) one share of preferred stock with a stated value of $24.00 per share (the "Preferred Stock"), per 100 shares of Common Stock. The Preferred Stock will be entitled to receive an annual dividend of 12.00%. Stockholders will be able to exchange blocks of 100 shares of Common Stock for one Unit consisting of (a) $2.00 in cash and (b) one share of Preferred Stock which values the Common Stock at $0.26 per share and represents an 82% premium to the November 6, 2026, closing price of $0.1429. The exchange offer will require that a minimum of 100 million shares of Common Stock be tendered by common stockholders. The Company will seek to list the Preferred Stock on the NYSE American. If the application to list the Preferred Stock is approved by the NYSE American, trading in the Preferred Stock is expected to commence within a 30-day period after the approval of listing. The Company expects to formally launch the proposed exchange offer around November 17, 2026, subject to board approval, regulatory approval and customary closing conditions. The proposed exchange offer reflects Hyperscale's view that its current market valuation does not accurately reflect the strength of its balance sheet, including its holdings of cash and Bitcoin. Milton "Todd" Ault III, Executive Chairman of Hyperscale Data, stated: "We believe there is a material disconnect between the intrinsic value of Hyperscale and where our Common Stock is currently trading. "The exchange offer is intended to provide shareholders with an opportunity for liquidity and an instrument that will allow stockholders to participate in the long-term growth of the Company while receiving a fixed payment. The exchange offer will, if consummated, also allow the Company to repurchase a meaningful percentage of its shares at what we believe are significantly undervalued levels. We believe this is a disciplined and shareholder-focused use of capital." Details regarding the proposed exchange offer and instructions for stockholders interested in participating will be provided in the Offer to Exchange and related documents, which will be filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the "SEC") and distributed to the Company stockholders. The exchange offer will not be made to any person in any jurisdiction in which either the exchange offer, or solicitation or sale thereof, is unlawful. This press release is for informational purposes only and shall not constitute an offer to buy or sell Common Stock or any other securities. Any solicitation of offers to buy the Common Stock will only be made pursuant to an Offer to Exchange and related materials to be sent to the Company stockholders on the commencement of the exchange offer. Company stockholders should read such materials carefully when they become available because they will contain important information, including the terms and conditions of the proposed exchange offer. The tender offer documents will be available without charge at the SEC's website at http://www.sec.gov and will be delivered without charge to all stockholders of the Company who so request it. artigo.texto: On one of the hottest nights of the year, South Australia‘s big batteries ran out of charge before the evening peak ended. That night shows why the next question for Australia’s grid isn’t how many batteries we build, but how long they can run. Australia has built big batteries at record pace. The grid-scale fleet in the National Electricity Market (NEM) now holds about 17.7 GWh of storage, yet it averages just 2.3 hours of discharge at full power.[1] HiTHIUM, a battery manufacturer focused solely on energy storage, thinks that number needs to grow. Its answer is the ∞Power 6.9 MWh, a system it describes as the world’s first battery built from the cell up for eight hours. A battery that runs out at 8pm is useful. A battery that runs past midnight is infrastructure. TL;DR - Duration is the new pressure point: Most of Australia’s grid batteries hold two hours or less, but high-price events are expected to stretch from about 1.5 hours today to 5–10 hours by the 2040s. - Policy is already moving to eight hours: NSW and South Australia now contract storage that can run for eight hours or more. - HiTHIUM has built for that standard: Its ∞Power 6.9 MWh uses a dedicated 1,300 Ah cell designed for eight-hour discharge, backed by a 25-year design life. What happened in South Australia on 26 January 2026? South Australia had the quarter’s most expensive evening, and its batteries ran low before the evening ended. The Australian Energy Regulator (AER) set out what happened in its report on significant electricity prices.[2] Parts of Adelaide passed 44°C. Evening demand topped 3,100 MW, within 300 MW of the state’s record. Wind output fell to around 337 MW, about 12% of installed capacity. Prices ran high from 6:30pm to 10:30pm, peaking at $20,158/MWh for a 30-minute period. AEMO declared an actual lack of reserve from 8:30pm to 9:45pm. Batteries delivered plenty of power early in the evening. But from around 7:50pm, operators began withdrawing offers, mostly citing state of charge. By 8:55pm, battery offers had fallen below 100 MW, down from an average of 839 MW when high prices began. The AER attributed the evening’s prices to more than heat alone: high demand, low wind, network constraints and rebidding all played a part. Yet much of that rebidding was itself a duration story — Neoen shifted 130–200 MW at Blyth toward the high-priced evening hours as its forecast state of charge fell, and Vena Energy withdrew 40 MW at Tailem Bend. The heat continued overnight. When prices spiked again the next morning, the AER found very little battery capacity was on offer. The batteries did their job. They simply couldn’t last long enough. A battery that starts discharging at 6:30pm with eight hours of storage could, in principle, keep going until 2:30am— through the morning spike that followed. The AER found that across that quarter, prices above $5,000/MWh added $63/MWh to South Australia’s average wholesale price.[2] Why is battery duration becoming the big question? The grid’s hardest hours are getting longer, while most of the battery fleet was built for short bursts. A battery’s duration is how many hours it can discharge at full power. A 100 MW / 200 MWh battery is a two-hour battery. Two-hour systems make up 5.2 GW of the NEM’s 7.3 GW of operating battery capacity, Modo Energy’s July 2026 long-duration outlook found.[3] Those batteries were designed for a grid with sharp, brief price spikes. That grid is changing. In the same analysis, Modo forecasts that price events above $300/MWh will lengthen from about 1.5 hours today to between five and 10 hours by the 2040s. The reliability outlook points the same way. Modo’s reading of AEMO’s 2026 Electricity Statement of Opportunities is that most shortfall events will run longer than four hours by 2030.[4] The existing fleet and pipeline can already cover shorter events. The industry has moved to four hours. Is that enough? Developers have already stretched duration. Four hours is now the default for new NEM battery investment, according to Modo Energy’s analysis of duration trends.[5] The future pipeline holds 24.4 GW of four-hour-or-longer capacity, but only 2.6 GW at eight hours, Modo’s July outlook shows. Four hours would have covered the high-price window on 26 January. It would not have covered the next morning, when batteries that had discharged overnight had little left to offer. As coal retires, the grid needs storage that can cover a whole evening and still have something left. How do Australia’s storage schemes treat duration? Australia’s storage schemes don’t agree on how long is long enough. National tenders mostly buy four-hour batteries, while NSW and South Australia now write eight hours into their contracts, and WA’s requirement is climbing towards seven. NSW: the country’s biggest long-duration tender In February 2026, ASL awarded LTESAs to six battery projects totalling 1.17 GW / 11.98 GWh, all eight hours or longer.[6] The largest, Neoen’s Great Western Battery, has a nominal duration of 10.6 hours.[7] The round took NSW’s contracted storage to 30 GWh. A further 12 GWh tender has been scheduled to start in Q2 2026, with another 12 GWh in 2027. South Australia: four-hour batteries derated to fit South Australia’s first FERM round shows what an eight-hour rule does to a fleet built around shorter durations. Modo Energy’s analysis found that the six winning batteries hold 1,334 MW of nameplate capacity but commit only 517 MW to the scheme.[8] That’s because four-hour batteries had to derate their power to stretch their energy across eight hours. The state still expects its large-scale battery capacity to grow from 1.1 GW to 2.5 GW.[9] Derating works. But it means buying more inverters, transformers and grid connection than the firm power you actually get. National tenders still default to four hours The federal CIS has been the biggest driver of new batteries, and it mostly buys four hours. Tender 8 projects needed at least two hours of storage

artigo.texto: One of the most resounding results of the midterm elections was that artificial intelligence (AI) is facing a big backlash from voters. Americans of both parties seem to agree on one big issue: They don't want AI data centers built in their backyards. According to data tracked by Ballotpedia, as of Nov. 4, voters decided on 47 local ballot initiatives to either support or limit the development of AI data centers. And 46 of 47 of these initiatives (98%) resulted in outcomes against the development of AI data centers. This is a big sign that the AI industry has a public relations problem. It's rare to get 98% of American voters to agree on anything, but in 98% of these local ballot measures, American voters expressed distrust of the AI build-out. A CNBC poll found that 56% of voters ranked data centers as a "crucial or major" factor in how they voted on Election Day. Many American voters are worried that AI data centers will raise utility costs. They don't want to offer up their local land and resources for data center construction without seeing economic benefits to their communities. And they support political candidates who are skeptical about AI data centers. In Ohio and Texas, newly elected Democratic governors have proposed moratoriums on new AI data center construction. Let's look at what the AI data center backlash means for investors -- and how you might want to position your portfolio as a result. A post-election sell-off in AI data center stocks The first few days after the Nov. 3 midterm election brought a big sell-off in AI-related stocks. The tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 dropped by 5.5% between Nov. 3 and Nov. 5, while the iShares Semiconductor ETF plummeted by about 15%. It's not just tech companies and chipmakers that are affected by the AI backlash. Construction manufacturer Caterpillar, a major pick-and-shovel AI stock that has benefited from the data center boom, lost about 11.3% during those two days after the election. Although all these names have recouped some of their post-election losses since Nov. 5, this is still a big sign that AI stocks are vulnerable to the will of the voters. If Americans are becoming hostile toward data centers, that could slow the AI boom -- and lead to downturns for other AI stocks. Warning signs of an AI data center slowdown Does the midterm election result mean that the AI boom is over? Not necessarily. But it could be heading for a slowdown. If states and local governments require more expensive regulations or slower approval processes for AI data centers, that could drive up costs and add delays for AI companies. If AI data centers are built more slowly and more expensively, there could be some new AI winners and losers in the short term. Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., has been an enthusiastically bullish voice on the AI boom, which he calls the "AI Revolution." But on Nov. 4, as reported by CNBC, Ives wrote a research note that said: "For tech investors the big focus is will these mid-term elections slow the pace of the planned 800 to 1,000 datacenters across the US fueling the AI Revolution...the answer in our view is a clear YES." Ives also wrote that his firm now believes that "Big Tech capex growth rate now peaks in 2027 vs. our previous view that would not happen until 2028/2029." If the boom in AI capex ends in 2027, that could be bad news for semiconductor stocks and various pick-and-shovel stocks whose earnings have been boosted by hundreds of billions of dollars in corporate investment in data centers. CNBC also reported that Dominique Toublan, Barclays Investment Bank head of U.S. credit strategy, wrote in a note from Nov. 4 that "AI pushback is bipartisan but local, making the buildout pricier rather than stalling it," and that "scarce power favors the biggest balance sheets." How to invest in AI stocks after the midterms If you believe AI data centers are about to become more expensive to build and you agree with Toublan's view that companies with the "biggest balance sheets" are likely to benefit from this new dynamic, the best AI stocks to buy now might be the large-cap AI hyperscalers. If AI data centers become more expensive to build, the companies best equipped to build them are likely to be the well-established, cash-rich companies like Alphabet (GOOG +2.00%) (GOOGL +2.11%) rather than neoclouds like CoreWeave (CRWV +24.71%). CoreWeave has recently drawn investor concern about its high level of debt and rising interest expenses. A slowdown in the AI data center build-out could add to those pressures. The landscape of the AI trade just got more complicated with the midterm elections. If you still believe in tech stocks but don't want to invest too much in any one stock or sector, you could buy a tech ETF like the Invesco Nasdaq 100 ETF (QQQM +2.29%). This fund holds 103 stocks of the largest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq. In the past five years, QQQM has delivered annualized returns of about 13.1%. QQQM Invesco NASDAQ 100 ETF NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/11/26 That 13.1% average annual return includes the bad bear market of 2022, when the Nasdaq-100 declined by about 33.1%. For long-term investors, QQQM is likely a good way to invest in the tech economy and perhaps own future big AI winners -- without concentrating too much on any one company or industry vertical. artigo.texto: Anthropic has spent billions developing Claude, one of the world's leading artificial intelligence models. Now it's preparing to spend a staggering amount of money to make sure Claude has somewhere to run. In its recent IPO filing, Anthropic disclosed approximately $895.4 billion in purchase commitments and lease agreements, substantially all related to computing and infrastructure. About $447.5 billion of those commitments are expected to come due by the end of 2030. But Anthropic isn't simply buying computing capacity from Amazon and Alphabet anymore. It's also pursuing dedicated data center infrastructure, including arrangements in which third parties develop facilities that Anthropic leases and operates through specialized partners. Anthropic isn't necessarily constructing or owning the buildings itself. And its filing doesn't identify most of the companies that will build and equip those facilities. Still, some interesting publicly traded companies do this type of work and offer investors exposure to data center construction. Sterling Infrastructure: Preparing the ground Before installing a server, someone has to prepare the site. My pick in this realm is Sterling Infrastructure (STRL +14.97%), which provides site development services for large industrial projects, including data centers and semiconductor manufacturing facilities. Sterling performs excavation and grading at construction sites and prepares infrastructure to support large buildings. Its electrical contracting business adds another source of revenue from complex construction projects. Business is booming. In the third quarter, Sterling's E-Infrastructure Solutions segment generated $1.30 billion in revenue, an increase of 212% from a year earlier. That segment accounted for 83% of the company's total quarterly revenue. Sterling also reported $4.14 billion in signed backlog and another $2 billion in unsigned awards. Management says its broader pipeline of identified work, including future project phases, approaches $8 billion. STRL Sterling Infrastructure NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/09/26 Quanta Services: Delivering the electricity Data centers need power, and a lot of it. Quanta Services (PWR +9.35%) provides transmission lines, substations, and other infrastructure to connect data centers to the power grid. AI data centers aren't the only customers demanding more electricity. Utilities are investing in grid modernization, while industrial facilities and other large electricity users need additional capacity. That gives Quanta a much broader opportunity than any single AI company's expansion plans. Revenue in the third quarter was $12.01 billion, up 57% from a year ago. Its Electric segment generated $9.80 billion, accounting for nearly 82% of total revenue. Meanwhile, Quanta's total backlog reached a record $63.7 billion, providing substantial visibility into future work. PWR Quanta Services NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/09/26 Vertiv: Keeping the chips cool AI chips and servers generate a lot of heat as they work together on AI tasks. And without a way to cool off, they won't work for long. Vertiv Holdings (VRT +9.63%) makes liquid cooling systems that help solve that problem, as well as power equipment and related infrastructure for data centers. The company's Q3 revenue was $4.31 billion, up an impressive 61% from a year ago. Organic orders more than doubled, and adjusted operating margin increased 290 basis points to 25.2%. The company's deferred revenue also reached $4.12 billion at the end of September, compared with $1.81 billion at the end of 2025. That reflects payments received for products and services that haven't yet been recognized as revenue. Converting that demand into completed deliveries remains important. VRT Vertiv NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/09/26 Three stocks to buy to invest in AI infrastructure Anthropic's filing makes clear that expanding computing capacity involves considerably more than purchasing advanced chips. It requires land, construction, electricity, cooling equipment, and specialized contractors. Sterling, Quanta, and Vertiv each participate in a different part of that process. While none is identified as an Anthropic contractor in the filing, all three serve customers beyond Anthropic. That's why they're worth examining.

artigo.texto: AI data centers raise questions about water use, cooling Artificial intelligence can answer a question in seconds, but behind that speed is a physical network of computers, power lines and, in many cases, water. Data centers running AI generate enormous amounts of heat and keeping that equipment cool can place new demands on local water supplies, especially during hot weather or drought. Shirley Clarke, a Penn State Harrisburg professor, said cooling is a major issue. “The biggest part that people need to know about air and water is this issue around cooling the computer chips that we use, which take a tremendous amount of water depending on what cooling system we use,” Clarke said. How data centers stay cool When an AI program summarizes a document or answers a question, that work happens on computers housed in data centers. Those computers use electricity, and as they work, their chips give off heat. How that heat is removed can make a major difference in how much water a facility needs. One common method uses water that moves through tubes near the chips to carry heat away. In some systems, that water circulates in a closed loop. But the water can become too warm to reuse directly, so some facilities use cooling towers, where water is sent outside and allowed to evaporate. That breaks the closed loop and requires new water to be added. Another option uses fans to move air across equipment, which uses very little water but can require more electricity on very hot days. Experts say the amount of water used can vary widely depending on the model, the length of the response, the location, the weather, the cooling system and the electricity supply. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that all U.S. data centers — not just those running AI — directly consumed about 17 billion gallons of water in 2023. Questions for local communities For communities considering a data center, the biggest questions are where the facility would get its water, how much it would need on average and on the hottest days, and what happens when supplies are low. “You know, does it go to the residents to do what? Shower, to clean, to drink, to cook? Or does it go to the data center or is there a balance in there? And that's what many of the parties are going to have to be dealing with and the water systems are gonna have to deal with,” Clarke said. Location also matters. A facility drawing from a small stream or heavily used groundwater source may raise different concerns than one served by a larger supply. Groundwater can also replenish slowly, and even where water is available, a utility may need new pipes, pumps or treatment capacity. There is also debate about using treated wastewater for industrial cooling instead of drinking-water supplies. “The other problem we have with this really is we're just not equipped for it. Oftentimes the data centers are not built next to the treatment plants. So now we'd be looking at running another set of infrastructure to get the wastewater to that,” Clarke said. The question, experts say, is not whether every data center uses the same amount of water. They do not. The question for each community is how a proposed facility will be cooled, where its water and electricity will come from, and what protections will be in place when supplies are under stress.

artigo.texto: Mundo Indonésios protestam contra data centers por falta de água Enfrentando uma seca severa e escassez de água para necessidades básicas como cozinhar e tomar banho, os habitantes da ilha de Batam, na Indonésia, manifestam-se contra a rápida instalação de ‘data centers’ que impulsionam o avanço da inteligência artificial. A região vem sofrendo uma seca prolongada, intensificada pelo fenômeno climático El Niño, segundo o responsável pelo serviço local de abastecimento de água, em depoimento à AFP. Como em outras nações, a população atribui a culpa aos ‘data centers’, que são instalações que mantêm aplicativos e ferramentas de IA em funcionamento e utilizam água para resfriar seus equipamentos. Juniardi Adinda Sembiring Gurukinayan, comerciante local de 54 anos, relatou que inicialmente a chegada dessa indústria parecia positiva para Batam, mas com os cortes recentes no fornecimento de água, os moradores enfrentam dificuldades como ficar sem banho em algumas ocasiões. Ele destaca: “Não podemos preparar arroz sem água, nem cozinhar verduras”. Em um período crítico, dezenas de moradores realizaram protestos diante do Nongsa Digital Park, um complexo de ‘data centers’ e outras instalações que foi designado como zona econômica especial. Os residentes creem que a escassez hídrica está relacionada à construção dessas instalações, afirmou Juniardi. A seca causou uma queda acentuada no nível do reservatório próximo a Nongsa, enquanto uma pane elétrica agravou as interrupções no abastecimento, explicou Ginda Alamsyah, porta-voz da empresa operadora de água Air Batam Hilir. Esse parque tecnológico é abastecido por outro reservatório, o de Duriangkang, conforme fonte do setor industrial. Em setembro, as autoridades orientaram os empreendedores a instalarem sistemas para dessalinização da água do mar para uso na refrigeração, evitando assim a pressão sobre os recursos locais. Empresas como BW Digital, com sede em Singapura, DayOne e Princeton Digital Group operam ou planejam operar no Nongsa Digital Park. Gaw Capital Partners, com sede em Hong Kong, declarou estar ciente das preocupações dos moradores e que seus centros de dados adotam tecnologias eficientes e energias renováveis para minimizar impactos, incluindo sistemas de circuito fechado que reutilizam água. Na cidade costeira vizinha de Mata Ikan, moradores têm utilizado água do mar para higiene pessoal após evacuações, relata o manifestante Rahmat, de 52 anos. Sulastri, de 38 anos, conta que a crise hídrica, que já dura um ano e piorou nos últimos seis meses, faz com que precise usar água engarrafada para lavar utensílios domésticos. O governo disponibilizou água por meio de caminhões-pipa, porém a qualidade foi criticada por moradores, pois estava malcheirosa e com coloração amarelada. Autoridades locais não responderam aos questionamentos da AFP sobre a situação. O prefeito de Batam, Amsakar Achmad, afirmou que as interrupções no abastecimento não são consequência dos data centers, mas sim de fatores climáticos. A rápida expansão tecnológica e seus desafios Relatório da KPMG indica que a capacidade dos ‘data centers’ no sudeste asiático deve triplicar entre 2025 e 2030, o que poderá aumentar a pressão sobre recursos hídricos e energéticos, já fortemente dependentes de combustíveis fósseis. A Indonésia e a Malásia viram crescimento acelerado destes centros, especialmente após Singapura suspender novos projetos temporariamente. Ginda ressalta que a empresa de água apoia o desenvolvimento desde que haja gestão eficiente, incluindo melhorias nos reservatórios de Batam e técnicas como semeadura de nuvens para combater a seca. Impactos e mobilizações na Malásia Na região de Johor, considerada um grande polo emergente para infraestrutura de IA, a capacidade dos ‘data centers’ aumentou consideravelmente, causando preocupações ambientais. Projeções do governo indicam que até 2035 esses centros poderão consumir um terço da energia total da Malásia. Moradores protestam contra poluição por poeira e alagamentos provocados pela proximidade das instalações a áreas residenciais, enfatizando que a situação está em um momento crítico, segundo Mohd Fadhil Md Din, da Universidade Tecnológica da Malásia. Em Kota Damansara, um projeto de ‘data center’ foi suspenso após forte oposição da comunidade, com mais de 9.000 assinaturas em petição e pressões políticas. Jahaidi Harun, aposentado de 72 anos, destacou que além do barulho, o consumo elevado de água é sentido por todos quando não chove por um período prolongado.

artigo.texto: Production of Airedale® Chillers for Data Center Customers Begins at New Texas Facility RACINE, Wis. , Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Modine (NYSE: MOD), a diversified global leader in thermal management technology and solutions, today announced that it has commenced commercial production of Airedale® chillers at a new purpose-built advanced manufacturing facility in Grand Prairie, Texas. The 682,000-square-foot facility is dedicated to manufacturing state-of-the-art 2MW and 3MW chillers with free cooling for the data center market, directly supporting the rapidly expanding infrastructure needs of the world's leading hyperscale cloud providers, colocation operators, and high-density AI computing environments. "The launch of our Grand Prairie facility is an important milestone in the plan we announced last year to expand U.S. manufacturing capacity for Airedale cooling technologies," said Neil D. Brinker, President and CEO. "Scaling our capacity close to our customers enables us to partner with them to deliver the right highly engineered cooling solutions to help them advance their progress and achieve their performance objectives." The Grand Prairie site is expected to become the largest Airedale chiller manufacturing facility within the organization's global footprint. The first production line began operations this month, and the company is targeting four operational 2MW production lines by the end of the current fiscal year, subject to equipment commissioning, workforce readiness, and other operational considerations. The facility currently operates one shift, with plans to systematically scale to a fully operational, three-shift model. In addition to chillers, Airedale offers a comprehensive portfolio of mission-critical thermal management solutions, including dry coolers, coolant distribution units (CDUs), and intelligent controls, engineered to optimize efficiency across diverse data center thermal architectures. Airedale's purpose-built, premium systems address the most complex, high-density thermal demands of today's data center operators while maximizing energy and water efficiency. About Modine For more than 100 years, Modine has solved the toughest thermal management challenges for mission-critical applications. Our purpose of Engineering a Cleaner, Healthier World™ means we are always evolving our portfolio of technologies to provide the latest heating, cooling, and ventilation solutions. Through the hard work of more than 9,000 employees worldwide, our businesses advance our purpose with systems that improve air quality, reduce energy and water consumption, and use environmentally friendly refrigerants. Modine is a global company headquartered in Racine, Wisconsin (U.S.), with operations in North America, Europe, and Asia. For more information about Modine, visit www.modine.com. As of 11:42 a.m. ET, the S&P 500 was down 57.20 points, or 0.76%, at 7,492.74, the Nasdaq Composite was down 269.19 points, or 1.07%, at 24,983.95, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 357.50 points, or 0.68%, at 52,032.25. Below the index level, companies that make the physical equipment behind AI data centers, from chip inspection tools and optical links to electronics manufacturing, cooling systems and backup generators, have reported quarterly results over the past two weeks, three of them on Monday. Active Companies from around the markets with current developments this week include: Onto Innovation Inc. (NYSE: ONTO), Coherent Corp. (NYSE: COHR), Sanmina Corporation(NASDAQ: SANM), AAON, Inc.(NASDAQ: AAON), and Generac Holdings Inc.(NYSE: GNRC). What the inflation report showed According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers increased 0.4 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in October after rising 0.6 percent in September. The index for all items less food and energy rose 0.3 percent in October, as it did in September and August. The agency said it did not collect survey data for October 2025 because of a lapse in appropriations and, as a result, cannot publish 12-month percent changes for October 2026 for indexes where October 2025 data are unavailable. Inside the chip: inspection and process control Onto Innovation Inc. (NYSE: ONTO) was up 1.41% as of 11:42 a.m. ET. In its third quarter 2026 results released November 9, the company reported record quarterly revenue of $410 million, an increase of 88% as compared to the third quarter of 2025, with revenue, operating margin and earnings per share all exceeding the high end of its previously announced non-GAAP guidance ranges. "Demand remains robust as increasingly complex device architectures for next-generation AI and high-performance computing drive greater process control requirements." artigo.texto: Hyperscale Data Sells Remaining Bitcoin Reserves to Reduce Debt and Fund Michigan AI Data Center LAS VEGAS , Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hyperscale Data, Inc. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced that as of November 8th, 2026, it had sold all of its remaining Bitcoin reserves at approximately $76,000 per Bitcoin. The Company sold approximately 211.56 Bitcoin and received gross proceeds of approximately $16.0 million. Since the Company initially sold a portion of its Bitcoin reserve in late July of 2026, the Company has sold approximately 1,113 Bitcoin for approximate proceeds of $74.4 million. Hyperscale Data is using the proceeds to pay down debt and fund the continued development of its Michigan AI data center. "Our highest priority is to energize the first 10 megawatts of critical IT capacity at our Michigan data center in December," said Will Horne, Chief Executive Officer of Hyperscale Data. "We believe bringing that capacity online is our quickest path to profitability. Selling our Bitcoin reserves reduces our exposure to Bitcoin price swings and gives us cash to pay down debt and fund the work in Michigan. We believe that's the best use of this capital for all our stockholders." Hyperscale Data continues to mine Bitcoin at its Montana mining site. Going forward, the Company expects any Bitcoin it holds on its balance sheet to come primarily from its own mining operations. The Company expects to file its Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, on or before Monday, November 23. In light of the recently announced proposed exchange offer for its Class A common stock (the "Exchange Offer"), the Company also expects to move its virtual Investor Day from November 12 to November 23. Management expects to update investors on debt reduction and progress toward the December energization target. When the Company commences the Exchange Offer, it will file the offer documents with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Stockholders should read those documents when available. They will be accessible free of charge at www.sec.gov. For more information on Hyperscale Data and its subsidiaries, Hyperscale Data recommends that stockholders, investors and any other interested parties read Hyperscale Data's public filings and press releases available under the Investor Relations section at hyperscaledata.com or available at www.sec.gov. About Hyperscale Data, Inc. Through its wholly owned subsidiary Sentinum, Inc., Hyperscale Data owns and operates a data center at which it offers colocation and hosting services for the emerging AI ecosystems and other industries. Another of Hyperscale Data's wholly owned subsidiaries, Ault Capital Group, Inc. ("ACG"), is a hybrid private equity firm and operating company that acquires, finances, builds and actively manages businesses across financial services, digital assets, industrial services, hospitality, defense technologies and other sectors. Hyperscale Data currently expects the divestiture of ACG (the "Divestiture") to occur in 2027. Upon the occurrence of the Divestiture, the Company would be an owner and operator of data centers to support high-performance computing services, as well as a holder of the digital assets and the third wholly owned subsidiary of the Company, Omnipresent Robotics, LLC. Until the Divestiture occurs, the Company will continue to provide, through ACG and its wholly and majority-owned subsidiaries and strategic investments, mission-critical products that support a diverse range of industries, including an AI software platform, equipment rental services, defense/aerospace, industrial, automotive and hotel operations. In addition, ACG is actively engaged in private credit and structured finance through Ault Lending, LLC, a licensed lending subsidiary. Hyperscale Data's headquarters are located at 11411 Southern Highlands Parkway, Suite 190, Las Vegas, NV 89141. On December 23, 2024, the Company issued one million (1,000,000) shares of a newly designated Series F Exchangeable Preferred Stock (the "Series F Preferred Stock") to all common stockholders and holders of the Series C Preferred Stock on an as-converted basis. The Divestiture will occur through the voluntary exchange of the Series F Preferred Stock for shares of Class A Common Stock and Class B Common Stock of ACG (collectively, the "ACG Shares"). The Company reminds its stockholders that only those holders of the Series F Preferred Stock who agree to surrender such shares, and do not properly withdraw such surrender, in the exchange offer through which the Divestiture will occur, will be entitled to receive the ACG Shares and consequently be shareholders of ACG upon the occurrence of the Divestiture. artigo.texto: Munters announces investments to strengthen data center supply chain and capacity STOCKHOLM , Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Munters Group today announced it has entered into an agreement with Lordan, a producer of high-quality fin and tube heat exchangers, to establish a joint venture for coil manufacturing in the US. The company also said it plans to expand its facility for chiller production in Italy. US joint venture Munters will invest MUSD 9.5 (approximately MSEK 90) and hold 45% in the joint venture company, with Lordan holding the remaining 55%. The joint venture will now proceed to establish a facility for coil manufacturing near Munters Data Center Technologies' facility in Selma, Texas. Production is expected to begin in 12-18 months. "Coils are a critical component in many of our cooling products. Through this collaboration with a well-established expert in heat exchangers, we are ensuring a flexible supply of high-quality coils and related components for products such as CRAHs and fan walls," says Frank Pellegrino, President of Munters business area Data Center Technologies. "The proximity to our existing facility is an added benefit from an efficiency and environmental perspective, and we're excited about the potential for this joint venture to contribute to our in-house expertise around thermal management and heat exchange," adds Pellegrino. The agreement with Lordan is valid for seven years and includes commitments from the parties to produce and acquire a certain quantity of coils over that period, at preferred lead times and price levels. Lordan will be responsible for day-to-day operations at the facility while Munters will contribute with supply chain and staffing resources. Italy expansion Munters has also decided to expand its existing facility in northern Italy for manufacturing of chillers, to better meet growing demand in Europe for these products. The company is acquiring an adjoining site and will over the course of the coming year develop new production lines, R&D capabilities and testing facilities. The total investment is estimated at around MEUR 25. "This investment signifies our commitment to growing chiller capacity for Europe, as well as the importance of our Italian operations as a hub for expertise in this area," Pellegrino said. artigo.texto: LITEON Showcases High-Speed Optical Interconnect and Key Optoelectronic Technologies at electronica 2026, Advancing AI Data Center Infrastructure with Intelligent Photonics MUNICH , Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- LITEON Technology (2301) participates in electronica 2026, held in Munich, Germany, from November 10 to 13, showcasing its optoelectronic semiconductor technologies under the theme "Intelligent Photonics." The portfolio spans high-speed optical interconnects, high-efficiency isolation and power control, intelligent sensing, and AR optics, demonstrating LITEON's broad deployment of core optoelectronic technologies across AI data centers, high-efficiency energy management, and intelligent applications. "AI is accelerating the transformation of computing and energy infrastructure, while driving growing demand for high-speed, low-power, and highly reliable optical connectivity," said Sander Su, General Manager of LITEON's Optoelectronics Products Solutions. "With deep expertise in optical communications and optoelectronic semiconductors, LITEON is positioning ourselves as a Digital Photonics Integrator, continuously integrating technologies across key components, modules, and system-level applications to help customers address the growing demands for high-speed transmission, greater efficiency, and intelligent sensing in the AI era." As AI computing scales, data centers require higher bandwidth, lower latency, and greater energy efficiency. LITEON showcases its VHP External Laser Source (ELS) technology and ELSFP solutions supporting CPO and NPO switch architectures, providing high-performance, scalable optical connectivity for AI clusters and future data centers. Designed to accommodate different system configurations, liquid-cooling architectures, and integration requirements, the solutions help customers build more efficient AI networking infrastructure. LITEON also showcases isolation and power-control technologies for 800 VDC power systems and AI data center power architectures, extending its optoelectronic expertise from data transmission to power conversion and control. The portfolio includes Isolation Amplifiers, Gate Drivers, high-speed Photocouplers, Photo Relays, and reinforced isolation platforms, providing safe and reliable power conversion as well as precise signal sensing and control in high-voltage, high-power environments. These technologies also support solar inverters, battery management systems, EV charging, and industrial automation, enhancing safety, reliability, and energy efficiency across diverse applications. Beyond data centers, LITEON showcases Multi-Zone ToF, Direct ToF, Metalens Dot Projectors and SWIR sensing technologies for robotics, machine vision, industrial automation, autonomous navigation and AR/VR applications. The showcase also features next-generation AR optical technologies, including MicroLED display modules, full-color optical engines, waveguide integration and AR optical system design, demonstrating LITEON's ability to extend its optoelectronic semiconductor expertise from sensing components to optical modules and integrated systems, further expanding its presence in emerging applications such as smart wearables and immersive computing. artigo.texto: Anthropic's S-1 Says It Will Expand Its Data Center Footprint. Here's Who Could Pour the Concrete, Wire the Power, and Cool the Chips. Anthropic has spent billions developing Claude, one of the world's leading artificial intelligence models. Now it's preparing to spend a staggering amount of money to make sure Claude has somewhere to run. In its recent IPO filing, Anthropic disclosed approximately $895.4 billion in purchase commitments and lease agreements, substantially all related to computing and infrastructure. About $447.5 billion of those commitments are expected to come due by the end of 2030. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » But Anthropic isn't simply buying computing capacity from Amazon and Alphabet anymore. It's also pursuing dedicated data center infrastructure, including arrangements in which third parties develop facilities that Anthropic leases and operates through specialized partners. Anthropic isn't necessarily constructing or owning the buildings itself. And its filing doesn't identify most of the companies that will build and equip those facilities. Still, some interesting publicly traded companies do this type of work and offer investors exposure to data center construction. Sterling Infrastructure: Preparing the ground Before installing a server, someone has to prepare the site. My pick in this realm is Sterling Infrastructure (NASDAQ: STRL), which provides site development services for large industrial projects, including data centers and semiconductor manufacturing facilities. Sterling performs excavation and grading at construction sites and prepares infrastructure to support large buildings. Its electrical contracting business adds another source of revenue from complex construction projects. Business is booming. In the third quarter, Sterling's E-Infrastructure Solutions segment generated $1.30 billion in revenue, an increase of 212% from a year earlier. That segment accounted for 83% of the company's total quarterly revenue. Sterling also reported $4.14 billion in signed backlog and another $2 billion in unsigned awards. Management says its broader pipeline of identified work, including future project phases, approaches $8 billion. Quanta Services: Delivering the electricity Data centers need power, and a lot of it. Quanta Services (NYSE: PWR) provides transmission lines, substations, and other infrastructure to connect data centers to the power grid. AI data centers aren't the only customers demanding more electricity. Utilities are investing in grid modernization, while industrial facilities and other large electricity users need additional capacity. That gives Quanta a much broader opportunity than any single AI company's expansion plans.

artigo.texto: Lawmakers eye data center moratorium as Virginia environmental coalition ramps up pressure ASHLAND, Va. (7News) — A coalition of more than a dozen environmental groups met in the parking lot of an animal shelter in Ashland, Virginia, Wednesday to call for a halt to any new data center construction within the commonwealth. Their backdrop: a data center approved in Hanover County with little-to-no public input. At a time when state lawmakers in Virginia are increasingly warming to the idea of pressing the pause button on Virginia's data-center build out, environmental groups are calling for a moratorium on new construction. ALSO READ | Virginia Democrats lay out 2027 agenda targeting affordability and data centers "We're here to say 'enough is enough. Our governor and our legislature need to pause data center construction to protect the Virginia we know and love," said Blair St. Ledger-Olson, Director of Advocacy and Campaigns for the Virginia League of Conservation Voters. More than one speaker Wednesday referenced shifting opinions within the Virginia General Assembly, as well as changing voter sentiment reflected in the midterm elections, a combination the coalition seeks to capitalize upon as Virginia lawmakers prepare to consider what one person Wednesday referred to as a "smorgasbord of legislative options." Senator Russet Perry, (D - Loudoun County) and Senator Glen Sturtevant, (R - Chesterfield), among others, are expected to back bills in the coming legislative session recommending a moratorium on data centers. With 685 data centers either built or in the planning stages, Virginia is far and away the data center capital of the world. Any new projects, the coalition insists, must protect the commonwealth's power, water and land. "We are paying more for power because of data centers, and the data centers are getting a sweet deal on the backs of Virginians," Nate Benforado, an attorney for the Southern Environmental Law Center said Wednesday. Jay Ford, a policy director with the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, cautioned that the 64,000 square mile Chesapeake Bay watershed sits at "ground zero." "Just this year, Virginia has faced historic strains on our water resources," Ford said. "We drink water from rivers and we drink it from ground water and both of those are under historic stress right now. " Julie Bolthouse, Director of Land Use for the Piedmont Environmental Council identified the commonwealth as "one of the fastest growing markets" in the nation's data center build out, "with about 280 million square feet of data centers space already approved locally." Bolthouse said that amount of land designated for data center development is "the equivalent of 1,500 Walmart supercenters or, if you're a football fan, 5,000 football fields." The question is whether the growing calls for a data center moratorium will sway the opinion of Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger, who has publicly supported greater restrictions on the industry through an executive order but not an outright pause on any new construction. Elena Schlossberg, who successfully battled a massive data center project in her home of Prince William County said Wednesday that Spanberger would do well to consider, what Schlossberg described as the shifting political winds. "If Governor Spanberger has higher aspirations, then I would recommend that she get on the right side of this issue," Schlossberg said.
