artigo.texto: Byhmgard signs loan agreement with Signet Bank for the financing of the SW Power battery storage plant in Rīga, 15 MW / 30 MWh Byhmgard AB (publ) ("Byhmgard" or the "Company") announces that its wholly owned project company SW Power SIA (the "Project Company") has signed a loan agreement with Signet Bank AS for a project loan of just over EUR 3.0 million, corresponding to 50 percent of the financing of the Company's battery storage plant at Ata iela in Rīga, Latvia (the "Plant"). The total financing requirement for the Plant amounts to approximately EUR 6.1 million (approximately SEK 67 million). The remaining 50 percent is intended to be financed largely through the Company's wholly owned subsidiary Byhmgard Invest AB, which in turn owns all shares in the Project Company, acquiring battery systems on a payment plan and contributing them to the Project Company as a contribution in kind. This credit is guaranteed with support from the financing agreement with Middelborg AS and Gimle Invest AS announced by the Company on 11 March 2026. The loan from Signet Bank is sized to be serviced by the group's revenue from energy arbitrage, which the Company estimates at approximately EUR 20 million over 20 years, with a further potential of approximately EUR 33 million from balancing and capacity services to the state-owned transmission system operator Augstsprieguma tīkls (AST). As previously announced, commercial operation is planned for the second quarter of 2027. Financing The financing requirement of approximately EUR 6.1 million is financed half by a project loan from Signet Bank AS, Rīga, secured on the Plant and the Project Company. The loan is disbursed against costs incurred during construction and is repaid monthly from autumn 2027. The other half is intended to be financed through the Company's subsidiary Byhmgard Invest AB, which in turn owns all shares in the Project Company, acquiring battery systems on credit and contributing them to the Project Company as a contribution in kind. The battery systems make up most of the portion of financing provided by Byhmgard Invest AB, and the balance, approximately 30 percent, is contributed in cash by Byhmgard Invest AB. The credit for Byhmgard Invest AB's acquisition of the battery systems is supported by guarantees from Middelborg AS and Gimle Invest AS in accordance with the financing agreement announced on 11 March 2026, under which these parties undertake to cover the part of the project cost not financed by bank debt. The financing of the Company's second plant in Rīga, SW Battery SIA, is being finalised and is intended to follow the same structure. Revenue calculation The loan from Signet Bank is sized on estimated revenue from energy arbitrage, that is trading on the Nord Pool day-ahead and intraday markets. According to the Company's revenue analysis, the Plant is estimated to generate revenue of approximately EUR 20 million over the period 2027 to 2047, which meets the bank's coverage requirement for interest and repayments. The Company's revenue analysis is based on historical price spreads on the Nord Pool day-ahead market for Latvia, one full charging cycle per day, assumptions on efficiency, degradation and availability, and an assumed price development over the period. Once the Plant has been approved for balancing and capacity services with the state-owned transmission system operator in Latvia (AST), further revenue of approximately EUR 33 million is estimated based on external market assessments that Byhmgard has requested from local third-party market participants. These calculations indicate total revenue of approximately EUR 53 million for the period 2027 to 2047 in the electricity, balancing and capacity markets. Any revenue from balancing and capacity services is, however, not necessary for the payment of interest and repayments on the loan. Estimated revenue varies with price spreads in the electricity market and in the balancing and capacity markets, and the actual outcome is expected to fall within the range of EUR 20 million to EUR 53 million. All amounts are estimated revenue before operating costs. The plant and timeline The Project Company is wholly owned by Byhmgard through its subsidiary Byhmgard Invest AB. The Plant has a grid connection of 14.99 MW and consists of six liquid-cooled lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery containers with two hours of storage, approximately 30 MWh. Land rights and the environmental decision have been obtained, and the grid connection agreement has been entered into. As previously announced, the Project Company has signed an EPC agreement with Latvijas Energoceltnieks (LEC) and an operation and maintenance agreement with Alstra Energy AB. LEC will only commence its work under the EPC agreement after Byhmgard issues a notice to proceed. Notice to proceed to LEC is issued when the building permit is registered with the relevant authority in Rīga. The building permit is expected to be obtained in mid-November 2026. Costs for LEC's work, approximately EUR 0.6 million, begin to accrue when the notice to proceed is issued and are included in the total investment of approximately EUR 6.1 million. Costs for Alstra Energy AB's work, approximately EUR 70 thousand per year, begin to accrue once operation has commenced and are included in the Plant's operating costs. Delivery of the battery systems to Rīga is expected in spring 2027 and commercial operation in the second quarter of 2027. An application for approval for ancillary services is planned to be submitted thereafter. The loan is sized on estimated revenue from energy arbitrage, which gives a robust base, while potential ancillary services to AST may provide a substantial upside. artigo.texto: Minneapolis City Council to vote on data centers Thursday In less than 24 hours, the Minneapolis City Council will make a pivotal vote on whether to allow data centers in the city. The current proposal would require data centers to be in two downtown districts, be 150,000 square feet or smaller, only operate in existing office space, and not be the primary use of a building. In an update Wednesday, Council Member Jamal Osman pledged to work “to preserve the tighter size limit, the renewable-energy requirement, and public review in the final ordinance.” Others are still pushing for a total ban, which did not advance in Committee this week. On Wednesday, Council Member Soren Stevenson said, “If a full ban fails again tomorrow, we will bring back a proposal that includes overlay zoning again as well,” which he explained would allow City Council members and the Planning Commission to hold public hearings when evaluating a proposed data center development on a case-by-case basis. Stevenson said he and the others plan to bring forward more amendments to “do everything we can to protect Minneapolis from the interests of AI and Big Tech.” There is a moratorium in place, but that expires in about two weeks. The City Council implemented the pause to allow the city to create new data center standards. “Will small-scale data centers be a cure-all for revenue generation? I’ve already said no,” said Council Member Elizabeth Shaffer. “Is it a step in the right direction for some revenue generation and property tax relief? Yes.”

artigo.texto: State clean energy programs and the communities they’re meant to serve want the same thing. Both want more resilient, more affordable, cleaner power. And yet, across solar and storage programs throughout the U.S. Northeast, projects stall, applications bounce back and forth, and entire counties opt out of battery storage altogether. This is not because anyone disagrees on the goal, but because the two sides are speaking different languages about cost, risk, and timeline. COMMENTARY The disconnect is a translation and timing problem, and underneath it, a fluency problem: clean energy is still young enough as an industry that we haven’t built a shared, baseline understanding of how it works, which is exactly the vacuum fear and misinformation grow fastest in. The technical, financial, and safety information communities need almost always exists somewhere; it just doesn’t arrive in a form, on a timeline, or in a language that matches the person who has to act on it. The Technical Handoff Gap Consider a state clean energy incentive program that requires applications to meet a minimum technical requirement, such as a shading threshold verified through third-party modeling software. Programs like this are purposely built to require licensed contractors, rather than homeowners, to submit on a project’s behalf. In practice, though, the person doing the actual submitting inside that contractor’s office is often administrative staff, handling documentation and portal logistics rather than the shading analysis itself. The friction shows up when an application gets flagged for revision. If a shading model overestimated sun exposure, if a battery specification sheet vaguely says it’s UL listed, or if a site location on a drawing is off, the fix requires looping back to whoever built the original technical analysis, understanding what needs to change, and resubmitting. For an administrative submitter without training to read these types of documents, it could be a multi-week round trip, and every round trip pushes a project’s timeline further from the one the applicant was promised. The review requirement is holding a consistent technical bar as intended, but it is colliding with an industry that hasn’t yet agreed on what baseline fluency should look like. As the technology moves from niche to standard, programs need to better explain their requirements, and applicants and communities need to get better at asking questions. The Bandwidth and Fit Gap Some states have built entire portfolios of clean energy incentive programs, including production-based solar incentives, demand-reduction standards that reward market participation, dedicated resilience programs, and more. We’ve worked directly on application reviews and feasibility studies for programs like these, as well as supported the people weighing whether to pursue them, including town officials, church administrators, and facility managers. Across nearly every one of those conversations, we found real interest and need, but simply not enough bandwidth to figure out which program actually solves their problem. These aren’t organizations with dedicated energy staff. Most of the people making these decisions have the same relationship to electricity most people do: they know what it costs, not how it works. They know their power went out last summer, or that heating bills wiped out half their annual budget, but they don’t have a working sense of peak demand, energy arbitrage, or how a given program lines up with either problem. For example, many states have built resilience-specific tracks alongside their standard incentive programs. Local leaders recognize that a community hub (Figure 1) worried about outages needs a different program than a homeowner just trying to lower a bill. But the program simply existing isn’t the same as someone knowing it’s the right fit. The real work is helping someone who’s never had to think about kilowatts vs. kilowatt-hours figure out which program they need. The Trust and Visibility Gap A string of BESS fires, layered on top of a wave of unrelated lithium-ion fires involving e-bikes and scooters, has created a perception problem for the industry. The largely negative image of battery storage that many community members hold is hard for any single conversation to undo, especially in dense urban areas or in smaller communities served by volunteer fire departments. Faced with that uncertainty, it was faster and safer for many municipalities to pass a moratorium than to build out permitting and zoning frameworks on their own, and the result was close to a domino effect, with moratoria spreading across counties and towns statewide. The irony is that most states had already responded substantively, not just rhetorically. They published model laws, a customizable zoning and permitting template local governments could adopt directly. These outlines stood up to a peer review program that puts technical experts in front of every project above a size threshold, reviewing design drawings, vetting proposed equipment, confirming fire suppression systems are in place, and checking third-party test reports, emergency response plans, and hazard mitigation analyses. Projects receiving state incentive awards go through this layer of scrutiny as a condition of funding. Very few communities living near these proposed projects seem to know that layer exists, which means a state-level solution and a community-level fear are running in parallel, as if unaware of each other. Information and trust broke down because nobody built a shared understanding before it was urgently needed. Developers typically don’t live in the communities where they’re proposing projects, which raises a fair question on both sides: How does that engagement avoid feeling staged, and how is a community supposed to know what to ask for or how to respond? What is Required There’s a version of developer-community engagement that gets this sequencing right from the start

artigo.texto: Washington County to consider yearlong pause on data centers The Washington County Quorum Court held a County Services Committee meeting on Monday. One of the issues discussed at Monday's meeting was a proposed yearlong moratorium on data centers in Washington County. The committee debated the item and discussed amendments that would be made to the original draft. The item was passed by the committee and will move to quorum court for a formal discussion and potential vote. The next Washington County Quorum Court meeting is scheduled for Thursday, Nov. 19. Evelyn Rios Stafford, the Justice of the Peace for District 12, is one of the supporters of the moratorium. She said that the proposed moratorium would allow time for the quorum court to look over planning and zoning rules. "We've heard a lot of concerns over the last year from residents of our county. They see data centers opening up in other places. And they are concerned about the amount of electricity they use, the amount of water. Is it going to raise people's utility bills? Are they going to create noise if they come into our county? And so I think we need to take the time and take a pause in order to see what we need to do to protect our residents," Rios Stafford said. According to Rios Stafford, there are currently no plans for data centers in Washington County.

artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Siemens eleva metas de crescimento com o avanço da IA industrial e a demanda por data centers Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Siemens elevou suas metas de crescimento de médio prazo em 12 de novembro de 2026, após os pedidos comparáveis aumentarem 25%, alcançando o recorde de €108,2 bilhões no exercício fiscal encerrado em 30 de setembro de 2026. A empresa associou as ambições mais elevadas à IA industrial, à digitalização, à eletrificação e à demanda por data centers. Para o grupo, excluindo a Siemens Healthineers, a meta de crescimento comparável da receita agora é de 7%–11%, ante 6%–9%, enquanto a ambição para o EPS pre PPA passou de crescimento de um dígito alto para crescimento de dois dígitos. EPS pre PPA corresponde ao lucro básico por ação antes da contabilização da alocação do preço de compra; o crescimento comparável exclui os efeitos da conversão cambial e das mudanças no portfólio. Data centers e software impulsionam a aposta em IA A Smart Infrastructure apresentou a evidência trimestral mais clara da demanda por data centers. Seus pedidos do quarto trimestre cresceram 39% em base comparável, chegando a €8,7 bilhões, com contratos maiores de eletrificação e produtos elétricos firmados com clientes de data centers, principalmente nos Estados Unidos e na Europa. A receita comparável aumentou 15%, para €7,2 bilhões, à medida que essas áreas executaram suas grandes carteiras de pedidos. A apresentação para investidores da Siemens informou um crescimento de três dígitos nos pedidos de data centers no exercício fiscal de 2026. Os data centers agora representam 20% da exposição da receita da Smart Infrastructure, tornando-se seu segundo maior segmento vertical, atrás dos clientes industriais. A empresa atribuiu o impulso sustentado à expansão da infraestrutura de IA. Grandes contratos ferroviários também contribuíram substancialmente para o recorde de pedidos do grupo. Os pedidos da Mobility aumentaram mais de 200%, chegando a €10,7 bilhões no quarto trimestre, incluindo um pedido alemão de €2,4 bilhões para trens de alta velocidade e serviços de manutenção. Além da eletrificação, a receita dos negócios digitais da Siemens, que abrangem software específico para cada segmento, IoT e serviços digitais, cresceu 16%, alcançando €10,9 bilhões. A Siemens também informou que seu Eigen Engineering Agent duplicou a velocidade dos trabalhos de engenharia na fabricante de máquinas ANDRITZ Metals, oferecendo um exemplo de cliente para sua estratégia de IA industrial. Lucro industrial recorde contrasta com queda no lucro líquido O lucro dos Negócios Industriais aumentou 13%, atingindo o recorde de €13,3 bilhões no exercício fiscal de 2026, mas o lucro líquido caiu para €9,5 bilhões, ante €10,4 bilhões. O valor do ano anterior incluía um ganho de €2,1 bilhões com a venda da Innomotics, o que ajuda a explicar por que o lucro industrial recorde não se traduziu em um aumento do resultado final. Perspectivas para o exercício fiscal de 2027 dependem dos investimentos em IA A Siemens inicia o exercício fiscal de 2027 com uma carteira recorde de pedidos de €143 bilhões. A empresa prevê crescimento comparável da receita de 9%–11% e EPS pre PPA de €10,20–€10,80, em comparação com a base comparável de €9,27 no exercício fiscal de 2026, excluindo a Siemens Healthineers. A previsão exclui a Healthineers porque a Siemens pretende desconsolidar o negócio por meio de uma cisão direta durante o exercício fiscal de 2027. Por isso, o valor de €9,27, e não o resultado divulgado pelo grupo, é a referência pertinente para comparar as perspectivas de lucro. A administração parte do pressuposto de que a expansão econômica global continuará, impulsionada principalmente por investimentos em IA e infraestrutura digital, programas de investimento público e uma retomada da atividade industrial. A Siemens também espera que a intensidade de capital seja substancialmente maior do que no exercício fiscal de 2026, medida pelos gastos de capital, incluindo arrendamentos operacionais, em relação à depreciação e à amortização, sobretudo devido à expansão da capacidade da Smart Infrastructure. As metas mais elevadas tornam a conversão da carteira de pedidos e a expansão da capacidade os principais desafios operacionais do exercício fiscal de 2027, enquanto a cisão planejada da Healthineers alteraria o perímetro de negócios usado para medir o crescimento e os lucros da Siemens.

artigo.texto: O governador de Mato Grosso, Otaviano Pivetta (Republicanos), divulgou nesta quarta-feira (11) imagens de sua presença na 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP31), sediada em Antália, na Turquia. O deslocamento do chefe do Executivo estadual tem como finalidade central a captação de investidores estrangeiros e a obtenção de validação para créditos de carbono originados da diminuição do desmatamento em território mato-grossense. A projeção do governo aponta para a possibilidade de fechar negócios na ordem de R$ 4,1 bilhões. Em manifestação publicada nas redes sociais, Pivetta declarou: “Estamos na COP 31 com uma missão importante: apresentar o trabalho de Mato Grosso na redução do desmatamento e buscar reconhecimento internacional para nossos créditos de carbono. Também vamos conversar com investidores e mostrar que é possível unir conservação ambiental, desenvolvimento e novas oportunidades para o nosso Estado”. Nas imagens divulgadas, o governador surge ao lado de membros da comitiva do Estado, ressaltando a relevância do contato com representantes de outros países. A proposta governamental prevê a certificação de cerca de 50 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono que deixaram de ser lançadas na atmosfera em decorrência da queda do desmatamento. Conforme números apresentados pelo Estado, a supressão de vegetação na área mato-grossense da Amazônia registrou redução de 46,7% quando comparados os períodos de 2024/2025 e 2025/2026. A expectativa de arrecadar US$ 750 milhões, montante equivalente a aproximadamente R$ 4,1 bilhões, está condicionada à certificação dos créditos e à efetivação de acordos comerciais. Para dar suporte a essas tratativas, Pivetta enviou à Assembleia Legislativa o projeto de lei nº 1.156/2026, que propõe a instituição da Companhia Mato-grossense de Ativos Ambientais S.A. (CMAA). A companhia de economia mista ficará responsável pela gestão e pela comercialização de créditos de carbono e de outros ativos ambientais. A comitiva estadual também tem agenda prevista com investidores vinculados à Coalizão LEAF, iniciativa internacional voltada ao financiamento da preservação florestal, da qual participam nações como Reino Unido e Noruega. A ausência do governador provocou alterações temporárias na chefia do Executivo estadual. Desde sexta-feira (6), o presidente da Assembleia Legislativa, Max Russi (Podemos), responde interinamente pelo cargo de governador. O retorno de Pivetta a Mato Grosso está previsto para 18 de novembro e, conforme o Governo do Estado, a viagem está sendo bancada com recursos próprios do governador. O evento em Antália conta ainda com a presença do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), reeleito em outubro, o que abre a possibilidade de um encontro institucional entre os dois governantes, que apoiaram candidaturas presidenciais rivais nas eleições deste ano.

artigo.texto: Southeast Asia's Semiconductor Rise: AI Reshapes Industry Stratification as Singapore Anchors a Regional Innovation and Demand Hub As the global semiconductor industry undergoes a structural revaluation driven by the AI computing boom, Southeast Asia is evolving from a manufacturing hinterland into a dual engine of innovation and demand. AI Reshapes Industry Stratification, with Southeast Asia at the Core The global semiconductor market is expanding faster than expected. According to the World Semiconductor Trade Statistics (WSTS) spring 2026 forecast, the global semiconductor market is projected to grow 90% year-on-year in 2026 to reach US$1.51 trillion, and to grow a further 27% in 2027, approaching US$1.9 trillion. The core driver of this cycle is sustained strong demand for AI infrastructure, high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and accelerated computing platforms. Memory chip sales are expected to rise about 250% year-on-year in 2026, while logic chips grow 37%, as AI redefines capacity priorities from advanced process nodes to advanced packaging. Southeast Asia's position in this cycle is particularly critical. According to the ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO) Quarterly Update of the ASEAN+3 Regional Economic Outlook (AREO), the region accounts for nearly half of global AI-related exports, with semiconductor sales accelerating further on the back of strong growth in 2025. As a regional hub, Singapore holds about 10% of global chip capacity and 20% of semiconductor equipment manufacturing share, making it one of the most attractive AI innovation hubs in Asia-Pacific. In 2026, the Singapore government launched the "SG Semiconductor" national brand, focusing on seven technology areas — including advanced packaging, silicon photonics, power electronics, high-frequency gallium nitride, piezoelectric MEMS, planar optics and IC design — to further strengthen its competitive edge across the semiconductor value chain. Singapore's Semiconductor Ecosystem Is Accelerating Its Expansion The decision to hold Asia Semiconductor Expo (ASE) in Singapore reflects the substantive expansion of the city-state's semiconductor supply chain. In September 2026, Advanced Substrate Technologies (AST), a joint venture between Broadcom and Toppan, opened its first high-end FC-BGA substrate manufacturing facility in Singapore, adding more than 330 engineering and technical positions. In the same month, VSMC, a joint venture between Vanguard International Semiconductor and NXP, opened its 12-inch wafer fab, with mass production expected in the first quarter of 2027 and capacity already booked. Dr. Tan See Leng, Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry), has emphasized on VSMC Grand Opening Ceremony that Singapore plays a trusted role in regional supply chains, and that this influence can extend beyond the semiconductor ecosystem to create opportunities for more local suppliers. From a regional perspective, Southeast Asia's semiconductor landscape is developing across multiple poles: Malaysia accounts for about 13% of global assembly and test capacity and 40% of automotive-grade chip assembly and testing; Thailand ranks among the world's top five in PCB capacity, with its automotive electronics market expected to grow to US$4 billion by 2030; and Vietnam's semiconductor industry output is valued at about US$20 billion, with a compound annual growth rate of around 11%. These dispersed yet complementary capabilities call for a platform at the regional hub that can showcase and connect them—and that is precisely the role Asia Semiconductor Expo is built to play. Take the Lead in the Upward Phase of the AI Chip Cycle WSTS's forecast sends a clear signal: the semiconductor industry has moved from a post-inventory-correction recovery into a phase of structural revaluation driven by AI infrastructure. However, this revaluation is uneven — capacity and customer priorities across AI core chains such as HBM, advanced logic chips, advanced packaging and high-speed interconnects are being redefined. For companies in semiconductor equipment, materials, components and compound semiconductors, whether they can appear in front of key buyers during the 2027 regional procurement decision window will directly affect their position in this cycle. As one of the three themed shows under Asia Photonics Expo 2027 (APE 2027), Asia Semiconductor Expo (ASE) will take place March 3–5, 2027 at the Sands Expo and Convention Centre, Singapore. Anchored in Singapore, reaching across Southeast Asia and connecting to global markets, ASE is dedicated to building an international exhibition and business-matching platform spanning the entire semiconductor value chain. Running alongside it, the newly launched Asia Electronics Expo (AEE) will also debut in Singapore, joining APE 2027 to form a three-show ecosystem spanning semiconductors, photonics, and electronics. Whether you are looking to showcase cutting-edge technologies, innovative products and solutions, or to connect with Southeast Asia's increasingly complete design–manufacturing–packaging and testing–application ecosystem, the show offers an entry point that only a three-show co-location can provide. Secure your booth now to put your innovations in front of key decision-makers — or register to visit and efficiently assess and procure across the entire value chain, all in one place. About the Author Eric Yang Eric Yang is Secretary General of the Asia Photonics Expo. (Source: China International Optoelectronic Exposition)

artigo.texto: Geraldo Campos Jr., Marisa Wanzeller e Lais Carregosa, da Agência iNFRA As negociações dentro do governo em torno do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter) avançaram, segundo relataram interlocutores à Agência iNFRA. No entanto, há alguns aspectos relacionados ao setor elétrico que ainda precisam ser pacificados, dentre eles, a possível exigência de aquisição de energia nova para abastecimento dos data centers. A expectativa é que o decreto seja publicado ainda em novembro, após a participação do presidente Lula na COP31, na Turquia. O setor aguarda o governo definir se será necessário que os empreendimentos comprem energia de usinas novas, construídas para o seu abastecimento, ou recém-construídas, conforme o conceito de “adicionalidade energética”. O tema divide agentes no setor. Outra negociação ainda na mesa é quanto à cobrança de encargos dos data centers. Segundo interlocutores, os investidores querem ser isentos do pagamento da CDE (Conta de Desenvolvimento Energético) por meio da celebração de contratos de autoprodução por equiparação. Também é esperada a lista de fontes de geração que serão aceitas, com expectativas do segmento de gás natural para que a molécula seja incluída. Adicionalidade A exigência de novas usinas para atender os data centers não é um consenso. De um lado, há empresas que veem na adicionalidade uma possibilidade de expansão dos negócios. Do outro, há geradores com usinas que ficarão descontratadas que miram esse mercado e avaliam que erguer novas plantas de geração tiraria a competitividade dos projetos e acarretaria custos para o sistema elétrico. Na última sexta-feira (6), o presidente Lula falou sobre o tema e defendeu que os empreendimentos de data centers construam suas usinas. O presidente disse que os centros consomem muita energia e que “quem vier investir [que] construa a sua própria energia”. Ele continuou: “Não vai ser a energia do povo que vai ser usada para data center”. A preocupação está em linha com o que se observa em países onde o desenvolvimento de data centers já está mais avançado, como os Estados Unidos. Lá, a população viu a conta de energia aumentar em algumas regiões. Autoprodução Também circula nos bastidores que o Ministério da Fazenda levou à mesa de discussão uma proposta para que os empreendimentos sejam enquadrados como autoprodutores de energia. Dessa forma, os data centers ficariam isentos do pagamento da CDE – a conta que reúne os custos dos subsídios do setor elétrico. Com a possibilidade aventada, os técnicos do MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) fazem agora o cálculo dos impactos dessa renúncia. Eles analisam se é possível “reduzir os danos”, disseram fontes. Na autoprodução por equiparação, o consumidor da energia se torna acionista da SPE (Sociedade de Propósito Específico) da usina. Dessa forma, é equiparado ao autoprodutor “clássico” – que investiu em geração própria para atender ao empreendimento consumidor. Gás natural Quanto às fontes de suprimento, a resistência de parte do governo federal à inclusão do gás natural está menor, segundo pessoas a par das tratativas. Agora, a tendência é que o decreto contemple o insumo, ainda que com condicionantes, como compensação pelas emissões de carbono. Os secretários-executivos dos ministérios de Minas e Energia, da Fazenda, da Indústria e Comércio e da Casa Civil reuniram-se na última semana, ocasião em que o MME defendeu o gás natural. Interlocutores afirmam que a Fazenda – que vinha travando a entrada do gás – passou a admitir a possibilidade de incluir a fonte. Falta, agora, fechar o modelo das condicionantes. No MME, a intenção é que as compensações de carbono mantenham os projetos de gás viáveis. No setor, no entanto, os agentes estão preocupados com os termos, que podem onerar os investimentos e acabar restringindo, na prática, a implementação de térmicas a gás para abastecer os data centers. Algumas possíveis formas de compensação aventadas nos bastidores são o uso de tecnologia de CCUS (Captura, Utilização e Armazenamento de Carbono, na sigla em inglês) ou a aquisição de créditos de carbono. Riscos Agentes ligados ao segmento de gás natural vinham demonstrando temor com a possibilidade de o gás ficar totalmente fora da regulamentação do Redata. Agora, admitem que esse risco é menor, mas ainda agem com cautela e dizem que será preciso ver os termos impostos pelo governo nas condicionantes. Uma regulamentação restritiva por causa das condicionantes, segundo um executivo, pode afastar investimentos em térmicas colocalizadas com data centers e pressionar as tarifas de energia. Isso porque os centros de dados poderiam ter de usar energia da rede nos horários com escassez de energia renovável, aumentando a demanda por potência. Caso o decreto vete ou restrinja o gás, o setor cogita buscar alterar os termos da regulamentação via Congresso. Isso poderia ser feito por meio de um PDL (Projeto de Decreto Legislativo). “Ficou claro que o Legislativo, ao aprovar o Redata, não quis restringir nenhum combustível de baixa emissão, como o gás natural”, comentou um agente termelétrico. Por outro lado, os geradores renováveis apontam que as termelétricas a gás natural emitem mais carbono do que os limites estabelecidos internacionalmente, de aproximadamente 0,10 tonelada de gás carbônico por MWh (megawatt-hora). Dessa forma, essas usinas não se enquadrariam na exigência da lei. Atraso O diretor de Relações Institucionais e Governamentais da Brasscom (Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação e de Tecnologias Digitais do Brasil), Sergio Sgobbi, diz que a demora na regulamentação tem afastado os investidores, que estão buscando outras alternativas. Ele aponta que é essencial a publicação das regras de habilitação e coabilitação dos empreendimentos, e a lista de equipamentos que terão os tributos federais desonerados para aquisição. “Enquanto a regulamentação não vier a público, tudo é incerto e, diante da incerteza, o investimento não

artigo.texto: Deutsche Bank and Rabobank are backing an €835 million (about $936 million) financing package to help energy storage company Return expand its battery storage business in Germany. The deal will support new projects as the country works to integrate more wind and solar power into its electricity system. The portfolio facility initially covers three battery energy storage projects with a combined capacity of 117 megawatts (MW). More eligible projects can be added as they reach financial close. The financing combines support for physical battery assets with Return’s Virtual Flexibility Portfolio (VFP). This model connects multiple storage facilities into one virtual system. Energy companies can access flexible electricity capacity through a single platform. The transaction involves several financial and technical advisers. Rabobank acted as financial adviser, while White & Case advised the lenders. Other firms involved included Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, Baker McKenzie, Baringa, DNV, EY, EY-Parthenon, and Marsh. The deal comes as Germany’s battery storage market grows. It also shows how private finance helps build the infrastructure for a power system with more renewable energy. A Financing Framework for Germany’s Battery Expansion The €835 million facility gives Return a way to finance several battery projects under one structure instead of arranging separate financing for every site. This approach could help speed up project development. Eligible facilities can access funding as they progress toward financial close, without having to restart the financing process each time. The initial portfolio includes three projects in Germany with a combined power capacity of 117 MW. Return stated that, with four-hour batteries running two full cycles each day, the facilities could provide enough electricity yearly to power around 100,000 German households. The company plans to add more projects to the financing framework through 2027. Return also has wider growth plans for the German market. It aims to install at least 1 gigawatt (GW) of battery storage capacity each year from 2027. The company estimates that this would require annual investment of €750 million to €1.2 billion, depending on market conditions. The financing is therefore part of a much larger expansion plan. The company has not said that the full €835 million will be used only for the three projects in the initial portfolio. Daniel Witvoet, CFO at Return, remarked: “As demand for energy flexibility grows, we need to scale not just our battery storage capacity, but also the way we finance it. By bringing together physical infrastructure financing and our virtual flexibility model, we can expand more efficiently and respond to our customers’ evolving needs. This is an important step towards our ambition to become a leading independent provider of energy flexibility in Germany.” Why Germany Needs More Battery Storage Germany is adding more wind and solar power to its electricity mix. However, these sources do not produce power at a steady rate. Solar generation changes with daylight and weather, while wind output can rise or fall depending on conditions. Battery storage can help manage these changes. It can store electricity when supply is high and prices are low, then release it when demand rises or renewable generation falls. This can help balance the grid and make better use of clean electricity. Germany’s Federal Network Agency explains that battery systems can respond to electricity market prices, support grid stability, and improve the use of renewable power. The need for this flexibility is becoming clearer as storage projects move through the development pipeline. According to data published by Germany’s Federal Network Agency in August 2026, network operators received 18,158 battery storage connection applications in 2025. These requests represented about 573.5 GW of planned power capacity and 1,583 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy capacity. However, these figures do not represent projects that are certain to be built. Developers sometimes submit applications for the same project at several possible locations. The regulator noted that only one location may ultimately be selected. A more advanced measure is the number of grid connection offers. In 2025, network operators issued 1,937 offers covering 54.2 GW of power capacity and 142.4 GWh of energy capacity. These offers provide a clearer picture of project progress because they are binding proposals for connection agreements. Even so, projects still need to secure financing, complete construction, and meet other requirements before they can operate. Germany’s Storage Pipeline Reflects a Growing Market Germany’s battery storage market has expanded as renewable energy has gained a larger role in power generation. Fraunhofer ISE reported that, in 2025, wind and solar power generated more electricity than any other source in Germany’s public electricity mix. The shift increases the need for storage and other flexible resources that can help match supply with demand. The International Energy Agency has also identified utility-scale battery storage as an important part of Germany’s energy transition. Large batteries can provide services such as frequency response and reserves, helping the grid remain stable as the electricity mix changes. Globally, battery storage is growing quickly as well. The IEA’s Global Energy Review 2026 reported that 108 GW of new battery storage capacity was deployed worldwide in 2025, 40% more than in 2024. Global installed capacity was 11 times higher than in 2021. These trends are creating opportunities for developers, utilities, and financial institutions. However, the scale of Germany’s connection requests also shows that grid access and project delivery remain important challenges. artigo.texto: (Photo: Courtesy of More Than Just Parks) As America grapples with the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence data centers, two brothers have set out to map infrastructure project proposals nationwide—including those near public lands and national parks. Will Pattiz is the cofounder of More Than Just Parks, an independent public lands publication that tracks AI data centers. According to his research, at least 14 proposed data center projects are within ten miles of a national park boundary. His data also shows that 38 sites are planned within 25 miles of a national park, and 131 are within 50 miles. “The basic idea is that a lot of these [projects] are being done under the cloak of darkness or secrecy, and we want folks to know where they’re coming in and who’s building them,” Pattiz, a resident of Portland, Oregon, told Outside. “The stance that we take is that we don’t want them on public lands.” “Places like Utah, for example, have a huge amount of data center projects and some of the biggest ones that are being proposed,” Pattiz said. “Just depending on the size and scale, they take up a massive amount of resources and will have impacts on public lands one way or the other, whether it’s taking water or the land itself.” Data centers are rapidly popping up across the United States, fueled by the computing needs of artificial intelligence and cloud-based software. These centers house massive servers, data storage systems, and networking equipment, and they require sizable amounts of electricity and water to run and maintain the hardware. “The question that we want to see asked is: ‘What is the public benefit from this?’” Pattiz said. “So far, the ones that have been proposed on public lands, there’s no public benefit that’s been outlined.” To use Pattiz’s map, a user inputs their zip code, and the site shows the closest data center or proposed facility. The site then suggests how the center will affect utility costs, as well as the groups that support the center. “You can go through that discovery process yourself to decide whether you support [the center] or not, because these are things that are going to impact all of us, and you can decide where you land on that,” Pattiz said. The map auto-populates as more information becomes available. As of this writing, the tool reflects 2,086 data centers, 741 of which are still in the proposal phase. Of those, 77 are located within ten miles of protected land like national parks, wildlife refuges, and wilderness or conservation areas. Roughly half are in the American West. In Virginia, 97 data centers are proposed, and 12 are within 25 miles of Shenandoah National Park. At least 25 data centers are proposed in Indiana, according to the map, and eight are located within 25 miles of Indiana Dunes National Park. The map also includes several construction proposals that are extremely close to iconic National Park Service sites. Arizona alone has 26 active proposals, with three within 25 miles of a national park. In January, the City of Page sold roughly 500 acres to developers planning to build a $10 billion data center next to Horseshoe Bend, an iconic viewpoint along the Colorado River. The 500-acre parcel was previously protected for outdoor recreation. According to the City of Page, the proposal is undergoing public review and has not yet been formally adopted, but a planning and zoning meeting is scheduled for November 17. According to Pattiz’s map, the center is also located about five miles from the northeastern edge of Grand Canyon National Park near Lees Ferry. Just outside of Price, Utah, Pattiz found that a company called Valar Atomics applied for more than 9,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management land for data center buildouts, including permits for hundreds of small nuclear reactors, a fuel plant, and nuclear waste storage. According to a report published by NPR, the so-called Project Beehive would produce about 9.6 gigawatts of power for data centers. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces less than half of that on average, NPR reports. The land is about two hours from both Arches and Canyonlands National Parks. Located about 40 miles from Zion National Park, Antelope Data Center is slated for development as part of a 640-acre, 1.5-gigawatt project that will include an on-site natural gas power plant, according to The Salt Lake Tribune. The Iron County Commission approved a conditional use permit in June 2026. Large-scale data center rollouts represent an inflection point in American history, Pattiz said. As construction crews have erected these centers, they have become political lightning rods in American towns and cities. Pattiz believes that giving Americans transparent, readily available information about where big tech is breaking ground will help them track what developers are building in their backyards. “At the end of the day, data is data,” he added. “Whether or not there’s a need for these things is a totally separate question from where they’re being built and what impact they’re going to have on you and the places that you love.”

artigo.texto: Leilão de baterias atrai mais de 6 mil projetos e movimenta setor elétrico BNDES destinará R$ 30 bilhões a empreendimentos com componentes nacionais, em certame que marca a entrada do armazenamento em larga escala no sistema brasileiro Atualizado 10/11/2026 Pela primeira vez, o sistema elétrico brasileiro está em via de investir bilhões de reais em tecnologias para armazenamento de energia. Com isso, se insere na tendência global. Apenas no segmento de baterias, em 2025 a capacidade instalada no mundo atingiu 108 GW (gigawatts), volume 40% superior ao de 2024 e 11 vezes maior que o de 2021, segundo a Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA, na sigla em inglês). O movimento foi impulsionado pela China, Estados Unidos e Europa. “Baterias são a tecnologia que mais cresce no mundo”, diz Donato Filho, CEO da consultoria Volt Robotics. O Brasil, devido à matriz majoritariamente hidráulica, também conta com as hidrelétricas reversíveis (com dois reservatórios). No entanto, esse mercado ainda é incipiente. Somente no fim de setembro, portaria do Ministério de Minas e Energia as incluiu nos leilões para contratação de reserva de capacidade a serem realizados em 2027, 2028 e 2029. As baterias, no entanto, já têm leilão marcado para o início de dezembro de 2026. Segundo o Plano Decenal de Expansão da Energia (PDE) 2036, elaborado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) e em consulta pública até o fechamento desta edição, ao final deste período o país deverá contar com 9,2 GW em capacidade de armazenamento. Deste total, 7,2 GW em baterias e 2 GW em hidrelétricas reversíveis. A função do armazenamento é acumular energia elétrica em momentos em que há excesso de produção para utilizá-la em períodos de escassez. Como registra o PDE 2035, “as tecnologias de armazenamento constituem um recurso estratégico para o provimento de capacidade e para a ampliação da flexibilidade operativa do sistema”. Para o período, o PDE estima uma expansão de 100 GW na capacidade instalada do país, totalizando 359 GW. Essa expansão viria da construção de usinas convencionais e de soluções de armazenamento. Leia mais: A diferença entre as hidrelétricas reversíveis e sistemas de baterias, também chamados de BESS (batery energy storage system), é que as primeiras demandam de sete a oito anos para entrar em operação, só podem ser erguidas em locais onde há reservatórios, são mais lentas para ligar e desligar, podem acumular energia por muitas horas e demoram também horas para descarregar essa mesma energia. Além disso, contribuem para o abastecimento em períodos de estiagem. Já os BESS são mais ágeis: podem ser erguidos em um a dois anos, acumulam energia em poucas horas e a descarregam em períodos de tempo mais curtos, como quatro a oito horas. Além de beneficiar a potência, tornam a operação do sistema mais flexível. Por isso, os BESS são particularmente adequados a parques eólicos e solares, que contam com excesso de produção quando o vento sopra e o sol está a pino, mas sofrem com a escassez de insumo nos outros períodos. Isso provoca dois problemas: excesso ou escassez de energia. As duas situações são perniciosas, pois podem provocar apagões de energia e problemas de variação de tensão e de frequência. Isso obriga o Operador Nacional do Sistema (ONS) a determinar o corte da produção das renováveis quando há excesso (curtailment) ou aumentar a produção das térmicas e das hidrelétricas quando há escassez, a um preço maior. A questão é acentuada pelo comportamento do consumo: menor durante o dia, quando a produção é farta, e maior no início da noite, quando há escassez. “O problema é que esses cortes não são ressarcidos. Nós temos contratos, não recebemos o que não geramos e, às vezes, somos até multados”, diz Rodrigo Sauaia, CEO da Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar), referindo-se ao curtailment. “Temos que colocar o consumidor como protagonista e induzi-lo a mudar o horário de carga”, afirma Luiz Eduardo Barata Ferreira, presidente da Frente Nacional dos Consumidores de Energia (FNCE). A expansão dos BESS tem sido beneficiada pela queda nos preços, que a partir de 2010 recuaram de mais de US$ 1.000/kWh (kilowatt/hora) para uma média global de US$ 108/kWh, conta Sauaia. Por isso, eles já são utilizados em projetos de média tensão, como indústrias, comércios e hospitais em substituição aos geradores convencionais. “Estamos vivendo uma onda que chega a 1 GW em projetos de menor porte e carga de média tensão”, diz Markus Vlasits, presidente da Associação Brasileira de Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae). A exceção é a subestação de Registro (SP), da ISA Energia Brasil, primeiro BESS de grande porte no Brasil, inaugurado em 2022, com 90 MW de potência e 60 MWh de energia. Agora, o setor elétrico prepara-se para introduzir os BESS no Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Pela primeira vez na história, em dezembro eles serão objeto de leilão específico organizado pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e pela Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE) para reserva de capacidade (LRCAP - Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade) na forma de potência. Isto significa que os projetos vencedores serão acoplados a subestações ligadas às linhas de transmissão de alta tensão do SIN, aumentando a potência e dotando o sistema de maior flexibilidade operacional. O leilão foi dividido em duas etapas. A primeira, no dia 2 de dezembro, para projetos com componentes nacionais. A segunda, no dia 4 de dezembro, para equipamentos nacionais e estrangeiros. Os primeiros contarão com financiamento de R$ 30 bilhões do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES), via Finame. Para os demais, o financiamento ainda está indefinido. Mas, como diz Donato Filho, “no momento há muitos recursos externos para projetos ligados à energia renovável”. “O acesso ao financiamento do Finame, associado a critérios de conteúdo local, pode fazer do leilão de baterias também um instrumento de política industrial.

artigo.texto: The Korea Overseas Infrastructure & Urban Development Corporation (KIND) will jointly develop an energy storage system (ESS) project in Ireland with Shinhan Asset Management, Hyosung Heavy Industries and Irish developer Lumcloon Energy. KIND said on the 11th that it signed a memorandum of understanding with the three companies at the Embassy of Ireland in Seoul on the 10th to jointly develop the ESS project and to pursue overseas infrastructure projects together. The agreement covers an ESS project being developed in the Coolpowra area of County Galway, Ireland. KIND and Shinhan Asset Management agreed to build a strategic cooperation framework with Hyosung Heavy Industries and Lumcloon Energy for the development of and investment in the project. The partners agreed to pursue grid connection for the large-scale ESS and to cooperate across the entire development process, from project permitting and transmission grid connection to deal structuring and financing. If the project moves ahead, it will stabilize output from renewable sources such as wind power and improve both the flexibility of electricity supply and grid stability, the parties to the agreement said. Ireland is expanding its use of renewable energy in response to rising electricity demand and the need to secure grid stability. The country is positioned to tap wind resources along the Atlantic coast, while the need to expand energy storage infrastructure to cope with the intermittency of renewable power is also growing. "Ireland is a market where the importance of grid stability and energy storage infrastructure is growing, driven by the expansion of renewable energy and rising large-scale power demand from facilities such as data centers," a KIND official said. "Using this memorandum of understanding as a starting point, we will work closely with local partners and Korean EPC companies to advance project development, and contribute to expanding Ireland's stable power infrastructure and to broadening Korean companies' entry into the European market."

artigo.texto: da Agência iNFRA Sete associações do setor elétrico enviaram carta ao governo federal solicitando apoio à aprovação do PL 3.716/2026, que propõe alterar as regras de custeio da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias no âmbito da reserva de capacidade. O documento pede prioridade na tramitação da proposta para garantir segurança jurídica à realização do primeiro leilão de reserva de capacidade voltado a baterias. A carta é assinada pela ABEEólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias), ABIHV (Associação Brasileira da Indústria do Hidrogênio Verde), Abrage (Associação Brasileira das Empresas Geradoras de Energia Elétrica), Abragel (Associação Brasileira de Geração de Energia Limpa), Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia), Absolar (Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica) e Apine (Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica). O projeto, de autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim, prevê a revogação do dispositivo da Lei 10.848/2004 que determina o rateio dos custos da contratação de baterias exclusivamente entre os agentes de geração. As entidades defendem que o custeio siga critérios semelhantes aos aplicados às demais tecnologias contratadas para a reserva de capacidade, considerando que o serviço beneficia todo o sistema elétrico. Segundo as associações, a concentração dos custos nos geradores não impede seu repasse aos consumidores, uma vez que os encargos podem ser incorporados aos preços da energia. “Esse encargo será incorporado aos preços da energia, conforme as condições contratuais e de mercado, e repercutirá nos custos de produção de bens e serviços, possivelmente de forma opaca ou pouco clara”, afirmam as entidades na carta. As associações também alertam que a manutenção das regras atuais pode elevar os riscos dos empreendimentos, encarecer as contratações e provocar questionamentos administrativos e judiciais, com possíveis impactos sobre o cronograma do certame. A carta foi encaminhada a seis ministros, incluindo os titulares de Minas e Energia, Fazenda e Casa Civil, e solicita articulação do Executivo para a aprovação do projeto.

artigo.texto: NYU Researcher: Data Centers Must Offer More to Local Communities Data center developers face growing pressure to deliver local benefits Kate Keith WASHINGTON, Nov. 11, 2026 — Data center developers must do more than minimize environmental and economic harms if they want to gain public support for new construction, according to a researcher at New York University. Scott Brennan, director of NYU’s Center on Technology Policy, said data centers should become more active contributors to the communities where they operate, including by paying property taxes, investing in local infrastructure and supporting workforce development. Brennen's research focuses on technology policy, media and misinformation. He previously held research and policy positions at the University of Oxford, Duke University and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. He holds a doctorate and master's degree in communication from UNC-Chapel Hill and a bachelor's degree in chemistry from Grinnell College. Before pursuing his doctorate, he served in the U.S. Peace Corps as a high school chemistry teacher in northern Mozambique. Speaking during a Fiber Broadband Association Fiber for Breakfast discussion, Brennan said the benefits of data center development, including lower computing costs, technological innovation and U.S. competitiveness in artificial intelligence, are largely shared across society. The costs, however, often fall on the communities hosting the facilities. “The purported benefits of data center buildout are all collective goods, but the harms are localized in specific communities,” Brennan said. “This mismatch between collective goods and local harms is not sustainable.” Public opposition to data centers has grown as residents raise concerns about electricity prices, water consumption, pollution, environmental damage and the effects of large facilities on nearby neighborhoods. Brennan said opposition also reflects broader public distrust of technology companies and concerns about artificial intelligence, including potential job losses and other economic disruptions. He said data center developers have spent years pursuing tax exemptions and other incentives from state and local governments while employing relatively few local workers. As a result, they have not necessarily developed strong constituencies within the communities where they operate. “If data centers are to survive and to gain public support, they need not only ask how to minimize the harms, but ask how to be positive additions to communities,” Brennan said. In a report released over the summer, Brennan's center outlined 10 recommendations for making data centers more beneficial to local communities. The proposals generally focus on improving energy infrastructure, supporting local economies and providing direct community benefits. Brennan said data center operators should help pay for necessary electricity infrastructure upgrades rather than allowing those costs to fall on other utility customers. He also suggested that new demand could create opportunities to modernize aging power grids and expand cleaner energy supplies. Another recommendation is for data centers to pay their fair share of local taxes. “I don't see any reason why data centers shouldn't pay their fair share of taxes,” Brennan said, pointing to the potential for property tax revenue to support local schools and other public services. He also advocated establishing local funds to support workforce development, environmental improvements and other community priorities. Community benefit agreements could provide another way to ensure residents receive something tangible from data center development. Such agreements could support local parks, educational institutions, broadband infrastructure and other projects identified by residents. Brennan said some state governors have begun referencing community benefit agreements in executive orders, but those directives have not necessarily established specific requirements for what the agreements should include. He said communities should have an opportunity to identify their priorities and negotiate agreements that reflect local needs. The growing number of temporary data center moratoriums could give local governments time to develop those expectations, Brennan said. He cautioned, however, that pauses in development should be accompanied by efforts to determine how future projects can benefit residents. Brennan also acknowledged the national competitiveness argument for expanding data center capacity, saying insufficient computing infrastructure could raise costs and limit access to artificial intelligence models. He said the United States needs sufficient computing capacity to remain central to the global AI economy but argued that expanding infrastructure and addressing community concerns should not be mutually exclusive.

artigo.texto: O avanço do mercado de carbono no Brasil tem alcançado territórios de povos indígenas, quilombolas e outras comunidades tradicionais, onde se localiza parte dos projetos de maior potencial, como os de redução de emissões por desmatamento e degradação florestal (REDD+). Nesse contexto, a advogada socioambiental Ana Carolina de Campos Honora, […] 11 de novembro de 2026, às 12:12 O avanço do mercado de carbono no Brasil tem alcançado territórios de povos indígenas, quilombolas e outras comunidades tradicionais, onde se localiza parte dos projetos de maior potencial, como os de redução de emissões por desmatamento e degradação florestal (REDD+). Nesse contexto, a advogada socioambiental Ana Carolina de Campos Honora, doutoranda em Mudança Social e Participação Política pela Universidade de São Paulo (USP), e a oceanógrafa (UFES) e mestre em Planejamento Energético (COPPE/UFRJ) Larissa Albino, gerente de Operações de Clima e Inteligência Artificial da Future Climate Group, examinam uma pergunta ainda sem resposta simples: quem fica com o valor do carbono. Para elas, o debate vai além do volume financeiro dos créditos. “A discussão não se limita à geração de valor: é preciso saber quanto efetivamente chega às comunidades, segundo quais regras e com que grau de influência sobre o desenho, a negociação e a governança dos projetos”, afirmam. Uma cadeia extensa entre o crédito e o território Segundo as especialistas, não há um número único que indique a fatia destinada às comunidades, e essa ausência integra o problema. A receita se dilui entre desenvolvimento do projeto, estruturação jurídica, auditoria, certificação, intermediação e venda. A parcela da repartição de benefícios costuma ser pactuada caso a caso, em contratos privados entre a comunidade, ou suas entidades representativas, e o desenvolvedor. O retorno também varia de forma. Estudo apresentado em 2023 no encontro da Sociedade Brasileira de Economia Ecológica (EcoEco) apontou que, em projetos REDD+ da Amazônia, os mecanismos vão de pagamentos em dinheiro a regularização fundiária, infraestrutura, apoio produtivo e fortalecimento de organizações locais. Para Ana Carolina e Larissa, essa diversidade dificulta a comparação entre iniciativas e pode ocultar quanto de fato permanece no território. O que a legislação já prevê No campo legal, a Lei nº 15.042/2024 criou o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SBCE) e trouxe a primeira garantia federal explícita no tema. O artigo 47 assegura a povos indígenas e comunidades tradicionais, via entidades representativas, o direito de vender créditos de carbono e Certificados de Redução ou Remoção Verificada de Emissões (CRVEs) gerados em suas terras, cumpridas as salvaguardas socioambientais. A comercialização depende de consentimento obtido em consulta livre, prévia e informada, nos termos da Convenção nº 169 da Organização Internacional do Trabalho (OIT), custeada pelo desenvolvedor. A lei exige repartição justa e equitativa, gestão participativa dos recursos em conta específica e garante às comunidades ao menos 50% dos créditos de projetos de remoção e 70% nos de REDD+ de abordagem de mercado. A operacionalização desses mecanismos ainda depende de regulamentação, iniciada parcialmente pela Resolução nº 19, de 1º de agosto de 2025, da Comissão Nacional para REDD+ (CONAREDD+). As duas lembram que a norma já foi questionada: em agosto de 2026, o Ministério Público Federal (MPF) recomendou a revisão do artigo 7º, por entender que planos de consulta feitos pelo Estado podem enfraquecer o veto de cada comunidade e ignorar protocolos autônomos. Certificação e integridade Outra camada de regras vem de padrões privados, como Verra, Gold Standard e Cercarbono, que exigem salvaguardas sociais e planos de repartição, mas priorizaram a comprovação de processos em vez de resultados distributivos uniformes. Em novembro de 2024, o Conselho de Integridade do Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (ICVCM) aprovou três metodologias de REDD+ e apontou que versões antigas da Verra, fora da avaliação, respondiam por cerca de um quarto dos créditos aposentados em 2023. Consulta não equivale a poder de decisão Para Ana Carolina e Larissa, a comunidade ser ouvida e poder recusar um projeto é fundamental, mas difere de ter assento real na negociação. “O direito de ser consultada e de recusar a implementação de um projeto não assegura às comunidades, por si só, condições equitativas de negociação sobre aspectos essenciais da relação contratual, como a definição de preços, a duração dos contratos, os critérios de reajuste, a governança dos fundos e a destinação das receitas”, observam. Assimetrias de informação técnica, jurídica e comercial podem desequilibrar essa participação. Por isso, as salvaguardas socioambientais devem ser rigorosas e integralmente observadas e cumpridas em todas as etapas do projeto, garantindo assessoria independente, acesso a informações claras e acessíveis, tempo adequado para a tomada de decisões, representação legítima, governança transparente e mecanismos efetivos de resolução de conflitos. O cumprimento dessas salvaguardas deve ser contínuo, verificável e não pode ser tratado como mera formalidade. A Future Climate Group atua com projetos de carbono baseados na natureza e em transição energética, consultoria e educação climática. Um deles é o Projeto Rio Madeira, de REDD+ agrupado, que, segundo a empresa, protege mais de 52 mil hectares de floresta em Rondônia e no Amazonas e capacita coletores de castanha em parceria com a Empresa Brasileira de Pesquisa Agropecuária (Embrapa). Os próximos passos O principal desafio de curto prazo, na avaliação das especialistas, é a regulamentação do SBCE, que deverá converter a repartição justa e equitativa em procedimentos verificáveis e exigíveis, como financiamento da consulta, gestão financeira participativa, monitoramento, prestação de contas e solução de controvérsias. artigo.texto: Neighbors protest data center developments in Fayette County PIPERTON, Tenn. (WMC) - Residents in Fayette County packed a city meeting Tuesday night to push back against potential data center developments in their quiet, rural community. Neighbors in and around Piperton, Tennessee, gathered at city hall, turning a local planning commission meeting into an open town hall. While no data center proposals were officially on the agenda, Piperton’s city manager says several rules will be in place before any project is considered. Even still, some residents want to make sure data centers never come their way. “I hope that you look at me as your neighbor in Fayette County and say, ‘I won’t do it to you,’ and I hope you know that I wouldn’t do it to you, and I hope the commission and our leadership can look at each of us and know that they won’t do it to us either,” said Laura Kate Jordan. “So, not just talking about the coding of what’s coming, but first and foremost, we’re not allowing this. Not at all. This is not coming here, and we’re not doing it.” Much of the pushback centers around land near I-269 and Macon Road, where residents say they recently spotted survey crews. artigo.texto: BYD planeja investir R$ 1 bi em nova fábrica no Brasil Nova unidade da montadora chinesa produzirá vans elétricas e caminhões; empreendimento deve criar 2.000 empregos A montadora chinesa BYD planeja investir R$ 1 bilhão na instalação de uma nova fábrica de vans elétricas e caminhões no Brasil. O empreendimento deve criar 2.000 empregos, de 2028 a 2029. As informações foram divulgadas pela CNN Brasil nesta 2ª feira (9.nov.2026). Minas Gerais, São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro disputam a instalação da unidade. A fabricante ainda não definiu a localização e considera os incentivos oferecidos pelos governos estaduais para decidir onde realizará o investimento. Os modelos que serão fabricados no novo complexo também não foram anunciados. A BYD, no entanto, apresentará os caminhões elétricos eT35 e eT75 na Fenatran, feira do setor de transportes que começa nesta 2ª feira (9.nov), em São Paulo. A montadora levará ainda uma versão do eT23 adaptada para o transporte de bebidas. BYD NO BRASIL O projeto faz parte da expansão industrial da BYD no país, iniciada com a abertura do complexo automotivo de Camaçari, na Bahia. Com a nova unidade, a empresa pretende ampliar a atuação no mercado de veículos comerciais e competir com fabricantes tradicionais de vans movidas a diesel. Com investimento anunciado de R$ 11,3 bilhões, o complexo de Camaçari é responsável pela produção dos modelos de carros Dolphin Mini, King, Song Pro e Atto 2. A BYD pretende ampliar a capacidade anual da unidade para 300.000 veículos na próxima etapa de expansão da empresa no país. Em balanço divulgado em 5 de novembro, a montadora informou que a fábrica baiana já ultrapassou a marca de 150 mil veículos produzidos e conta com 9.500 empregos diretos desde a inauguração, em outubro de 2025.

artigo.texto: Trending BOARDMAN -- Don't be quick to dismiss data centers. There's room for talk, understanding and opportunity. That’s the message from an organization of business, union and educational leaders that emerged Monday to promote data center development in the Mahoning Valley. The co-founders of Mahoning Valley Coalition for a 21st Century Economy -- the Youngstown/Warren Regional Chamber and the Western Reserve Building Trades -- said at a news conference that education and conversation are needed to understand how the high-tech facilities can benefit the region and its economy. Their effort is backed by 29 entities -- from Youngstown State University and Brilex Industries to the Cafaro Company and SoftBank Group. "We now have an opportunity, if we do this right, to reverse decades of brain drain, create a 21st century economy that helps us retain our best and brightest, and be the destination for other people's best and brightest," said Guy Coviello, president and CEO of the Regional Chamber. The group's initiative comes as some Valley communities have rejected data center development. Moratoriums have been enacted in Niles, McDonald, Girard, Warren, Newton Falls, Vienna, Howland, Braceville, Boardman, Cortland and Ellsworth Township. Voters in Hubbard voted to ban data centers in last week’s general election. "Come to mutual agreements without moratoriums," Coviello said. "The indirect impact of moratoriums on the data center industry is it sends a message out to all industries that one slight thing and you might slap a moratorium on my industry or my business. "When you say no to data centers, you say no to Hynes Industries. You say no to Wheatland Tube. You say no to Foxconn." The Ohio Supreme Court recently backed the village of Lordstown in a zoning issue involving a data center developer. During her campaign, Gov.-elect Amy Acton said she supported a conditional moratorium on data centers. She set six standards a developer must meet before coming into the state. "As we start talking about bans and moratoriums and different things like that, that’s not the right way to go," said Marty Loney, president of the Western Reserve Building Trades. "What we don’t understand, or what we don’t have, is then an avenue to be able to sit down with these companies and make those community benefit agreements where it works for everybody." Loney said the monetary benefits to the Valley are considerable. "Everybody talks about temporary jobs, right?" he said. "An average-sized data center is about 1,700 construction jobs over a several-year period. That to me doesn’t sound temporary. That sounds like community benefits for our tax base. "It’s a great way for young folks to have a great future here in the Valley." He said the new coalition is designed to deliver accurate information to the public and to dispel fears. "What we can’t lose sight of, though, is that people have legitimate concerns. ... We can't allow a small group of critics to dictate what's best for our local area." Rick Organ, CEO of Austintown-based Hynes Industries, told the audience that the century-old steel company has evolved and grown. Data centers have played a role. "It has profoundly impacted our business in a positive way," he said. "Over the course of the past two years, we have invested over $30 million in our business. We’ve doubled down to produce components and parts into the data center marketplace. "We’ve been in it for a number of years. It represented about 10% of our business as recently as two years ago. Today, it represents 40% of our business." Besides Hynes Industries, supporting the initiative are BBM Railway Equipment; Brilex Industries; Cafaro Company; Discover Global; Edge City; Foxconn; HBK CPAs & Consultants; HSH Contractor; Humtown Products; McDonald Industrial Development; Methodica Capital; North Jackson Commerce Park; Ohio Business Roundtable; Oppidan; Platz Realty Group; QUICKmed; Roemer Industries Inc.; Sharon Tube; SoftBank Group; Sunbelt Solomon; Taylor-Winfield Technologies; Top Property Holdings; Warren Area Chamber of Commerce Economic Development Foundation; Warren Area Chamber of Commerce Education, Civic and Cultural Foundation; Western Reserve Port Authority; Wheatland Tube; Youngstown State University; and Zekelman Industries. Covielli said he and Loney have already met with Boardman Township's zoning commission and the Trumbull County Council of Governments. "We want to continue to offer ourselves to be available to come and speak to any public body that wants to receive our information, our handouts and also to ask us questions directly," he said. That includes trips to communities opposed to data centers. "We’ll certainly go everywhere that we are welcome to go and meet with folks."

artigo.texto: Vanderburgh County data center committee hosts meeting Tuesday EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE) - Residents from across Vanderburgh County spoke out about data centers at a public forum hosted by the Vanderburgh County Data Center Committee Tuesday at Ivy Tech’s auditorium. Most who spoke opposed data centers. Others backed them, saying the facilities would bring jobs and strengthen the community. The committee decided at its last meeting to hold the forum, making a point to hold at least one. Water, noise and security concerns Opponents cited concerns about water usage, noise, data security and environmental impact. Several questioned whether data centers are needed at all. Leann Rippy said she wants answers about the county’s water supply. “A geologist told us that all of our water is going to be dried up within 5 mile radius and within a short period of time. The data center representatives say different. Who’s correct? Who’s going to fix our water well if it’s damaged or drained?” Beverly White-Rowley urged the committee to reject data centers outright. “If you love your family, just say absolutely not to data centers. We don’t need any more data. I can find out about you and you and you and you and everyone in here on the Internet today. I don’t need to know all your dirt.” Many opponents spoke two or even three times, arguing data centers should not be in the county. Supporters point to jobs Supporters said data centers would create work. Ryan McRoberts said construction alone would employ many people. “These data centers will provide hundreds and thousands of jobs for construction over the next couple of years. They will also provide dozens and dozens of maintenance jobs after the facility is up and going.” Money questions Some opponents said data center supporters stand to profit. Kaleb Brown said the people speaking in favor have a financial stake. “The only people who’ve had anything positive to say about this data center all have financial gain to make from the situation. They all have construction businesses. The only people that are for this have a financial incentive. When does the money stop? I guarantee you every single person sitting in this chair makes more money than I do.” What’s next A moratorium on data centers has been in place for the past few months while the committee researches their impacts. The committee is preparing a report and recommendation for the Vanderburgh County commissioners. Committee officials said they will consider all of the public comment as they prepare for their next meeting, scheduled for Nov. 17. Copyright 2026 WFIE. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Bolivar city council discusses possible data center moratorium BOLIVAR, Tenn. (WBBJ) - Bolivar City Council members discussed a possible moratorium related to data centers as they consider how such a facility could affect the community. Mayor Julian McTizic said an inquiry was made about a potential data center at the city’s industrial complex, but it did not lead to a property sale. “The council just decided not to take any action but also make sure we do some studies on what it will look like for a data center to be in our community,” McTizic said. McTizic said multiple people have expressed interest in coming to the community, although he has not recruited data centers. Some community members have raised questions about the potential financial and environmental effects of a data center. Bolivar sits along the Hatchie River, which Councilwoman Caroline Miller described as an important local resource. “We are here on the Hatchie River. That’s one of our greatest resources,” Miller said. “We have water and, you know, we want to maintain that. We want to honor that.” City leaders said they want to stay ahead of the issue, be transparent and keep the community informed as they consider potential interest in a data center before property is purchased. Members of the public were given an opportunity to address the council during the meeting, but no one spoke. Copyright 2026 WBBJ. All rights reserved.
