artigo.texto: How BYD Is Combining Solar Power, Batteries And 5-Minute Charging Chinese car manufacturer BYD has announced the launch of a new integrated charging system in the Abu Dhabi desert. The installation combines solar power generation, battery energy storage, ultra-fast charging, and robotic charging technology in a single location. While each of those elements already exists independently, BYD says this is the first time it has brought them together in a fully integrated system. BYD Flash Charging Reducing charging times, alongside increasing range, remains one of the most effective ways to convince drivers to switch from internal combustion engines to EVs. BYD's answer is FLASH Charging, technology that's claimed to charge a car from 10% to 70% in around five minutes, or from 10% to 97% in roughly nine minutes. Rather than relying solely on the grid, the site captures solar energy, stores it in batteries and then delivers it to vehicles when required. By integrating generation, storage and charging into a unified system, BYD hopes to reduce dependence on existing power infrastructure while making charging more viable in remote locations. It's a concept that could prove particularly relevant in regions where electricity networks are under strain or where connecting high-power charging stations remains challenging. Why The Desert? The desert environment provides an abundant supply of sunshine while also presenting some of the harshest operating conditions for energy infrastructure. High temperatures, dust, and limited rainfall create a demanding test bed for both solar generation and charging equipment. Although many consumers know the company primarily as an automaker, BYD has built a substantial renewable energy division over the past two decades. The company says its solar business operates in more than 100 countries and regions, supplying everything from photovoltaic cells to complete energy systems. Where Does Robotics Fit In? Rather than requiring a driver to retrieve a charging cable and connect it manually, a robotic arm handles the process automatically. Using cameras and force-feedback technology, it identifies the charging port, opens the flap, and inserts the connector. Likewise, drivers can leave the vehicle, lock it, and walk away, while the car navigates itself to an available charging bay. Once parked, the charging robot takes over. In locations where temperatures regularly climb well above comfort levels, eliminating the need for drivers to stand outside connecting heavy charging cables may be genuinely appealing. Almost 20 Years In The Making BYD frames the project as the latest step in a strategy first outlined by chairman Wang Chuanfu in 2006. At the time, he described what the company calls its "Three Green Dreams": generating clean electricity from solar power, storing that energy in batteries and then using it to power electric vehicles. Nearly two decades later, the Abu Dhabi installation represents perhaps the clearest physical expression of that idea. Solar panels generate energy, batteries store it, and electric vehicles consume it, all within a single integrated system. It is also a sign of how far EV technology has progressed. Concepts that once sounded ambitious, such as ultra-fast charging and large-scale battery storage, are increasingly becoming commercial realities. Global Expansion BYD says it plans to deploy 6,000 FLASH Charging stations worldwide by the end of 2027, significantly expanding access to its ultra-fast charging technology. Whether every site will eventually incorporate solar generation, battery storage, and robotic charging remains unclear. But the Abu Dhabi project offers a strong indication of the direction BYD wants the industry to travel. This article was originally published on Forbes.com

artigo.texto: Minneapolis City Council advances data center plan, lays out rules Minneapolis leaders moved a data center ordinance ahead as members remained split over tax relief, oversight and environmental concerns. The Minneapolis City Council moved the ordinance forward Monday, with the city’s moratorium set to end in two weeks. The proposal is headed to a full council vote later this week. There were more than 1,600 public comments as the council debated the rules. The ordinance would require data centers to be downtown, 150,000 square feet or smaller and only in existing office space. Other restrictions included that data centers cannot be the primary use of a building or be on the first two floors. Supporters said the projects could help as downtown property values slump and the tax base falls. “I have heard some say that the economic benefit of these small-scale data centers is wishful thinking; I beg to differ,” Minneapolis City Council Member Elizabeth Shaffer said. “Will small-scale data centers be a cure-all for revenue generation?” Shaffer asked. “I’ve already said no. Is it a step in the right direction for some revenue generation and property tax relief? Yes.” Councilmember Aurin Chowdhury backed an all-out ban, but that effort failed Monday. Chowdhury said residents wanted stronger limits and raised concerns about environmental effects. “What I hear from my constituents is, ‘Don’t sell us out to big tech, don’t sell it out to this industry that oftentimes tries to go around the rules and find loopholes,'” Chowdhury said. “It could have absolutely gone further,” Chowdhury added. “Residents asked for far more.” The council also failed to approve an overlay district that would have required future data center projects to get council approval. Mayor Jacob Frey’s office said he did not support that step but does support the ordinance the full council will take up later this week. His office shared the following: “The Mayor had been in conversation with council members ahead of today’s meeting. He supports the regulatory framework that was approved today.”

artigo.texto: Power Entergy Powers Up Texas, Louisiana for Data Centers Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $33 billion of projects from Entergy, with nearly $16 billion attributed to grassroot developments Released Wednesday, November 11, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by Will Ploch, Assistant Editor-in-Chief for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary Entergy is turning to Texas and Louisiana to build out some of its highest-profile power-generation and transmission projects, including several attached to data centers. Powering Up the Pelican State Entergy Incorporated, a utility that serves parts of Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Arkansas, is taking a bigger role in powering up the data center market, while scrambling to reinforce a regional power grid under growing stress. Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $33 billion worth of active and proposed projects from Entergy, nearly $16 billion of which is attributed to grassroot developments. According to Industrial Info Resources data, more than 50% of the total investment is attributed to projects in Texas and Louisiana. In a quarterly earnings-related conference call last week, Andrew Marsh, the chief executive officer of Entergy, said his company has more than 1,000 miles of transmission lines planned, "primarily in Louisiana and Texas, 85% of which are 500-kilovolt lines. Approximately 70% of the investment is already approved." Last month, the Louisiana Public Service Commission (LPSC) approved Entergy's Babel-to-Webre Transmission Project, a 147-mile line connecting the company's Babel Substation in South Toledo Bend, Texas, which already is under development, to the existing Webre Substation in New Orleans. The project is part of the Midcontinent Independent System Operator's (MISO) 2025 Transmission Expansion Plan (MTEP25), which comprises 432 transmission projects intended to support rapid load growth and improve system reliability. Industrial Info Resources offers more information on the Babel-to-Webre project in its Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Power Project Database, where subscribers can find details--including construction schedules, investment values and necessary equipment--in reports on the transmission line and substation. Marsh also said the U.S. Gulf Coast was a hotspot for its power-generation business: "We also have nine plants in regulatory review in Louisiana, with schedules to support decisions later this year. We have an additional four plants that are in our supply plan, but later in the cycle. That leaves eight units that are available for new growth opportunities." Hyperscalers are among the customers for Entergy's power-generation projects in Louisiana, Marsh said: "We have been innovative in expanding our investment by accessing less-traditional markets. For example, in October, we closed on our second build-to-suit lease" for a unit addition at its Waterford Power Station in Killona, Louisiana, which is being developed partly to service Facebook parent Meta Platforms Incorporated's Hyperion Data Center in Rayville, Louisiana, the first phase of which is under construction. Subscribers can learn more from detailed reports on the Waterford addition and the first phase of Hyperion. Subscribers also can consult a full list of project reports for Meta's nearly $79 billion worth of data center projects in Louisiana. By the Numbers - More than $33 billion: Total investment value of active and proposed projects from Entergy - More than 50%: Share of the total investment attributed to projects in Texas and Louisiana - $940.3 million: Entergy's third-quarter net income, a 35.5% year-over-year increase Shaking Hands with Google Renewable energy also is in Entergy's project mix, including one project intended to serve a data center: the Cypress Solar & Battery Storage Project in Wright, Arkansas, which is designed to generate 600 megawatts (MW) from photovoltaic (PV) panels provided by Canadian Solar Incorporated and store up to 350 MW in a battery energy-storage system (BESS) unit. The Cypress complex will serve Google parent Alphabet Incorporated's West Memphis Data Center, nicknamed "Project Pyramid," a $10 billion investment across five buildings. To ward off public criticism surrounding data center growth, Google agreed to cover all power and infrastructure costs, including $600 million in new grid enhancements. The grid enhancements include a 250-MW BESS unit at the Driver Solar Plant in Osceola, Arkansas, and the 100-MW, standalone Jones Mill BESS unit in Malvern, Arkansas. Both projects are owned by Entergy. Subscribers can learn more from detailed project reports on Cypress, Driver and Jones Mill. Subscribers also can consult a list of reports for projects related to the West Memphis Data Center. Entergy reported consolidated operating revenues of $4.37 billion for third-quarter 2026, a 14.7% increase from the same period last year. Net income stood at $940.3 million, a 35.5% increase. The Industrial Info Resources GMI Project and Plant databases offer a full list of detailed reports for projects mentioned in this article, and a full list of related plant profiles. Industrial Info Resources also offers a full list of reports for active and proposed projects from Entergy. artigo.texto: Anthropic proposes IPO price as data center communities ask who benefits Company could be valued at up to $1.4 trillion; residents near projects seek a direct financial stake GREEN BAY, Wis. (WBAY) - Anthropic, the company behind the AI assistant Claude, proposed a share price of $70 to $78 on Tuesday for its initial public offering. Communities that host data centers are questioning whether the economic benefits last beyond construction. At the high end, the offering could raise up to $64 billion. The stock sale could value the company at up to $1.4 trillion. The sale has not happened yet. Data centers need land, power and approvals The industry’s growth depends on more data centers. Those projects require land, electricity, infrastructure and local approvals. Janine Yorio, CEO of Community Digital Technologies, works with residents near data center projects. She said there is a difference between building the facilities and sharing in the wealth they generate. “Part of the reason why people were so upset about data centers is because they see billions of dollars being poured into their local community to build them,” Yorio said. “But then the local prosperity ends there. After construction stops, there are very few jobs for local workers.” Tax revenue does not necessarily reach homeowners Data centers can generate tax revenue. Those benefits do not necessarily reach individual homeowners. Communities are pushing for residents to have a more direct financial stake in projects built near them. They also want more control over what gets built and who pays the price. As communities question the impacts, developers may face more pressure to offer benefits beyond tax revenue. Yorio said approaches used in the past may not be enough. “Developers have already tried lots of different things. They’ve tried giving towns new schools and paying taxes. And even that hasn’t been enough,” Yorio said. “So the next step is to talk to the neighbors like potential partners and offer them a piece of the upside. People want to understand that they are not going to get left behind by the AI economy that’s being built in their neighborhood.” Payments and ownership stakes Possible benefits include direct payments or ownership stakes for homeowners near data centers. There is no guarantee developers would agree. Copyright 2026 WBAY. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Em um agronegócio que amplia a área cultivada e depende de janelas climáticas para plantar e colher, manter tratores e colheitadeiras disponíveis é parte da gestão da produtividade. Com esse foco, a Moura apresenta na Fenatran 2026, de 9 a 13 de novembro, em São Paulo, a M100HA, bateria de […] 10 de novembro de 2026, às 17:42 Em um agronegócio que amplia a área cultivada e depende de janelas climáticas para plantar e colher, manter tratores e colheitadeiras disponíveis é parte da gestão da produtividade. Com esse foco, a Moura apresenta na Fenatran 2026, de 9 a 13 de novembro, em São Paulo, a M100HA, bateria de sua linha pesada desenvolvida para atender às exigências elétricas cada vez mais complexas de máquinas agrícolas. Segundo levantamento da Companhia Nacional de Abastecimento (Conab), a safra brasileira de grãos 2026/27 poderá alcançar 367,1 milhões de toneladas, alta de 1,4% sobre o ciclo anterior. A área prevista de plantio chega a 85,4 milhões de hectares, expansão de 2,3%. Ao mesmo tempo, a Anfavea registra queda de 15,8% nas vendas de máquinas agrícolas de janeiro a agosto de 2026. Com a renovação mais lenta, preservar a disponibilidade dos equipamentos ganha peso na gestão da safra. A indisponibilidade de uma máquina pode exigir socorro, reparos e reprogramação de atividades, além de afetar o ritmo de outros equipamentos envolvidos no plantio ou na colheita. Ao apresentar a M100HA, a Moura reforça sua atuação em soluções de energia para o agronegócio, com suporte de sua rede nacional de pós-venda e destinação ambientalmente adequada das baterias ao fim da vida útil. “No campo, a produtividade não depende apenas da capacidade da máquina, mas de ela estar disponível quando o clima permite operar. Uma falha na partida pode interromper uma frente de trabalho inteira. Por isso, a escolha da bateria deve considerar o motor, as condições de uso e a instalação elétrica”, afirma Felipe Godoy, Diretor de Negócios Corporativos e Novos Mercados da Rede Moura. Além do esforço exigido na partida de motores a diesel, tratores e colheitadeiras incorporam atualmente computadores de bordo, GPS, telemetria, sensores e iluminação auxiliar. Esses recursos exigem conexões elétricas confiáveis. Com o motor ligado, o sistema de geração assume o fornecimento de energia. À bateria cabe garantir a corrente de partida e as funções previstas no projeto. A M100HA é uma bateria chumbo-ácido de 12 volts e 100 ampères-hora, com corrente de partida a frio de 930 ampères. Um de seus diferenciais é o posicionamento dos terminais, adequado aos chicotes originais de determinadas máquinas agrícolas. Quando a aplicação é compatível, a configuração dispensa extensões, emendas e esforços indevidos nos cabos, fatores que podem comprometer conexões sob vibração. A estrutura interna também contempla proteção e sustentação das placas, além de ligas de chumbo e separadores de alta retenção, recursos voltados à resistência mecânica e à durabilidade. Esses elementos são relevantes para máquinas submetidas à trepidação e ao uso intensivo no campo. A escolha exige observar as especificações do equipamento e não dispensa manutenção preventiva. artigo.texto: Power DTE Boosts Spending Outlook, Eyes Data Center Growth Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $6 billion worth of active and proposed projects from DTE Released Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by Will Ploch, Assistant Editor-in-Chief for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary DTE Energy is raising its five-year investment plan in an effort to boost lower-carbon resources, including battery storage, and to cater to the U.S. data center market. Leaning into a Changing Economy DTE Energy Company is shifting its focus to some of the most energy-hungry parts of the U.S. economy: The Detroit, Michigan-based power provider announced last week it plans to sell off a non-utility subsidiary for $3 billion, so it can focus more on its regulated electric utility and fund a newly revamped five-year investment plan. Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $6 billion worth of active and proposed projects from DTE. Last week, DTE raised its five-year investment plan, which covers 2027-31, to $44.2 billion. Specifically, the company aims to invest $39 billion at its DTE Electric subsidiary and $5.2 billion in its gas operations; the previous, 2026-30 investment plan totaled $34.5 billion, with $30 billion for DTE Electric and $4.5 billion for gas operations. The DTE Electric investment "includes approximately $23 billion of cleaner generation investment, supporting cleaner and more affordable energy for our customers while meeting demand growth," said Joi Harris, the chief executive officer of DTE, in a quarterly earnings-related conference call. "The plan includes 7.6 gigawatts (GW) of new solar and wind resources, 2.1 GW of new combined-cycle natural gas generation, and 2.7 GW of energy storage." According to Industrial Info Resources data, battery energy-storage system (BESS) projects account for more than $1.8 billion of DTE's active project slate. The two highest-valued projects both are just south of Detroit: the 350-megawatt (MW) Monroe I Energy Center in Monroe and the 200-MW Fermi Energy Center in Newport. Both are set to begin construction in the spring of 2027. Industrial Info Resources offers more information on these BESS developments in its Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Power Project Database, where subscribers can find details--including construction schedules, investment values and necessary equipment--in detailed reports on the Monroe and Newport projects. DTE's energy-storage efforts got a boost earlier this year, when it partnered with LG Energy Solution Vertech to develop Michigan-made BESS units across the Wolverine State. Under the agreement, the two companies will invest $1.6 billion across eight projects, which will deliver 1.5 GW of battery storage over a two-year period. By the Numbers - More than $6 billion: Total investment value of active and proposed projects from DTE - $44.2 billion: Total value of DTE's five-year investment plan, which covers 2027-31 - $470 million: DTE's net income for third-quarter 2026, a 12.2% increase from the same period last year Making Room for New Partnerships Shifting priorities also were seen in DTE's recent decision to sell subsidiary DTE Vantage, which focuses on non-utility operations, to institutional investors advised by J.P. Morgan Asset Management in a deal valued at roughly $3 billion. Harris said the deal, which was announced in the earnings call, is expected to close in the first half of 2027. Industrial Info Resources is tracking activity at eight operational plants owned or co-owned by DTE Vantage. Subscribers can learn more from a detailed list of plant profiles in Industrial Info's GMI Power Plant Database. Last month, the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) approved special contracts between DTE and Google, in which the utility will provide electricity for Google's planned Belleville Data Center Campus near Van Buren Township, which is about 30 miles southwest of Detroit. DTE Electric will develop, own and operate the data center, which will be paid for by Google, according to the MPSC's website. Under the agreement, Google must finance DTE's development of up to 1.6 GW of renewable energy and 480 MW of battery storage to serve the Belleville complex. The data center, which is expected to begin service by the end of 2027, will be fueled by energy from a variety of power-generation facilities, rather than a single plant. Subscribers can learn more about Google's Belleville project from a plant profile and a detailed list of project reports. "Looking ahead, our data center development pipeline remains robust," Harris said in the earnings call. "We continue to see approximately 5 to 6 GW of additional opportunities, including 2 GW currently in advanced discussions." DTE reported net income of $470 million for third-quarter 2026, a 12.2% increase from the same period last year. Consolidated revenues stood at $2.25 billion, a 12% decrease. The Industrial Info Resources GMI Project and Plant databases offer a full list of detailed reports for projects mentioned in this article, and a full list of related plant profiles. Industrial Info Resources also offers a full list of reports for active and proposed projects from DTE. artigo.texto: Virginia organizations push for pause in new data center construction Groups say they want better safeguards put in place HANOVER, Va. (WWBT) - A coalition of more than a dozen Virginia-based environmental organizations hosted a press conference Wednesday at the Hanover Humane Society to unveil a “Pause to Protect” policy platform, which calls for a pause on data center construction. The event was held at the Hanover Humane Society, where a new data center is under construction just feet away from the walking trails. “Our goals are not that lofty,” said : Blair St. Ledger-Olson with the Virginia League of Conservation Voters. “We simply want data centers to be better neighbors.” The coalition said the event comes as Virginians across the Commonwealth demand a data center moratorium. “There is no more time to waste. Urgency is now,” said Elena Schlossberg with the Coalition to Protect Prince William County. “We don’t have six months, we don’t have a year. The pause needs to happen now.” The groups believe a statewide moratorium would to develop and implement regulations to protect Virginia’s air and waterways. “We need to get those protections and safeguards put in place before any more of these data centers are getting permitted at the local level, so we’re not creating essentially a gold rush and before they’re getting interconnected so we can make sure our grid is protected,” said St. Ledger-Olson. This demand comes on the heels of the upcoming General Assembly session, where state lawmakers have filed bills for a data center moratorium. However, the Data Center Coalition believes a statewide moratorium is the wrong approach. Nicole Riley, director of Virginia government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, sent 12 On Your Side the following statement: “Data centers can play a crucial role in advancing Virginians’ top priorities including affordability, job creation, local tax revenue, and bringing investment and opportunity to communities. Our industry remains committed to being responsible partners, engaging with residents and local leaders to understand community priorities, and ensuring digital infrastructure meets local standards and delivers the clear benefits that communities are seeking. We join the many local governments, economic developers, business leaders, and labor unions who believe a top-down, statewide moratorium is the wrong approach to regulating this economically impactful industry. States and communities that signal that they are closed for business and investment risk relinquishing substantial long-term economic investment, high-wage jobs, and critical tax revenue to neighboring areas or other states. As we approach the 2027 General Assembly session, DCC looks forward to working with Governor Spanberger, legislators, local communities and state leaders to maintain trust, support responsible development, and help build a stronger economic future for every Virginian.” However, the groups pushing for a statewide moratorium believe the time for a pause is now. “That we can build on the foundation of a pause to deliver a future that all Virginians deserve,” said Tim Cywinski, communications director of the Sierra Club Virginia Chapter. artigo.texto: Empery Digital Announces Update on Midwest Data Center Investment and Share Repurchase Program Empery Digital Has Repurchased an Additional 155,040 Shares Empery Digital Has Repurchased Approximately 26.7 Million Shares AUSTIN, Texas--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 9, 2026-- Empery Digital Inc. (NASDAQ: EMPD) (the “Company” or “Empery Digital”) today provided an update on its Midwest data center investment and its share repurchases. The Company and Hunt Properties, Inc. (“Hunt Properties”) continue to advance lease negotiations for the Midwest AI data center facility and expect to execute a lease in the near term. While these negotiations continue to progress, the definitive agreement to purchase the property has been amended and extended to maintain flexibility while lease negotiations continue. Management believes that the Midwest data center facility is ideally positioned to serve hyperscalers due to the immediate availability of 150 megawatts of power with an owned substation and the potential to expand to approximately 300 megawatts of power. Share Repurchase Update In the week ended November 6, 2026, the Company repurchased 155,040 shares of its common stock under its $200 million share repurchase program at an average price of $2.36 per share, including fees and commissions. As of November 6, 2026, the Company has repurchased an aggregate of 26,686,348 shares of its common stock. Following these repurchases, Empery Digital has 29,372,106 shares outstanding, after giving effect to the potential exercise of 1,653,686 pre-funded warrants, and approximately $49 million remains available under the share repurchase authorization. About Empery Digital Empery Digital is focused on building long-term shareholder value through its disciplined capital allocation strategy. The Company employs a bitcoin treasury strategy and is strategically expanding into AI infrastructure and data center investments, partnering with operators that have decades of real-estate and energy infrastructure development experience to capture growth at the intersection of digital assets and next-generation compute. Empery Digital is committed to transparency, efficiency, and accountability, applying rigorous decision-making to drive sustainable, long-term shareholder value. artigo.texto: Data centers need power – lower income, rural residents pay the price By Caitlin Hayes, Cornell Chronicle As the engines of artificial intelligence, large data centers can consume as much power as medium-sized cities, straining grids and prompting expensive upgrades to U.S. energy infrastructure. New research finds that residents, and especially lower-income and rural residents, are disproportionately bearing the costs. In the study, published Nov. 9 in Nature Energy, Cornell researchers analyzed growth in energy demand and infrastructure projects for four major U.S. power grids from 2020 to 2025 and found that data centers have hiked wholesale energy prices and on average paid only 38% of the infrastructure costs linked to their growth – $3.12 billion of an $8.25 billion bill in 2025. The remaining $5.13 billion, or 62%, fell largely on residents, with the lowest income households seeing extra energy costs up to 28% of their incomes. “We were trying to answer a very simple question: With the booming of data centers, who pays for that expansion and who benefits?” said Fengqi You, the Roxanne E. and Michael J. Zak Professor in Energy Systems Engineering in the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering. “It’s not just a question of generating enough electricity but of whether the rules for paying for the grid are keeping pace with who is driving new demand.” The research is the first multi-region, long-term assessment of how data center development impacts infrastructure growth and how costs are distributed across communities. It comes amidst a boom in data center construction. The researchers found that transmission investment in energy infrastructure projects increased from $2 billion in 2020 to $34 billion in 2025, with data centers driving much of that rise. Debates are ongoing – from local communities to state governments to Congress – about who picks up the bill as growth accelerates; data centers are projected to consume between 8% and 17% of U.S. electricity by 2030, with 70% to 80% of that attributed to AI. With first author and postdoctoral researcher Cheng Feng, You also looked at data centers’ economic benefits, finding that each gigawatt of data center capacity can create 15,000 jobs across the economy, with an average 2,700 jobs directly associated with the data center (although not necessarily all on-site). “In a lot of discussions right now, people take one side or the other, completely yes on data centers or completely no,” said You, director of the Cornell AI for Sustainability Initiative. “But there are benefits and costs, and the key issue in the end is how to balance the trade-offs.” Sharing the cost of power infrastructure The team analyzed data from 4,000 existing and proposed data centers, as well as power-price records, rate filings from utilities, power-line plans, and federal household and job data. The major grids they studied encompass regions with the largest clusters of data centers, including the southern San Francisco Bay area; north Texas around Dallas-Fort Worth; the Midwest; and the mid-Atlantic region, including northern Virginia, where the biggest concentration of data centers has been built to date. State incentives for data centers have provided returns on the investments, if inconsistently, the researchers found. Some states, such as California, reaped $180 in worker income for every dollar spent, while Virginia increased income $2 for every dollar invested. The researchers determined that the presence of an existing, qualified workforce was a stronger indicator of high returns than the amount of incentive spending. Data centers also increased wholesale electricity prices, the amounts utilities pay regional power markets before delivering the electricity to homes. In the most-affected hubs, data center growth raised those prices by nearly 10% or more by 2025. In Virginia, the costs jumped 15% and in California’s southern Bay Area, 20%. In contrast, residents in New York and New England, where data center construction has been limited, have not seen clear price increases due to data center expansion, the researchers found. “I think that means we’re at a good starting point in New York to think about the next steps,” You said. “Economic benefits, job benefits, investment, fairly allocating the costs – these are the dimensions and trade-offs we need to consider.” A key problem is how the costs of new infrastructure projects are currently shared: The allocation is often based on previous patterns of energy consumption. “It’s kind of a chicken-and-egg problem,” You said. “Because if you’re going to build a data center, you need to expand this power infrastructure. Otherwise, there’s no electricity for them to run. But before they build, they’re not using energy. So with this model of relying on past consumption, households end up taking on much of the infrastructure costs.” Many more rural and lower-income residents saw proportionally higher bills; the share of rural families shouldering a high energy burden – spending more than 6% of their incomes on energy – rose 76% more than among urban residents. The authors cite a national survey finding that rural residents are also less likely to use AI tools like ChatGPT than urban residents. The impact on energy bills also has a wide geographical reach. For example, residents in New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Ohio help pay for grid upgrades linked to data center growth in Virginia, the researchers said. “You do not have to live next to a data center to help pay for its power infrastructure,” You said. “The grid connects communities across states, and cost-sharing rules connect them financially.” Using insights from the data, You and Feng recommend changes to cost-sharing rules and strategies to lower burdens. In all four regions, they found that, if data centers cut back power use during 22 of the region’s peak demand hours each year, they would relieve strain on the grid and minimize the need to expand. artigo.texto: Protect Kansas circulating 3-part petition to ban hyperscale data centers TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW) - Both Topeka and Shawnee County now have a moratorium in place for data centers. Similar to what we just saw happen in Emporia, the group Protect Kansas is collecting signatures to ban hyperscale data centers. Even with moratoriums in Shawnee County and the city of Topeka, Protect Kansas is taking matters into their own hands. “The city can change their moratorium at any time. They’ve let us know that they could vote that in and change that any day,” Colleen Campbell, Protect Kansas co-founder, said. The petition is broken into 3 parts: - No data centers over 25 megawatts - Preventing Topeka from supplying water to data centers outside city limits - “No annexing the data centers from the county into the city,” Campbell said. “So it’s not completely banning data centers. It’s just saying, ‘hey, we don’t want these hyperscale ones that use a lot of resources,’” Campbell said. It’s not just about protecting people in the city. “The county doesn’t have any recourse for a petition or any kind of way for them to have their voices heard,” Campbell said. The petition needs 6,000 signatures that can be verified by the city clerk. “The city council actually has a chance to just accept the petition as is so they can go ahead and make it as law,” Campbell said. If city council doesn’t accept it, the petition could be challenged in court or put it to a public vote. Though the moratoriums are in place, Protect Kansas wants this to go beyond the expiration dates. “This gives us long-term protection, and it’s really mirroring what the moratorium has already done, so we’re just looking for that longer-term, more solid protection,” Campbell said. WIBW reached out to the city for comment on the petition, but the city has not responded. The Shawnee County moratorium expires at the end of Feb. 2027, and the Topeka data center moratorium expires in mid-July 2027. Copyright 2026 WIBW. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Maine developer revives plan to turn former Jay paper mill into AI data center JAY (WGME) -- A local developer has revived plans to turn a former paper mill in Jay into an AI data center, teaming up with the same national partner that pulled out of the original project in June. The local developer intends to file permit applications with the Maine Department of Environmental Protection to redevelop a portion of the former Androscoggin Paper Mill in Jay into a data center. Six years ago, a wood pulp digester exploded at the paper mill in Jay, eventually leading to the closing of the mill and a loss of 170 jobs. The $550 million facility Sentinel Data Centers wants to build wouldn't bring back all those jobs, but it could significantly ease some of the tax burden in Jay. "If we have nothing there, we have no tax base, and we have a property just sitting there with really no purpose,” Jay resident Jason Mancine said. “So, I think it's an opportunity." "I think it's a good idea,” Jay resident Elizabeth Bates said. “If not that, something else. They should do something with it." Some people in town say they're concerned about all the electricity and water data centers use. - Also read: After Mills vetoes statewide pause, Maine towns move to halt data center projects locally Town leaders say it would be about the same as what the paper mill used, and they don't expect much of an environmental impact change. "It's a former industrial site, so it's not as though we're putting this in the middle of a forested wetland or something like that," Jay Town Manager Shiloh LaFreniere said. "I understand people's concerns about environmental impacts, but I think it would be miniscule compared to what paper mills were," Mancine said. CBS13 reached out to the developer and was told they are not commenting at this time. Earlier this year, Governor Janet Mills vetoed a moratorium on data centers after lawmakers refused to carve out an exception for the Town of Jay. Governor-Elect Hannah Pingree has said she would sign a bill to ban new data centers in Maine. "I don't know how that will play out," LaFreniere said. "My hope personally is that what they're coming out with at the state level will be met by this developer anyway." Developers plan to hold a public meeting at the Jay mill site in one month to talk about the impact of water and electricity use by the proposed data center.

artigo.texto: Safety remains a concern as the use of batteries spreads throughout the economy but they’re getting safer, Christopher Rahn, a professor of mechanical engineering at the Pennsylvania State University, said in an interview. Lithium-ion batteries pose the greatest fire risk because they have high density and use a flammable solvent. But manufacturers are getting better at shipping packs with fewer bad cells, said Rahn, who serves as co-director of the Battery and Energy Storage Technology Center at Penn State. “If you’re going with a well-known supplier, like LG Chem, they do a lot of testing to weed out the weak cells,” he said. Battery management systems are getting better, too, he said. “They make sure you don’t over-charge, don’t over-discharge,” he said. “They make sure they’re working normally and, if anything’s abnormal, they alert you so you stop using the pack. That can help prevent a thermal runaway event.” Manufacturers are also getting smarter about how they control propagation, whether cell-to-cell, pack-to-pack, module-to-module or container-to-container. “The individual cells have different types of materials between them so they don’t propagate to a module-level event,” said Rahn, who’s worked with research teams to develop algorithms for monitoring battery health. At the module level, manufacturers are improving venting to enable gases to escape more effectively. “If there's anything burning and it needs to vent hot gases, you give them an exit from that module,” he said. And at the container level, battery system suppliers are spacing containers further apart during set-up. “If there’s an issue with one container, it doesn’t affect the other ones,” he said. “So, there are three levels of safety, and all of that is maturing,” Rahn said. “The technology of the cells and the quality of manufacturing, the ability to detect when there are anomalies and the ideas and concepts of how to prevent propagation are all maturing." Manufacturers are also investing more resources into alternatives to lithium-ion, which remains the go-to battery despite its risks because its high density makes it the most efficient rechargeable battery on the market. Rahn said he’s seeing manufacturers release more batteries that have aqueous, water-based chemistries, which are considered safer because they don’t rely on a flammable solvent. That means the market is seeing new approaches to traditional lead-acid batteries but also improvements to nickel-zinc batteries to lengthen their lifespan and to iron-air batteries, which use rust conversion to store and discharge energy. He’s also seeing greater use of lithium iron phosphate batteries, which have a lower density than lithium-ion but are less likely to have a thermal event. “So, there’s a spectrum,” he said, “everything from very high-energy density lithium-ion that would typically be used in vehicles through lithium iron phosphate, which is less energy dense but has a safer chemistry, to aqueous chemistries like lead-acid, nickel-zinc and iron-air.”

artigo.texto: O Ministério das Comunicações aprovou R$ 46,3 milhões do Fundo para o Desenvolvimento Tecnológico das Telecomunicações (Funttel) para o projeto Prisma, plataforma que usa inteligência artificial para distribuir o processamento de dados entre infraestruturas, inclusive mini data centers, segundo o ministério em 9 de novembro de 2026. O Centro Brasileiro de Inovação em Tecnologias da Informação e da Comunicação (CPQD), de Campinas (SP), executa o projeto, e a Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep) gere os recursos. O prazo é de 36 meses, contados a partir do convênio entre as duas instituições. Leia também - João Pessoa já sedia data center que vai quadruplicar de tamanho; Nordeste tem vantagem de US$ 17,4 bilhões no setor, aponta Redata - Brasil lidera expansão de data centers na América Latina - IA pressiona consumo de energia dos data centers O que o projeto Prisma prevê Segundo o Ministério das Comunicações, a plataforma deve decidir com IA onde e como os dados serão processados, distribuindo recursos computacionais entre diferentes infraestruturas. Os objetivos são reduzir o consumo e os custos de energia, cortar custos operacionais, acelerar o acesso à informação e proteger dados estratégicos. Os mini data centers são instalações menores, que processam dados mais perto de onde são gerados. O projeto prevê estimular a expansão dessas unidades em diversas regiões do país, sem informar quantidade nem localização. - Setores atendidos: saúde, defesa, segurança pública, educação e telecomunicações. - Energia: soluções de armazenamento de eletricidade, para dar mais autonomia e continuidade aos serviços. - Segurança e governança: padrões internacionais de segurança e diretrizes da Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD). De onde vem o dinheiro O Funttel é um fundo de natureza contábil, alimentado por contribuição de 0,5% sobre a receita bruta das prestadoras de serviços de telecomunicações, segundo o Ministério das Comunicações. Nos últimos anos, o fundo destinou mais de R$ 362 milhões a empresas do setor, segundo a pasta. O Prisma já aparecia entre os projetos do pacote de cerca de R$ 104 milhões do Funttel para o CPQD, anunciado em março de 2026 para 6G, nuvem e IA, com execução entre 2026 e 2028. O comunicado de 9 de novembro não informa se os R$ 46,3 milhões fazem parte desse total. O que dizem os envolvidos Frederico de Siqueira Filho, ministro das Comunicações, afirmou que investir em tecnologia nacional garante ao Brasil mais autonomia para proteger informações e reduz a dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior. Gustavo Correa Lima, diretor de Tecnologia e Inovação do CPQD, destacou que a arquitetura permite “maior controle sobre o dado que está na borda”, ou seja, nas unidades próximas a quem gera a informação. Joana Meirelles, superintendente da Área de Saúde e Transformação Digital da Finep, citou o objetivo de disponibilizar uma plataforma nacional segura e sustentável. O que falta para o projeto sair do papel O aporte mostra a direção do governo, que é a de levar processamento para perto dos usuários com tecnologia desenvolvida no país. O que falta para isso se concretizar são os detalhes de execução. O comunicado não informa se o convênio entre Finep e CPQD já foi assinado, em quais regiões os mini data centers serão instalados, quantas unidades serão e quantos empregos o projeto gera. No Prisma, o ponto em aberto é a execução do convênio.

artigo.texto: RWE has started construction of its first battery energy storage system (BESS) in Italy. The 62.5 MW Ragusa battery will be located in Sicily. It will consist of 42 containers with lithium-ion batteries, being able to deliver its maximum output for four hours. This corresponds to a nominal storage capacity of 262.5 MWh. Commissioning is scheduled for the end of 2027. Sopna Sury, CEO RWE Renewables Europe & Australia, said: “The start of construction of our Ragusa battery storage marks an important milestone. We have been operating in Italy for many years, using the energy from the wind and the sun. In a world of growing renewable energy, battery storage systems are crucial for stabilising the grid and ensuring that electricity is used when it is needed most. Ragusa battery will be capable of covering the evening peak demand of around 21 000 households for four hours. We look forward to establishing further battery storage capacity in Italy soon – in addition to wind and solar power – in order to support Italy in building a resilient energy system.” Ragusa battery will provide balancing energy to stabilise the electricity grid. It also features the technology necessary to provide new grid forming services such as instantaneous reserve (inertia). In addition to the batteries, RWE will build the associated grid infrastructure. This includes a high-voltage transformer to connect to the 150-kV grid. artigo.texto: ProLogium and Rimac Technology Advance Next-Generation EV Battery Development Paris, France, October 12, 2026 – ProLogium today announced progress in its collaboration with Rimac Technology on next-generation electric vehicle battery pack development. The companies signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) in September 2025 to develop a next-generation battery platform and have completed a battery pack concept mockup, which will be displayed at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. The next phase will focus on developing a functional battery segment to establish a basis for testing the thermal management and cell-integration concepts and support battery pack applications in the battery electric vehicle (BEV) market. The collaboration combines ProLogium’s next-generation cell technology with Rimac Technology’s battery system development expertise, focusing on a pouch cell-to-pack architecture. Through a staged development path from concept mockup to functional battery segment, full-scale functional battery pack and in-vehicle testing, the companies will progressively evaluate cell and system integration approaches, connecting next-generation cell technology with automotive product development. From Concept Mockup to Functional Hardware Bringing cell technology into automotive applications requires more than cell-level performance. It also involves addressing thermal management, cell integration and battery pack architecture at the system level. With battery pack integration at its core, the collaboration brings together cell technology and systems engineering to examine the design requirements for next-generation batteries in automotive applications. The completed concept mockup is an initial milestone in this development process. The ongoing development will move the project from a conceptual representation toward functional hardware, using a battery segment as the platform for subsequent testing. This work will assess the feasibility of thermal management and cell-integration concepts and inform full-scale battery pack development. By developing a battery segment before expanding to a full-scale system, the companies will gather test results and design feedback at each stage to assess whether the integration approach can meet automotive battery-systems requirements. Vincent Yang, Founder and CEO of ProLogium, said: Since jointly announcing our collaboration with Rimac Technology at IAA in 2025, both teams have continued to advance the project, translating our shared technical vision into concrete engineering development work. ”What we are presenting at the Paris Motor Show is the baseline of that collaboration. Building on the completed concept mockup and the functional segments currently in development, we are preparing to move into the development and production of a functional battery progressing toward a full-scale battery pack and subsequent vehicle integration validation. Bringing next-generation batteries to the automotive market requires more than cell technology. It also takes the engineering expertise to integrate those cells into a battery pack with optimized architecture and thermal management. We look forward to combining our technical strengths through hardware development and testing to address the engineering challenges of automotive integration and translate the value of next-generation cell technology into solutions that can be adopted in vehicles.” Daniel Kišić, Principal Product Architect of Rimac Technology said: Rimac Technology is developing a scalable cell-to-pack integration technology for solid-state pouch cells, designed to meet and exceed the requirements the automotive industry is expected to set over the coming decade. ”A wide range of integration solutions is currently being evaluated and tested in parallel on functional battery segments, covering thermal management, swelling management, cell integration and system-level design. Some of these solutions are oriented towards maximum energy density and reduced space and weight, while others are oriented towards delivering performance. The work starts from vehicle-level requirements and aims to improve every aspect of the battery design by reducing complexity, combining functions and reducing weight. It does so with cost in mind, while still delivering state-of-the-art charging times and power output. Once validated at vehicle level, the solution is expected to deliver significant weight savings, improving driving efficiency and extending range. OEMs could then choose between more energy on board at the same weight, a smaller and lighter battery for the same range, or any combination in between.” A Clear Pathway to Full-Scale Battery Packs and In-Vehicle Testing According to Rimac Technology’s current development roadmap, the functional battery segment currently in development is planned for display at CES 2027, with the full-scale functional battery pack identified as a development milestone for the second half of 2027. Subsequent targets include in-vehicle and public-road testing in the second half of 2028.These stages will progressively expand the scope of validation, from assessing integration concepts in a functional battery segment to a full-scale battery pack, followed by vehicle installation and road testing to evaluate system performance in an automotive environment. At the Paris Motor Show, the companies will present the concept mockup stage of the collaboration and outline the next steps in functional hardware development and integration validation. By combining cell technology with battery systems engineering, ProLogium and Rimac Technology will continue to advance next-generation battery integration technology development from concept design toward automotive applications. artigo.texto: Since I became a Climate Justice Fellow at ANCA, I’ve learned a lot about energy in New York and the North Country, including the important role that battery storage could play. As we continue to discuss what battery storage looks like in the region, I wanted to share some of what I’ve learned in the last few months. What is BESS? Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are large battery installations that connect to a home, business, or the larger electrical grid. As shown in the diagram below, BESS consist of cells, modules and racks, which are then controlled with a Battery Management System (BMS). The BMS is the brain of the battery system and monitors the whole system down to individual cells. There are two options for BESS. First, it can be part of a renewable energy installation, like a solar farm, and be charged when more energy is being produced than the grid needs at that time. Then, when energy is needed, the batteries can send that stored energy to the grid. READ MORE: In Northern NY, Battery energy storage system moratoriums and bans stack up The second option is a standalone BESS, meaning it is not “co-located” with clean energy generation. In this case, it charges directly from the grid when energy demand is low and costs are cheaper, before discharging when costs and demand are high. Both of these options can help keep energy costs from spiking and reduce the need to turn on peaker plants, which operate when demand is especially high, are expensive to operate, and burn fossil fuels. New York’s electric grid is facing strain due to increasing electricity demand and aging infrastructure. Adding BESS to the grid will support the grid by responding to energy supply and demand quickly and without burning polluting fossil fuels. Day to day, BESS can help meet peak energy demand and create a balance of electricity supply. This is referred to as “peak shaving” since we’re “shaving” the top of the energy demand spike. Long term, BESS can also reduce or defer the need for expensive grid infrastructure upgrades needed to meet future peak demand. Grid infrastructure upgrades contribute to increased delivery charges on your electric bill, and deferring or eliminating expensive upgrades would help keep costs down. BESS and the North Country In the North Country, we have lots of hydropower, as well as wind and solar, so I wasn’t sure at first why we would need batteries too. But as we shift our reliance from fossil fuels, batteries are needed to enable the transition to renewables and energy independence. By supporting the state-wide grid, batteries can improve energy affordability, as mentioned before, by supporting peak demand and reducing the need for more expensive grid upgrades. Just like your taxes go to paying for upkeep of the roads in your town, but you drive roads of other municipalities too, the energy made and used in the Adirondacks isn’t confined by the Blue Line. We’re part of the larger state-wide grid, and the system needs to be evaluated and supported as a whole. There have been some BESS proposals made by developers in communities all over the state recently, including the North Country, such as part of a solar installation in Elizabethtown and standalone BESS in St. Armand. Developers look for locations based on factors such as size, local zoning and avoiding sensitive environmental areas. Crucially, they also look for locations which have strong grid connections with enough extra energy that can be stored for later to be able to support additional infrastructure like a BESS, and there are some locations in the region that meet those requirements. Fire risks and solutions Historically, the main risk commonly associated with BESS, as with any electrical infrastructure, is fire. Fires can happen when components of the battery overheat, including by “thermal runaway,” where battery temperatures self-accelerate. Battery fires, especially lithium-ion batteries, which are currently the most common type used in BESS, are not like a house fire we may be more familiar with. For lithium-ion battery fires the recommended strategy is to monitor and let the fire burn itself out. Obviously that sounds very scary, but studies have shown no lasting environmental impact on soil, air or water after this type of fire, which I know is a concern for me, personally. Because of the unique nature of BESS fires, there are specific, detailed trainings for first responders that are required to be provided to EMS with BESS nearby. For example, in 2023, in East Hampton on Long Island, the way that a BESS was handled led to PFAS contamination in local wells, but this was due to firefighters using water to suppress the fire and washing the built-in fire suppressant chemicals out of the system which would have been self-contained if not for the water used. This just goes to show how important site-specific training is. Since 2023, there were four cases of BESS facilities catching fire in New York, such as in Warwick. As a result, the state has taken major steps to improve fire safety around BESS, including New York’s Inter-Agency Fire Safety Working Group, which created the new Fire Code of the State of New York. They gave 11 recommendations, including requiring “industry-funded peer review” of BESS projects and increased monitoring and fire detection, which were incorporated into the fire code and made it much more rigorous. For anyone interested, those documents and more can be accessed on their website. There are also site-specific, annual trainings for first responders that are required to be provided to local EMS by the owner of BESS facilities for installations of a certain size. Technological advancements also mean that lithium batteries are safer than they were a few years ago. So fires that have happened at older BESS facilities are much less likely to occur in ones built today, as shown in the orange line on the graph below. artigo.texto: Indonesia Accelerates Energy Transition with Landmark Carbon Market Agreement at COP31 November 11, 2026 Category Norway and Indonesia sign Indonesia’s first Mitigation Outcome Purchase Agreement under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, marking a significant milestone in the country’s carbon market implementation. ANTALYA, TÜRKIYE, November 11, 2026 – Norway and Indonesia have signed a Mitigation Outcome Purchase Agreement (MOPA) at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye. The agreement is facilitated by GGGI and marks Indonesia’s first MOPA to operationalize Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, representing a significant milestone in the country’s participation in the international carbon markets. Supported through the Norwegian Article 6 Climate Action (NACA) Fund – a carbon fund hosted under GGGI’s Carbon Transaction Facility (CTF) – the agreement is expected to be among the largest transactions under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement to date. It represents an important step in translating international carbon market cooperation into practical implementation and mobilizing climate finance for Indonesia’s energy transition. The signing took place at the Indonesia Pavilion during COP31. The agreement signing was witnessed by Moh Jumhur Hidayat, Minister of Environment/Head of Environmental Protection Agency of Indonesia, and Sigrun Aasland, Minister of Climate and Environment of Norway, serving as witnesses. Following the signing, GGGI will work closely with the Government of Indonesia, PT PLN (Persero) – Indonesia’s state-owned electricity company, and the Norwegian Ministry of Climate and Environment to finalize implementation and operational arrangements. “This agreement marks a concrete step in implementing the Article 6.2 bilateral agreement between Indonesia’s Ministry of Environment/Environmental Protection Agency and Norway’s Ministry of Climate and Environment. Through this cooperation, we seek to mobilize carbon finance to support Indonesia’s energy transition and contribute to the achievement of our national climate targets. This cooperation will also support efforts to strengthen Indonesia’s SRUK (Carbon Unit Registry System) and ensure transparent recording and tracking of international transfers. Our priority is to ensure that this cooperation delivers credible mitigation outcomes, upholds environmental integrity, and is implemented in line with Indonesia’s national climate commitments,” said Moh Jumhur Hidayat, Minister of Environment/Head of Environmental Protection Agency of Indonesia. The MOPA supports the implementation of Indonesia’s Generation-Based Incentive (GBI) Program, a results-based crediting mechanism designed to accelerate investment in new and additional clean, grid-connected electricity generation. As a sectoral financing mechanism, the GBI can be applied across renewable energy technologies. Its initial technological window in Indonesia focuses on floating solar photovoltaic (PV), in line with national priorities and Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. “Indonesia’s emissions are growing rapidly. Norway’s cooperation with Indonesia is helping ensure that more of the country’s electricity comes from solar power rather than coal. This demonstrates how international cooperation can contribute both to reducing emissions and accelerating the transition to renewable energy,” said Sigrun Aasland, Norway’s Minister of Climate and Environment. The program addresses financial, regulatory, and grid-related constraints that have slowed renewable energy investment in Indonesia. It provides additional incentive payments when the standard power purchase price is insufficient to make an eligible project financially viable. By prioritizing new and additional renewable energy generation paired with battery energy storage systems (BESS), the program enables renewable electricity delivery during peak and evening hours, when grid emissions are highest. This approach aims to reduce intermittency, enhance grid stability, and support the transition to a low-carbon power system. Under the GBI Program, participation is voluntary. Independent Power Producers (IPPs) may apply for inclusion if they meet established financial, technical, and geographic criteria and demonstrate genuine additionality, measurable emission reductions, and positive sustainable development impacts. The program uses a digital Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) system to capture electricity generated and supplied to the grid. The data is reviewed through an independent audit process to ensure accuracy, transparency, and environmental integrity. Following verification, carbon payments are issued to project operators based on actual performance. The resulting emission reductions are aggregated, authorized, and traded as Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs) under a cooperative approach between Indonesia and the Norwegian Ministry of Environment, as part of the Norwegian Global Emissions Reduction (NOGER) Initiative. The program applies dynamic baselines anchored in Indonesia’s unconditional Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), helping safeguard environmental integrity while supporting national climate objectives. “Article 6 is moving from readiness to implementation, and this agreement is a clear example of what that transition requires: strong national drive and dedicated partners. GGGI is proud to have facilitated this agreement between Norway and Indonesia, building on our support to countries as they prepare for and take part in carbon markets. Results-based mechanisms like this can give governments and investors the clarity they need to mobilize finance for climate action at scale.” – Sang-hyup Kim, Executive Director of GGGI. This signing demonstrates Indonesia’s continued efforts to translate climate commitments into bankable projects, commercial agreements, and sustained implementation. artigo.texto: Power PPL Pours Capital into PJM as Data Center Plans Grow Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $7 billion worth of active and proposed projects from PPL, nearly half of which is attributed to grassroot projects Released Wednesday, November 11, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by Will Ploch, Assistant Editor-in-Chief for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary PPL expects growing energy demand from data centers in the PJM region will necessitate the development of more gas-fired and T&D capacity. Data Dominates the Agenda PPL Corporation, an important energy provider on the PJM Interconnection, is building out its gas-fired power-generation capacity to meet the ever-growing demand from data centers--especially in Kentucky and Pennsylvania, which have emerged as investment hotspots for the company. Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $7 billion worth of active and proposed projects from PPL, nearly half of which is attributed to grassroot projects. Companywide, PPL plans to raise its base capital expenditures for 2027 through 2030 to $25 billion, which is $2 billion more than the 2026-29 plan. In Kentucky alone, the company's spending is set to increase from $2.3 billion in 2026 to $3.6 billion in 2027. "Through 2032, additional capital investment opportunities could reach a total of $12 billion to $16 billion," in addition to the amount projected through 2030, said Vince Sorgi, the chief executive officer of PPL, in a quarterly earnings-related conference call. "This includes additional regulated generation investment in Kentucky required to meet continued increases in potential demand growth." The increased spending in Kentucky is attributed largely to the proposed construction of a 645-megawatt (MW), natural gas-fired, combined-cycle (NGCC) turbine, subject to regulatory approval. But that approval could be a tough process: The Kentucky Public Service Commission (KPSC) has denied several requests from PPL in recent years to add new gas-fired capacity. However, KPSC did grant a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) in October 2025 for the proposed Unit 6 at Mill Creek Power Station in Louisville, Kentucky, which also is a 645-MW, NGCC unit. Louisville Gas and Electric Company (LG&E), a PPL subsidiary, owns Mill Creek and is developing the project, which is set to follow the ongoing construction of the 621-MW Unit 5. PPL expects Unit 5 will be completed sometime in the second half of 2027. Together, the two new units would nearly double capacity at Mill Creek, which has an operational output of at least 1,361.7 MW. Industrial Info Resources offers more information on the Mill Creek developments in its Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Power Plant and Project databases, where subscribers can find details--including construction schedules, investment values and necessary equipment--in a plant profile and detailed project reports on Unit 5 and Unit 6. Concurrent with the Mill Creek 6 approval, the KPSC granted a CPCN to PPL's proposed, 621-MW unit addition at the E.W. Brown Power Station in Harrodsburg, Kentucky, which currently has an output of at least 1,457.6 MW. Subscribers can learn more from a detailed plant profile and project report. By the Numbers - More than $7 billion: Total investment value of active and proposed projects from PPL - $25 billion: The company's base capital expenditures for 2027 through 2030 - $12 billion to $16 billion: Additional capital investment opportunities from 2031 to 2032 Keystone State Key to Growth Sorgi announced in the earnings call that Invitium Energy, a joint venture between PPL Corporation (with a 51% stake) and Blackstone Infrastructure (49%), "signed a letter of intent (LOI) with Quality Technology Services (QTS) to be their generation solution provider in portions of Pennsylvania. Under that LOI, we have agreed with QTS on all key commercial terms for approximately 2 gigawatts (GW) of generation capacity for its Salem Township Data Center project, with a 20-year initial term allowing for multiple five-year renewals." According to Industrial Info Resources data, the Salem Data Center, which is located in Luzerne County, comprises 12 buildings and more than $10 billion of investment value. Sorgi also noted PPL's large load tariffs "require data centers to cover the cost of serving them, so existing customers don't bear that burden." Subscribers can learn more from a plant profile and a detailed list of project reports. Through Invitium, PPL has proposed the Luzerne County Power Station, which is designed to generate at least 1.5 GW for data centers in the area. The company also is looking into additional transmission and distribution (T&D) capacity to support the load growth. Subscribers can learn more about the Luzerne County Power Station from a detailed project report. PPL's net earnings for the third quarter were reported to be $367 million, a 15.4% increase from third-quarter 2025. Operating revenues stood at $2.5 billion, an 11.5% increase. The Industrial Info Resources GMI Project and Plant databases offer a full list of detailed reports for projects mentioned in this article, and a full list of related plant profiles. Industrial Info Resources also offers a full list of reports for active and proposed projects from PPL. Key Takeaways - Regulated generation investment in Kentucky accounts for a significant share of PPL's investment plans. - The company is building out its NGCC capacity in Kentucky, with several projects at various stages of approval. - PPL has proposed the gas-fired Luzerne County Power Station to support data centers in eastern Pennsylvania. artigo.texto: SMUD discusses policies for large data centers as two major electricity inquiries advance The Sacramento Municipal Utility District held a public meeting Wednesday night to discuss how it would serve large electricity customers as two potential data center projects enter the feasibility stages and community members raise concerns about energy use, pollution, water consumption and transparency. SMUD confirmed it has received two inquiries from prospective large-load customers, each seeking more than 50 megawatts of electricity capacity. According to a SMUD spokesperson, one megawatt of power is enough to supply approximately 1,000 homes. That means each inquiry represents a potential electricity demand equivalent to more than 50,000 homes. If both projects move forward, they would represent the largest electricity demands among SMUD's 16 data centers, according to the utility. The inquiries come as communities across the country debate the potential costs and benefits of large data centers, including their demands on electricity, water and local infrastructure. SMUD says it has longstanding policies and procedures intended to ensure the costs of serving large electricity customers are not passed on to existing ratepayers. Those principles were the focus of Wednesday night's public meeting. However, SMUD spokesperson Gamaliel Ortiz told CBS News Sacramento the discussion was not centered on any specific projects. One company that has confirmed early conversations with SMUD is Link Logistics, a New York-based real estate company owned by Blackstone Inc. The company said it has owned and operated Depot Park for many years. "We regularly evaluate opportunities to make the best long-term use of the property in ways that support jobs and economic growth in the community, and that includes early conversations with SMUD about the site's potential," a Link Logistics spokesperson said in a statement. The company confirmed it has not submitted an application for a new project. "Any future proposal would go through the City of Sacramento's full public entitlement and environmental review process, with opportunities for community input, and we look forward to sharing more with the community at that time," the spokesperson added. SMUD did not confirm the conversations involving Depot Park. In a separate statement, a spokesperson reiterated the utility's policy on large electricity customers. "It is a longstanding SMUD policy and procedure that costs associated with serving large electrical load customers are paid for by the customer, ensuring these costs are not passed on to existing customers," the spokesperson said. SMUD does not make land-use decisions. Those decisions fall to local jurisdictions. Any data center of this scale proposed within Sacramento city limits would require approval from city leaders. During a Sept. 15 City Council meeting, Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty called for a review of the city's policies and additional information about how potential data center projects could affect the community. "I want Sacramento to be prepared if and when a project comes our way. I'm asking our city manager and staff to consider a policy that considers potential impacts on our communities, energy, water, infrastructure, neighborhoods and what safeguards we may need if such a proposal is forwarded to the City of Sacramento for consideration," McCarty said. SMUD leadership is scheduled to vote next week on the large-load customer service principles discussed Wednesday.

artigo.texto: Minneapolis City Council to vote on data center regulations Go Deeper. Create an account or log in to save stories. Like this? Thanks for liking this story! We have added it to a list of your favorite stories. Quick Read The Minneapolis City Council is poised to pass zoning regulations Thursday that limit the size of new data centers and restrict them to the city’s downtown. City leaders agree that, at a minimum, data centers must be regulated. But they disagree on how strict those regulations should be, and some back a full ban. Supporters of data center development argue it can bring in needed jobs and tax revenue to communities. “Look around our city. We do not see cranes. We are not building, and our construction trades need work,” said council member Elizabeth Shaffer, who was one of the lead writers of the regulations. Turn Up Your Support MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all. “Do data centers drive a lot of permanent jobs? No. Do they drive more jobs than vacant space? Absolutely,” she said. Proponents also argue new centers are required to support cloud storage and the computing needs of artificial intelligence. Data centers emerged as a key issue nationally ahead of the 2026 midterm election as communities protested the massive utility usage, noise pollution and secretive deals that can come with their development. The most controversial centers are supersized facilities located in rural communities and suburbs, but even small projects have prompted public outcry. The Minneapolis regulations on the table Minneapolis leaders are trying to put regulations in place before a six-month moratorium on most new data centers expires Nov. 21. The moratorium exempted downtown projects under 350,000 square feet and went into effect without Mayor Jacob Frey’s signature. The city of Minneapolis received about 1,600 written public comments about potential regulations of data centers. The vast majority opposed data centers and almost half called for an outright ban, according to an MPR News analysis. However, labor organizations including the Minnesota AFL-CIO and the Minneapolis Building and Construction Trades Council wrote in favor of looser rules, including allowing data centers outside of downtown and dropping or raising the size cap. The mayor supports specific regulations for data centers and told WCCO in August he believes data centers should not be the sole use of a building. "It generates tax revenue that helps drive down taxes for everybody else. But, too, it enables the owner to do something awesome that helps the community," Frey said. City staff proposed allowing new data centers only in downtown, with server space capped at 175,000 square feet. The city’s planning commission recommended stricter rules: a rigid 50,000-square-foot cap and a council vote on each new data center. A compromise measure was unanimously passed at a council committee meeting Monday — with council member Jamison Whiting absent — to be taken up for a final council vote Thursday. The ordinance would limit the server space of new centers to 150,000 square feet, which is in between the 175,000 square feet suggested by city staff and the 50,000 square feet recommended by the planning commission. It would also restrict new centers to existing buildings downtown, require mixed-use of buildings with data centers and require any center with server space over 50,000 square feet to buy into a renewable energy program. Regulate or ban? Attempts by progressive members to pass a full ban or require council approval for each new center failed on a 6-6 vote Monday. “We don’t need more computers in our downtown,” said council member Soren Stevenson. “We need people down here, and so I want to fight for a vision where people are thriving in our city, not for a vision where stockholders are thriving in our city.” A potential mayoral veto hung over the committee meeting, which included the full council. Several council members called for Frey to publicly state what proposals he would veto. “If you’re gonna veto, email us. Let us know. Let the public know your stance,” said council member Jason Chavez. Instead, the mayor indicated his position through statements from his office to the press and conversations with city staff and council members. Council member Linnea Palmisano said the mayor authorized her to share his position. “Mayor Frey does not support the planning commission’s amendments. If those are included in the final package, he will veto it,” she said. “The reality we live in is that any action we take today that's not supported by the mayor will get vetoed,” council member Jamal Osman said Monday. Osman said he’d heard from city staff and other council members that Frey would veto both a full ban and creating an overlay district, which would have required any new center to earn council approval. If no new rules pass before the moratorium expires, data centers would fall back under the city’s existing zoning code, which allows them with a permit in 10 of the city’s 15 zoning districts. Frey’s office confirmed to MPR News that he “supports the regulatory framework” of the compromise ordinance approved Monday. Some council members said they’d propose additional amendments at Thursday’s meeting, which starts at 9:30 a.m. The council needs a minimum of seven votes to pass legislation and a minimum of nine votes to override a mayoral veto. MRP News correspondent Matt Sepic contributed to this reporting.
