artigo.texto: Opposition to AI data center helped to fuel the nationwide "blue wave" on Election Night for Democrats at the ballot box. This summer, New York became the first in the nation to pass a one-year statewide moratorium on new data center construction. The push continues for Gov. Kathy Hochul to sign more restrictive legislation that passed the state legislature back in June. “Seeing the wins across New York state and the country is a signal that many of the things we’ve been talking about are incredibly popular,” said Democratic state Sen. Kristen Gonzalez. Gonzalez’s Responsible Data Center Development Act passed the state legislature in June. The following month, Hochul signed the nation’s first one-year moratorium on new data centers in New York state. Advocates maintain Gonzalez’s measure covers a broader range of large facilities starting at 20 megawatts or more. The governor’s moratorium has a threshold of 50 megawatts or more. Gonzalez believes data centers helping to fuel turnout nationwide makes her case stronger in having Hochul sign her legislation. “I absolutely think that’s the case,” she said. “We always knew that data centers was a bipartisan issue across the country, but even in New York state. A recent poll said that 63% of New Yorkers would support our moratorium being extended at the end of the one year.” In a statement to Spectrum News 1, a spokesperson for Hochul’s office said in part: "New Yorkers across the state have made abundantly clear that the rapid growth of AI and data centers cannot come at their expense. Governor Hochul listened, acted and is proud to have delivered the first data center moratorium in the nation. The Governor will continue to strengthen protections around artificial intelligence that will put New Yorker's and their future first." Critics argue stricter guidelines on data centers will come at an economic expense, with some states missing out on investments. Political expert Grant Reeher says it will depend on if this issue gets worked out on the national level. “If it remains something states are taking different positions, I think the states that aren’t doing it will pay some sort of economic price,” he said. Reeher says he believes what we’ve witnessed at the ballot box in reference to data centers is a “physical proxy” about voters’ much more “general anxiety about the future when it comes to AI.” In a CBS 60 Minutes interview on Sunday, President Donald Trump explained why he’s an advocate for AI data centers. “The level of power of winning that race is very important,” said Trump. “China has no problem with data centers. China has no problem with electricity. By the way, neither do we because I’m demanding that they build their own electric plant.” Despite the arguments, Gonzalez is continuing to advocate. In August, she embarked on a statewide data center tour. On Tuesday, her tour will stop at the First Unitarian Church of Rochester. The event is in partnership with Democratic state Sen. Samara Brouk.

artigo.texto: O Programa Paraná Energia Rural Renovável (RenovaPR) passará a apoiar a instalação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em propriedades rurais do estado. A medida vale também para quem já gera energia própria por meio de solar ou biogás e quer reforçar a segurança do abastecimento elétrico. O incentivo consiste em uma subvenção de três pontos percentuais na taxa de juros, operacionalizada pelo Banco do Agricultor Paranaense. O produtor pode contratar o financiamento com o agente financeiro de sua preferência, e o Governo do Estado equaliza parte dos juros. A política conta com R$ 320 milhões em recursos do Fundo de Desenvolvimento Econômico e da Fomento Paraná e está presente em 398 municípios. Os sistemas de baterias para atividades rurais custam entre R$ 35 mil e R$ 800 mil, conforme o porte da propriedade e a quantidade de equipamentos que precisam funcionar durante interrupções no fornecimento. O investimento médio é estimado em R$ 78 mil, com prazo de retorno entre quatro anos e meio e sete anos. Segundo Herlon Almeida, coordenador da Área de Energias Renováveis e Conectividade Rural do IDR-Paraná, a adoção de baterias precisa avançar junto com a melhoria da infraestrutura elétrica no campo. Entre as prioridades estão a ampliação das redes trifásicas e o uso de sistemas com inversores híbridos, que armazenam o excedente produzido durante o dia. A tecnologia mantém equipamentos essenciais em operação em falhas da concessionária, o que é importante para avicultura, suinocultura, produção de leite e piscicultura. Desde agosto de 2021, o Paraná soma 45.274 unidades rurais de geração distribuída, com potência instalada de 1,11 GW e investimentos estimados em R$ 6,4 bilhões. A potência média é de 24,58 kW por unidade, a maior do país. Levantamento do IDR-Paraná aponta média de 4,3 interrupções no fornecimento e 7,17 horas sem energia por consumidor, com prejuízos que já alcançaram milhões de reais em ocorrências graves.

artigo.texto: Jefferson County leaders hold workshop to discuss potential data center impacts Commissioners have seven more months before the county’s data center moratorium, which was put in place this summer, is up MONTICELLO, Fla. (WCTV) - Jefferson County residents and leaders are discussing the potential impacts of data centers as the county’s 12-month moratorium remains in place. County Manager Doug Baber said the workshop on Monday was an opportunity for commissioners to hear from experts about the potential impacts of data centers. “Data centers have been known as the boogeyman for quite a while, and I don’t disagree with a lot of that stuff because it’s unknown,” Baber said. “We want to make sure we bring in the experts on both sides of the field to talk about how much water it would use, how much electricity it would demand, how many acres they would have to have, how many jobs they create per acre.” Attorneys and professors from Florida State University and the University of Florida were among several experts sharing their knowledge, including the potential costs of studying the impacts. Andrew Fay, an attorney with the Digital Infrastructure Industry Group at Greenberg Traurig, discussed the cost of engineering studies needed to help commissioners make informed decisions. “The cost for the engineering studies for the expertise to make a decision on the impacts for water, the impacts that maybe the noise will have on the area, the light, the impact to the natural environment that it could be built in, all are extremely expensive and can be extremely time-consuming,” Fay said. Experts discussed both the potential jobs data centers could bring and concerns about light, noise and water. More news out of the Big Bend: Those concerns resonated with District Four Commissioner Austin Hosford, who pointed to issues residents have already raised about the Trulieve cannabis facility in the county. “Just right off the top, hearing the issues in these other places Texas, Virginia, light, noise, and water. I know how aware y’all are of what we’ve been dealing with in Jefferson County; we’ve got a major operation that has caused light, noise, and water problems for quite a lot of people, so that jumps off to me big time,” Hosford said. Residents also had a chance to ask questions and share their concerns, with many worried a data center could change the county’s rural character. Jefferson County is known for its natural resources, including the Wacissa River and springs. Some residents questioned whether the community has the resources to support a data center. “We don’t have the baseline to support it. Tallahassee could. We just don’t have it. I don’t see how it benefits us long term. I’m not opposed to data centers; I just don’t see how our county could support the construction of it or even the employment that we really want from it,” Jefferson County resident Tracy Place Allison II said. Baber also said there have been no applications for data centers in Jefferson County. No action was taken Monday night. Commissioners have seven more months before the county’s data center moratorium, which was put in place this summer, is up. artigo.texto: Oklahoma City extends moratorium on data center projects OKLAHOMA CITY, Okla. (KOKH) — Oklahoma City is keeping its pause on data centers development requests in place. The city council voted on Tuesday to extend a moratorium on new rezoning requests for data center projects through the end of next year or when the zoning code is updated, whichever comes first. A moratorium was already place through the end of this year, with the exception of one project. "We originally approved this in April and then in May. We hired a consultant to help us looking at our code to see what kind of updates or changes we might make. We have since approved one item...a hyperscale data center that was already in process, approved the zoning, and have a CBA that we're still going to negotiate with them. We feel like there's just a lot more information that we can collect working with our consultant and what we'll learn in this process," said City Manager Craig Freeman. On October 27, the city council approved a rezoning request for the hyperscale data center Freeman was referring to. Many OKC residents were not happy with that decision, including Le'Shauhndin Kirkendoll. On Tuesday she demonstrated to the city council what she says living next to a data center would sound like by playing the noise on her phone during her allotted public comment time. "This really is a time for comments. I think you've made your point. Are you going to speak anymore? If not, we'll move on," Mayor David Holt said. "Within, 90 seconds, 30, 60 seconds Holt was already irritated and annoyed with the noise quality. But that's what our elected officials are wanting to force the constituents to live with for whatever reason," Kirkendoll told FOX 25. Kirkendoll said she has been showing up to city council meetings to advocate for those who can't, since they are held every other Tuesday morning. "I've heard a lot of people in opposition for the data centers. I haven't heard one person that wants the data center in their neighborhood," she said. Kirkendoll said she was glad to see the moratorium extended. "I also hope that they implement some type of construction hold, because Oklahoma just needs to pump the brakes a little bit until we can get a bigger picture of what's going on," she said. As for the data center campus the city council already approved a rezoning request for, the next step will be to finish negotiating the community benefits agreement.

artigo.texto: The nearly $100 million facility received special exemptions that skirted the traditional oversight provided by the county. The U.S. Air Force and U.S. Space Force have maintained that the 56,000-square-foot laboratory and data center under construction in Kīhei is not expected to be a significant added strain on the region’s infrastructure. But federal officials still won’t say how much water the project is expected to use. The nearly $100 million facility at Līpoa, the mixed-used development formerly known as the Maui Research and Technology Park, is intended to consolidate some of the military’s operations on the island into one location. It is being engineered to meet high federal energy and water-efficiency benchmarks, according to a 2022 environmental assessment. However, no specific details about the facility’s projected water usage have been made public, nor has that information been shared with county officials who make decisions about whether to approve applications for new construction projects in the area. Those decisions are based, in part, on where and to what extent the island’s water infrastructure can handle new development. Typically, plans for new development would prompt the Maui Department of Water Supply to reevaluate the subdivision’s water meter reservation and adjust it as necessary, according to a department statement provided Monday by county spokesperson Lila Lawrence. The military’s data center project was granted a federal exemption, so the department has not reviewed the subdivision since December 2022 — when there were no proposed buildings or other permit plans — and the water meter reservation was determined based on the lot’s square footage, according to the department. Water is already limited in South Maui, which receives almost all of its water from the ʻĪao and Waiheʻe aquifers in Central Maui. The Central-South Maui water system has for years been operating dangerously close to capacity, and Kīhei residents are often subjected to water conservation advisories due to dry conditions and issues related to the region’s aging infrastructure. Projects like the nearly 1,000-unit Ledcor South Maui Properties, the 652-unit Mākena Mauka project and the 1,150-unit Honua‘ula project — also known as Wailea 670 — have come under fire in part because of concerns about the availability of potable water. Given those challenges, no building project’s anticipated water consumption should be hidden from the public, said Hina Kneubuhl, an organizer with Protect Haleakalā, a collective of Hawaiian cultural practitioners, environmentalists, community leaders and others working to protect culturally significant landscapes. “I’m tired of these kinds of things being opaque. It’s not fair,” she said. “We’re living on an island with limited water and power resources. How is it just or fair to keep those kinds of figures from the public, and how can County Council members or the Planning Commission or anybody involved in making decisions make an informed decision without that kind of information?” Kelly King, who was recently elected to represent South Maui on the Maui County Council, said her decision-making related to future development projects would absolutely be affected by whether she has access to information about the military facility’s water consumption. “But I think that we shouldn’t just sit back and wait for information that may not be forthcoming. I think we need to actually call them into the chambers,” she said. “They need to come clean and tell us what they are doing.” She added, “The scrutiny for all the development is going to get much, much more detailed, I think, and the community is going to want more answers before the council makes any more moves.” When asked directly about the Kīhei project’s anticipated water usage, a spokesperson for the U.S. Space Force provided an emailed response from department representatives that did not include specific figures. Instead, representatives shared information about some of the water efficiency measures planned for the new facility. In its environmental assessment, Air Force officials did not consider the project’s impact on future development that had not already been approved, and it only considered developments in the neighboring community. artigo.texto: O mercado regulado de carbono do Brasil pode acrescentar 5,8% ao Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) até 2040 e 8,5% até 2050, segundo estimativas do Banco Mundial divulgadas pelo Ministério da Fazenda. A projeção também aponta uma redução de 27% nas emissões dos setores submetidos ao sistema até meados do século. Os números foram apresentados pela Secretaria Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono (SEMC), vinculada ao Ministério da Fazenda, durante a 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (COP31), em Antália, na Turquia. O encontro ocorre até 20 de novembro e marca a apresentação dos resultados da primeira etapa de implementação do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE). Criado pela Lei nº 15.042/2024, o SBCE estabelece um limite para as emissões de gases de efeito estufa de empresas de setores regulados. As companhias recebem cotas de emissão, que diminuem gradualmente ao longo dos anos e podem ser negociadas entre os participantes do mercado. O objetivo é criar um incentivo econômico para que as empresas reduzam a poluição. Quem emitir menos do que o limite poderá negociar cotas excedentes com outras companhias que precisem delas. Mercado regulado de carbono terá adesão gradual Em outubro, o Ministério da Fazenda divulgou o cronograma para que os setores industriais iniciem o monitoramento das emissões e cumpram as exigências de Mensuração, Relato e Verificação (MRV). O conjunto de procedimentos determina como as empresas devem medir, registrar e comprovar a quantidade de gases de efeito estufa que lançam na atmosfera. As regras alcançam operadores com emissões a partir de 10 mil toneladas de CO₂ equivalente por ano. Segundo o governo, esse grupo representa menos de 1% das empresas brasileiras. A secretária extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono, Cristina Reis, afirmou que o sistema oferece previsibilidade regulatória para atrair investimentos sustentáveis. A expectativa do governo é que a implementação do mercado contribua para a modernização industrial e para a transição a uma economia de baixo carbono. Coalizão liderada pelo Brasil reúne 42,2% das emissões globais A participação brasileira na COP31 também marca o primeiro ano da Coalizão Aberta para Mercados Regulados de Carbono (OCCCM), iniciativa apresentada pelo país durante a COP30, em Belém (PA). Presidido pelo Brasil e copresidido pela China e pela União Europeia, o grupo reúne jurisdições responsáveis por 42,2% das emissões globais de gases de efeito estufa e por US$ 49 trilhões do Produto Interno Bruto mundial. O Plano de Trabalho 2026-2027 da coalizão foi aprovado em setembro, em Wuhan, na China. Durante a COP31, a delegação brasileira conduz uma reunião de alto nível e prevê a entrada de novos participantes. Também está prevista a assinatura de um Memorando de Entendimento para a adesão do Banco Asiático de Investimento em Infraestrutura (AIIB). Segundo o Ministério da Fazenda, a instituição será o primeiro banco multilateral de desenvolvimento sediado na Ásia a integrar formalmente a governança da coalizão. Desmatamento na Amazônia e no Cerrado recua O Brasil também apresenta na conferência dados recentes sobre a redução do desmatamento. Segundo o Programa de Monitoramento dos Biomas Brasileiros (BiomasBR), do Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (Inpe), a taxa de desmatamento na Amazônia caiu 41,8% no período 2025/2026, para 3.335 quilômetros quadrados. O resultado é o menor da série histórica, iniciada em 1988. No Cerrado, a redução foi de 23,8%, com área desmatada de 5.516,69 quilômetros quadrados. De acordo com os dados apresentados pelo governo, esse é o menor índice desde 2001. O Sistema de Estimativas de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SEEG), iniciativa do Observatório do Clima, atribui à contenção da perda de vegetação uma contribuição para a queda de 6% nas emissões brutas do Brasil em 2025.

artigo.texto: I'm a firm believer in investing in what you know—and what you use. During a recent visit to my parents' New Hampshire property, my brother and I tackled overdue maintenance, and having the right equipment on hand was critical to finish the work in the limited time we had. He and I rented both a compact track loader (CTL, not pictured) and a bulldozer (pictured above) from United Rentals (NYSE: URI) to push through some of the heavier work. For those who may not be familiar with the company, United Rentals can quickly deploy heavy equipment to a remote site. Here's why I believe it sets up well for a defined-risk, moderately bullish options trade. The good news is that United Rentals is currently trading at a below-market forward multiple — both on a Price-to-Earnings (P/E) basis, currently ~17.3x forward estimates of ~$61.10/share, and on an Enterprise Value-to-EBITDA (EV/EBITDA) basis at ~8.8x $9.25 billion in FYE2027 EBITDA. This despite the fact that the company is compounding revenues, earnings, and EBITDA at a noticeably faster clip than the cap-weighted S&P 500. Effectively, one can buy superior, market-beating growth at a discounted market multiple. The recent third-quarter earnings confirmed this trajectory. URI delivered a beat and raise, pointing to robust underlying demand across its end markets, and the sell-side is scrambling to catch up, revising its forward estimates upward. Improving earnings estimates is one of the most reliable, time-tested short-term investment factors. Stocks with positive estimate revisions tend to meaningfully outperform those burdened with declining estimates in the short term. The macro backdrop provides a sturdy foundation for this growth. We are in the midst of a broader nonresidential construction recovery, which has driven an environment of improving and resilient rental rates. Although admittedly a potential slowdown in data center construction could become a future headwind, broader infrastructure demand remains robust. A balanced view requires acknowledging the risks. While URI looks cheap relative to the broader market, it is not exactly cheap relative to its own history. The stock is currently trading roughly 20% to 25% above its five-year average multiple. One could easily argue that the historical multiple was simply too cheap for a business of this quality, scale, and capital efficiency. Still, mean reversion back to historical levels of "cheapness" remains a downside risk. This brings us to the options market. When you have a stock with solid momentum, fundamentals, and positive estimate revisions, but you're hesitant to pay a premium to its historical valuation, outright unhedged equity accumulation isn't always the optimal route. Instead, selling cash-covered puts offers a highly strategic entry mechanism. The trade With URI's implied volatility currently hovering in the 42% to 45% range, the options market is pricing in enough movement to offer a decent premium. By selling a cash-covered put, we acknowledge both the good and the bad. It respects the aggressive growth, market share capture, and the recent beat-and-raise quarter, while appropriately hedging against the risk of that elevated historical multiple. If the stock continues its upward march, the puts expire worthless, and we pocket a high-probability yield that easily beats fixed income. If the stock pulls back—perhaps toward that 5-year average multiple—we are assigned the shares at a lower effective cost basis, which, if it happens, we could lower even further by writing upside covered calls against it. (This approach to entering a stock, then writing covered calls if assigned, is sometimes referred to as "the wheel strategy"). So either we acquire an attractive stock at a price we dictate (the short strike, less the premium collected for selling it) or we simply collect premium for assuming that risk if the stock does not decline. For a company that provides the literal heavy lifting for infrastructure growth, that's a structural advantage worth trading. artigo.texto: UK singer-songwriter Bess Atwell is back with a bold new chapter. Her fourth studio album, 'Cut a Figure', is officially set to land on 5th February 2027 via Nettwerk. Alongside the announcement, Atwell has treated fans to the striking lead single 'Glass', complete with a brand-new music video and news of a sprawling 2027 world tour. Following her acclaimed 2024 record 'Light Sleeper', which was produced by Aaron Dessner, Atwell sought a drastic change of scenery. A spontaneous nine-month relocation to Quebec, Canada, provided the distance she needed to craft her most fiercely honest work yet. Ditching some of her usual creative habits, she eventually teamed up with renowned producer Chris Coady—known for his work with Beach House, DIIV, and Foals—in Los Angeles to bring the project to life. The shift in her approach was highly intentional. “The songs I really enjoyed performing from my last record were the rare moments where I put down any instruments, and it was just me singing to my audience, which can be a bit scary,” she says. “But those were the songs that seemed to connect the most, and where I felt most free to actually live with the song and what it was about.” The album’s emotional anchor is undoubtedly the new single, 'Glass'. Powered by a cathartic indie-pop arrangement and crystalline vocals, it tackles the paradox of vulnerability. Bess explains, "I knew I wanted to name the album after a line in this song as it feels like the heart of the record. Sometimes, an eagerness to be seen and understood can have the opposite effect - you can be so transparent that you end up invisible. When I was a teenager, I was really into doing 'personality tests'. One test had you imagine a cube and then describe it (the cube supposedly representing how you express yourself). All my friends and family pictured various different sizes and colours, while I saw a transparent glass box floating in space." 'Cut a Figure' sees Atwell turning the lens inward, processing long-held anger, untangling toxic dynamics, and exploring her own health struggles. From the Eighties-tinged bite of 'The Act' to the shimmering analogue synths of 'Tonight I Am Allowed', the record is a defiant, self-accepting shedding of people-pleasing tendencies. Be sure to stream 'Glass' on your favourite digital platforms today and check out the brilliant new video. To stay updated on the upcoming album and secure tickets for her upcoming 2027 world tour, follow Bess Atwell on Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, and X.

https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBM.resumo: A Eletronet anuncia o ELET1, seu novo Data Center em São Paulo, que ampliará a oferta de serviços de colocation, conectividade e interconexão da companhia e fornecerá mais escala ao atendimento de provedores de nuvem, operadoras de telecomunicações e provedores de Internet (ISPs), e hyperscalers. Com investimento de R$ 25 milhões, o centro terá aproximadamente 350 m², capacidade para cerca de 90 racks e potência inicial de 0,5 MW, podendo chegar a 1 MW na segunda fase de expansão. Com as obras já iniciadas, a previsão de lançamento é para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. O projeto acompanha o aumento da procura de empresas dos segmentos de cloud, streaming e telecomunicações por infraestrutura de Data Center em regiões estratégicas de São Paulo, com alta disponibilidade e acesso a um amplo ecossistema de conteúdo. O ELET1 estará em uma localização com elevada concentração de redes de telecomunicações e provedores de conteúdo.  O Data Center também abrigará o PIX (Ponto de Interconexão) da Eletronet no IX.br São Paulo, o maior ponto de troca de tráfego de Internet do mundo, tanto em volume quanto em número de participantes. O PIX da companhia se destaca por liderar o volume de tráfego de download entre as operadoras participantes do IX.br São Paulo. Para os clientes, estar nesse ambiente aumenta as possibilidades de conexão com diferentes redes e provedores de serviços digitais. “O ELET1 representa um passo estratégico para fortalecer nossa atuação no segmento de Data Centers. Estamos ampliando nossa estrutura para atender às necessidades dos clientes que já utilizam nossos serviços e abrir novas oportunidades de negócios, em um contexto no qual a hiperconectividade e a disponibilidade se tornam cada vez mais essenciais”, afirma Rogerio Garchet, CEO da Eletronet. Segundo ele, o projeto acompanha o avanço de aplicações em nuvem, inteligência artificial, streaming e serviços digitais, que exigem suporte para volumes cada vez maiores de dados. “Queremos ir além das necessidades atuais e antecipar os próximos ciclos do mercado, fortalecendo nossa capacidade de conectar clientes, redes e ecossistemas digitais”, diz. Com segurança, tecnologia de última geração e resiliência operacional entre os pilares da iniciativa, o ELET1 seguirá as melhores práticas globais de infraestrutura, com soluções voltadas à proteção física e lógica, alinhadas às diretrizes da norma ISO 27001. O Data Center também contará com aplicações modernas e práticas de gestão ambiental e energética, tendo como referência os padrões ISO 14001, ISO 50001 e LEED, apoiando no melhor desempenho energético e na redução do PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness). Entre os recursos previstos estão dois geradores redundantes de 500 kVA, dupla entrada de rede, backbone DWDM protegido, sistema de gerenciamento predial (BMS) atualizado, monitoramento contínuo e um Centro de Operações de Rede (NOC) de contingência. “Mais capacidade precisa vir acompanhada de eficiência, resiliência e previsibilidade operacional. Por isso, o ELET1 foi concebido com uma arquitetura que otimiza o uso dos recursos e oferece mais flexibilidade à operação. A modernização dos sistemas críticos também nos permitirá atender a diferentes perfis de uso e níveis de demanda, mantendo o ambiente preparado para operações críticas”, afirma Emerson Hioki, Chief Technology Officer (CTO) da Eletronet. O ELET1 integra a estratégia da Eletronet de fortalecer sua atuação em Data Centers e complementa a expansão de sua rede nacional de fibra óptica. A nova unidade também contempla a migração da infraestrutura atualmente instalada no Data Center da companhia em São Paulo para o novo ambiente, em um processo planejado para preservar a continuidade dos serviços.

artigo.texto: Genoa residents seek to restrict data centers as push to limit them grows across Ohio Residents say a potential project could affect quality of life, but getting the issue on the ballot could be difficult GENOA, Ohio (WTVG) - Some residents in the village of Genoa are joining a growing push across Ohio to restrict large-scale data centers. They face obstacles in their effort to stop a potential project. According to Ohio State University, 18 Ohio communities have had ballot issues related to data center development. Voters sided against data centers in each case, often by a wide margin. Genoa residents who want similar restrictions could have difficulty getting the issue on the ballot. Marc Hanneman of Residents Against Genoa Environmental Destruction said residents want to take action. “If we sit back and let it roll over us, we’ll get it,” Hanneman said. Residents are concerned about a potential data center on 430 acres south of State Route 163 along Reiman Road. Hanneman said residents worry about the effect on water resources and wildlife. They also worry about noise and light pollution a project near residential neighborhoods could bring. “If we stand up and exercise our rights as citizens and residents of this community — that is [a] peaceful, loving community — we might just turn them away,” Hanneman said. The village annexed the property three years ago, which led to studies of what could be built on the empty fields. “I wish they’d slow down, moratorium, re-zone it. We could put it into apartments, we could put it into residential, we could do a lot of things… greenhouse, warehouse,” Hanneman said. Residents looking to stop a possible data center face a key challenge. Some Ohio communities have added bans or restrictions to their charters. Genoa does not have a charter, so residents are looking into creating one. “We’re looking into a charter, turning our village into a charter,” Hanneman said. Hanneman said a charter could give the community a way to put guardrails in place. Residents are also joining a statewide effort with Conserve Ohio to petition for a ban on large-scale data centers. Hanneman’s group plans to collect signatures Friday at the Genoa Retirement Center from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. near the potential project site. Hanneman said the group also conducted exit polling after the recent election. “92% is against a data center coming into Genoa,” Hanneman said. “This is registered voters coming from the polls saying that they don’t want it.” Latest Local News | First Alert Weather | Crime | National | 13abc Originals Copyright 2026 WTVG. artigo.texto: Desenvolve SP e Möbius lançam fundo de R$ 70 milhões para provedores e data centers FIDC terá R$ 50 milhões da agência paulista e R$ 20 milhões da gestora para recebíveis, equipamentos e operações de consolidação. A Desenvolve SP e a Möbius Capital lançaram um Fundo de Investimento em Direitos Creditórios (FIDC) de R$ 70 milhões destinado ao financiamento de infraestrutura digital no Estado de São Paulo. O fundo tem como público provedores regionais de internet e data centers de pequeno porte e poderá financiar a compra de equipamentos, antecipar recebíveis e apoiar operações de fusão e aquisição. A estrutura conta com R$ 50 milhões subscritos pela Desenvolve SP em cotas seniores e R$ 20 milhões pela Möbius Capital em cotas subordinadas. O comunicado não informa quando os recursos estarão disponíveis para contratação nem detalha taxas, prazos ou limites de crédito por empresa. Uma das modalidades previstas é a antecipação de recebíveis dos provedores, originados em contratos com clientes pessoas físicas e jurídicas. O fundo também poderá investir em operações de crédito para a aquisição de equipamentos de infraestrutura tecnológica e para a expansão das empresas, incluindo compras e fusões de negócios do setor. “Temos um histórico de realizar financiamento para aquisições de provedores de internet, operações via mercado de capitais para fomentar o crescimento de empresas do setor, além de dar apoio no avanço da profissionalização e governança dessas companhias”, afirma Roberto Savaris, sócio e fundador da Möbius Capital. Segundo o anúncio, o fundo pretende ampliar o acesso ao crédito em regiões subatendidas, especialmente nas cidades do interior paulista. Entre os objetivos estão a expansão da conectividade em localidades com baixa penetração e a ampliação do acesso à infraestrutura de data centers. Composição de recursos públicos e privados A Desenvolve SP é a agência de fomento do Estado de São Paulo, vinculada à Secretaria de Desenvolvimento Econômico. Seu diretor-presidente, Ricardo Brito, relacionou a participação no fundo à estratégia de combinar recursos públicos e privados. “Nossa meta é ampliar o acesso ao crédito e facilitar recursos para negócios inovadores. Por meio do blended finance, conseguimos atrair investimento privado, potencializar o impacto do recurso público e alcançar mais empreendedores”, afirmou Brito. Os valores anunciados correspondem a recursos subscritos. O material divulgado não esclarece se os R$ 70 milhões já foram integralizados. A Möbius Capital foi uma das gestoras selecionadas na chamada pública da Desenvolve SP para FIDCs e Fundos de Investimento em Participações (FIPs). O processo incluiu a apresentação de uma Carta-Consulta com informações sobre a tese de investimento, estrutura, estratégia, governança, equipe, histórico e valor solicitado. Após a análise de elegibilidade e uma apresentação presencial, a proposta passou pela diligência da gestora e do fundo. Concluída essa etapa, o Comitê de Investimentos da Desenvolve SP aprovou o compromisso de investimento. Na sequência, foram implementados os termos e condições do compromisso, conforme os processos internos da agência. O comunicado não detalha os critérios de acesso ao financiamento pelas empresas interessadas. (Com assessoria de imprensa)

artigo.texto: Expansão de data centers – A Noruega decidiu interromper temporariamente a concessão de novas conexões elétricas para data centers. A medida, anunciada pela operadora estatal Statnett, busca evitar uma sobrecarga na rede diante do crescimento acelerado dos projetos no país. A previsão é que a restrição permaneça em vigor até, no máximo, 1º de agosto de 2027. A expansão dessas estruturas ocorre em escala global, impulsionada pelos investimentos de empresas de tecnologia em infraestrutura para desenvolver e operar sistemas de inteligência artificial. O avanço, porém, também provoca resistência de comunidades na Europa e nos Estados Unidos, principalmente pela demanda por terrenos e eletricidade e pelos possíveis impactos nas tarifas de energia. LEIA: IA permite que hackers ataquem empresas em diferentes países “Queremos data centers na Noruega, mas não podemos aceitar todos os tipos de data centers” afirmou o ministro da Digitalização, Torgeir Micaelsen. “Portanto, precisamos controlar o crescimento e garantir que a Noruega receba os data centers de que realmente necessita, aqueles que proporcionam os maiores benefícios para a sociedade.” De acordo com a Statnett, 800 megawatts (MW) de capacidade de data centers já estão conectados à rede. Outros 4.200 MW têm reservas aprovadas, enquanto 9.100 MW aguardam disponibilidade. Há ainda pedidos adicionais para conectar 18 mil MW. Somados, os projetos pendentes representam 27.100 MW, volume superior ao pico de consumo de eletricidade da Noruega, que ultrapassa pouco os 25 mil MW. Um relatório recente do Conselho Norueguês de Tecnologia também apontou limitações econômicas do setor. Segundo o documento, os data centers geram poucos empregos permanentes após a conclusão das obras e cerca de 90% das instalações pertencem a empresas estrangeiras. artigo.texto: A data center owner specifies 400 pieces of owner-furnished, contractor-installed equipment. The purchase orders go out. The manufacturers confirm ship dates. The construction schedule is built around those dates. Six months later, a generator arrives at the jobsite with undocumented damage. Nobody knows when it happened. Nobody knows who touched it last. The vendor says it left the factory clean. The carrier has no record of an incident. The site crew is pointing fingers. This is the accountability gap. And it costs the industry more than most owners realize before they've lived through it. The OFCI model creates accountability risk by design Owner-furnished, contractor-installed programs make financial sense. Owners can leverage their purchasing power, standardize equipment across a portfolio, maintain direct relationships with manufacturers, and build a data record that — if captured correctly — can improve how future programs are planned and executed. On paper, it looks like control. In practice, most OFCI programs distribute that equipment across a chain of custody that nobody fully owns. A manufacturer ships to a freight forwarder. The freight forwarder hands off to a carrier. The carrier delivers to a warehouse. The warehouse holds it until the GC is ready. The GC coordinates final delivery. The installation crew takes it from there. At each handoff, responsibility technically transfers. But accountability rarely does. Each party documents what they received, in whatever format their own system requires, and hands the equipment forward. If something is missing, damaged, or mislabeled, the discovery almost always comes late, usually at the point in the project when it causes the most disruption. The data problem underneath the accountability problem Most owners believe their OFCI equipment is being tracked. In many cases, it is; loosely, across multiple systems, with inconsistent standards and no shared source of truth. A manufacturer has a ship date in their ERP. A carrier has a delivery confirmation in their TMS. A warehouse has a receiving record in their WMS. The owner's project team has a schedule in their construction management platform. None of these systems talk to each other. The data lives in silos, and nobody is reconciling it in real time. When the project team needs to know where a piece of critical equipment is, they start making phone calls. When they need to know its condition, they hope someone took photos. When a discrepancy surfaces, they spend days reconstructing a chain of events from fragmented records. That is not visibility. It is archaeology. Research has found that US construction professionals spend an average of 14 hours per week on non-optimal activities such as searching for project data, correcting mistakes, and managing rework. That is 35% of their working hours. For the US construction sector at large, this accounted for over $177 billion in excess costs in 2018. What the gap actually costs The damage is rarely dramatic. It accumulates in the places that are hardest to measure. A generator arrives at the jobsite before the pad is ready. The site team has nowhere to put it, so it sits on the trailer longer than planned. That costs money. When the pad is finally ready, the equipment needs to be repositioned. That costs more money. If it was sitting in an uncontrolled environment, there may be questions about condition. That costs time. A switchgear unit ships with components missing — a configuration issue at the manufacturer that nobody caught on the way out. The project team discovers it during installation. Replacement parts have a 14-week lead time. The schedule absorbs the hit. None of these costs appear on a single line item. But they accumulate, and they all count toward the total cost of ownership for a program that looked predictable on paper. A pallet of equipment arrives at a warehouse and is logged as received. When it is released to the jobsite three months later, three pieces are missing. Nobody knows if they were missing at receipt or left during storage. The warehouse record is a single line item. The investigation goes nowhere. Each of these incidents has a specific cause. But the underlying condition is always the same: nobody owned that equipment at the moment the problem was created. A joint study by PlanGrid and FMI found that roughly 48% of US construction rework is directly attributable to inaccurate, inaccessible, and incompatible project data, costing the industry more than $31.3 billion annually. Chain of custody is a process, not a document The common solution to accountability gaps is paperwork. Bills of lading. Receiving records. Inspection checklists. These create documentation, but documentation is not the same as accountability. A receiving record captures what the warehouse accepted. It does not necessarily capture condition. A bill of lading records that a delivery was made. It does not capture what the driver saw when they opened the trailer. A checklist completed quickly and filed away creates a paper trail that is almost impossible to use as evidence when something goes wrong months later. Research bears this out. Project teams with centralized, easy-to-locate documentation are twice as likely to feel confident proving which party was responsible when a dispute arises. Teams whose documentation lives in email threads, text messages, and phone calls report the lowest confidence. Documentation structure determines whether it can actually be used. Real chain of custody means every touchpoint captures the same data — condition, serial numbers, quantities, photographs — in a format that feeds a single record the owner can actually use. Exceptions get flagged in real time, not discovered months later. And one party owns the continuity of that record across the entire chain, not just their piece of it. artigo.texto: Envision and ju:niz Energy Extend Partnership With 442 MWh Battery Storage in Bavaria The Smareg 13 project in VÃ¶hringen becomes the third joint project for the two groups. According to them, it relies on the Gen 8 platform, four-hour storage and a low-noise design. Envision Energy and ju:niz Energy are expanding their partnership with Smareg 13 (VÃ¶hringen II), a 442 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Bavaria. According to the two groups' press release, it is their third joint project, bringing the total volume of their collaboration to nearly 600 MWh. Elsewhere in Europe, other players are developing smaller capacities, such as PGE Dystrybucja, which secured a grant for a 4 MW energy storage system in Lutomiersk. Storage also remains in focus across the Rhine on the gas side, where German gas storage is at a record low and the INES organisation is calling for reform. A developer and operator role for ju:niz Energy ju:niz Energy is responsible for the development, financing and realization of Smareg 13. The company will operate the system over the long term. The project forms part of its German BESS portfolio, which the company says is growing. The site is located adjacent to the operational Smareg 12 facility. According to the press release, the project would strengthen storage capacity in Bavaria and provide greater flexibility and balancing capability as Germany integrates a growing share of renewable energy. Envision's Gen 8 platform at the core of the project Smareg 13 will deploy Envision's Gen 8 BESS platform, which combines four-hour energy storage, advanced battery technology and grid-forming capabilities. The two companies say its low-noise design allows deployment in acoustically sensitive environments. According to the press release, this feature addresses one of the key site challenges. artigo.texto: Fort Worth considers 90-day pause on data center development as residents raise concerns Fort Worth is considering new restrictions on where and how data centers can be built, including a potential 90-day pause on new development, as residents raise concerns about the impact on their neighborhoods. Tuesday marked the first of two public hearings required before the city can move forward with the proposed moratorium. The next hearing is tentatively scheduled for Jan. 12, with a possible vote in February. Dozens of residents brought their concerns directly to city leaders Tuesday, citing potential effects on the environment, quality of life, and the pace of development. "There's environmental concerns ... where I live, just about a mile away there's a data center in the works so I am concerned for my own quality of life but even more so for others," resident Ellis Maxwell said. "Data center developments are being very much rushed, rushed through the process," Brian Patman said. "So they are very much being pushed through before there is any regulation available to sort of rein them in." A city commission led by TCU Director of the Institute for Environmental Studies Michael Slattery presented its findings Tuesday after months of studying the potential impact of data centers on power, water and nearby communities. "The questions we looked at came out from a number of sources, one of which was the surveys that we got to look at … about 1,500 surveys that came back to the city from residences … and just lots and lots of conversations," Slattery said. The commission presented 19 recommendations, including requiring non-evaporative, closed-loop cooling systems to conserve water, zoning standards to protect residential neighborhoods, noise limits that account for surrounding areas and a pilot study of low-frequency noise. "I think it would give the city a roadmap on how to move forward," Slattery said. "Our city has an opportunity to be the city that did not just react to this technology, but has helped to understand it. That starts with doing what you asked us to do, get the facts, say them plainly, and say when you don't know." Maxwell said he hopes the proposed moratorium leads to lasting changes. "I want to make clear with the moratorium that it's not just a moment to sort of give us this concession and then wait for public pressure to die down, but that it's actually something that we're going to continue speaking out," Maxwell said.

artigo.texto: - Utah House Speaker Mike Schultz criticizes MIDA's role in data center decisions. - Schultz cites public concerns and process flaws in the Stratos Project's approval. - Reforms may include giving local governments more authority over data center approvals. SALT LAKE CITY — Utah House Speaker Mike Schultz agrees that the general public had "fair concerns" regarding the Stratos Project as the massive data center project, led by celebrity businessman Kevin O'Leary, was going through the state approval process. That's why he bemoans how those concerns and the whole process were handled. "You have Kevin O'Leary saying, China this and China that and whatever else, and I wanted to bang my head against the wall as that was happening. ... I've never been more frustrated than that," said Schultz, R-Hooper, recalling the drama during a joint Deseret News/KSL editorial board meeting on Monday. O'Leary worked out a framework for the data center proposal in a remote area of Box Elder County with the Military Installation Development Authority, a board made up of government appointees. It seeks to bolster the U.S. military's access to artificial intelligence and cloud-computing capabilities. Box Elder County leaders carried out additional votes to move it forward. One of the leaders who voted in favor said they felt pressured to accept it to avoid costly lawsuits. They could have rejected it and "the project area would not exist," MIDA executive director Dan Hemmert said last month. Project officials recently filed a new water application, which states the facility would include 11 data center building clusters along with a 7.5-gigawatt generation facility comprised of 15 500-megawatt combined-cycle natural gas power plants. It plans to use a little more than 1,700 acre-feet annually from Salt Wells Spring Stream. Meanwhile, multiple Utah residents who opposed the project have sued O'Leary and Fox News in recent months, claiming that the billionaire defamed them by falsely claiming they were agents of the Chinese government during interviews with the network for objecting to the plan. While O'Leary has sought a dismissal in at least one of the suits, the whole series of events was difficult to watch and proved that process adjustments are needed for data centers, Schultz said. "The thing that broke down on that was the process. That's where it went awry," he said. "Really getting back to fundamentally following the process on these controversial issues will help alleviate those concerns." A 'huge mistake' Data center reform may be one of the priorities during the 2027 legislative session, which is expected to be different following a drastic change in the Utah Legislature, said Schultz and Senate President-elect Evan Vickers, R-Cedar City. Senate President Stuart Adams, who serves as the MIDA board chair, was ousted in the Republican primary. Republicans also lost a supermajority in the House of Representatives for the first time in decades, the Associated Press projected on Monday. It's unclear how much of that was tied to data centers, but top state leaders acknowledged that it may have factored in lost public trust. Reforms to data center policy may start with giving local governments a greater say when it comes to approving data centers. Utah stepped up to oversee data centers when it became clear that they could overwhelm the state's energy grid without coordination between local governments, Schultz explained. However, he believes the recent backlash shows that the current process is broken. "MIDA should never be doing data centers," he said. "That was a huge mistake. ... I think it's important to know that and recognize that and make sure that doesn't happen again." Data centers can bring short-term property tax relief for Utahns and drastically improve local property tax bases in rural counties, the University of Utah Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute noted in August, which could help affordability challenges — likely another key subject next year. If you can go through this process and check those boxes, it really comes down to a local decision. Do you want it or don't you? –Utah Senate President-elect Evan Vickers But the institute warns that they can create future tax increases and "greater volatility" in some areas. That's on top of environmental concerns, which typically include urban heat, water consumption, and strains on electricity grids, the Yale School of Environment points out. The state, Vickers said, has already passed requirements tied to utility rates and water consumption. Modern facilities might be able to offset additional concerns, but the debate over pros and cons should be taken up on a local level. It's something that might require local entities to break down each request to see if it's the right fit. "If you can go through this process and check those boxes, it really comes down to a local decision," he said. "Do you want it or don't you?" Other adjustments? Utah may also examine other concerns, such as the rate of tax increments handed out for projects, Schultz noted. He and Vickers spoke on the issue weeks after fellow state lawmakers grilled Hemmert on the Stratos Project during interim meetings at the Utah Capitol. Some wondered if MIDA provided adequate notice about the project to the public or questioned whether local officials are facing pressure when considering MIDA partnerships. Others worried that public trust in MIDA was waning. Gov. Spencer Cox also called for major reforms to MIDA in August, largely over concerns tied to the Stratos Project. It's unclear how that will factor into future legislation, but Schultz said he prefers a future system where the state sets coordination guidelines and local governments decide on future projects. "The state shouldn't be making decisions," he said. artigo.texto: Publicidade O desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial e de data centers no mundo tem colocado um grande desafio para os países, incluindo o Brasil, em termos de estrutura. De acordo com o Itaú BBA, a necessidade de grandes fontes de energia e de sistemas robustos de distribuição que a estrutura demanda pode ser especialmente favorável para a WEG (WEGE3) aqui no país. A avaliação veio depois de uma reunião entre o banco e a Scala, uma das maiores desenvolvedoras de data centers de grande escala da América Latina. Segundo a empresa, o Brasil possui uma vantagem importante em se tratando da disponibilidade de energia elétrica, especialmente, quando comparado a mercados norte-americanos, com maiores restrições de oferta de energia. Para a WEG, a demanda elevada de equipamentos e a oferta de fornecedores locais ainda limitada e com prazos de entrega longos, coloca a companhia em uma posição favorável para capturar os benefícios desse ciclo de investimentos. Após “sell-off” com midterms em meio a temores de IA, bancões recomendam compra A forte correção das ações ligadas à inteligência artificial após as eleições legislativas nos Estados Unidos abriu oportunidades de compra em diversos segmentos do setor JBS, Minerva e MBRF: como será o 3º trimestre dos frigoríficos? Melhora no cenário internacional e pressão no Brasil podem gerar efeitos diversos Atualmente, a companhia já fornece boa parte dos equipamentos que compõem a cadeia elétrica de um data center, enquanto a oferta de fornecedores locais ainda é bastante limitada. Por esse motivo, também, o BBA reforçou a WEG como sua principal escolha no segmento de transportes e bens de capital. Além disso, reforçou a recomendação outperform (desempenho acima da média do mercado), com preço-alvo de R$ 56. Continua depois da publicidade Cenário favorável De acordo com a administração da Scala, o projeto planejado próximo a Porto Alegre, o Scala AI City, já obteve autorização da ANEEL para dispor de 5 GW de energia elétrica, o que dá suporte ao potencial desenvolvimento do projeto ao longo do tempo. Segundo a empresa, um projeto de 1 GW pode exigir a disponibilidade de transformadores em aproximadamente oito meses. Ao mesmo tempo, os prazos de entrega de alguns equipamentos elétricos podem chegar a até três anos. Para a administração da Scala, uma empresa que já possua capacidade produtiva instalada no país, como a WEG, teria vantagem competitiva em relação aos concorrentes que ainda precisem estruturar suas operações locais. Continua depois da publicidade Fabricantes de equipamentos, como a Vertiv, também têm sido negociados no mercado a múltiplos de avaliação superiores aos das empresas operadoras de data centers. Isso sugere, segundo os analistas do BBA, que o mercado pode atribuir um valor relativamente maior às empresas que fornecem os equipamentos necessários para a expansão dessa infraestrutura do que às próprias empresas responsáveis por operar os data centers. Amparo fiscal Atualmente, os servidores dos data centers, estão sujeitos a uma carga tributária efetiva de aproximadamente 70% no Brasil. Esses equipamentos representam cerca de 80% do investimento total em bens de capital de um data center. Continua depois da publicidade De acordo com a administração da Scala, essa mesma carga tributária tem sido a justificativa para que cerca de 40% das cargas de trabalho brasileiras ainda sejam executadas no exterior. Estimativas do BBA apontam que o Redata, o programa que estimula investimentos em centros de dados no Brasil, poderia reduzir essa carga tributária para aproximadamente 20%, tornando mais atrativa a realização desses investimentos diretamente no Brasil. Os analistas explicam que, na prática, uma redução da tributação sobre servidores diminuiria o custo de implantação dos data centers no país. Com isso, empresas que hoje preferem instalar sua infraestrutura no exterior poderiam passar a considerar o Brasil uma alternativa economicamente mais interessante. Continua depois da publicidade

artigo.texto: Romulus City Council voted to temporarily ban data centers, discuss Flock cameras ROMULUS, Mich. (FOX 2) - The City of Romulus is getting ahead of the data center debate before it even begins, as they are temporarily banned before they even open. Data Centers and Flock, oh my! Big picture view: Data Centers and Flock cameras were the hot topic of discussion at Romulus City Hall on Monday. Residents joined the meeting expressing a number of environmental concerns and that they do not need one in their neighborhood. Meanwhile, the city council stressed that nothing has been proposed. A six-month moratorium would prevent them from even looking at proposals or applications, so the city council voted unanimously for the moratorium. Besides Data Centers, Flock cameras became another topic of discussion. The city has twenty up and running with thirty more scheduled to go up. Residents at the meeting questioned how they are being funded. Residents asked: Is it paid for by the city's Tax Increment Finance Authority, also known as ‘TIFA Board?’ Or was it the police department? Some say the original contract with Flock was for $47,500 but allege a short time later it was $90,000. What they're saying: When FOX 2 asked Mayor Robert McCraight about this discrepancy in October, he said it was a "typo by a clerical person." "It’s just a way to clean it up. We want to make sure everybody’s on board and on the same page," he said. "The TIFA Board knew what they were voting on to support and help alleviate some of that drain or general fun which is public safety dollars. But Romulus is a different community. We housed DTW. We talked about it before with 30-million travelers. That’s more than Disneyland and the Magic Kingdom. "So when you talk about 60–70 percent of the violent crime in Romulus is committed by people who don’t live here, we need to use tools to push that number down and our accredited police department is doing such. But we’re always going to look at one's venues. Is that the best technology that we have right now? It seems like. Can we get better? Absolutely." Última atualização em 11 de novembro de 2026 às 14h03. O Redata é um regime tributário que pode atrair até R$ 2 trilhões em investimentos privados em data centers ao longo de dez anos. O decreto que detalhará as regras para empresas se habilitarem ao regime deve ser assinado por Lula em até duas semanas após seu retorno da COP31. A regulamentação definirá como as empresas comprovam contrapartidas em pesquisa e desenvolvimento, e exigirá que atendam a critérios de sustentabilidade energética e uso de água. O decreto que vai definir como os data centers poderão acessar os incentivos do Redata deve ser assinado pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva depois de sua volta da COP31, na Turquia, nas próximas duas semanas a partir da terça-feira, 17. A previsão foi dada pelo presidente da República em exercício, Geraldo Alckmin, em reunião nesta quarta-feira, 11, com a Associação Brasileira das Empresas de Software (ABES), segundo informações enviadas com exclusividade à EXAME. Alckmin indicou um prazo de até duas semanas, sem fixar uma data para a assinatura. A entidade pediu apoio para concluir a regulamentação e entregou a Alckmin um estudo sobre experiências internacionais de governança digital. A proposta é que o próximo governo reúna, em uma estrutura vinculada à Presidência, a coordenação de políticas hoje distribuídas entre ministérios. Segundo a ABES, Alckmin se comprometeu a considerar as recomendações na preparação do próximo mandato. Para Marcelo Almeida, diretor de Relações Institucionais e Governamentais da ABES, um dos pontos em aberto para o setor de software é saber quais produtos importados poderão receber o incentivo. “Tem uma minuta de decreto pronta, não sabemos o teor do decreto, mas sabemos que vão ter anexos”, diz Almeida à EXAME. A expectativa da entidade é que o texto venha acompanhado de dois anexos. A lei que criou o Redata prevê uma lista geral de produtos elegíveis e outra, específica para a suspensão do Imposto de Importação, limitada a bens sem produção nacional equivalente. Depois de publicadas, essas listas só poderão ser alteradas para acrescentar itens. A ABES aguarda o texto final para saber se o incentivo alcançará softwares importados para uso nos data centers. A lei também permite que empresas cumpram a contrapartida de investimento em pesquisa e desenvolvimento em parceria com instituições de ensino. Os procedimentos para comprovar esses investimentos dependem da regulamentação. O Redata pode atrair até R$ 2 trilhões em investimentos privados em data centers ao longo de dez anos, segundo estimativa do Ministério da Fazenda. A projeção foi divulgada em 17 de setembro de 2025, quando Lula assinou a medida provisória que lançou o regime. A medida provisória perdeu a vigência em fevereiro de 2026. O Congresso aprovou depois um projeto de lei próprio, sancionado por Lula em setembro, que prevê a suspensão de tributos federais sobre a compra de equipamentos e componentes por empresas habilitadas. O decreto vai detalhar como as empresas poderão solicitar a habilitação à Receita Federal e comprovar as contrapartidas. Em 6 de novembro, a ministra da Casa Civil, Miriam Belchior, já havia indicado que o governo esperava anunciar as regras na semana de 16 de novembro. Na avaliação de Almeida, a discussão sobre o abastecimento elétrico dos data centers atrasou o decreto. Ele afirma que Lula pediu que a regulamentação priorize investimentos sustentáveis. A lei exige que as empresas habilitadas atendam toda a demanda de eletricidade com fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, por meio de contratos de fornecimento ou geração própria. O texto também fixa um limite de uso de água de 0,05 litro por quilowatt-hora, com aferição anual. Caberá à regulamentação estabelecer os procedimentos e prazos para demonstrar o cumprimento dessas exigências. O ICMS é um imposto estadual. Uma eventual desoneração para equipamentos de data centers depende de negociação no Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz), que reúne os estados e o Distrito Federal. Para Almeida, a publicação do decreto federal é o momento em que as entidades do setor pretendem levar a discussão ao conselho. “Estamos fazendo com outras entidades reuniões periódicas para manter acesa essa luz de que, tão logo tenhamos a publicação do decreto, possamos ter a pauta do Confaz”, diz. Na agenda regulatória que publicou em março, a ABES defendeu uma estrutura ligada à Presidência para definir prioridades nacionais em inteligência artificial, infraestrutura digital e semicondutores. Hoje, áreas como pesquisa, política industrial e tributação passam por pastas diferentes. A entidade quer que uma instância com autoridade política coordene essas decisões e acompanhe sua execução. O Redata dá uma dimensão do problema que a associação levou a Alckmin. Para o mesmo investimento, as empresas acompanham regras federais de habilitação, critérios de fornecimento de energia e uma negociação tributária com os estados. A proposta entregue pela ABES procura dar à Presidência um papel mais direto na coordenação da política digital no próximo mandato. Segundo o relato da reunião obtido pela EXAME, Alckmin indicou que Lula deve assinar o decreto após voltar da Turquia, em até duas semanas. A assinatura ainda não tem uma data anunciada. O Ministério da Fazenda divulgou a projeção em setembro de 2025, quando o governo lançou a medida provisória do Redata. artigo.texto: Harrisburg data center offers insight into technology and community concerns A Harrisburg data center operated by Alerify provides a closer look at the technology behind the cloud, as concerns grow over the development of larger hyperscale data centers in Pennsylvania. Video above: Top news stories from News 8 at 5 p.m. Inside a smaller data center "This data center here isn’t one of those large AI hyperscale data centers. It's actually only 2,500 square feet. And it fits in this commercial building right behind me," said Andy Kochanowski, CEO of Alerify, during a tour of the facility. Kochanowski explained that customers trust the center with their data and equipment, emphasizing the importance of security. "Customers trust us with their data and their equipment, and they don’t want anybody, you know, getting into it," Kochanowski said. Inside the facility, the hum of machines and air conditioning systems is constant. "That noise, is that all of the machines and everything?" asked News 8's Maegan Summers during the tour. "That noise is at some of the machines, but mainly it's the air conditioning systems to keep the equipment cool," Kochanowski said. The center houses computer servers and data storage rented by various customers, essentially serving as the physical form of the cloud. "It's almost like your personal belongings when you put them in storage. But we're doing it for computer equipment. So that's called co-location," Kochanowski said. "Virtual server hosting is basically, instead of owning equipment, you want to create a private server up in the cloud. This is the cloud," he added. Cooling and power demands The facility operates at about 50% capacity, with aisles of equipment rotated between hot and cold zones to regulate temperatures. "It's comfortable in here. It’s probably like 71 or 69. Yeah. So it's reasonable. But if you come in here, it’s probably going to feel like a temperature difference," Kochanowski said. Between cooling the building and powering the machines, the data center uses 40,000 to 80,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity per month. Despite its relatively small size — about 2,500 square feet, comparable to a tennis court — larger hyperscale data centers can span hundreds of thousands of square feet. One such center being built in Lancaster is 850 times larger than the Harrisburg facility. "We've seen more of these hyperscale data centers start to come up. Do you think that they're necessary?" Summers asked. "They need to go somewhere. You know, obviously I'm a consumer. I have a home. I don't want to see my electric rates go up either. And I don't want to deal with the noise. But they do need to go somewhere," Kochanowski said. Community concerns about hyperscale centers The rapid development of hyperscale data centers has sparked concerns among community groups like Lancaster Stands Up. Taylor Enterline, a member of the group, outlined their worries about the environmental and community impact. "The electric grid. What happens when there's a blackout? If there's a blackout, the data center is going to keep running. They have all these backup generators. But where does the help come from? For our neighbors, our biggest one is water. Our beautiful Susquehanna, down the road, is sacred. It's beautiful. How are we protecting our water?" Enterline said. Enterline suggested state-level regulations on hyperscale data centers and artificial intelligence, as well as community benefit agreements to hold developers accountable. "Testing and control. Right. We're not just like testing beforehand. We're testing during and we're testing afterwards. And if they are not following through on that, who is holding them accountable? Who knows if these large, you know, monstrosities of AI hyperscale data centers are going to be needed in five to 10 years? Who's responsible for shutting those down, cleaning them up? It should not be on the community who didn’t want them in the first place," Enterline said. Exploring more efficient practices As a smaller data center owner, Kochanowski shared his perspective on environmentally friendly practices, including partnering with Penn State students to develop more efficient air conditioning systems. "There are a lot of dilapidated, old foundries and steel mills that already have the power into those places but are just barren. We have to redo something like that versus starting brand new. We also need to be very conscientious of the noise, especially in communities. And the power draw, you know, to the extent they can produce their own power, that's great," Kochanowski said. He also highlighted the benefits of closed-loop cooling systems for water conservation. "I think that’s the best way to go, honestly. I mean, to the extent you can recirculate that water through that computer equipment and not have to continue to tap the challenges making that water cool itself down before it cycles back through," Kochanowski said. The future of data centers Looking ahead, Kochanowski predicted continued growth in the data center industry but noted that advancements in equipment could reduce the need for large facilities. "I think it's going to continue to grow. The question becomes whether or not the equipment needed shrinks. Then it may not be as big an issue in the future as what it is today," Kochanowski said.

artigo.texto: As AI data centers drive up demand for electricity, a growing question is who should foot the bill to expand the Texas electric grid to support them. Georgia said it has taken steps to protect families from those costs, freezing electric rates and requiring data centers to cover the costs of grid expansion. NBC 5 Investigates traveled to Georgia to see whether those protections are working and if Texas could do the same. Watch NBC 5 free wherever you are "Unprecedented" demand for power In Georgia, the electric grid already sizzled during hot Atlanta summers before the arrival of AI data centers that can contribute to soaring power use. "It's truly unprecedented, off the charts," said Bob Sherrier, an attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center, a legal advocacy group working to protect electric customers from higher bills. Sherrier said Georgia could need twice as much power in just five years. "So if you think about it, it took us a hundred-some-odd years to build up to where we're at -- now we're gonna double that in five," Sherrier said. His group wants to shield average consumers from higher bills as Georgia adds new electric lines and power plants to support data centers. Sherrier fears utilities will spend a fortune expanding the grid, only to see the data center market suddenly change. If data center companies then left the state, he worries families could be left facing higher electric rates for years, paying off the costs of that construction. "It's a big bet that the power companies and the data centers are making and we don't want to backstop it," Sherrier said. But Georgia regulators said they have already put protections in place to prevent that from happening. "I honestly think that what we've done to date has got all the protections in place and more," said Jason Shaw, chairman of the Georgia Public Service Commission, the state's electric regulator. Last year, the commission announced a deal with the state's major electric provider, Georgia Power, to freeze electric rates for three years. The PSC said it's also required the power company to sign long-term guarantees with new data centers, committing them to pay for grid expansion for years, even if they leave. Shaw believes electric bills will eventually go down, not up, because data centers will cover a bigger share of the costs. "We're going to do everything we can here at the commission to continue to take advantage of these benefits using the leverage that we have in negotiating these large load rules and contracts," Shaw said. Critics question protections But not everyone in Georgia believes the state is setting an example Texas should follow. Patty Durand, a former candidate for the Georgia PSC, leads Georgians for Affordable Energy, an advocacy group. Durand argues the state's rate freeze is deceptive. First, she says the freeze came after years of rate increases, effectively locking in higher prices. She also said it delayed state hearings on new electric rates for three years, making it harder for the public to see how much grid expansion is costing right now. "The rate freeze means there's no scrutiny on the spending and no ability to stop it or change direction until it is too late," Durand said. Durand also complains the contracts requiring data centers to backstop costs are not open to the public. She and other watchdog groups fear those contracts could contain exit clauses, potentially letting data centers off the hook before the advertised long-term guarantees expire. "It's really the secrecy that is concerning people," Durand said. Sherrier shares concerns about the lack of public access to those agreements. "We have to take a lot of this at how they've described it publicly without being able to actually evaluate language and what's in there itself," Sherrier said. The PSC said its own staff scrutinizes those contracts, but Georgia has laws, like other states, that prohibit the release of information companies deem to be trade secrets. The commission said the contracts include guarantees lasting 15 to 25 years, and if a data center exits early, the commission points to a letter agreement the power company signed with regulators, promising it will "not seek to recover" those costs from residential customers. Shaw said he's confident even if the AI bubble bursts, Georgia families won't end up stuck with the bill. "No, in this case it would be the data centers and the shareholders of the for-profit regulated utility," Shaw said. Shaw said he has also been in contact with other states adopting similar rules. "If you don't have these rules and these protections that we've developed here in Georgia, somebody's assuming the risk, and I'm afraid if it's not done right then it's the rate payers that will be taking those risks," Shaw said. Could Texas adopt similar protections? What Georgia has done may be harder to accomplish in Texas because the two states have very different electricity markets. In the ERCOT power market, most Texans choose from multiple electric companies, unlike Georgia, where regulators set the rates charged by one utility serving most customers. That means Texas cannot simply freeze electric rates the way Georgia regulators did. But the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUC) is working on other rules aimed at financially protecting consumers. Beth Garza served for five years as ERCOT's Independent Market Monitor, a watchdog tracking the Texas grid. "Well, the concept of the financial security is written down. It's in a proposed rule right now. All of this evolves on the speed of regulation," Garza said. She explained that Texas lawmakers passed SB 6 in 2025, creating rules requiring large electric customers, including data centers, to pay grid connection costs upfront and post financial security. artigo.texto: Brasil apresenta avanços do mercado de carbono durante a COP31 na Turquia Governo federal detalha implementação de sistema que limita emissões de grandes empresas e projeta crescimento econômico com a transição para uma economia de baixo carbono 🎧 Ouça esta matéria — narrado por IA O governo federal apresenta, durante a 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (COP31), realizada em Antália, na Turquia, os resultados da primeira fase de implementação do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE). A iniciativa busca reduzir a emissão de gases de efeito estufa e incentivar investimentos em tecnologias sustentáveis. A apresentação é conduzida pela Secretaria Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono, vinculada ao Ministério da Fazenda. A primeira etapa de implantação do sistema deve ser concluída nos próximos meses. A conferência climática segue até 20 de novembro. Como funciona o mercado de carbono Instituído pela Lei nº 15.042/2024, o SBCE estabelece um modelo de limite e comércio de emissões, conhecido como cap-and-trade. Nesse sistema, grandes empresas recebem limites para a emissão de gases de efeito estufa, que poderão ser reduzidos gradualmente ao longo dos anos. As empresas que conseguirem emitir menos do que o permitido poderão comercializar suas cotas excedentes, enquanto aquelas que ultrapassarem os limites precisarão adquirir permissões adicionais para cumprir suas obrigações. As exigências de monitoramento e declaração de emissões abrangem operadores que liberam a partir de 10 mil toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente por ano. Segundo o Ministério da Fazenda, a medida alcançará menos de 1% das empresas brasileiras. Estimativas do Banco Mundial divulgadas pelo governo indicam que o mercado regulado de carbono poderá proporcionar expansão acumulada de 5,8% no Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) brasileiro até 2040 e de 8,5% até 2050. As projeções também apontam potencial de redução de 27% nas emissões dos setores regulados até meados do século. Redução do desmatamento A participação brasileira na COP31 ocorre após a divulgação de novos dados sobre o desmatamento no país. Segundo o Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (Inpe), a taxa de desmatamento na Amazônia caiu 41,8% no período 2025/2026, atingindo 3.335 quilômetros quadrados, o menor resultado da série histórica iniciada em 1988. No Cerrado, a redução foi de 23,8%, com 5.516,69 quilômetros quadrados desmatados, a menor taxa desde 2001. Dados do Sistema de Estimativas de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SEEG), do Observatório do Clima, também apontam queda de 6% nas emissões brutas brasileiras em 2025, associada à redução da perda de vegetação. Cooperação internacional Durante a conferência, o Brasil também apresenta os avanços da Coalizão Aberta para Mercados Regulados de Carbono, criada na COP30, em Belém, e presidida pelo país, com copresidência da China e da União Europeia. A coalizão reúne países e jurisdições responsáveis por 42,2% das emissões mundiais de gases de efeito estufa e busca aproximar os sistemas nacionais de comércio de carbono. A agenda brasileira na COP31 inclui reuniões com representantes internacionais e iniciativas de cooperação para fortalecer a regulamentação e a integração desses mercados. Segundo a secretária extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono, Cristina Reis, o sistema brasileiro pretende oferecer segurança regulatória para atrair investimentos sustentáveis e estimular a modernização industrial.
