artigo.texto: A new battery energy storage system (BESS) being built on the former coal power station at Fiddler’s Ferry has passed a major milestone, with the installation of key electrical equipment. The site is owned by SSE Renewables, with infrastructure specialists OCU Energy and Fluence building the 150 MW BESS. When complete, it will be capable of providing power for approximately 250 000 homes for a two-hour period at a time. An SSE Renewables spokesperson previously said: “Similar to our Ferrybridge project, our grid scale battery at Fiddler’s Ferry will be built on what was a former SSE-owned coal-fired power station and highlights the transition away from fossil fuels towards a net-zero future.” Kiosk buildings, which will house electrical relays, switchgear, control panels, and communication systems, are now in place, fabricated by RSK Group companies AJ Engineering & Construction Services and Northern Engineering & Welding Co. (NEWCo). AJ Engineering & Construction Services Pre-Construction Manager, Lee Binks, said: “When fully operational, the BESS site will store power for release back to the UK national grid when it is needed the most – helping to manage peaks of energy demand and supporting a transition away from fossil fuels. “We have designed, fabricated and cladded two auxiliary transformer buildings and one portable relay room for the site in a modular format, reducing the time spent on site. These buildings provide compact, weatherproof enclosures that house the equipment that ultimately connects the battery system to the national grid. In addition to this, we have fabricated and erected the switch room, which is a structural steel portal frame building with insulated cladding. “Usually, for the aux buildings and portable relay rooms, these types of small buildings are manufactured using glass reinforced plastic or brick and built on site. To speed up delivery and reduce complexity, we built them off-site using fabricated steel modules. They were then transported to the site and lifted into place, already cladded and ready for fit-out.” Binks explained that because they are widely used in both the water and the en-ergy sectors, they are in high demand, and lead times for their procurement can be significant. He concluded: “Having been built with steel and cladding, the kiosks were ready to be installed on site within six weeks. Normally this team of structural designers, detailers, fabricators, steel erectors and site management would have to do this on-site. By building the kiosks off-site, we have avoided adding further complexity to an already busy construction site.” Fellow RSK company, Acies, carried out the connection design on the structural frame for the switch room, working in collaboration with AJ Engineering while it carried out the modelling of the building. With the kiosks in place, OCU Group will begin the fit-out process of the internal equipment that will connect the site to the national grid. It is expected to be operational in 2027. artigo.texto: The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission recently approved AES Indiana’s plan to serve a Google data center in a contested case that highlights the complex challenges regulators and utilities face in allocating system costs for large computational loads. According to the Oct. 7 order, AES will acquire or build new generation, storage and grid infrastructure for a 390-MW data center planned for Monrovia, a town Southwest of Indianapolis, at an estimated project cost of about $737 million. The new generation, storage and transmission assets included in the Monrovia Project will go into the utility’s rate base. AES says its electric service agreement with Google is designed to ensure the revenues will be sufficient to “reimburse at least 100%” of the project’s incremental direct costs. But the contract itself is heavily redacted, and an estimated $74 million in network upgrades has been explicitly allocated to all customers as a reliability need, prompting criticism from consumer advocates that the arrangement is shifting costs onto other ratepayers. What are ‘reasonably allocable’ costs? Indiana state law requires large load customers to reimburse at least 80% of project costs “reasonably allocable” to them. Claire Wayner, a senior associate at the clean energy nonprofit RMI, said in an interview that while local projects are fairly easy to trace back to a specific data center, broader regional system upgrades raise more complex questions about who benefits and how costs are allocated across jurisdictions. “Maybe they're upgrading a part of the grid that they were going to have to upgrade anyway because it's aging infrastructure,” Wayner said. “If that's the case, they should have to demonstrate that, and then maybe cross socialization makes sense.” But, she continued, “If that upgrade was not going to be built without the data center, without benefits modeling or just a demonstration of the benefits to the rest of the zone, it's difficult to make the claim that all ratepayers in that zone should pay for it.” AES Indiana will serve Google’s data center from its portfolio of shared generation and battery assets. The new generation and storage assets built to meet the additional demand will be owned through a subsidiary by the utility and go into its rate base. In testimony to the commission, a utility representative said the transmission infrastructure included in the Monrovia Project falls into three basic categories: interconnection infrastructure for the generation and storage; “direct connection” infrastructure for connecting the data center to the system; and network upgrades necessary “primarily” to serve Google “but also to meet other customer demand or energy needs.” Google will pay about $32 million upfront for the direct connection, but $73.8 million in network upgrades will be included in AES Indiana’s transmission rate base and recovered through future rates from all customers, including residential ones. Commissioners approved the proposal 5-0, saying in their order that “although the Customer may be the impetus for the network upgrades being made, this does not preclude the upgrades from providing system-wide benefits.” “Network upgrades, as the name implies, are upgrades or additions to the transmission network intended to provide reliability, resiliency, and stability to the system at large,” it said. “Just as the Customer will be allocated a portion of the existing network transmission infrastructure, it is reasonable for existing customers to also be allocated a portion of the network upgrades.” The Midcontinent Independent System Operator approved some of the network upgrades, which include a new substation, citing reliability and load growth. Although the order says the portfolio proposed in AES’ filing is for 390 MW of new load with 460 MW of new 4-hour storage and 130 MW of solar generation, the substation planned for the project is designed for 1,200 MW of load, creating opportunity for future expansion at the site. The generation and storage resources consist of one 200-MW and one 130-MW battery energy storage system, called Foundry Works and Hardy Hills, respectively, as well as a 130-MW solar facility paired with a 130-MW BESS called Crosstrack. Their cost is redacted in the case filings. ‘Cost allocation and cost recovery are two different concepts’ Ben Inskeep, program director at the Citizens Action Coalition, a consumer advocacy group that intervened in the case, sees the deal as running counter to President Donald Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge signed earlier this year by tech companies and utilities, including Google and AES Indiana. “These network upgrades are specifically driven by the Google data center,” Inskeep told Utility Dive in an interview. “Instead of making the cost causer pay, AES Indiana has decided to spread the costs out to other ratepayers, and our commission has unfortunately approved that.” Ben Gavelek, a spokesperson for the commission, declined to comment on the deal. Google did not respond to requests for comment. Claire Rice, a spokesperson for AES Indiana, said in an email that although the transmission assets are being allocated through the normal cost-of-service process, Google’s rate includes a “separate incremental-cost test designed to recover the incremental costs required to serve Google, including the network upgrades.” “Cost allocation and cost recovery are two different concepts,” she added. Many of the exact terms of the service agreement, including monthly energy and demand charges and riders, are redacted in the public record. Parts of other contracts underpinning the deal are also confidential. The assets will be included in future base rate case filings. Until those new rates are established, the utility plans to recover those costs through its Environmental Cost Recovery and netted with contract revenues. The commission’s order says AES Indiana’s accounting and ratemaking proposals enable it to “match” the project

artigo.texto: Lea County commissioners may vote next week to approve up to $134 billion in industrial revenue bonds for a 1,890-acre hyperscale Google data center on Hobbs’ outskirts. Google officials, in their first public appearance in Southern New Mexico, held town halls in Lovington, Tatum and Hobbs on Monday and Tuesday to discuss the project, which is similar in size to the 1,400-acre Project Jupiter in Santa Teresa. That development secured $165 billion in industrial revenue bonds from Doña Ana County. Google said ground work will begin in 2027, and construction will continue through 2030. While Google touted its potential to generate over 1,000 construction jobs and “substantial” tax revenue for the county, and proposed an $18 million housing fund, critics said the company had few answers to attendees’ questions, and the town halls didn’t feel like a meaningful attempt for the technology giant to engage with the community. “The meetings were hosted to ensure every member of Lea County had an opportunity to speak directly to members of the Google team and get their questions answered,” Google said in a statement provided by spokesperson Leslie Schuman. Clayburn Griffin, a business owner in Lovington, is pushing for a six-month data center moratorium in Lea County. Project opponents had called for independent experts to respond to their concerns about water and energy use, said Griffin, who attended all three events, but commissioners instead set up the Google town halls. “We knew it was going to be a Google PR event, which was not what we were asking for,” Griffin said in an interview Wednesday. “… The commission said that they would be transparent, but they obviously have not been fair in this process.” Lea County commissioners did not immediately respond to The New Mexican‘s requests for comment Wednesday. The Hobbs meeting at the Lea County Event Center — set up like a science fair, with multiple information booths for various topics — prevented any kind of public conversation, Griffin added. Notably, deputies from the Lea County Sheriff’s Office attended the town halls, including a sizable group at the Lovington event. Members of Protect Lea County, an organization that opposes the data center project, were told they could not bring clipboards, petitions or pamphlets inside the building, attendee Pam Keller said, adding people also were not permitted to film Google representatives’ responses to questions. A Google spokesperson denied attendees were prohibited from recording the events. In its flyer distributed at the meetings, Google said: “We will continue to listen, learn and support our local communities wherever we operate.” Google representatives at the town hall framed the newly dubbed “Project Rancho” as a “potential” data center, which would “power the essential technology that America relies on daily, from emergency 911 systems and electronic health records, to local small business operations and digital classrooms.” The project would be developed on county land under an option-to-purchase agreement with Excelsior Hobbs Power LLC, a company created for the project with ties to private equity firm Excelsior Energy Capital. Excelsior Energy would be responsible for constructing a 2-gigawatt solar field three miles away to help power the data center, a fueling decision few data center developers in New Mexico have turned to so far. For the 125 to 130 full-time positions that eventually would be offered at the site, one Google representative said the salaries would be between $85,000 and $100,000. And Google pledged to cover 100% of its energy costs, replenish more water to the community than the data center will consume, and “utilize high-tech, low-noise equipment and sound walls to meet or exceed all noise ordinances.” Like Project Jupiter, Google said it will use a closed-loop cooling system to recirculate its water, which requires a one-time initial fill of up to 9.7 million gallons. The site will then use roughly 40,000 gallons a day for activities like bathroom and kitchen use — or about 14.6 million gallons a year. However, asked for specific details on the expected energy consumption, the company’s promises when it comes to water use and timeline for the project, Google representatives were hesitant to provide official statements. Lorraine Villegas, a member of Protect Lea County, spoke about the county’s consideration of up to $134 billion in industrial revenue bonds for the project: “They want us to pay for it, but we don’t even know what they’re doing or how they’re going to do it,” she said in a statement. “… If they can’t find the decency to properly inform us, then I think the $3 trillion company is fully capable of funding itself.” “Just having Google sales pitches for the community is not a democratic way to go about this. And I think people deserve to have their voices heard,” Griffin said. “For that to happen, we need to have, first of all, a moratorium to give us more time on this … and then actual proper town halls set up so that the community can come out and discuss this issue.” Clayburn has collected almost 900 signatures in favor of a six-month data center moratorium, which he plans to bring to commissioners at a special meeting scheduled Thursday. The only items on the agenda were certification of the canvass for the Nov. 3 election and an executive session to discuss potential real estate transactions. The commission’s next regular meeting is scheduled Nov. 19. An agenda for the meeting is not yet available. Data center moratoriums have been proliferating nationwide as controversy grows over the facilities. artigo.texto: A Botetourt County resident’s lawsuit alleging that the county’s board of supervisors violated the state’s open meetings and open records law when it greenlit a Google data center campus is legally sufficient to move forward, a circuit judge ruled Tuesday. But after nearly three hours, which featured some testimony and a lot of arguments about the case’s merits, substitute Judge Michael Doucette said court schedule issues forced him to postpone a further hearing on the matter until next week. Robert Dallas, who lives near the Botetourt Center at Greenfield site, filed suit Nov. 2, seeking to invalidate the county’s economic development performance agreement with the limited liability company behind the project. His case alleges that the county violated the Virginia Freedom of Information Act when it approved documentation advancing the Google project. Dallas’s suit also asks the court to “rescind all actions” carried out in connection with the June 2025 document. Respondents in the case are the county, its board of supervisors, its economic development authority and Google-owned Helio Capital LLC. Julian Harf, representing the county, elicited testimony showing that Google has transferred $2.5 million of a promised $4 million to the county, helping pay for ambulances, fire trucks, heart monitors, body cameras and more. Further testimony showed ground clearing work has already started. Harf used the testimony to help support a plea filed in response to the suit. He asked the court to find that even if Dallas’ allegations are true, his case is legally insufficient. “Remedies” for a FOIA violation “do not include rescission” of the agreement and its effects, Hart said. An invalidated agreement would not be the court’s problem, said John Fishwick, who leads Dallas’ legal team. Google, the county and Helio could work out those ramifications among themselves, Fishwick said. FOIA law calls for a hearing within seven days of a suit’s filing, but it took eight before Doucette could be available. By the time the recently retired Nelson County judge decided in the plaintiff’s favor, the hearing time had bumped up against an already scheduled criminal court docket that included several cases in which jail sentences could be ended. “I won’t force an inmate to spend one more day in jail,” he said as he told those gathered in the courtroom that the trial would be set for 9 a.m. Monday. It was unclear why Botetourt County Circuit Judge Joel Branscom was unavailable to hear the case. According to the suit, the county’s board of supervisors did not disclose on its published agenda that it would be discussing the agreement or a resolution to enact it in a closed meeting on June 24, 2025. After the board returned to public session, it voted 5-0, with no discussion, to approve the resolution and the agreement, after they were added to the agenda during the meeting as so-called “walk-on” items, the case alleges. After a recess, the board returned to address another walk-on item — announcing the data center project. Yet another item that hadn’t appeared on the agenda was a board resolution approving Google’s agreement with the Western Virginia Water Authority, Dallas alleges. Harf and Helio’s lawyer, Graham Bryant, told the court that information on the agenda denoted an economic development project in the industrial park, which they argued was the most the board needed to disclose, to protect the negotiations. Harf said that county officials discussed the matter in detail after the vote, and any violation committed was “technical.” Fishwick said the board sneaked the matter into its meeting that day, part of an atmosphere of secrecy it had developed. “They treat FOIA like it’s a little technical thing, and they can run roughshod,” Fishwick said, adding that the supervisors’ later announcement of the project was more of a “cheerleading session” than an information share.

artigo.texto: Residents of Jacumba Hot Springs gathered Monday night at the community center for their monthly Jacumba Community Sponsor Group meeting. But one agenda item dominated the discussion – preliminary plans for a data center north of Interstate 8. For years, back country residents in communities like Jacumba have fought large energy projects. Most recently, the Jacumba and Boulevard communities battled two solar and battery energy storage projects that the County Board of Supervisors ultimately approved. “At the end of the day, we’re going to represent ourselves at that table,” said Jeff Osborne, the community group’s current chair. “We’re going to ask for things. We’re gonna ask for representation. We hope to get some response on this specific topic of data centers from the supervisors soon so we can have some indication. Because this is kind of a whole new thing.” There are few things these days that have inflamed communities more than data centers. The massive buildings powering the AI boom can have huge impacts on local land use, water and power. “I’m pro business. I was a contractor for 30 years. But something like that out here in the mountains,” said Ray Tiffany, a longtime Jacumba resident. “It’s just not right.” Osborne first heard about the data center plans after members of the Boulevard Community Planning Group were tipped off by a local landowner. The Jacumba group confirmed the proposal through County records obtained under the California Public Records Act. The tentative plans come from the Spain-based renewable energy company, IGNIS. Tahir Fazal, an IGNIS representative, said in an interview with KPBS that the company is in the early phases of deciding whether to do the project. “We have not done an application, so this project right now is nothing more than a consultation to the county to assess what the permitting path will be, to assess whether there are any limitations that are in place for this project,” Fazal said. Fazal said if the company does decide to pursue the project, it will do community outreach. “We're gonna be transparent on this, as we progress, with the community,” Fazal said. “Right now, I cannot give you an accurate answer on when we will take action on the application. As I mentioned, we are evaluating the guidelines that we received.” The project would ultimately need approval from the San Diego County Board of Supervisors, a county spokesperson confirmed Tuesday.

artigo.texto: Do ronco ao silêncio: qual a diferença entre dirigir um carro elétrico e um a combustão? César Urnhani, piloto e especialista automotivo, mostra quais são essas diferenças e dá dicas para quem está fazendo essa transição. Crédito: Estadão Gerando resumo A TIM fechou um contrato com a BYD para fornecer internet a toda a frota de veículos leves da montadora chinesa no Brasil, além do seu polo industrial. Com a parceria, os diferentes modelos da marca passarão a contar com chips virtuais (eSIM) da TIM, com conexão 4G em 100% das cidades brasileiras e 5G em 1,1 mil cidades onde a operadora oferece cobertura. A previsão é de que cerca de 200 mil veículos da montadora chinesa contem com essa conectividade embarcada nos próximos 24 meses. Assim, a BYD busca avançar no desenvolvimento de novas funcionalidades que envolvam serviços conectados. Com o crescimento de serviços como inteligência artificial e uso de funções como mapas e streaming a bordo, um carro já tem consumo de dados quase equiparável a de um plano básico pós-pago, tipo ‘controle’. Do lado da TIM, o negócio representa uma expansão no setor automotivo, onde já oferece conexão para cerca de 630 mil veículos. A tele italiana possui uma parceria com a antiga Fiat Chrysler Automóveis (FCA) – hoje parte do grupo Stellantis – para fornecer conectividade 4G e eSIM em veículos das marcas Fiat, Jeep e Ram no Brasil. Essa é a maior fábrica de veículos eletrificados da América Latina, com 4,6 milhões de m². O projeto prevê a instalação de sete pontos de cobertura externa e 63 equipamentos distribuídos entre os galpões e as áreas operacionais, garantindo uma rede preparada para acompanhar o crescimento da produção e as demandas tecnológicas do complexo.

artigo.texto: Stanton annexation request raises residents’ questions about possible data center STANTON, Tenn. (WBBJ) - Wednesday evening a Stanton municipal planning commission meeting took place at Stanton town hall. Members of the community filled town hall with the intention of getting a better understanding on the city’s plans and to express concerns about possible data centers moving into their region. Thomas Stringer, Stanton landowner said, “That’s really why we’re all here, you know, just so we can be in the know and nothing gets swept under the rug.” Stanton’s planning commission agenda listed a public hearing and consideration of an annexation request for land owned by the Juanita Buchanan and children’s trust. The agenda describes the request as approximately 164 acres. Residents say they want clear answers about what is being proposed such as the real reason the area needs to be re-zoned as industrial. They say they are worried about the developments the re-zoning would bring and how it would impact their town. “This is our home, this is where we live. The proposed land is right behind my property, you know, I could throw a rock and hit it. So, if it does come in it will disrupt everything that we have worked so hard for,” continued Stringer Town hall was so full of Haywood county residents that many were even standing outside to hear what leaders had to say in response to their concerns. A data center has not been confirmed as the proposed use for the land. There will be another meeting held next week for further discussion and a possible vote on whether or not to approve the proposed annexation of the land. Copyright 2026 WBBJ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Indonesia requires support from developed countries and private partnerships to ensure climate financing is accessible. Benefits for local communities are a key priority. 11 Nov 2026 10:47 WIB · Lingkungan AFP ANTALYA, KOMPAS – The Indonesian government has reaffirmed its readiness to actively develop the carbon market as a strategic instrument to accelerate climate action and mobilize sustainable financing. This initiative has moved beyond mere ambition and has entered a phase of tangible implementation, with the preparation of regulations for carbon economic value and the offering of high-integrity carbon projects to global investors. President's Special Envoy for Climate and Energy Hashim Djojohadikusumo emphasized that Indonesia's natural wealth, encompassing forests, peatlands, mangroves, and oceans, is not merely a collection of resources but a national heritage and a significant contribution to the health of the planet. To maximize this potential, the government is enhancing carbon market governance through Presidential Regulation No. 110 of 2025 and developing a national carbon unit registry system (SRUK) to ensure transparency and investment certainty. "Indonesia views the carbon market as a strategic instrument to accelerate climate action, achieve our NDC targets, and mobilize sustainable financing," Hashim emphasized in a keynote speech during the discussion session titled "Unlocking Indonesia's Carbon Market Potential for Climate Action and Sustainable Finance" on Tuesday (10/11/2026) at the Indonesian pavilion at the 31st Conference of the Parties to the Climate Change Convention (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey. Hashim added that the development of a credible carbon market must deliver tangible environmental benefits and attract long-term investments, with a key requirement being the availability of a robust monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) system. In the maritime sector, Deputy Minister of Marine Affairs and Fisheries Irwan Meilano emphasized the urgency of incorporating the ocean into climate solutions, given the long-standing impacts felt by fishing communities and coastal ecosystems. The Ministry of Marine Affairs and Fisheries is currently working on reforesting 600,000 hectares of mangroves and optimizing seagrass beds as part of its efforts to mitigate and adapt to climate change. "The challenge before us is no longer ambition; it's implementation," Irwan said at the same event. As a tactical step, Irwan stated that the Ministry of Marine Affairs and Fisheries will soon issue derivative regulations to implement the national carbon policy. The ministry is scheduled to launch a ministerial regulation on the economic value of carbon on November 18-19. Simultaneously, the government will also present three candidate blue carbon project sites to potential partners and investors. Furthermore, Hashim and Irwan agreed that the commercialization and preservation of carbon ecosystems must not overlook the welfare of surrounding communities. Hashim emphasized that conservation and natural restoration must create meaningful economic opportunities for local residents living alongside these ecosystems. In line with this, Irwan also emphasized the importance of support from developed countries and private partnerships to ensure climate funding is easily accessible. "We need straightforward access to funding, support for mobilizing private investment, and partnerships that transform good projects into viable investment models, while ensuring that the benefits reach local communities," he stated. During a press conference on Tuesday, COP31 Negotiation Presidency Chris Bowen set an ambitious target to increase global electrification levels to 35 percent by 2035. This initiative is seen as an essential requirement and the only way to prevent global temperatures from rising more than 1.5 degrees Celsius amid the threats of a global polycrisis. "We are meeting in a time of polycrisis, when the world is under immense pressure. Unlike previous COPs, we are now confronted with the rise of artificial intelligence and the pressures it places on energy networks. At the same time, the climate crisis has not disappeared; in fact, it is worsening," Bowen stated. Coinciding with Energy and Transport Day at COP31, Bowen emphasized the importance of accelerating electrification as a key solution to various crises. Currently, the global electrification rate stands at just 23 percent, a slow increase from 17 percent in 2005 and 19 percent in 2015. For years, the global electrification rate has increased by an average of only 0.3 percent per year. To achieve a leap target of 35 percent within less than a decade, the COP31 presidency is urging participating countries to sign an electrification pledge and engage in consultations to ensure this target is included in the conference's final decision. We want people to leave here saying, ‘Yes, things changed at COP31.’ Murat Kurum, COP31 President COP31 President Murat Kurum emphasized during the same press conference that electrification is a central theme of COP31. The presidency is advocating for the expanded use of clean energy-based electricity in the transportation, building, and industrial sectors to reduce dependence on the vulnerability of supply and prices of imported fossil fuels. The crisis in the global energy market has served as a harsh lesson for many countries. According to Kurum, from March to August 2026, fuel-importing nations will face an additional cost surge of approximately $330 billion due to price volatility. With the increasing affordability of electrical technology, electrification is seen as a golden opportunity to enhance energy security while also reducing emissions. artigo.texto: Os alunos do curso Técnico em Manutenção e Suporte em Informática do Instituto Federal do Pará (IFPA) – Campus Conceição do Araguaia realizaram, na noite da última segunda-feira (9), uma visita técnica ao data center da JC Telecom. Durante a atividade, os estudantes foram recebidos por Raylan Matias, técnico em Telecomunicações, que apresentou o funcionamento da estrutura e compartilhou informações sobre os sistemas de redes de computadores e o grande volume de dados que circula diariamente por essas redes. A visita foi marcada por muito aprendizado, troca de conhecimentos e curiosidade. Os alunos tiveram a oportunidade de esclarecer dúvidas, conhecer de perto uma fibra óptica e compreender melhor a infraestrutura tecnológica que possibilita a transmissão de informações e a conexão entre diferentes sistemas. A experiência proporcionou uma aproximação entre os conteúdos estudados em sala de aula e a realidade do mercado de trabalho, especialmente na área de Redes de Computadores, componente curricular ministrado pelo professor Ailvan Silva. Mais do que conhecer equipamentos e estruturas, os estudantes puderam ampliar seus conhecimentos e perceber, na prática, a importância das redes de computadores para o funcionamento da sociedade conectada. (Viviane Fialho/Ascom IFPA Conceição)

artigo.texto: Energy storage is expanding across Europe, but its growth remains constrained by obstacles that extend beyond technology. This is the conclusion of Energy Storage Deployment in the EU: Drivers, Barriers and Policy Pathways, published by the Joint Research Centre (JRC), the European Commission’s science and knowledge service. The analysis identifies grid connection delays as the most widespread barrier, while regulatory uncertainty and unpredictable revenues limit projects’ ability to secure financing. The report combines market data, policy analysis and a stakeholder consultation that received 19 responses. The JRC treats these contributions as qualitative evidence rather than a statistically representative sample. Grid connections remain the main bottleneck Insufficient capacity at targeted connection points and lengthy procedures for securing connection agreements are delaying new installations. In the report’s stakeholder consultation, insufficient grid capacity received an average severity rating of 4.1 out of 5, followed by long lead times for connection agreements, at 3.9 out of 5. The study also highlights how applications for projects that fail to progress, or reserve several potential locations, can block capacity for developments that are ready to proceed. Measures examined include prioritising projects that demonstrate maturity, improving transparency on available grid capacity and simplifying administrative procedures. Flexible connection agreements offer another route to earlier grid access. However, they may impose temporary network access restrictions that developers must account for in their business models. Predictable revenues are critical to financing The JRC warns that projects relying exclusively on market revenues still face difficulties attracting financing in many countries. Price volatility and uncertainty over future income make it harder for lenders to assess projects’ ability to repay debt. There is also a risk that the entry of additional batteries and other flexible resources will erode some revenue opportunities, particularly in markets vulnerable to saturation. The report identifies long-term contracts, capacity and flexibility remuneration mechanisms, and agreements combining renewable generation with storage as ways to improve revenue predictability. It also examines tolling agreements, under which a counterparty pays an agreed fee for commercial use of a storage facility. These arrangements can support financing, although they transfer part of the risk to the counterparty and require an assessment of its creditworthiness. Regulation still limits the value storage can capture Fragmentation across national markets represents another obstacle. The report highlights double charging when storage withdraws electricity from and injects it into the grid, high network tariffs and incomplete rules for participation in certain markets. It also finds that some services storage can provide, such as relieving local grid congestion, do not always receive adequate remuneration. The JRC therefore argues that policies should reward measurable contributions to the electricity system—including duration, availability and security of supply—while maintaining technology neutrality. Co-location with renewables creates opportunities The report highlights the potential of installing batteries alongside solar or wind farms. These configurations can share infrastructure, capture electricity that might otherwise be curtailed and shift delivery to higher-value hours. Power purchase agreements combining renewable generation and storage can provide an electricity supply profile better aligned with buyers’ requirements. However, securing financing requires clear contractual provisions on revenue allocation, operational responsibilities and risk sharing. Modelling points to 172 GW of EU storage needs by 2030 The report cites PRIMES modelling results that put the European Union’s power sector storage requirements at 172 GW by 2030, combining batteries and pumped hydropower. For 2040, projected requirements range from 213 GW to 275 GW, depending on the scenario. These figures represent modelled system requirements, rather than a specific binding storage deployment target. The JRC concludes that accelerating deployment requires action on permitting, grid connections, market rules and revenue stability. Falling technology costs support growth, but converting that potential into operating projects also depends on a framework that enables developers to finance and connect their assets.

artigo.texto: 9 de novembro de 2026, às 16:22 A TIM fechou um contrato com a BYD para fornecer internet a toda a frota de veículos leves da montadora chinesa no Brasil, além do seu polo industrial. Com a parceria, os diferentes modelos da marca passarão a contar com chips virtuais (eSIM) da TIM, com conexão 4G em 100% das cidades brasileiras e 5G em 1,1 mil cidades onde a operadora oferece cobertura. A previsão é de que cerca de 200 mil veículos da montadora chinesa contem com essa conectividade embarcada nos próximos 24 meses. Assim, a BYD busca avançar no desenvolvimento de novas funcionalidades que envolvam serviços conectados. Com o crescimento de serviços como inteligência artificial e uso de funções como mapas e streaming a bordo, um carro já tem consumo de dados quase equiparável a de um plano básico pós-pago, tipo ‘controle’. Do lado da TIM, o negócio representa uma expansão no setor automotivo, onde já oferece conexão para cerca de 630 mil veículos. A tele italiana possui uma parceria com a antiga Fiat Chrysler Automóveis (FCA) – hoje parte do grupo Stellantis – para fornecer conectividade 4G e eSIM em veículos das marcas Fiat, Jeep e Ram no Brasil. O contrato entre a TIM e a BYD envolve também a implantação de infraestrutura dedicada de redes 5G e 4G no complexo industrial da montadora em Camaçari, na Bahia. Essa é a maior fábrica de veículos eletrificados da América Latina, com 4,6 milhões de m². O projeto prevê a instalação de sete pontos de cobertura externa e 63 equipamentos distribuídos entre os galpões e as áreas operacionais, garantindo uma rede preparada para acompanhar o crescimento da produção e as demandas tecnológicas do complexo. artigo.texto: Norwegian shipping firm Hoegh Autoliners will install marine battery systems supplied by China's BYD on its upcoming ammonia-fuelled car carrier Aurora No. 12. The companies signed a strategic and technical cooperation agreement to integrate BYD's battery technology with the vessel's existing energy systems, according to a emailed press release. The ship will combine ammonia fuel, batteries, a shaft generator and solar panels, making it the first deep-sea car carrier to bring together these technologies, according to Hoegh Autoliners. The integrated system is expected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by around 1,000 tonnes of CO2 equivalent annually while improving fuel efficiency. Scheduled for delivery in May 2028, Aurora No. 12 will be part of the company's Aurora class, which can carry up to 9,100 cars and is designed to cut carbon emissions by up to 58% compared with conventional-fuelled pure car and truck carriers.

artigo.texto: Data centers become a political flashpoint after midterms, putting AI industry on notice HOBART, Ind. - The message from voters was hard for the data center industry to ignore: communities want a say in what gets built in their backyards — and they're increasingly demanding answers before those projects move forward. Data center debate The backstory: President Donald Trump has been one of the biggest supporters of the data center boom, arguing these facilities will bring jobs, investment and economic prosperity to communities across the country. On August 31, in a post on Truth Social, Trump said in part, "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want data centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let data reign." "You have to convince your community how great these things," said Trump. "You can't fight it. You have to go with it. And you're going to make a tremendous amount of money. You're going to reduce taxes." But that message hasn't necessarily resonated with residents who are worried about the potential consequences of these massive developments. And those concerns became a political talking point during the midterm elections. The Associated Press reports Democrats who campaigned on tighter restrictions on data centers made significant gains in several key gubernatorial races, including Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada and Iowa. In fact, 32 of the 34 winning gubernatorial candidates in races where AP called a winner supported stronger regulations or restrictions on data centers. Twelve supported outright bans or moratoriums. At the local level, the opposition was even more pronounced. An analysis by Redbud Consulting found voters approved restrictions in 44 of 45 completed local data center referendum elections across the country. And the opposition wasn't confined to one political party or one part of the country. The AP Voter Poll found roughly three-quarters of Americans opposed building a new data center in their community. For Wannie Park, founder and CEO of Pado AI, an energy orchestration software company that works with data centers, this backlash has been building for some time. "I think the dynamics of growth sometimes, which is what we're kind of going through, is oftentimes full brute force without thoughtfulness and good planning," said Park. "And I think with that, what you have is sort of what we have now, which is the backlash, right? Moratoriums and just people saying like, 'hey, let's take a breath here and figure out what's the right way to deploy this stuff.'" Park says the issue has become increasingly bipartisan, as residents question whether the economic benefits promised by developers are actually materializing. "People are saying, well, like, 'hey, I'm not getting what I thought I was getting' or ‘the economic development is not there’ or 'you're using up and polluting all our water' or ‘my rates are going up.’ Like all those types of things started to trickle in," said Park. Hobart meetings on data centers In northwest Indiana, Fox Chicago has reported increasingly heated public meetings in Hobart over proposed data center developments, with some residents even being removed after voicing their opposition. And the concerns being raised locally mirror what is happening across the country. On Fox News, Compass Data Centers CEO Chris Crosby acknowledged that not every developer has done a good job addressing those concerns. "I think it's fair. Their questions are real. Not everybody who develops and owns data centers does a good job of it. And, you know, there is a bar that needs to be raised," said Crosby. He says developers need to be more transparent, pay their own way when it comes to electricity and provide tangible benefits to the communities where they operate. Park agrees the industry needs a different approach. And he takes issue with the idea that opposing data center development means someone doesn't understand the importance of artificial intelligence. "I think that's just the wrong position, right?" Park argues the industry has been operating inefficiently, with opportunities to get more out of existing facilities rather than simply building more. He says older data centers could be repurposed, potentially reducing the need for some of the massive new construction projects being proposed. And he pushes back against the argument that slowing development automatically means America will fall behind China in the AI race. "I don't think it's that dire. Sometimes the industry kind of speaks to it like it's a binary. We have to build, build, or we're going to fall behind China or whatever. We're not going to lead. It's not that dire," said Park. What's next: Instead, Park says the next phase should focus on making better use of existing infrastructure and proving that these projects produce meaningful benefits. He also believes the political backlash is already affecting the industry's bottom line, with stricter regulations and uncertainty making investors and lenders more cautious about financing new developments. The Source: The information in this report came from statements by President Donald Trump, reporting and polling by The Associated Press, an analysis by Redbud Consulting, interviews with Pado AI CEO Wannie Park and Compass Data Centers CEO Chris Crosby, and previous FOX Chicago reporting on data center developments in Hobart, Indiana.

artigo.texto: A world leader in the provision of battery manufacturing assembly equipment, Gloucester-headquartered TBS Engineering plays a crucial role in keeping the vehicles and infrastructure used by millions of people up-and-running, right across the globe. SoGlos looks at five of its biggest customers and the products they power, from high-end cars like Porche, Bentley and Jaguar, to everyday essential infrastructure, like rail signals and telecoms. Exide With roots going all the way back to the 19th century, Exide is a US-founded company steeped in history, having made batteries used to launch torpedoes in World War Two, and by NASA to land on the moon in the 1960s. Now split from its former North American operations, the company supplies batteries for the automotive and energy sectors, operating from facilities across Europe and Asia Pacific as Exide Technologies. Bringing in annual revenue of around €1.6 billion, it supplies world-leading vehicle manufacturers from Citroen, Volkswagen and Mini, to Alfa Romeo, BMW and Jaguar, powered by TBS Engineering's state-of-the-art battery manufacturing assembly equipment. Clarios Clarios is a global giant in the automotive battery manufacturing sector, serving 1.5 million customers across more than 100 countries – and boasting the claim that one in three vehicles worldwide are powered by a Clarios battery. Bringing in $10.6 billion in annual revenue, a long list of renowned vehicle manufacturers use Clarios batteries, from Nissan, Renault and Skoda, to Porche, Bentley and Mercedes Benz. TBS Engineering has built up a strong partnership with Clarios, providing critical battery manufacturing assembly equipment that has accelerated capacity expansion for the company globally – a valued collaboration that was recognised with an award at the Clarios Supplier Summit in 2026. Enerya Served by TBS from its Mexico office, Enerya is dedicated to the manufacture of electrical batteries for the vehicle industry. Based in Nuevo León in Mexico, it's a leading North American brand, manufacturing batteries that power everything from passenger cars and commercial trucks, to motorcycles and marine vessels. TBS established its Mexico office in Monterrey in 2024, in order to provide its customers in the region with aftermarket spare parts, technical support, service, account management and streamlined logistics. East Penn A private, family-owned business operating the largest single-site lead battery manufacturing facility in the world, Pennsylvania company East Penn serves the North America and Asia Pacific markets. Making batteries for all types of vehicles, from cars and trucks, to boats, along with reserve power for things like rail signals and telecommunications, the company boasts annual revenue of around $3 billion. East Penn and TBS have a long-standing relationship which goes back to 1987, with Robert Flicker, COO of East Penn, saying of working with the Gloucester company: 'Their commitment to customer satisfaction and their willingness to work with their customers to provide the state-of-the-art equipment with high-level quality and standards makes them a great partner to satisfy our equipment needs.' Amara Raja Indian company Amara Raja Energy & Mobility manufactures a range of batteries for the automotive and industrial sectors, bringing in annual revenue of more than £1 billion. The company is the largest automotive battery manufacturer in India, supplying major auto manufacturers like Ford, Suzuki and more, while it also makes industrial batteries for sectors including telecoms, railways and defence. This year, TBS Engineering opens its TBS India office in Pune, Maharashtra, where it will provide aftermarket and technical support services for its clients in the region. To find out more about TBS Engineering, its global operations, and the equipment and services it provides for its customers, visit tbseng.co.uk.

artigo.texto: Frontier Institute announces lawsuit against Missoula’s data center zoning ordinance MISSOULA, Mont. — On Nov. 9, Frontier Institute announced attorneys from Arizona’s Goldwater Institute will represent CubCloud AI in a lawsuit regarding Missoula’s zoning regulations after the city passed an ordinance in October that would change the way it zones for data centers. “There’s a lot of things we should be requiring of data centers, I just don’t believe that what we’re doing should be in the same category of a multibillion-dollar facility,” Joshua Rhines, founder and CEO of CubCloud AI, said. The ordinance adopted by Missoula simply changed what is defined by a data center in regard to zoning. “It currently reads as a facility or portion of a facility housing network computer systems, servers and appliances and telecommunications equipment. It goes on. I simply would like to or propose that it read and slash or telecommunications,” Justin Ponton, the ward 2 city council member, said when he proposed the amendment back in October. The ordinance passed unanimously, and the addition of that one word may place protections on high-scale data centers. But, according to the lawsuit, it violates Montana’s Right to Compute Act and jeopardizes small tech businesses and their ability to grow in Montana. “Lawmakers go about regulating for data centers they need to make sure that they’re being thoughtful in the way they go about it. They can’t just enact sweeping bans on an entire category of technology without potentially sweeping in the little guys and these local small businesses like CubCloud who are real assets to our community,” Kendall Cotton, CEO and president of Frontier Institute, said. CubCloud AI is a local Missoula tech company founded on the belief that Montana had a need for local AI infrastructure and provides local organizations looking to implement AI an alternative to large-scale data centers like Microsoft or Meta. “You know it was never going to be like a hyperscale data center that would be 20 megawatts like Bonner or 100 megawatts or any of that it always planned to be like 2 or 3, you know obviously those plans are off the table right now you until we figure out what’s going on with ordinance here,” Rhines said. The city is aware of the lawsuit and issued this statement to NBC Montana regarding its current stance. It reads: “The city is aware of the lawsuit filed by CubCloud, however it has not been served the lawsuit as of the present moment. The city is aware of the Right to Compute Act. It is the city’s position that the Right to Compute Act does not give data center companies the right to locate wherever they please. The city plans to vigorously defend the City Council decision in this case. However, the city will not comment on the specifics of this case pending litigation.” CubCloud AI is not seeking a monetary settlement and simply is looking to work with the city to revise the current ordinance. “Our hope is we can have a productive dialogue and hopefully come out with an ordinance that addresses small business interest and saves the city from getting a Trojan horse situation which I think is probably why they passed the ordinance and their main fear,” Rhines said.

artigo.texto: Patrocinado por: (VCG/VCG/Getty Images) Repórter de Inteligência Artificial e Tecnologia Publicado em 9 de novembro de 2026 às 10h01. A ByteDance, dona do TikTok, planeja expandir suas operações de data centers no Brasil. O primeiro complexo está em construção no Ceará, com investimentos bilionários, enquanto negociações avançam para uma segunda instalação voltada ao mercado brasileiro. O projeto enfrenta questionamentos jurídicos sobre licenciamento ambiental e consulta indígena. Com seu primeiro data center na América Latina ainda em construção, a ByteDance, dona do TikTok, já procura uma empresa para desenvolver a segunda fase do complexo no Pecém, no Ceará. Em paralelo, o grupo chinês abriu conversas preliminares sobre outra instalação, fora do complexo portuário, que atenderia clientes no Brasil, segundo a Bloomberg. A expansão no Pecém pode superar em porte a obra atual, estimada em US$ 10 bilhões e que terá demanda elétrica de cerca de 300 megawatts (MW). A segunda fase segue em avaliação, e o projeto voltado ao mercado brasileiro está em estágio inicial. As obras da primeira etapa começaram em janeiro de 2026. A Omnia, plataforma de data centers do Pátria Investimentos, desenvolve o projeto para a ByteDance em parceria com a Casa dos Ventos. A previsão informada pela Omnia à Reuters é iniciar a operação no terceiro trimestre de 2027 e ampliar as atividades gradualmente até 2029. O projeto original do Pecém foi anunciado em dezembro de 2025 com investimento estimado em cerca de R$ 200 bilhões para o complexo completo, previsto em fases. Na etapa em obras, os servidores terão 200 MW de capacidade de tecnologia da informação. A demanda elétrica total, próxima de 300 MW, inclui os sistemas que mantêm os equipamentos em funcionamento, como a refrigeração. A energia é uma parte do negócio que já tem contrato. Em maio, Omnia e Casa dos Ventos acertaram um fornecimento de 20 anos, avaliado em cerca de US$ 2 bilhões. A maior parte virá do complexo eólico Ibiapaba, no Ceará, com uma parcela menor de um parque no Piauí, segundo as empresas. Perto do Pecém, os cabos submarinos que chegam a Fortaleza dão ao estado conexões de fibra óptica com os Estados Unidos, a Europa e a África. O empreendimento em construção fica na Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) do Pecém. O conselho federal que administra o regime aprovou o projeto da ByteDance para prestação de serviços exclusivamente ao mercado externo. Na prática, os servidores ficam no Ceará e processam dados para operações em outros países. Já a instalação em discussão fora do Pecém teria como destino o mercado brasileiro, segundo a Bloomberg. As conversas ocorrem enquanto o governo prepara as regras do Redata, regime federal sancionado em setembro que prevê incentivos tributários para equipamentos de data centers. Entre as contrapartidas previstas na lei estão critérios de eficiência hídrica e a oferta de pelo menos 10% da capacidade beneficiada ao mercado interno, compromisso que pode ser substituído por investimento adicional em pesquisa e inovação. Na sexta-feira, 6, a ministra da Casa Civil, Miriam Belchior, disse que o governo espera anunciar a regulamentação na semana de 16 de novembro. Em setembro, o Ministério Público Federal e a Defensoria Pública da União entraram com uma ação civil pública para impedir o início da operação antes de uma consulta livre, prévia e informada ao povo indígena Anacé e da elaboração de um estudo de impacto ambiental. Os órgãos também pedem que sejam avaliados os efeitos do empreendimento sobre a água, a rede elétrica e as comunidades do entorno. Em resposta à agência eixos, a Omnia afirmou que o licenciamento segue o rito da Superintendência Estadual do Meio Ambiente do Ceará (Semace) e que possui as autorizações válidas para as atividades que exerce. No início de novembro, o Fórum Nacional pela Democratização da Comunicação divulgou as conclusões de uma missão dos conselhos nacional e estadual de direitos humanos que recomendou a revisão do licenciamento e a consulta às comunidades afetadas.

artigo.texto: A computational and experimental investigation of calcium-iron-manganese oxide perovskites has revealed that tailoring iron concentrations to lean levels yields a notable surge in chemical energy storage capacity, surpassing standard benchmark materials under identical operating conditions. In research detailing the redox behavior of CaFexMn1-xO3-δ across its full compositional range, an iron-lean formulation containing approximately six and a quarter percent iron achieved an energetic thermochemical storage density of fifty-three kilojoules per mole of oxygen when reduced at twelve hundred and fifty degrees Celsius and re-oxidized at seven hundred and sixty degrees Celsius. This chemical capacity exceeds that of the established state-of-the-art comparator material, calcium aluminum manganese oxide, by approximately twenty percent under identical thermal and atmospheric boundaries. The storage potential peaked at sixty kilojoules per mole across an expanded temperature divergence of eight hundred and fifty degrees Celsius, establishing iron-lean compositions as exceptionally effective media for capturing and releasing high-grade thermal energy through cyclical chemical transformations. The search for resilient energy storage technologies stems directly from the expanding diversification of renewable generation and the fundamental intermittency challenges that afflict clean power infrastructure. Renewable sources including solar photovoltaic panels, wind turbine arrays, and concentrated solar thermal plants experience environmental fluctuations that disrupt steady electricity delivery, impair load-following capabilities, and create severe supply-demand mismatches across distribution networks. Thermal energy storage systems serve as critical operational buffers by holding surplus generation as thermal energy for dispatch into downstream industrial processes or thermal power generation cycles. While traditional sensible heat storage materials absorb energy via plain temperature elevations without changing phase and reach volumetric storage densities of around two hundred megajoules per cubic meter, latent storage media exploit phase changes to achieve three hundred to five hundred megajoules per cubic meter. In contrast, thermochemical energy storage operates through reversible chemical reactions without undergoing destructive structural melting, offering superior reported theoretical and experimental energy densities spanning 0.5 to 3 gigajoules per cubic meter. Thermochemical energy storage in redox-active metal oxides operates via a closed two-step thermochemical cycle that stores thermal input directly within reversible chemical bonds. During the charging stage, high-temperature heat drives the endothermic reduction of the metal oxide lattice, freeing oxygen gas from the crystalline framework and generating vacancies across the anionic sublattice. During the subsequent discharge cycle, ambient or compressed air streams flow across the reduced material, initiating an exothermic re-oxidation that takes up oxygen into the vacant sites and releases the stored chemical enthalpy as high-temperature heat. Unlike systems that undergo crystallographic phase shifts across distinct solid phases, vacancy-driven perovskite frameworks maintain structural integrity through cyclical bond formation while offering high reaction enthalpies and exceptional physical durability. Iron substitution within calcium manganese oxide systems presents an attractive route to calibrate reaction thermodynamics, because replacing expensive cobalt modifiers with abundant iron significantly suppresses raw material expenses while tuning the operational enthalpy of reduction across demanding thermal envelopes. Despite the recognized theoretical advantages of the calcium-iron-manganese oxide family, substantial information gaps previously hindered the deployment and optimization of these perovskites in high-temperature storage systems. Prior thermodynamic evaluations were restricted to a single linearized van ‘t Hoff modeling investigation that surveyed only three isolated iron concentrations, leaving the vast majority of the compositional spectrum uncharacterized. Linearized van ‘t Hoff approximations introduce significant compounding errors, impose rigid assumptions regarding temperature-independent enthalpies and entropies, and cannot continuously predict the thermodynamic consequences of complex cation-cation interactions. Consequently, the temperature dependence of enthalpy, entropy, and non-stoichiometry remained unknown across broad operating regimes. To resolve this deficiency, researchers implemented the advanced CrossFit Compound Energy Formalism algorithm, a thermodynamic modeling architecture capable of integrating theoretical quantum simulations with empirical thermal measurements to yield continuous, temperature-dependent, and composition-dependent representations of metal oxide reduction and re-oxidation behavior without relying on simplifying linearity assumptions. The CrossFit Compound Energy Formalism constructs an analytical solution model for the system free energy by unifying the distinct thermodynamic contributions of endmember configurations, configurational entropy, and excess interaction expressions. In the formulation developed for the calcium-iron-manganese system, calcium cations exclusively occupy the A-sublattice, while the B-sublattice incorporates four distinct transition metal species representing trivalent and tetravalent manganese alongside trivalent and tetravalent iron. The associated oxygen sublattice accommodates divalent oxygen anions alongside neutral oxygen vacancies. Site-fraction equations were mathematically derived from iron concentrations and the degree of oxygen off-stoichiometry, reflecting an equal distribution of reduction charge across active transition metal sites. artigo.texto: Política de minerais críticos vai priorizar imãs, baterias e fertilizantes Secretário de Mineração sinaliza cadeias que serão classificadas como prioritárias para liberação de instrumentos fiscais e de financiamento O Cimce (Conselho Nacional para Industrialização de Minerais Críticos e Estratégicos) deve enquadrar como prioritárias para a nova Política Nacional de Minerais Críticos as cadeias de imãs, baterias e fertilizantes, sinalizou nesta 4ª feira (11.nov.2026) o secretário nacional de Geologia, Mineração e Transformação Mineral do MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia), Anderson Arruda. O governo deve definir na próxima reunião do conselho, no final de novembro, as cadeias de minerais que receberão prioridade na aplicação dos instrumentos de financiamento e benefícios fiscais criados pela nova política. “Se a gente for pegar os debates que têm sido feitos sobre os projetos estratégicos, são esses: ímãs, baterias e fertilizantes. Obviamente, o Ministério de Minas e Energia e o Mdic [Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços], a gente está estudando, vendo quais são as outras cadeias que a gente pode atender também”, disse Arruda a jornalistas após participação no seminário “Fertilizantes: da dependência externa à resiliência do agro brasileiro”, organizado pelo Poder360, em Brasília. Segundo o secretário, a discussão sobre as cadeias levará em conta a demanda nacional pelos produtos que têm como matéria-prima os minerais classificados como prioritários na lista aprovada na 1ª reunião do Conselho. Questionado sobre eventual mudança na configuração da lista, Arruda disse não ver como “factível” que alterações sejam feitas agora. Como mostrou o Poder360, o Ibram (Instituto Brasileiro de Mineração) pediu uma revisão da relação para subir o potássio e o fosfato da classe 2 para a classe 1. Os minerais são matéria-prima para o setor de fertilizantes. “Não adianta a gente ter 27 minerais e não ter projeto. E agora, o governo vai se debruçar sobre essa carteira de projetos do Brasil. Quais são os projetos de maturidade, por exemplo, para ter um daqueles instrumentos [de financiamento e crédito fiscal]? Isso eu tenho falado para o setor de fertilizante. Houve uma seleção de classes, mas isso não quer dizer que o fertilizante não seja prioritário”, disse o secretário. URÂNIO FICA SEPARADO Arruda voltou a afirmar que o mineral será debatido separadamente das outras cadeias, por estar sob regime de monopólio da União e por demandar investimento público. Segundo o secretário, o Brasil tem alto potencial de desenvolver o setor em curto prazo, por ter reservas e tecnologia para transformar o mineral em combustível nuclear. “A gente já tem a cadeia adensada no Brasil e a gente já tem a demanda que é Angra 1 e 2 e possivelmente Angra 3. Então, a gente tem reserva, demanda e tecnologia. No curto prazo, a gente consegue inclusive atender esse interesse do presidente Lula, que é desenvolver uma indústria nacional”, declarou. O avanço da exploração de urânio, no entanto, depende de um debate maior sobre o setor nuclear prometido pelo ministro Alexandre Silveira (Minas e Energia) na última 6ª feira (6.nov). Segundo Silveira, o governo apresentará um plano de reestruturação do segmento ainda em 2026. Apesar de a reforma ter sido anunciada para e este ano, Arruda afirma que a discussão deve ficar para 2027. “O fato de o Urânio ter entrado na lista, na classe 1, demonstra que isso é uma atenção que o governo já está dando. Agora, nós precisamos, obviamente, a partir do novo governo Lula, sentar e definir como desenvolver isso”, declarou.

(First Alert 4) -An ex-employee of OnderLaw is suing the law firm, claiming harassment and an online campaign to sway public perception of a proposed data center in Ferguson. The lawsuit, filed on Thursday, was filed by an ex-employee referred to in court documents as Jane Doe. The lawsuit names the defendants as OnderLaw and James ‘Jim’ Onder. Onder’s lawyer told First Alert 4 he is declining to comment for the story. First Alert 4 has also reached out to OnderLaw for comment. As of publication time, we have not heard back. Court records show Onder’s lawyer had filed to have the case sealed by the court. In a Friday ruling, Judge Heather Cunningham denied the request. The 30-page lawsuit alleges a series of sexually inappropriate actions taken by Onder against Doe, along with allegations he pressured her to participate in a campaign against Ferguson and its city council regarding a vote against his proposed data center. The lawsuit alleges OnderLaw discriminated against Doe after she exercised her workers’ compensation rights and that the company violated Missouri’s whistleblower protection act. Against Onder himself, Doe alleges assault and battery The Ferguson Project On May 4, Ferguson’s City Council rejected tax breaks for Onder’s proposed data center at the former Emerson campus. The project would have received $1.5 billion in tax breaks over the 15 years of the agreement. After the rejection by the City Council, Doe claims that Onder ordered her to create a negative campaign about the city and residents. Onder told Doe the campaign would be pushed through Meta to residents in Ferguson; the content would appear as real news stories and paint the city as overrun with crime, the lawsuit states. The lawsuit says that Onder told Doe this would get him back to the approval process through a loophole and his relationships with officials and leaders at the Port Authority. Days after the rejection, on May 7, Doe was in a closed-door meeting with Onder, a St. Louis County official and a crisis public relations consultant. In this meeting, Doe alleged Onder again detailed his campaign plan. During the meeting, Onder said he wanted to instill fear about safety in Ferguson with exaggerated stories, making the data center “the only way out for these people,” documents state. While planning the campaign, Doe claims that Onder mocked Black people. Doe said during one meeting, while discussing what graphics to use during a Ferguson town hall, Onder said: “They [Black people] can’t read, so it doesn’t matter.” Doe says after the May 7 meeting she told Onder and Lisa Frederick, who served as the Chief Operating Officer, Chief Financial Officer, and President for OnderLaw, she would not work on the Ferguson project. Doe says that Onder persisted and told OnderLaw Director of Special Projects, Don Bertelsmann, to use bots to manufacture comments about Ferguson on social media that would look like they were coming from ordinary people. Doe alleges Onder instructed Bertelsmann to use computers in his home lab to do the botting. Months earlier, in January 2026, Doe alleges she was given a 2025 expense folder by Bertelsmann, showing a charge on his personal credit card for two “labs”; one at his house and another at his father-in-law’s house, according to the lawsuit. Bertelsmann wanted a reimbursement of $8,000 for equipment, software and internet service, the lawsuit states. At the time, Doe alleges that Bertelsmann wouldn’t tell her what the labs were for. Months later, Onder directed Bertelsmann to use his home lab and the computers in it to run bots for the Ferguson campaign. Allegations of violating Missouri lobbying law The lawsuit states that Onder’s goal was to influence Ferguson’s City Council’s decision on the data center’s tax breaks by pushing down real residents with fake accounts. The lawsuit states that Onder’s campaign efforts violated Missouri’s Lobbying Law, which requires every lobbyist to register with the Missouri Ethics Commission and prohibits hiring a person not registered as a lobbyist by the state. According to the lawsuit, Onder knew that Bertelsmann was not a registered lobbyist but still hired him. Doe claims she refused to be part of the campaign, as well as her team. She says she reported the campaign to Faith Earley, who was the firm’s new COO. The reports were done in mid-May; Doe says she reported her concerns multiple times after. The suit shows a text message exchange between Onder and Doe, in which Onder says, “So I shouldn’t announce to the World the illegal bribes each one requested to buy their votes?” in reference to the Ferguson City Council. artigo.texto: Building owners are turning to battery energy storage systems to lower energy costs, add resilience against grid disruptions and support decarbonization. Despite momentum, their adoption faces a number of persistent obstacles, said panelists at the Greenbuild conference last month. Nationwide, nearly 58 gigawatt-hours of on-site battery storage capacity was installed in 2025, the largest single year of new battery capacity on record, according to a report by the Urban Land Institute and UL Standards & Engagement, drawing on data from the American Clean Power Association. Looking ahead, the sector is expected to install 500 GWh of battery storage between 2026 and 2032, the report says. Notwithstanding the success of these models, several barriers are keeping the market from growing more quickly, according Jill Maltby-Abbott, senior environmental and sustainability standards engineer at UL Standards & Engagement, a panelist who contributed to the ULI and UL report. Location-specific challenges. Even when a project makes economic sense, it can be stopped by interconnection and permitting woes, unclear approvals, shifting local requirements and unfamiliarity with the technology, according to Maltby-Abbott. Even where interconnection and permitting processes exist, commercial-scale storage projects can take years to deliver, the report said. Long and unpredictable timelines can cause projects to accumulate soft costs — like time and money spent on community engagement or engineering fees — and be exposed to changing market conditions, incentive structures and regulatory requirements, adding to the financial risk of implementation, per the report. Risk thresholds. Another key consideration is how municipalities view the risk and governance of these assets, Maltby-Abbott said. “How are [municipalities] defining the [risk] thresholds that they’ll accept? It’s very much on a per-project, per-owner basis, and this is a challenge that a lot of people experience with multiple emerging technologies.” Concern over risk can lead to delays as local officials put up hurdles, Dean Apostoleris, practice leader of renewable energy development at Kimley-Horn, said at the conference. “What we see as a really big barrier in terms of penetration into new markets and, even in some situations, mature markets is resistance from the regulatory, zoning, land use and siting perspective of these batteries,” he said. Even in really population-dense markets, where storage development has been a priority for quite some time, there has only been increased adoption of on-site battery energy storage in the past five or so years, according to Apostoleris. “That issue stems from a lack of education and lack of knowledge about what battery energy storage really is,” he said. For example, New York state has established a mandate to procure 6 GW of battery energy storage by 2030, with Illinois and Massachusetts setting targets of 3 GW and 5,000 MW as well, respectively. But with those targets close to just three years away, New York only has 415 MW of battery storage installed, or 7% of its target, as of the presentation, Aposoleris said. State mandates aim to spur battery adoption but development "comes down to the local and community level,” Apostoleris said. “And a lot of these communities have not yet had the bandwidth, the knowledge or the education to implement some of these regulations.” “As a result, when you actually go to permit and construct BESS, ultimately the reviews and approvals are … preventing a lot of that mandate and that goal from being achieved,” he said. Fire risk. Of all the risks, fire is one of the first localities worry about, said Kara Kokernak, senior director of the ULI Lewis Center for Sustainability in Real Estate. “That is something that became very apparent” when conducting research for the report, she said. “That was tagged in most of our conversations, but having fire safety teams part of that education can help ease those concerns.” Because of this pushback, Apostoleris said, it can be much easier to implement these projects in jurisdictions that have already established BESS safety requirements and review processes, which provide more prescriptive guidance on how projects will be evaluated. He points to the Massachusetts Energy Facilities Siting Board as a good example. It “allows a lot of developers to push through their projects in a very prescriptive manner that reduces some of the risk that often comes with uncertainty of reviews and approvals they might have at the state level,” Apostoleris said. Even when requirements are stringent, this predictability can help project teams incorporate safety considerations earlier while supporting fire department preparedness and confidence in how potential incidents will be avoided or managed, the report says. Community engagement, or lack thereof, can often delay, constrain or stop otherwise viable projects, the report says. For that reason, early engagement, before formal filings, is a “consistent recommendation from those who have successfully navigated community opposition,” the report says. “This gives developers the opportunity to understand specific concerns, explain safety and emergency response approaches, and adjust the project so that community input is reflected in project planning from the start.”
