artigo.texto: Sodium-ion batteries are moving into commercial production, supported by growing interest in diversified supply chains and reliable performance across a wide range of temperatures, according to new analysis from Wood Mackenzie. The report, Sodium-ion batteries: commercialisation begins, economics to follow, examines developments in China, the United States, Germany and India. It finds that supply agreements now exceed 70 GWh, signalling growing confidence among downstream customers. Wood Mackenzie expects leading manufacturers to achieve cell-level cost parity with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries by the end of 2026. However, parity at module and complete system level is not expected until after 2030. Supply security and temperature performance support adoption The consultancy identifies supply chain security, cycle life and a broad operating temperature range as key advantages of sodium-ion technology. Its performance in cold conditions strengthens its appeal for applications where low temperatures can affect battery operation. According to Ankita Chauhan, Director of Global Supply Chain and Integrated Power & Renewables Research at Wood Mackenzie, these characteristics, alongside geopolitical supply advantages, are driving near-term commercialisation. China leads manufacturing expansion China is leading the development of sodium-ion manufacturing capacity. Wood Mackenzie reports that BYD has 30 GWh of planned capacity in the country, while CATL is targeting at least 1 GWh of sodium-ion battery shipments by the end of 2026. China, the United States and Europe have significant offtake agreements, while India remains at an early stage of commercial validation. Manufacturing capacity, however, is expanding ahead of demand. The consultancy estimates a learning rate of 18–20% for China during 2026–2035, reflecting the potential for costs to decline as production scales and manufacturers gain experience. Higher upfront investment, lower lifetime costs The analysis puts average global upfront costs for sodium-ion systems at US$229/kWh, compared with US$200/kWh for LFP. Despite this initial premium, it estimates that sodium-ion can deliver a 21% lower total cost of ownership over a 20-year project. The projected savings stem from lower operating expenditure and avoiding capacity additions needed to compensate for battery degradation. According to Wood Mackenzie, system economics remain stable across storage durations of two to four hours. Near-term deployment nevertheless faces several obstacles. The report highlights Chinese export controls, India’s underdeveloped supply chain, slow gigafactory expansion in the United States and German trade policies as potential constraints on growth. Policy plays a central role in commercialisation Wood Mackenzie finds that taxation, trade measures and domestic manufacturing incentives are shaping sodium-ion deployment alongside technological progress. According to the report, China’s reintroduction of a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries in July 2026 exempts sodium-ion technology through the end of 2028. LFP batteries face a 2% levy from September 2026, rising to 4% from September 2027. In the United States, the consultancy identifies Section 301 tariffs of approximately 58% on Chinese energy storage cells as an incentive for domestic sodium-ion production, complemented by manufacturing credits under Section 45X of the Inflation Reduction Act. In Europe, carbon-footprint disclosure requirements under the EU Battery Regulation provide further support. India is developing local capacity through a US$1.25 billion incentive programme and duty exemptions on manufacturing equipment, the report notes. The economics could shift decisively between 2030 and 2035 Wood Mackenzie identifies 2030–2035 as the period when sodium-ion economics could become significantly more competitive. For projects being deployed today, however, it considers LFP the established, bankable choice for storage assets with durations of two to four hours. Sodium-ion manufacturers still need to scale production, refine cell materials and establish a consistent operating track record. The consultancy therefore expects several battery technologies to coexist, each serving different applications and storage durations.

artigo.texto: ENERGY Governor’s energy council recommends data centers, large users cover grid costs Report offers 22 recommendations, including zero-carbon standard shift A council appointed by Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham is urging lawmakers to make data centers and other large power users pay for the grid costs they create, according to a report released this month. In April, Lujan Grisham established the 13-member Energy Affordability and Grid Reliability Council through an executive order to develop recommendations addressing energy affordability, grid reliability, infrastructure investment and economic development. State Economic Development Secretary Rob Black, acting Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Secretary Erin Taylor and Rep. Meredith Dixon, D-Albuquerque, were among the public officials appointed to the council. El Paso Electric President and CEO Kelly Tomblin and TXNM Energy President and CEO Don Tarry also serve on the council. The council’s report includes 22 recommendations to inform future legislative, regulatory and administrative actions. Among them: Large industrial customers should “bear costs attributable to serving them and existing customers should be held harmless from costs and financial risks caused by new large loads,” the report said. The report said the state Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Department should develop a database of large electricity users, noting that industrial customers accounted for about 47% of New Mexico’s 2025 electricity sales, followed by commercial users at 30% and residential at 23%. “Meeting growing demand requires careful planning and prudent investment,” Tarry said in a statement announcing the report. The report notes that future energy demand is expected to grow, though the “scale, timing and location of that growth remain uncertain.” “New Mexico’s three major (investor-owned utilities) are all evaluating significant load growth scenarios, including growth from data centers, manufacturing, electrification of oil and gas operations and in other industrial processes, transportation electrification, and broader economic development,” the report said. Already, most New Mexicans have seen increases on their monthly electricity bills — under a staggered rate increase approved last year — to help cover the cost of system expansions for the Public Service Company of New Mexico. Lujan Grisham in 2019 signed into law the Energy Transition Act requiring utilities to go carbon-free by midcentury. The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission in May 2025 approved PNM’s phased-in rate increase request to help cover the costs of renewable energy buildout. That PRC approval hiked average monthly residential bills by roughly $12. The report also recommends that lawmakers shift the state’s renewable-energy standard to a “zero-carbon” standard, giving utilities more flexibility to meet clean energy targets with non-emitting resources such as nuclear power. The council’s report also suggests other measures, such as broadening the availability of energy infrastructure securitization for utilities, which would allow utilities to recover infrastructure costs via bonds backed by ratepayer revenue, thereby reducing financing costs and passing on savings to ratepayers. In a statement, Lujan Grisham said the recommendations “give us a path to protect ratepayers, bring more power onto the grid and keep our energy clean, all at the same time.” Added Dixon, “These recommendations give legislators a practical starting point for protecting customers while supporting responsible growth.” Justin Horwath covers tech and energy for the Journal. You can reach him at jhorwath@abqjournal.com.

artigo.texto: The Telangana Electricity Regulatory Commission (TGERC) has granted in-principle approval to state distribution companies, Telangana State Southern Power Distribution Company Limited (TGSPDCL) and Telangana State Northern Power Distribution Company Limited (TGNPDCL), to procure 7,300 MW of renewable energy along with advanced energy storage systems. The proposed procurement will involve long-term power supply agreements ranging from 15 to 25 years and aims to meet the state’s growing electricity demand while supporting national renewable energy targets. The approval follows a petition submitted by the distribution companies highlighting the need to strengthen Telangana’s future power supply. According to the Central Electricity Authority’s (CEA) Resource Adequacy Plan, the state’s annual energy requirement is expected to increase from 1,08,125 million units (MU) in FY 2026-27 to 1,77,219 MU by FY 2035-36. Peak electricity demand is also projected to rise by nearly 49.4% during this period. The distribution companies are also preparing for the expiry of several existing power purchase agreements, which could create gaps in energy availability and peak power supply. At the same time, meeting the Ministry of Power’s increasing Renewable Consumption Obligation (RCO) targets has become important to avoid regulatory and financial penalties. The approved procurement plan includes four major renewable energy components. The first involves 800 MW of standalone wind power under a 25-year agreement. This capacity is expected to complement solar generation and improve the overall renewable energy supply profile. The second component covers 3,000 MW of solar power integrated with a 6,000 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), configured at 1,000 MW for six hours. The project will operate under a 25-year agreement, allowing electricity generated during periods of high solar availability to be stored and supplied during evening peak demand. The third component includes 2,000 MW of Renewable Energy Round-the-Clock (RE-RTC) power for 25 years. This arrangement is intended to provide a more consistent renewable electricity supply and support the state’s base-load requirements. Additionally, the plan includes 2,000 MWh of Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE), configured at 500 MW for four hours, under a 15-year agreement to address peak demand periods. During the public consultation process, consumer groups and industry stakeholders raised concerns about the procurement process, demand projections and the possible impact on electricity tariffs. Some participants questioned the initiation of tendering activities before obtaining formal regulatory approval. They also highlighted the importance of promoting distributed renewable energy projects and creating opportunities for local micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs). In response, TGERC directed the distribution companies to obtain prior approval from the Commission before initiating bidding for future long-term or medium-term power procurement. The Commission also clarified that DISCOMs can participate in competitive procurement processes conducted through the Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) or use state-level tendering mechanisms. The selection between these routes should be based on the most cost-effective landed tariff at the Telangana periphery. The approved renewable procurement is expected to strengthen the state’s energy security, reduce dependence on conventional power sources and limit consumer exposure to rising fuel-linked electricity costs.

artigo.texto: Reports related to this article: Written by Eric Funderburk for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary U.S. battery energy storage systems are growing larger, often exceeding hundreds of megawatts in capacity and racking up substantial construction investments. A Big Market The deployment of battery energy storge systems (BESS) across the U.S. has represented a major shift in the U.S. power sector, opening the door to a utility-scale power source that was virtually unknown only a few years ago. And that door has opened in a big way. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) in August reported that nearly 52 gigawatts (GW) of battery energy storage was deployed in the U.S. at the end of June 2026, with 8.3 GW of that coming in the first half of 2026 alone. A previous article from Industrial Info Resources noted that $3.8 billion worth of standalone BESS projects were lined up to break ground in September. In addition to standalone battery facilities, dozens of BESS units are lined up to accompany solar installations, evening out power supply at times when solar power isn't actively being generated. Industrial Info Resources data show more than 1,400 U.S. BESS projects, valued at nearly $642 billion, either underway or on the planning table, although these frequently include solar power and a handful of wind projects accompanying the battery storage. Current construction represents more than $25.5 billion in investments. The Bigger, the Better? So where are the largest BESS projects currently being built in the U.S., and what is driving this $25 billion in current construction? One BESS installation rises to the top of the list: Intersect Power's Darden Clean Energy Project in Fresno, California. This massive 1,150-megawatt (MW) battery installation will be able to match the output of the accompanying 1,150-MW solar power plant at maximum discharge for a period of up to four hours with its 4,600-megawatt-hour discharge rating. The BESS unit plans to employ Tesla's lithium-ion-phosphate (LFP) battery technology and is expected to begin operating in 2028. Subscribers can access details of the project, including construction timelines, key contact details, and equipment and service needs on both the solar BESS components of the project, by clicking here. Battery storage also is a major component of the Steel River Energy Center being built near Osceola, Arkansas, which will feature 720-MW/2,880-MWh of battery capacity at full buildout. Work is underway on the first two phases of construction, which will add 480 MW of battery capacity to accommodate 1,000 MW of solar generation. A third phase of construction to add more solar generation along with an additional 240 MW of battery energy storage capacity is planned to get started at a later date. Work is just getting started on SB Energy's Libra hybrid energy center in which 700 MW of solar capacity is equally matched a 700-MW/2,800-MWh BESS unit. SB Energy has employed SOLV Energy to construct the project on federal lands managed by the U.S. Bureau of Land Management (BLM) near Yerington, Nevada. The project has a targeted in-service of 2028. Oregon a Prime BESS Destination Planned BESS builds are a more slippery target, but a few substantial projects seem to likely to move forward, including an anticipated 1,400 MW of battery storage at an Oregon project backed by Amazon. Ownership of the Sunstone solar/BESS project in northeastern Oregon was transferred to a subsidiary of Amazon earlier this year, but drawing on Amazon's substantial resources and a hard deadline of November 2027 to get moving on construction, the project seems likely to move forward. The first two phases of construction will add a combined 400 MW of BESS capacity, while a projected third phase would add a massive 800 MW of additional battery energy storage, although work on this final phase remains a few years out. Another substantial BESS project is on the books for Sherman County, Oregon, in the form of the Buckley solar/BESS facility, which could begin construction next year. The project planned by Boise, Idaho-based Clenera Renewable Energy would include 1,200 MW of solar and matching 1,200 MW of battery capacity with a four-hour discharge time. Substations, transmission tie-ins and all manner of equipment are part of the project, so an anticipated completion date of early 2029 could prove somewhat optimistic, depending on when construction kicks off and the pace at which is performed. Key Takeaways - BESS capacities are growing larger, often matching the solar generation capacity it frequently accompanies. - Oregon is the destination for two substantial BESS projects, each planned to add 1,200 MW or more of battery capacity. artigo.texto: Google’s Utah Deal Puts Geothermal Power on the Data Center Map Key Highlights - Fervo expects the first of eight generating units dedicated to Google’s 396 MW contract to deliver power in mid-2028. A separate expansion option could bring geothermal electricity directly to a proposed Utah campus. - Indonesia’s Pertamina Geothermal Energy is studying a 5 MW data center pilot at an existing field, where it must account for electricity already committed to the national utility. - Google’s first geothermal agreements in Asia target 10 MW for Taiwan’s grid. In Kenya, available power and disagreements over capacity payments have delayed Microsoft and G42’s proposed cloud campus. - New Zealand and Iceland offer two operating examples. Microsoft buys renewable attributes from a 51.4 MW plant supplying New Zealand’s grid, while Verne operates an Icelandic campus served by geothermal and hydroelectric power. In its November 9 project update, Fervo Energy identified the eight geothermal generating units it is building in southwestern Utah to supply Google with 396 megawatts of grid-connected power. As Fervo explained on its third-quarter earnings call, Google has agreed to pay for the power over 15 years even if it never builds the proposed Beaver County data center. The expansion option ties geography more closely to the deal. If Google elects to buy roughly 600 MW more, the companies are pursuing a direct connection that could carry that power from Cape Station to the proposed campus. Years before the AI boom, data centers gave other industries a working example of how a large electricity customer could bring renewable generation to market. In October 2014, Rich Miller reported for Data Center Knowledge on a field of more than 57,000 solar panels serving the QTS Princeton campus in New Jersey. The array could produce up to 14.1 MW. That same year, Facebook, Hewlett-Packard, and Intel joined General Motors, Walmart, Mars, and six other companies in asking utilities for competitive renewable power, access to new projects, and contracts long enough to support investment. By January 2017, 65 companies had signed those buyers’ principles. When Miller revisited the subject in DCF in March 2017, he found that data center providers had contracted for more than 1.2 GW of renewable power in the preceding year. In 2025, Google alone signed agreements for more than 12 GW of new clean energy. Corporate buyers have learned how to help finance power plants at a scale few would have imagined a decade ago. What a data center developer still needs to know is how much electricity will be available on its local grid at two in the morning, through a lull in the wind, and on the day the next hall opens. That question runs through the new DCF Global franchise, most recently in our examination of Britain’s bargain with the AI data center industry, where access to power comes with obligations to host communities and electricity customers. DCF’s geothermal reporting traces one route toward meeting those obligations. In 2023, Google and Fervo’s Nevada pilot began delivering electricity to the local grid. We subsequently examined the case for locating geothermal generation behind the meter. In Utah, Fervo and Google are now pursuing both approaches at the same field. Utah’s First 33 MW Is Operating. Google’s Eight Units Come Next. The clearest measure of progress at Cape Station comes from three generating blocks in different stages of commissioning. The first, rated at 33 MW, entered commercial operation on September 30. By November 9, the second had synchronized with the grid and was delivering test electricity. The third was mechanically complete, with crews checking equipment and systems ahead of live operation. Fervo expects the latter two units to reach commercial operation by January 1, 2027, completing the first phase. Google’s contracted supply will come from blocks four through 11, a group Fervo calls Cape Google 400. Fervo expects first power from those units in mid-2028 and is targeting full contracted capacity by the end of that year. Under the take-or-pay agreement, Fervo has a committed customer as it drills wells and builds generating equipment. Google can secure a substantial block of new supply before settling the scope and location of its Utah data center. The additional 600 MW involves a different decision. Under the agreement announced in September, Fervo committed to offering Google an option to increase its purchases to nearly 1 GW by June 2030. The companies are pursuing behind-the-meter delivery for that expansion under Utah’s SB132 framework. If the arrangement proceeds, proximity to the field would become a condition of receiving that power directly. The nearly 1 GW figure describes potential electricity purchases. The campus remains subject to engineering, approvals, and a commercial decision by Google. In Indonesia, Who Has a Claim on the Next 5 MW? At Kamojang in West Java, Pertamina Geothermal Energy is approaching site selection from the opposite direction. PGE already operates a producing geothermal field and wants to allocate 5 MW to a data center pilot there. Before the company can offer those megawatts to a new customer, it must account for its existing deliveries to Indonesia’s national utility, PLN. At a November 4 briefing covered by Indonesian news agency ANTARA, PGE executives said they had completed an initial technology study for a pilot designed to run entirely on power from the field. The company was examining commercial terms, prospective data center partners, and revisions to the project’s environmental assessment. According to ThinkGeoEnergy’s account of the proposal, PGE expected the reviews to run through late 2026 or early 2027 and envisaged a pilot lasting one to two years. The proposed 5 MW is an allocation at the plant. The share available to servers would depend on cooling and other facility loads. artigo.texto: PRESS RELEASE: Utility-scale solar developers are increasingly co-locating battery storage with new solar photovoltaic capacity. As of September 2026, over 16% of new utility-scale solar capacity added this year is co-located with operable battery storage, compared with 2% in 2017, according to data reported to EIA by operators. Reported plans for solar additions scheduled to come online in the last three months of this year show that the share with co-located battery storage could increase to 19% this year. Longer-term plans indicate that this trend will continue, with the portion increasing to more than 30% in plans submitted for 2027 and 2028. When operators co-locate battery storage with solar, they can direct solar electricity output to the grid or to the battery, depending on the wholesale prices. Wholesale prices in regions with large solar participation tend to fall when solar contributions are high and rise as they decrease. Plants with both solar and battery storage can manage the combined output of their generating resources to maximize their value in a changing wholesale price environment. Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, EIA-860M, Monthly Update to the Annual Electric Generator Report We publish unit-level generator inventory data based on our annual and monthly data collections, including information on design attributes for all utility-scale plants. Although battery storage and solar units at the same plant often enter commercial service at different times, the EIA-860 and EIA-860M data collection program tracks these developments and provides a monthly summary that can be used to identify co-located technologies. Southwest states have higher-than-average solar capacity shares relative to their total generating capacity and also have higher levels of co-located utility-scale solar and battery capacity. As of September, 13% of the total U.S. utility-scale generating capacity is solar photovoltaic, and 18% of that is co-located with battery storage. The share of solar generation co-located with battery capacity in California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Nevada is more than double the national average. Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, EIA-860M, Monthly Update to the Annual Electric Generator Report Principal contributors: Glenn McGrath, Alex Mey

artigo.texto: BOISE, Idaho — No mega data centers are currently proposed within Boise city limits, but with large-scale projects emerging elsewhere in Idaho, Mayor Lauren McLean says she doesn't want to wait until one arrives to determine whether the city is prepared. In an interview with Idaho News 6 on Monday, McLean explained what prompted her call for a six-month moratorium on large data center development, what questions she wants answered and why she believes the city needs to act now. "A lot of people are asking that, and they're asking why now, but I wouldn't want them to ask tomorrow, why didn't you do it," McLean said. WATCH: Boise mayor explains preemptive data center pause McLean pointed to recent data center proposals in other Idaho communities as a major factor behind her decision. South of Boise, a developer has proposed a project involving nearly 3,700 acres of federal public land, including a 4 million-square-foot data center. Meta already operates a data center in Kuna, while city leaders in Pocatello recently rejected another large-scale proposal. McLean said developments like those have raised questions about whether Boise has adequate protections in place. "This is a preemptive step. We don't want to be too late, so we're going to get ahead of this and ask the questions we need to ask to make sure we're advocating for Boise," McLean said. Those questions extend beyond the environmental impacts of data centers to whether the facilities provide enough long-term economic benefits for the communities hosting them. "The impact that it would have on water, the power that's needed, the number of jobs that might or might not exist, and also the noise," McLean said. Under her proposal, Boise would temporarily prohibit new data centers larger than 100,000 square feet or requiring more than 20 megawatts of power. The city has no pending applications meeting those thresholds. The proposal also raises questions about how Boise evaluates major industrial development, particularly as the city supports Micron Technology's multi-billion-dollar semiconductor expansion. Like large data centers, semiconductor manufacturing requires significant electricity and water resources. Asked how Micron's expansion differs from the facilities she wants to study, McLean emphasized the company's commitment to permanent jobs and investment in Boise. "Micron is not a data center," McLean said. "Yes, they require water, power. They're investing in the community, and they're creating opportunity for our kids and grandkids to come home with high-paying jobs." Her response highlights another consideration the city intends to examine: whether the economic benefits of large data centers justify their demands on local infrastructure and resources. McLean said she wants Boise to attract companies that invest in the community and provide lasting employment opportunities. Rather than responding to a specific development application, McLean said the proposed moratorium would allow city officials to study potential impacts before deciding what long-term regulations may be necessary. She also wants residents involved in determining what protections the city should establish. "Part of the six months is going to be a conversation with the community. I want to hear from residents on what they expect," McLean said. Asked whether six months would provide enough time, McLean said the city intends to use the period to examine existing regulatory tools, identify potential gaps and determine what additional steps may be needed. The mayor also suggested Idaho communities need more support at the state level when evaluating large data center developments. "The state needs to create guardrails so that communities can advocate for themselves," McLean said. For now, McLean's proposal is less about responding to a project already seeking approval in Boise and more about determining what rules should be in place if one eventually arrives. The Boise City Council will hold a public hearing on the proposed moratorium Tuesday, Nov. 10, before considering whether to approve it.

artigo.texto: Less than a month before leaving office, Gov. Mike Dunleavy announced that his administration had formed a public corporation intended to attract data centers to Alaska, along with a new platform to allow individuals to invest in the projects. The initiative is led by the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority, an embattled state-owned corporation whose board members were appointed by Dunleavy. AIDEA partnered with Plural, a California-based startup whose chief executive, Adam Silver, met with Dunleavy several times last year. The Monday announcement about the partnership is part of a flurry of activity as Dunleavy seeks to cement his policy priorities before he leaves office. His administration also announced this week that it transferred thousands of acres in state land to AIDEA to develop an industrial park that could include data centers, and separately approved a 50-year lease for a data center in the Arctic. AIDEA is the sole owner of Alaska Data Corp. LLC, a corporation that formed in March. The company’s president is listed as Brandon Brefczynski, who is AIDEA’s deputy director. The company’s vice president is listed as Dave Stieren, a former talk radio host. Both Brefczynski and Stieren have worked for Dunleavy or AIDEA since 2019. AIDEA board members voted earlier this year to send $20 million to the newly formed Alaska Data Corp., as first reported by the Anchorage Press. Data centers and their construction were a topic of debate in Alaska leading up to this month’s elections. Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who is poised to succeed Dunleavy as governor, said he would support a moratorium on data center construction in Alaska until the state adopts a comprehensive regulatory package. Kreiss-Tomkins has also said he would support additional oversight of AIDEA, which has been used in recent years to promote Dunleavy’s policy priorities with little public input or oversight. Dunleavy, who has not spoken publicly about what he intends to do after he leaves office next month, released a statement Monday calling for data centers to be built in the state. “As the country debates data centers, in Alaska, we have an opportunity to learn from what has occurred in other states and do it better here in our great state,” Dunleavy said. “If there is an opportunity for data centers here in Alaska, let’s do it right. Let’s build them the right way, let’s locate them in the right places, and let’s explore how individual Alaskans can have an ownership stake so that they clearly and directly benefit all Alaskans. Here in Alaska, we can demonstrate to the world how to do data centers well, so they are a positive, not a negative.” Dunleavy’s spokespeople did not respond to questions about the state’s partnership with Plural, the California startup backing the initiatives, which launched in 2024. Neither did Stieren. Dunleavy first met Plural’s chief executive, Adam Silver, in San Francisco in June 2025, according to his public calendar. In the ensuing months, Dunleavy met with Silver at least seven times, including four times in Washington, D.C. Two of those meetings also included Alaska’s Republican U.S. Rep. Nick Begich. The meetings also included leaders of AIDEA and Dunleavy’s former acting attorney general, Stephen Cox. The fate of the project — and AIDEA itself — remains up in the air with Dunleavy’s impending departure from office. Aubrey Wieber, founder of a progressive advocacy group called the 907 Initiative, said Dunleavy is “using AIDEA to move hundreds of millions of public dollars to Lower 48 corporations he and his closest political allies are tied to,” as he prepares to leave office. “Dunleavy is shelling out our cash to some company named Plural to build multiple data centers as quickly as they can, when he has less than a month in office,” Wieber said. “If Plural had any real interest in doing this, they would hit pause and start building a relationship with the incoming governor’s administration.” A representative of Plural did not respond to an email seeking comment.

artigo.texto: Phillips 66 stock adds SAF portal to carbon-market strategy Published on 11/10/2026 at 14:40 | Editorial responsibility: Rafael Müller, Editor-in-Chief AD HOC NEWS SAF Portal Broadens Phillips 66 Offering - The new platform lets companies buy sustainable aviation fuel environmental attributes through a book-and-claim model. - Customers receive documentation covering the emissions reductions linked to their purchases. - The initiative expands Phillips 66's sustainable aviation fuel sales and distribution strategy. Phillips 66 launched an Environmental Attributes Portal on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, giving companies a direct way to purchase environmental attributes linked to sustainable aviation fuel. Biofuels International Magazine reported that the platform is designed for businesses seeking to address emissions from business travel and upstream transportation. The portal uses a book-and-claim model. Companies can purchase the environmental attributes even when the physical sustainable aviation fuel is not available at their location, allowing the environmental benefit to be separated from the fuel's physical delivery. New Channel For SAF Customers Phillips 66 said the platform lets customers select the environmental attributes they want and complete purchases through flexible payment methods, including credit cards. There is no minimum purchase requirement, which broadens access beyond large-volume fuel buyers. After a purchase, customers receive an Environmental Attribute Document summarizing the associated carbon dioxide emissions reduction. That documentation can support internal emissions analysis and corporate reporting, making the portal a commercial tool as well as a transaction platform. Sunny Lopez, senior director of aviation and sustainable fuel sales at Phillips 66, said the company built the portal around its experience across feedstock sourcing, production, fuel delivery and distribution. The comments underline the company's effort to simplify access to SAF-related claims as corporate buyers face pressure to reduce transport emissions. Building A Broader SAF Platform The portal adds to Phillips 66's recent SAF initiatives. The company announced an agreement with Chooose in 2026 to integrate the technology provider's platform into existing SAF processes, with the aim of streamlining fuel delivery, distribution and documentation. For investors, the portal offers a route to serve sustainability demand without requiring every customer to take physical SAF at its operating locations. Its financial contribution will depend on transaction volumes, customer adoption and the availability of qualifying SAF attributes. The launch therefore supports Phillips 66's commercial positioning in renewable fuels, while the article does not provide revenue or earnings guidance for the portal. Phillips 66 stock traded at 220.80 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 14:33 CET on Tuesday, November 10. artigo.texto: The Nefer Benban Solar and BESS (Battery Energy Storage System) project in Egypt, developed by Infinity Power, secures US$127 million in financing to advance construction. The project is being developed by Nefer Benban for Renewable Energy, a special-purpose company owned by Infinity Power and HAU Energy and is designed to strengthen Egypt’s renewable electricity capacity and grid reliability. Meanwhile, Egypt’s Obelisk solar and battery project has begun operations, marking further progress in the country’s renewable energy expansion. The financing package includes a US$65 million construction bridge loan from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). Meanwhile, Germany’s development finance institution, DEG, will provide an equal amount. Together, the funding will support a 200MW solar plant and a 120MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) at Benban Solar Park near Aswan. Additionally, the EBRD identifies HAU Energy as the borrower, while Nefer Benban is the project company. The solar-storage development will combine daytime solar generation with battery storage that can release electricity during evening peak-demand periods. Therefore, the project is intended to help manage fluctuations in renewable generation and improve the reliability of electricity supplied to the national grid. The electricity will be sold to the Egyptian Electricity Transmission Company (EETC) under a 25-year power purchase agreement. Project Scope and Technical Specifications The project will use solar PV panels to generate electricity. Meanwhile, the 120MWh battery system will store excess daytime output. It will then release the stored electricity when demand rises or solar generation declines. Project disclosures list the solar plant’s installed capacity at approximately 200MW. However, the EBRD’s November 2026 announcement specifies a 258.5MWp photovoltaic (PV) array. Additionally, the project is among Egypt’s early utility-scale developments combining solar generation with battery storage. The facility will store surplus daytime electricity and release it after sunset. Consequently, it will extend the availability of solar power beyond daylight hours. It is also expected to reduce fluctuations in renewable electricity supply. The project is located within the wider Benban Solar Park, one of Egypt’s major renewable energy hubs. Furthermore, the established site provides an opportunity to expand solar generation and integrate additional flexibility into the electricity grid. Financing Structure and Project Partners The US$127 million financing package comprises a US$65 million construction bridge loan from the EBRD and an equal contribution from DEG. Additionally, the funding will cover eligible development and construction costs. These include engineering, procurement, installation, testing and commissioning. However, the package represents construction debt financing, not the project’s total capital cost. The project has also secured a separate EBRD financing commitment of up to US$63.5 million for Nefer Benban for Renewable Energy. This comprises up to US$56 million from the bank’s own resources and US$7.5 million from the Clean Technology Fund. Additionally, the package supports the combined solar and storage development. However, the two financing arrangements represent separate facilities and should be reported separately when outlining the project’s total funding. Infinity Power is a joint venture between Infinity and Masdar. It focuses on developing renewable energy projects across Africa. Meanwhile, HAU Energy is an investment platform established to develop renewable energy projects in Egypt. It is associated with Hassan Allam Utilities, Meridiam and the EBRD. Additionally, Nefer Benban for Renewable Energy serves as the project-specific company for the Benban development. Construction Status and Expected Impact The financing is intended to support construction and commissioning activities of the Nefer Benban Solar Project. However, the financing announcement alone does not establish that the facility has completed construction or entered commercial operation. The EBRD’s project information describes the development as an implementation-stage investment, while its latest announcement confirms the planned solar and battery configuration. Once operational, the facility will supply electricity under a long-term power purchase agreement with EETC. Additionally, the battery system will release stored solar power during peak demand after sunset. Consequently, it will help the grid accommodate a greater share of variable renewable energy. The Nefer Benban Solar Project also supports Egypt’s energy transition goals. These include expanding private-sector renewable energy capacity and reducing reliance on fossil-fuel generation. However, its long-term contribution will depend on timely construction, successful commissioning and grid integration. Furthermore, its impact will depend on the facility’s operational performance. artigo.texto: Land & Expand: Texas’ AI Boom Meets a New Political Reality Key Highlights - Democrat Gina Hinojosa's election as Texas governor, alongside Democratic gains in the state House and statewide offices, raises the prospect of an extended data center permitting pause and new legislation in 2027. - Riot Platforms disclosed a 910 MW, approximately $28 billion lease with Anthropic at its Corsicana campus, while Hut 8 advanced its gigawatt-scale Beacon Point project. - CenterPoint Energy increased its 10-year capital plan to $70.7 billion as Greater Houston prepares for major industrial and data center electricity demand. - Fermi's proposed 222 MW TensorWave lease missed its closing deadline, while Microsoft declined to exercise an expansion option for capacity at Nscale's Texas project. - From San Antonio to Hudspeth County, developers increasingly face demands for greater transparency, water and power safeguards, and clearer community benefits. In DCF's Land & Expand series, we track where North American data center development is taking root, where it's accelerating, and the forces shaping which projects actually get built. Today we examine how Texas has become one of the clearest demonstrations of the extraordinary scale of AI infrastructure development — and of the challenges now facing the industry as it attempts to turn that investment into operating capacity. In the space of several weeks, the state has seen major new data center leases, expanded utility investment plans, new behind-the-meter generation proposals, and continued construction on large AI campuses. At the same time, regulators have tightened oversight, municipalities have adopted additional development controls, and several high-profile transactions have encountered financing or execution challenges. Then came the November 3 midterm elections. Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the first Democrat elected Texas governor since Ann Richards in 1990. Democrats also won the Texas House and the lieutenant governorship, although Republicans retained their majority in the state Senate. The results introduce a new political dimension to a data center market already undergoing substantial regulatory change. Hinojosa made the industry's rapid expansion a campaign issue, calling for a moratorium on new approvals until lawmakers establish stronger protections for communities, water supplies, electricity customers, and local decision-making. In a November 5 interview reported by Reuters, the governor-elect reaffirmed her intention to pause further approvals until those protections are in place. As Data Center Frontier reported in August, Texas was already moving toward a more restrictive regulatory framework under Abbott, who ordered audits of prospective data centers and suspended certain approvals pending the results. Hinojosa's election could extend that process and place new requirements on developers seeking to move projects forward. Yet the state's AI infrastructure market is hardly standing still. The emerging Texas story is not simply one of growth versus regulation. It is about a new set of conditions under which massive capital commitments, available power, established customers, and community acceptance may determine which developments actually reach operation. A $28 Billion Agreement Shows That Texas Is Still in Expansion Mode One of the largest recent transactions illustrates the continuing strength of demand. On November 4, Riot Platforms announced a 15-year, triple-net powered-land lease covering 910 MW of critical IT capacity at its Corsicana campus in Navarro County. Although Riot initially described its customer as a leading frontier AI laboratory, the company's quarterly SEC filing identifies Anthropic as the tenant. Riot estimates that the agreement represents approximately $28 billion in contractual revenue over its initial term, with an average of about $1.8 billion annually. The contract became effective November 4 after the applicable approvals and technical conditions were satisfied. The development model is noteworthy. Riot will provide land, powered pads, and high- and medium-voltage electrical infrastructure, while Anthropic will supply and operate its modular computing equipment. The lease covers a contiguous 332-acre site, with deliveries expected in three phases extending through July 2028. The first phase comprises 400 MW, followed by 200 MW and 310 MW. Under the agreement, Anthropic is responsible for electricity costs and other operating expenses, while Riot retains responsibility for the site's power infrastructure. Rent is structured around contracted capacity rather than actual computing utilization. The result is a substantially more defined commercial arrangement than a speculative gigawatt-scale development announcement. Nevertheless, construction, financing, commissioning, and scheduled delivery remain significant obligations. It is also an example of the changing role of former cryptocurrency infrastructure operators in the AI market. Sites originally assembled around access to large electrical loads are increasingly being repositioned to serve customers requiring high-density computing capacity. The transaction underscores the continuing appetite for large-scale Texas developments, extending the expansion trend documented in DCF's previous Land & Expand roundup. Riot's agreement was announced one day after Hinojosa's election victory. The timing is striking, although the transaction was negotiated and signed before the election and should not be interpreted as a response to its outcome. Instead, it demonstrates the simultaneous forces now shaping Texas: substantial demand for power-ready infrastructure and growing uncertainty over the rules governing future development. artigo.texto: BYD investirá R$ 1 bilhão para produzir vans e caminhões no Brasil Minas Gerais, São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro disputam a próxima unidade da fabricante chinesa, que prevê gerar dois mil empregos A BYD vai instalar uma nova fábrica no Brasil para produzir vans elétricas e caminhões. A coluna apurou com exclusividade para a CNN Brasil que o projeto prevê investimento de R$ 1 bilhão e a criação de 2 mil postos de trabalho entre 2028 e 2029, início da produção. Minas Gerais, São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro foram selecionados pela fabricante e disputam o investimento. A escolha final do estado ainda está em aberto porque virá acompanhada pelo pacote dos incentivos. O projeto marca a segunda fase da expansão industrial da BYD no país. Depois de colocar em operação a fábrica de automóveis de Camaçari, na Bahia. A greentech prepara a nova unidade voltada aos veículos comerciais. Com as vans elétricas, a montadora entra numa disputa com as clássicas, que vendem os modelos a diesel. Durante a semana, a SAIC, com a Volks Caminhões, exibirá sua defesa no segmento das vans, trazendo novidades. Na Fenatran, que começa nesta segunda (9) em São Paulo, a BYD vai trazer os caminhões elétricos eT35 e eT75, além de uma configuração do eT23 para o transporte de bebidas. O eT35 usa a bateria Blade, enquanto o eT75 é voltado à distribuição urbana e regional. Os modelos que sairão da nova fábrica ainda não foram detalhados e devem ser anunciados nos próximos meses. Na Bahia A fábrica de Camaçari ultrapassou 150 mil veículos produzidos e 9,5 mil empregos diretos pouco mais de um ano após a inauguração, segundo balanço divulgado pela montadora em 5 de novembro. O investimento anunciado para o complexo chegou a R$ 11,3 bilhões, ante os R$ 5,5 bilhões informados em julho. A unidade baiana, que produz Dolphin Mini, King, Song Pro e Atto 2, tem capacidade instalada de 150 mil veículos por ano, com previsão de chegar a 300 mil na próxima etapa. A BYD já concluiu as obras civis dos galpões de soldagem e pintura e realiza testes operacionais nas duas áreas. Mais de 1.100 profissionais foram contratados para atuar nessas estruturas, que permitirão incorporar novas etapas da fabricação em Camaçari. Quem vai crescer? A BYD levou seus concessionários a Mendoza, na Argentina, para mostrar os carros que vêm por aí. Mas o recado mais direto da convenção foi para os donos das lojas. Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente sênior da companhia, deixou claro que, na próxima rodada de expansão da rede no Brasil, vai crescer com a BYD quem mantiver a exclusividade entre as marcas chinesas. Na prática, o grupo que quiser abrir mais pontos de venda com a fabricante terá de deixar as rivais asiáticas fora do portfólio. No encontro, a montadora apresentou um plano com sete lançamentos e novos pontos de venda. Um dos SUVs já tem nome e ano para chegar. O Ti7, antecipado por esta coluna, é um híbrido plug-in boxy de sete lugares confirmado para 2027. Com carroceria de linhas quadradas e porte do Denza B5, ele coloca a BYD na disputa por compradores de modelos como o Jetour T2 e o GWM Haval H7. O Dolphin GT será o próximo nacional e nós já cravamos aqui na CNN sobre o híbrido plug-in flex, que será feito na Bahia em fevereiro.

artigo.texto: UK and EU officials are on the brink of an agreement that would link their carbon emissions markets, a move that would save companies millions of euros in carbon border taxes, as the diplomatic push for deeper EU-UK integration accelerates ahead of a key post-Brexit summit next week. The deal would enable carbon permits to be traded across the two emissions systems. The UK’s post-Brexit emissions trading scheme was modelled on the EU’s. The UK’s carbon border adjustment mechanism, which is set to come into force early next year, is also based on the EU’s carbon border levy, a tax on imported industrial goods which are linked to high carbon emissions. Once the UK and EU emissions trading systems are linked, that would pave the way for them to be exempted from their respective CBAM laws. On Tuesday (10 November), UK trade minister Jonathan Reynolds and Europe minister Hamish Falconer held talks with EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič to push for a UK inclusion in the EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ initiative, that would allow UK firms to retain access to the EU’s industrial supply chain. Meetings with vice-president Stéphane Séjourne and defence commissioner Andrius Kubilius were also on the agenda.

artigo.texto: Publicidade SÃO PAULO, 11 Nov (Reuters) – A transmissora de energia Taesa (TAEE11) decidiu que não participará do leilão inédito do próximo mês voltado à contratação de baterias para o setor elétrico brasileiro, disse à Reuters a diretora financeira e de relações com investidores da companhia. Segundo Catia Pereira, a decisão foi tomada devido à falta de clareza regulatória para a participação das transmissoras no certame. A agência reguladora Aneel indicou que, caso saiam vencedoras do leilão, as empresas desse segmento terão que reverter parte das receitas do negócio de baterias para modicidade tarifária. ‘Essa questão da modicidade tarifária, quem vai pagar a conta (da contratação), tem essas inseguranças que a companhia falou: ‘não, acho que tem que ter uma maturidade maior”, disse a diretora. Ela reiterou com a Taesa mantém o interesse nas baterias e está realizando estudos e conversas com fornecedores para atuar futuramente no segmento, mas não se sentiu confortável para disputar esse primeiro certame. Outra grande empresa do segmento, a ISA Energia (ISAE4) também expressou insegurança recentemente com as regras colocadas para as transmissoras no certame, embora tenha dito que ainda não havia tomado uma decisão final sobre sua participação. A Taesa divulgou nesta quarta-feira o balanço financeiro do terceiro trimestre, com um lucro líquido regulatório de R$363,8 milhões, aumento de 12,5% na comparação anual. Já o Ebitda regulatório avançou 25,2%, a R$687,2 milhões. Continua depois da publicidade A melhora do desempenho do trimestre vem na esteira de um importante ciclo de investimentos que a companhia concluiu nos últimos meses e que envolveu a entrega de três projetos de transmissão, reforços na rede existente e a compra de ativos operacionais da Energisa. ‘Nesse ciclo de investimento, a gente investiu R$6,7 bilhões, R$2,9 bilhões só este ano. Aí tem uma mensagem muito importante, porque esse investimento trouxe para a companhia R$812 milhões adicionais de receita anual permitida’, afirmou Pereira. A Taesa continua avaliando novas oportunidades de crescimento por meio dos leilões de transmissão e eventuais aquisições, além de reforços e melhorias em sua rede existente, uma ‘avenida’ que tende a ganhar mais relevância no futuro, observou. Continua depois da publicidade ‘A gente tem R$600 milhões hoje na carteira de reforços e melhorias… A gente não vai ter uma carteira do tamanho da Axia, da ISA, principalmente porque a gente tem muita linha de transmissão, e o que gera mais necessidade de reforço é a capacidade de transformação (em subestações)’, explicou. ‘Mas o último projeto que foi entregue agora, o Tangará, e a compra dos cinco ativos da Energisa aumentaram a nossa capacidade de transformação, o que significa que também criamos oportunidade de aumentar no futuro a avenida de reforços e melhorias’, acrescentou.

artigo.texto: Insurance shortfalls, financial losses crippling St Bess business recovery Loading article... WESTERN BUREAU: Crippling financial losses, inadequate insurance coverage and mounting borrowing costs are threatening the survival of several businesses across St Elizabeth, leaving some operators contemplating permanent closure as they continue to reel from Hurricane Melissa’s devastating 2025 blow. Kadian Myers-Brown, president of the Black River chapter of the St Elizabeth Chamber of Commerce, and businessman Jason Henzell, chairman of the South Coast chapter of the Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association, believe that financial pressure continues to undermine recovery efforts. Myers-Brown said several long-standing, family-operated businesses in Black River remain shuttered because of the inability to finance repairs or replace equipment and stock destroyed during the hurricane, which struck as a Category 5 system just over a year ago. “Some persons are saying, ‘Hey, I’m just gonna give up.’ Some persons are saying that they are not going to reinvest ... not knowing what the plans truly are from the Government,” she told The Gleaner. Myers-Brown, an attorney-at-law, said some establishments had operated for generations without adequate financial reserves or insurance protection, leaving their owners particularly vulnerable to the hurricane’s devastating impact. “Some of them were like mom-and-pop stores operating for almost a century,” she said. A survey commissioned by the St Elizabeth Homecoming Foundation revealed that 46 per cent of Black River businesses suffered devastating or total destruction, with average rebuilding costs estimated at $17 million. Only 1.4 per cent had insurance coverage. It also found that 28 per cent of businesses reported income losses ranging from 70 to 100 per cent, with full recovery projected to take approximately 26 months. Among the establishments yet to recover are the popular Sunrise Bakery, several furniture stores, variety shops, barbershops, and farm supply businesses. Myers-Brown said supermarkets, pharmacies, hardware stores and medical offices were among businesses that had reopened, largely through the determination of their operators. Meanwhile, Henzell, who is also CEO of Jakes Hotel and chairman of the Treasure Beach Foundation, said tourism operators were receiving insurance settlements much lower than anticipated, creating additional financial difficulties. “If I were to take a survey of what people have told me in terms of the settlement that they got, it was probably two-thirds of what they were expecting. You know, it’s probably 65 per cent of what they were hoping for,” he said. Henzell further explained that lengthy delays in processing claims had forced some operators to borrow money. “If you have to go and borrow money now, because of the delay, remember you have to add that interest cost,” he said. He warned that dissatisfaction with insurance settlements was prompting some business owners without outstanding bank loans to reconsider renewing their policies, potentially leaving them exposed to future disasters. Henzell also stressed the importance of understanding insurance conditions, deductibles and underinsurance, suggesting educational workshops to help tourism operators make better financial decisions. “You could have the best hotel operationally, but you had the wrong mix of insurance,” he said, in highlighting the need for sound financial decisions. However, despite the setbacks, Henzell said all accommodation properties in Treasure Beach have reopened, noting that the recent Food, Rum and Reggae Festival generated strong occupancy across southwest St Elizabeth, extending into Junction. However, Myers-Brown said uncertainty surrounding the Government’s proposed Black River urban centre continued to discourage reinvestment, particularly among coastal operators, who are worried about what protection will be put in place to combat future hurricanes and storm surges. “It would not make sense to regain or restore business as per usual, not knowing what the effects of another storm will be like,” she said. “People are suffering. Businesses are suffering. Businesses want to really regain some sort of restoration at their peak level.” albert.ferguson@gleanerjm.com

artigo.texto: Maxell Begins Mass Production of All-Solid-State Battery Backup Modules for Industrial Equipment Power Supply Module Incorporating All-Solid-State Battery Helps Reduce Maintenance Workload and Improve Equipment Maintainability TOKYO–(BUSINESS WIRE)–Maxell, Ltd. (TOKYO: 6810) will begin mass production of its “All-Solid-State Battery Backup Module” incorporating the ceramic packaged all-solid-state battery, PSB401010H, and will start sales in Japan for industrial equipment applications in early November. Maxell has been conducting field tests*1 of power supply modules incorporating its all-solid-state batteries in manufacturing equipment at customers’ factories since 2024, with the aim of reducing the workload associated with battery replacement at production sites. The tests confirmed stable backup performance under actual manufacturing conditions, and customers highly valued the modules for their ability to improve equipment maintainability. Based on these results, Maxell developed four models of the All-Solid-State Battery Backup Module. The module is available with output voltages corresponding to those of ER batteries (3.6 V) and CR batteries (3.0 V), which are widely used as backup power sources. Two battery capacity options are available for each voltage type, offering a lineup of four models that can be selected according to the application. The all-solid-state battery incorporated into the module has an expected service life of more than 10 years*2. As a result, the module is expected to reduce the labor associated with primary battery replacement and the risk of downtime caused by unexpected battery depletion. In addition, the module can operate at temperatures of up to 85°C. Maxell will exhibit the module at Maintenance Munich 2026 (October 14-15, 2026; MOC – Event Center Messe München, Germany) and at other exhibitions in Japan. artigo.texto: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity Big Tech sees a culture war over progress. But the real fault line is electricity: drawing it from the grid and generating it onsite provoke different kinds of backlash, neither easily solved by public relations. This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here. As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid. One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport. Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out. Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid. But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out). The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale. Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency). Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do. But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? artigo.texto: Na Turquia para COP31, Pivetta busca investidores para créditos de carbono de MT Governador participa da COP31 e pretende apresentar resultados da redução do desmatamento em Mato Grosso, além de buscar oportunidades de financiamento ambiental. O governador de Mato Grosso, Otaviano Pivetta (Republicanos), anunciou nesta quarta-feira (11) que já está em Antália, na Turquia, para participar da 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP31). A viagem tem como um dos principais objetivos buscar reconhecimento internacional para os créditos de carbono do estado e estabelecer diálogo com possíveis investidores. Em publicação nas redes sociais, Pivetta compartilhou uma fotografia no evento e afirmou que pretende apresentar os resultados de Mato Grosso no combate ao desmatamento. “Estamos na COP31 com uma missão importante: apresentar o trabalho de Mato Grosso na redução do desmatamento e buscar reconhecimento internacional para nossos créditos de carbono”, escreveu. O governador também afirmou que a agenda inclui conversas com investidores para apresentar oportunidades relacionadas à conservação ambiental e ao desenvolvimento econômico do estado. A busca por reconhecimento internacional é uma etapa importante para que os créditos de carbono de Mato Grosso possam atrair interessados no mercado ambiental. Entretanto, a participação na conferência não significa que acordos comerciais tenham sido fechados. Mato Grosso quer ampliar atuação no mercado de carbono A viagem ocorre em meio às iniciativas do governo estadual para estruturar a participação de Mato Grosso no mercado de créditos de carbono. Nesse mercado, a redução de emissões de gases de efeito estufa ou a remoção de carbono da atmosfera pode gerar créditos negociáveis, desde que os resultados sejam medidos, verificados e atendam às regras aplicáveis. No caso da conservação florestal, mecanismos de financiamento podem remunerar resultados comprovados na redução do desmatamento e das emissões associadas. Para Mato Grosso, a proposta é transformar resultados ambientais reconhecidos em oportunidades de financiamento para ações de conservação e desenvolvimento sustentável. A obtenção de reconhecimento internacional, porém, depende de critérios técnicos e processos de validação. Por isso, ainda não é possível afirmar quanto o estado poderá arrecadar com eventuais negociações. Agenda internacional Além das discussões sobre créditos de carbono, Pivetta informou que pretende apresentar a investidores iniciativas de conservação ambiental e oportunidades de desenvolvimento em Mato Grosso. A COP31 reúne representantes de governos, organizações internacionais, especialistas e integrantes do setor privado para discutir medidas de enfrentamento às mudanças climáticas.

artigo.texto: Camila Valadão questiona licenciamento e impactos socioambientais A deputada estadual Camila Valadão (PSOL) apresentou uma indicação ao Governo do Estado, sob gestão de Ricardo Ferraço (MDB) solicitando a realização de consulta e audiência pública sobre a instalação de um data center voltado à inteligência artificial em Baixo Guandu, no Noroeste do Espírito Santo. A parlamentar protocolou um requerimento de informações sobre o licenciamento ambiental e os possíveis impactos socioambientais do empreendimento, além de questionar a participação da população e a disponibilidade de recursos hídricos. O empreendimento integra o Projeto Rubi, apresentado pela empresa capixaba Line Solution, e prevê investimento estimado em R$ 7,4 bilhões. Além do centro de processamento de dados, com capacidade inicial anunciada de 100 megawatts (MW), o complexo inclui condomínios logístico e industrial. A área total prevista é de aproximadamente 11 milhões de metros quadrados. A iniciativa da deputada ocorre em meio à falta de informações públicas sobre a origem da água que será utilizada pelo complexo e os procedimentos necessários para autorizar sua captação. Em resposta ao Século Diário, a Agência Nacional de Águas e Saneamento Básico (ANA) informou que não possui registro de pedidos de outorga de direito de uso de recursos hídricos destinados especificamente a data centers. O órgão esclareceu, entretanto, que a competência para autorizar a utilização de águas subterrâneas é dos estados. Na indicação encaminhada à Secretaria de Estado do Meio Ambiente e Recursos Hídricos (Seama), Camila solicita a realização de consulta pública, na modalidade de reunião participativa, e audiência pública para apresentação do empreendimento e dos estudos ambientais. A parlamentar também pede ampla divulgação das atividades para assegurar a participação dos moradores de Baixo Guandu. “Não podemos permitir que um projeto desse tamanho seja discutido apenas entre empresas e governo, sem ouvir quem vive no território. Estamos falando de um empreendimento que pode transformar a realidade de Baixo Guandu, com impactos sobre a água, o meio ambiente e a vida da população. É fundamental que as pessoas tenham acesso aos estudos, possam fazer perguntas e participar das decisões sobre o futuro da cidade”, afirma. O requerimento de informações foi encaminhado à Seama e ao Instituto Estadual de Meio Ambiente e Recursos Hídricos (Iema). Entre os questionamentos estão a existência de estudos de impacto ambiental e outros documentos apresentados pelos responsáveis pelo projeto, além da disponibilização dos materiais para consulta pública. A disponibilidade hídrica é uma das principais questões levantadas sobre o empreendimento. Em reportagem publicada anteriormente pelo Século Diário, o prefeito de Baixo Guandu, Lastênio Cardoso (MDB), afirmou que a água necessária ao funcionamento do data center viria de uma represa no Rio Doce. Ele não soube informar se os estudos ambientais já haviam sido apresentados e direcionou as perguntas sobre essa etapa ao empresário Mário Rodrigues, fundador e CEO da Line Solution. Procurado novamente por Século Diário, Mário Rodrigues ficou de retornar à reportagem para prestar explicações sobre o projeto, mas não encaminhou informações até o fechamento da edição. Questionada agora sobre a existência de autorizações para o uso de água por empreendimentos desse tipo, a ANA respondeu: “Até o momento a Agência Nacional de Águas e Saneamento Básico não tem registro de pedidos de outorga de direito de uso de recursos hídricos para a finalidade específica de data centers”. O órgão acrescentou que, caso o Projeto Rubi utilize águas subterrâneas, os pedidos de outorga devem ser apresentados à Agência Estadual de Recursos Hídricos (Agerh), uma vez que esse tipo de recurso é de domínio estadual, conforme a Constituição Federal. A distinção é importante porque a competência para autorizar a captação depende do manancial escolhido. O Rio Doce é um curso d’água de domínio da União, enquanto rios e demais corpos hídricos estaduais estão sujeitos à competência dos órgãos estaduais, por isso a definição da fonte de abastecimento é fundamental para identificar os procedimentos de autorização aplicáveis ao empreendimento. Em resposta ao Século Diário, a Agerh informou que não havia recebido pedidos de outorga de direito de uso de recursos hídricos ou de autorização da empresa responsável pelo Projeto Rubi e afirmou que, por essa razão, não dispunha de informações sobre eventual previsão de captação em mananciais da região para atender às necessidades do empreendimento. A preocupação com a água também foi levantada pelo coordenador do Observatório Capixaba da Água e do Meio Ambiente, Merci Fardin. Ao comentar o projeto em reportagem anterior, ele defendeu que os impactos sejam analisados de maneira conjunta, considerando os demais empreendimentos previstos para a região. Segundo o ambientalista, a instalação de novas estruturas industriais e logísticas pode ampliar a pressão sobre os recursos naturais e a infraestrutura local. Por isso, a avaliação não deve se restringir à disponibilidade de água nas proximidades do terreno destinado ao data center. A Line Solution informou à midia capixaba que pretende utilizar um sistema fechado de resfriamento, com reutilização contínua da água e reposição mensal estimada em volume equivalente ao consumo de três casas populares. A empresa também divulgou a previsão de criação de até 550 empregos, sendo 500 durante as obras e 50 na operação, além de arrecadação anual de R$ 50 milhões a R$ 60 milhões em Imposto Sobre Serviços (ISS). As projeções são da própria companhia e ainda dependem da implantação do complexo. Para além dos números anunciados, a definição da demanda hídrica efetiva, da fonte de abastecimento e das condições de disponibilidade dos recursos naturais permanece necessária para avaliar os efeitos do empreendimento sobre o território.
